Marconi Sailing Club CAMPING RULES – 2010 • No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday • Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid. • Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members. • No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site at all times. • The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area. • All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present. • Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times. • Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc. • Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected. • Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc. • Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are probably not paying much attention to traffic. • Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS. • The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed. • All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access. • All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight. THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE POINTS.

Membership Renewal Guide 2011 1 Classes of Membership A FULL MEMBER - Shall be a single person over the age of twenty-two. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote A FAMILY MEMBER - Shall include a married couple, or couple living together as a family, one of whom is over the age of eighteen, one or two parents, one of whom is over the age of eighteen, and all children under eighteen years of age. The family unit shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote exercisable by one person over the age of eighteen. A RETIRED MEMBER - Any member over the state retirement age shall pay one half of the full fees paid for Full or Family Membership as appropriate A YOUNG ADULT MEMBER - Shall be a single person who at the commencement of the subscription year is aged eighteen and is under the age of twenty two. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote A JUNIOR MEMBER - Shall be a single person who at the date of election or at the commencement of the subscription year is under the age of eighteen and joins the club other than as a Family member. They must be supported by a sponsor who is a full or family member and who will be accountable for his or her conduct. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities but may not purchase alcoholic drink or cigarettes from the bar and shall have no vote A SENIOR LIFE MEMBER shall be a single person who is over the State Retirement age (currently 65 years), has been a FULL or FAMILY member for the a minimum of the preceding fifteen years, has paid the senior life member fee, does not keep a boat at the Club and shall have one vote. 2 Annual Boat Permit Fee All craft incur a Boat Permit Fee. The first boat of a member is always deemed to be the craft incurring the highest fee. Subsequent craft under 10ft used solely as tenders are free of charge. 3 Winter Storage Storage Fees are payable in advance at these rates on boats, trailers and cradles to be kept at Stansgate during all or part of the period 30th November to 1st March following the date of renewal. th Any person who has a boat, trailer or cradle on site after the 30 November, and has not paid the appropriate storage fee will be liable for payment of a penalty fee in accordance with Bylaw 2.3. 4 Trailer Storage Fee A summer and winter storage fee is payable (as specified below) on second or subsequent trailers not associated with a boat for which a boat permit fee has been paid. Per winter or summer season: Cruiser trailer £47.00 Catamaran dinghy trailer £43.00 Monohull dinghy trailer £35.00 (A dinghy or catamaran is permitted to have one launching and road trailer on site before incurring the summer storage fee.) 5 Car Stickers A car sticker will be supplied free to each member, which should be displayed on all cars parked at Stansgate. If extra (free) stickers are required please specify the number required. 6 Resignations Persons wishing to resign their membership at renewal must indicate so on the form and return it together with all MSC Ltd keys by the end of January to the Registrar. 7 Late Renewal Renewal fees are due on 1st January and are payable by the last day in January. Renewals received after this date incur the Penalty Fee; Bylaw 2.3. 8 Is Our Data Correct? Will all members please fill in your boat details and amend any printed information that is incorrect so that we may keep our database up to date. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Marconi Sailing Club Summer Cruise To The Walton Backwaters & Beyond! The official date for the start of the Marconi Sailing Club's Summer Cruise to The Walton Backwaters & Beyond, was Saturday the 24th of July. However, for Evenstar & her crew, it started the week before. We went down to her to take down some of the stuff that we would need the following week. This coincided with the departure of the single-handers, who were leaving that Sunday for their preliminary weeklong cruise to the Rivers Alde & Ore. They would then join the MSC Summer Cruise at Titchmarsh Marina, on the Walton Backwaters the following Saturday. Sunday morning dawned & I eventually surfaced at 09:30, the allotted departure time, to find that they had gone. Was this an omen for what was to come? However they had gone, as far as Brightlingsea & we had a lazy day before returning home after getting Evenstar ready for our return the following week. Leaving work that Friday morning, I wasn't too sure if we would be going, but thankfully Angela drove me down. For what was to follow, I am very grateful. Anyway, we got our stuff on-board, I thought we were only going for a week! Would it all fit? However, with everything stowed, we proceeded to the 'Briefing Room' for the 'briefing' (the Mamgu Bar!). Roger & Jackie Camp & John Walker were unable to make it, but Mike & Cheryl Cutmore (Shadowfax), Danny & Carol Ainge (West Marie) & Dave Taverner (Sea Pearl) made it. After the 'briefing', we retired to our respective vessels, with an agreement to slip at 11:30hrs. Saturday dawned nice, bright & sunny with light winds. John gave us the slip & slipped early to get his sails up. As we went down the river, there was an unusual occurrence, very unusual; Southern Hey put her sails up! Then Roger turned the engine off, time to sit down. All became clear as we approached Bradwell. There was a huge fleet of dinghies racing, I would estimate their fleet to be over 100. Fortunately the wind was to = a Ae ——_ > starboard for Roger. We (I), chickened out & went around the 2 = | back of them as we were over that side & only had to dodge a = few. Roger called "Starboard", & went straight through them! 72 Followed in close succession by John. We then seemed to separate on our ways, with Dave on Sea Pearl keeping us company. We managed to sail all the way to Pye End before having to get the engine on in the channel. Here the winds died & Titchmarsh were warning of a very low level over the sill. This was heeded by some, but not all. I am saying no more, but Roger got my good lady to open up. Humph! Here we were met some members of MSC, Jan & Peter Reay who keep a Hurricane cat at the club. When I first got their email, I had to read it again. I thought they were going on the cat! No, they have a cruiser, Hebridean Girl, at Shotley & joined us for the week. Saturday evening was spent socializing & on Sunday afternoon we had a Squadron Dinner at the Harbour Lights Restaurant. After dining, something odd occurred & a photo for proof was required. Yes, that's neat coffee with nothing added! Not Gaelic or French, just coffee. I then gave an informal briefing, outlining the need to be at Woodbridge Haven at approximately 11:00 to have sufficient water to clear the entrance. Most agreed to leave at 08:00 the following morning. However, on Monday morning, one yacht gave us the slip at 07:05, to “have a nice sail”! We left, at 08:00, with a “Line Astern” & crossed the shipping lane off Harwich at 09:35. Some went the inshore route, claiming local knowledge of calmer waters, but I preferred to be a bit further out to dodge the lobster pots which were very poorly marked. Lots of them too! John, on Charlotte, was weaving all over the place along with some others. We had a direct route & made up some ground without the hassle, getting to the entrance at 10:27. We had heard a lot of scare rumours about this place, that it sounded like stones in a washing machine, but thankfully it was rather quiet. We then had a lovely run up the Deben, getting to Woodbridge at 12:30 to find Neil waiting to help us in. When we were safely moored alongside, I went to help some others… Here the fun started! Bob on Chappie was next in, being told to go to starboard when he entered. He promptly turned to port! Dave on Sea Pearl was next in, when Bob had managed to turn, he was after Dave. Dave's berth was occupied, so he took the next available berth, this was Bob's. He said, “that's mine” & I told him there was another a few berths down & returned to helping Dave. At this point, a man on a yacht on the other side of the marina said, “your mate's just gone in”, to which I replied, “yes that's right, just down there”. February 2011 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk “No, he's gone in” urgently came his reply. Being occupied with Dave, I said “yes, that's right, thank you”. “NO! He's fallen in the water!” in a Spike Milliganesque way. To which I left Dave to his own resources & went to help Bob. When I got there, Chappie was about six feet away, with Bob, whilst treading water saying, “grab hold the boat!”. Not wishing to follow him, I apologized as he clambered back on board. After I helped him alongside, I returned to Dave, who had just finished tying up. I returned at that point, to my good lady, for a well earned cup of tea! The access to Woodbridge Marina is extremely limited, to say the least! As the panoramic shots show. We were joined here by Pat Black on Tamarisk, who we had passed on the way. Mark Whitely (Reflection) also joined us, along-with Doug Rowe who arrived from Ipswich on the Tuesday. Tuesday also saw a fractioning of the Squadron, with Southern Hey, Reflection, Shell Seeker & Tamarisk leaving us for a few days. The rest of us departed on the Wednesday for Shotley Point Marina, Hebridean Girl's home base. Locking in was fairly straightforward & we were soon all in safely. That evening we had a barbecue arranged on the “beach” by the lock gates, fantastic backdrop. Somebody was heard to laugh at the misfortune of the barbeque of those that departed early the previous day, when they were rained upon. It all started well, with Bob G, Bob W, John & Neil dining in style with a table, table-cloth & Napkins. Then the rain came, torrentially! Three disposable barbecues were put out, Danny sported a new design of coat (his chair), Doug & Pat grabbed their food and went back to their yachts, with Bob W grabbing his & hiding under a motor- boat! The coats & pictures tell the rest. After a short time, the shower(?) passed & we enjoyed the evening. A few hardy souls ventured to Harwich the following day, well it has been experienced! That evening, we enjoyed a lovely meal at The Bristol Arms, in Shotley Point village. At about 21:00, a strange thing happened. All the single handers got up together, paid & left. The rest of us thought no more of it, thinking they had gone elsewhere to round off the evening with a drink. However, when we got back to Evenstar later that evening, we were greeted on the pontoon by Neil, who informed us that he & a couple of others were leaving early the next morning owing to the weather forecast. A force 4-5 gusting 7 was forecast at Selsy Bill, with 3-4 off Walton on the Saturday. I said that we had no intention of going home that way & were going to stay & finish February 2011 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk the tour. The next day, we were greeted by a near empty pontoon, (see the ubiquitous “before & after” photos) with a very confused looking Bob Whitaker looking up & down the pontoon. I asked him what the problem was & he asked where the rest were. I said that they had gone back, where to Lavington Bob replied, no to Marconi I said. He replied with, “what rotters, they didn’t say anything to me!” This left Bob W, Mike & Cheryl Cutmore, Dave Taverner, ourselves & naturally Jan & Peter Reay as they are berth holders at Shotley. Anyway, I called a flotilla meeting at 09:50 at the Shipwreck to formulate an agreed plan. We listened to the weather forecast at 10:10 & agreed that it was safe to carry on, as the forecast was much the same. We then slipped moorings at about 11:30 & proceeded to Pin Mill for Lunch. A place where most of us had hoped to visit by yacht. We picked up a mooing, with Jan & Pete picking up one astern of us. Dave & Mike rafted up alongside Hebridean Girl & lunch was commenced, a rather liquid one, aboard HG. Many thanks to Jan & Pete for the wonderful spread. Bob arrived soon & also rafted alongside Sea Pearl, four up on a mooring, not really ideal, or recommended! After lunch, we proceeded back down the river to Suffolk Yacht Harbour (Lavington) for the evening where we had a meal booked in their clubhouse, the Haven Ports Yacht Club, a dis-used lightship. A few other Marconi yachts even managed to sneak in & claim “Club Rates”, what nerve! I had the task of explaining to an upset Bulgarian chef that the numbers would be somewhat curtailed that evening. However, we (Mike & Cheryl, Bob W, Pete & Jan, Danny, Dave & ourselves) had a lovely meal, even if the numbers were depleted. I also had to explain to the Commodore of SYH as to the reason we were so few, however he understood & we had a great evening. We all left the next day, after bidding our goodbyes to Pete & Jan & headed for Brightlingsea. There we were joined by Reflection, Southern Hey, Serupin & Peter & Sue with their new yacht Last Dream. It was a tough sail with a nasty chop created by wind-over-tide, again. There was also a power boat race that morning, allegedly confined to the bay off Harwich according to the Notice To Mariners. It would appear that somebody got the charts wrong, as they were racing to North Foreland & back. They came up VERY fast, & I don’t think that calling starboard would have made much difference. However, they bracketed us, with immense speed, & we all made it February 2011 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk safely. We all went to Winkies that evening, where we were looked after in the usual excellent manner. Sunday morning dawned & after turning a couple of boats, some were stuck fast initially, we proceeded back to Marconi. A sail was tried, in the extremely light wind but it eventually gave in with Reflection, Evenstar, Sea Pearl & Shadowfax line abreast off Bradwell. Oh well, sails down & motor back. I have to say that it was an eventful cruise, although I also have to say on our part a very enjoyable one, Angela didn’t go much on the trip to Brightlingsea though! We met & made new friends, Jan & Peter who we hope to catch up with again on future cruises, & visited new places. I must say on my part that I enjoyed organising the cruise & I am extremely thankful for the help & support of all those taking part. It was extremely well supported, with 14 yachts making the first port of call, Titchmarsh, for the Start of Cruise Meal. It was a shame that a few more couldn’t make the meal at The Haven Ports Yacht Club, but individual decisions have to be made. George Male 2010 COMMODORE'S REPORT Marconi SC Remarks to 2010 AGM (held 23rd Jan 2011 following a postponement due to bad weather) Simon Elwell - Commodore LADIES AND GENTLEMEN As usual, I start my report by reminding you that our club is a company, limited by guarantee and that our principle activity during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our members. Responsibility for the company and thus the club rests with the board -- elected here by you each year. The board during the last financial year comprised six directors: Myself (Simon Elwell) -- I acted as managing director and chair Peter Clayton -- whose responsibilities cover moorings and equipment Murray Bates -- Murray looks after premises and the site Bryan Spencer, our rear commodore for sailing who has responsibility for sailing activities at the club and cadet training Michaela Glynn, who as our second rear commodore is on point for the events programme and Maurice Balfe-- our treasurer Once again Ray Ball has acted as honorary secretary for the company and club and, as ever, shoulders a significant part of the administration burden that the club generates. I'd like to offer a personal thank you to Ray for his support during my tenure as Commodore. Without his unfailing eye for detail and tireless management of our administration, we would have achieved only a fraction of what we have in recent years. The board has met regularly throughout the year -- as has the management committee. Additionally a number of sub-committees meet to manage and organise the day-to-day activities and events of the club. On your behalf I'd like to express our thanks to all those whose service in this way makes the continued running of the club possible. Following the postponement of the AGM, and to facilitate the smooth transition of the chairmanship of the board, I resigned as Commodore so that the board could co-opt Neil - the only candidate for the role. I'm grateful to Neil for stepping in and picking up the reins. I'll return to the subject of the club generally in a minute or two. Before I do that, I wanted to explain why I stepped aside as Commodore and to reflect for a moment on the last four years. It's not about wanting to spend more time with the family or anything like that. I think that the club deserves an injection of fresh ideas, new motivation and for someone to bring a new perspective to the board from time to time. That's the Commodore's job, and whilst others may serve longer in other roles at the club, I think it's right that there's a different hand on the helm to stop us becoming staid and unimaginative. Some time before I took on the role of Commodore, we had witnessed the Marconi company facing financial difficulty, and we had taken the bold step of buying the site and assuring the secure future of the club at Stansgate. Clive Shenton and Neil Pembleton led us through those troubled waters superbly, followed by Chris Davies. Chris was the first managing director of Marconi Sailing Club ltd - the limited company that sits behind our club. Suddenly we no longer had the support and resources of either Marconi or MASC and we had to stand on our own two feet. When I was elected Commodore, four years ago, Chris had already put wheels in motion by defining our strategy and setting priorities. Stretching out in front of me, however, was the challenge of making it happen... of realising the ambition. Four years later, I think I can say we've taken some important steps, but the journey is by no means over. We've updated our clubhouse - or part of it. In so doing we've thrown the other parts of our clubhouse and site into sharp relief - and there are already calls for further modernisation. We achieved this during a difficult financial climate and still maintained a February 2011 Navigans 10

healthy financial position which must be a factor in any future plans. In addition, the club has updated, replaced and repaired key pieces of equipment - tractors, winches, hoists as well as carrying out continuing maintenance on the jewel in our crown - the hard. Our web site, too, has proved an invaluable asset - many of our new members first find us on the internet, and email communication has proved a useful and cost- effective alternative to post. As time goes on the work that Andy Dowley does to improve and maintain the site will be crucial in keeping us up to date in more ways than one. In recent years, we have expanded the training we provide for youngsters beyond cadet week itself, with the introduction of our popular training days. Bryan Spencer has, as you know, driven this forward and needs your collective support to continue the good work. Reflecting on some of the things I hear, I am sometimes dismayed by the way in which criticism ignores the laws of physics and travels faster than others of support and help. I am also pleased to see that a new generation of younger members is taking up its rightful place within the leadership of our club. You know who you are; and you are the future of Marconi Sailing Club - I urge you to stay involved and to stay vocal. Now, at this point I'd like to present a couple of awards; The Seamanship trophy is awarded to someone who shows outstanding seamanship, sometimes in the face of adversity or in an emergency, but this year honouring a crew that has made a passage I suspect many of us envy. Just to compound things, the skipper also wins the Mamgu trophy for the best log - for the #rst time an online entry. So, this year's Seamanship trophy and Mamgu trophy goes to... Dave Onyons and the crew of Happy Morning for their Atlantic crossing. The other trophy I'd like to present is the Commodore's plate. I broke with tradition last year and awarded it to Murray Bates. I'd like to revert this year to the practise of awarding it to a non-committee member who has made an outstanding contribution to the club. This year's Commodore's plate, therefore, goes to the member who single-handedly designed, built and installed our new card entry system: Andy Redman. Going forward, it's no longer for me to set the agenda, but I know that there is much to do. A number of you are concerned that support for racing at the club is not as strong as it once was - and a number of initiatives are already in train to address this. Please support those who are sincerely trying to improve matters in this respect. We need even more participation from the dinghy and cat fleets as all too often they are under-represented among the club's leadership. This will only be remedied, however if people from the dinghy and catamaran fleets step up and get involved. Whilst our clubhouse modernisation has been successful, there is still much work to do around the site. Our buildings and infrastructure require constant maintenance and improvement and we'll need to prioritise investment carefully. Finally we will need to continue our efforts to attract and retain members. We've been successful in this in recent years but a slight fall in membership this year shows we mustn't be complacent. I've enjoyed working on your behalf and working closely with many of you - it's been a pleasure and a privilege to have been Commodore. As I said before, however, I think it's time for someone else to take charge, as I sincerely believe a fresh injection of ideas and perspective is vital for any organisation. Thanks to everyone for your superb support - which I'm sure you'll offer unhesitatingly to my successor. That's it from me - I'd be happy to answer any questions you have.

Marconi Sailing Club CAMPING RULES – 2011 THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES. • All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight. • No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday • Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid. • Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members. • No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site. • No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site. • No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site at all times. • The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area. • All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present. • Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times. • Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc. • Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected. • Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc. • Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are probably not paying much attention to traffic. • Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS. • The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed. • All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access.

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk On Another Tack or “Such Larks” Coming on over the last couple of years, like a growing itch was this feeling when sitting on the boat on the mooring, considering the latest forecast for the upcoming weekend cruise there didn’t seem to be quite the same tingle of excitement that I used to get. Don’t get me wrong I love these “Muddy Waters” of ours. As an example - a glorious day sail then the experience to be had of nosing into Pyefleet Creek on a mid summers late afternoon past all the other boats, dropping the hook and gaining the peace and solitude that the top of the creek provides. Taking an evening meal in the cockpit washed down with a couple of glasses of a good red whilst watching one of Pyefleet’s spectacular sunsets. All the while knowing you will get a good nights sleep because your anchor is safe at the end of its chain nicely dug in to gloriously sticky Essex mud. Cruising experience hard to surpass! But – and here’s the rub - for me in cruising the thing I get the biggest kick out of is planning a new passage, starting off, ticking off the waypoints, watching the pierheads or entrance to some new destination appear over the horizon. The excitement of entering a new harbour, tieing up then finding out what this new destination has to offer and shall we stay or go – it wasn’t there anymore. We’d become familiar with pretty much all of our cruising ground from North Foreland, the Thames to St Kat’s, Medway and all the rivers to Wells Next the Sea. The itch persisted though and with work dominating life, a weekend or even our two weeks annual leave meant we couldn’t get much further and the itch grew. The remedy though was at hand – retirement in late 2009 meant the 2010 season could be planned to venture into sailing pastures new. The boat, a bilge keel Sadler 26 called “Edal” was pretty much already equipped to go further afield as I’d spent like an idiot in previous years replacing pretty much everything that could be replaced. So that winter was spent just making sure she was ready and a plan hatched or in corporate speak “an overall strategy developed” to sail round the UK. Now, back in the day we reckoned if you get 80% of a strategic plan to work you’ve done pretty well – I though didn’t want to tie myself to anything rigorous – it would be take it as it comes – no strict plan to be anywhere at any time, yes it would be going round – but if I liked somewhere I’d stay, if not, I’d move on, if I wanted to spend some time at home I would - if it took two/three years then so be it. So on the 19th May “Edal” and me left Titchmarsh marina on a singlehanded odyssey, to crawl up the East coast with an outline plan to get to the West Coast of Scotland through the Caledonian canal to lift out for the winter somewhere by mid September. The night before we left when I did that check of the forecast, this time the itch had gone and the tingle was very definitely back. As we left Titchmarsh I remembered the thoughts I’d had when I left work for the last time – and now - as Joe said to Pip in Great Expectations, “what larks we shall have, such larks ! The table below shows the sequence of destinations to Loch Creran just North of Oban where Edal is now ashore for the winter. It clearly doesn’t tell the whole story we had a wonderful summer. Don’t believe what people say about the East coast of England and Scotland being grey and uninteresting with long distances between harbours – not so. A small capable boat particularly one that can take the ground or lean against a harbour wall can cover the distances with relative ease in daylight and there’s lots of interesting places to see. Enter/leave +/- HW 4hrs must call sea lock 21 Corpach - Loch Creran 28 Loch Creran strong ebb, enter on flood, moorings at Barcaldine Total distance 634 The two longest passages came at the beginning of the trip and were both achieved OK. The 54nm Lowestoft to Wells passage can be shortened in quiet weather and with bilge keels/shallow draft by anchoring overnight inside the breakwater at Sea Palling - something over four hours out of Lowestoft. We (me and Edal) did the passage in one go by timing for a neap and punching the tide either end of the passage, this meant the middle part where the fair tide was fastest as it sweeps round the corner of East Anglia gave us pace over the passage speed to reach Wells by HW. The 52nm from Wells to Grimsby had almost no tide against as the tide on leaving Wells sweeps East out of the Wash and along the East Anglia coast so was more or less on the beam for the first part of the passage. I followed the advice of Wells HM Bob Smith to go due North out of Wells and at the East Docking Buoy turn Nth West catching the fair tide. Closer to the Humber as the tide turns South again – if you are close enough to the mouth of the river it sweeps you into the Humber. Bob says this route does make the passage a bit longer but as well as not facing the tide quite so much early on you also stay in deep water which in rougher weather is more comfortable than the shallow water of the more direct route. All the other passages were much shorter and they pretty much matched the planning. The only one that came out a bit different was from Peterhead to Whitehills where the HM said “Reeds is wrong you need to set out two hours earlier” we did – and he was right. So if you get to Peterhead and intend going round into the Moray Firth – go have a chat with him ! Guess the point about both of the above is – it’s always someone’s local waters and they will tend to know the local wrinkles. Places I didn’t particularly like? Only a couple Whitby and Arbroath, strange because they’ve both a strong reputation for seafaring. Whitby is an attractive town to visit walk round and see the sights. But its harbour is controlled by the local council who seem to have a take it or leave it attitude to anyone visiting the marina by boat. The charges for a day’s visit are not frantically high just shy of £20 per day for Edal (high enough though) But I couldn’t avoid going home for a few days to get something done – and Whitby’s policy is to charge the day rate on a continuous basis. So nine days in total – just shy of £20 per day for a restrictive harbour that’s only +/- HW 2hrs. It cost me more to stay in Whitby for nine days than it did to stay in Anstruther for nearly a month and most harbours along the whole East Coast have a weekly or longer stay rate – so much for being a seafaring town, what if you were storm bound! Arbroath is well placed as a stop over on the way up Scotland’s East Coast, its charges too were close to £20 per night and you pay extra for showers, electricity and – water. The toilets and showers on the fish quay were filthy. I walked in the town and felt it had a sort of threatening atmosphere. A chap on the pontoons took his wife to a local hostelry for dinner and in the end walked out as they felt intimidated – maybe we picked the wrong time and places. Guess my opinion would be - both Whitby and Arbroath are well placed to use as stopovers on the way North but personally I would only stay one night if I had to. Places that are good passage ports? Grimsby, easy entrance behind dock gate and for a singlehander a huge outer dock in quiet water to drop sails and rig fenders before entering the HCA marina. The HCA remind me of Marconi they are self help and funding and have made a terrific job building their pontoons clubhouse yard and security fencing. They have oil and diesel available in the yard plus water and electricity on the pontoons. The town itself feels a bit down at heel though and it’s a fair walk from the dock. Sunderland, wide and easy entrance with the marina just inside off to starboard. A real Geordie welcome, good modern facilities. Water, electricity and diesel available. Good walks along the river to enjoy the industrial heritage. Blyth, again an easy entrance with the RNYC pontoons in a large dock off to port where you have room to stow sails and rig fenders etc. RNYC write the pilot book so advice on going North from these chaps is worth having. There is water and electricity on the pontoons, a bar and food in their clubhouse, provisions and diesel in the rather dismal town couple of miles away – terrific sandy beach for walks. Peterhead, enormous harbour, wide easily gained entrance with a modern marina in Southern corner. Good facilities, water, electricity and diesel available. Make sure you have chat with the HM about the timing of the tide ! Inverness, modern marina with an easy entrance to port after Kessock bridge. It’s in an industrial area a couple of miles out of town. I’ve got a folding bike on the boat so could get into Inverness which is pretty much like a lot of other provincial large towns having I think lost its identity to “retailisation”. There are still some good buildings though and along the banks of the Ness are some fine villa’s and the footways along the Ness are very pretty. Places most liked on the way North were, Wells Next the Sea, very friendly place, bustling quayside atmosphere, terrific walks and countryside with places to go inland and along the coast. Good clean facilities and a laundry. Bridlington, earthy kind of place with a busy fishing harbour, friendly, a fisherman even moved his boat so I could get a more comfortable berth. Basic but clean facilities. You have to lie along the wall or raft and take the ground – but it was only £15 for three days! April 2011 Navigans 14

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Holy Island, an absolutely magical place, where else can you sit on a mooring with two castles in sight Bamburgh and Lindisfarne, golden beaches to one side Holy Island to the other and the sea and Farne islands in the distance – bliss! Eyemouth, a serious fishing harbour, bustling activity, welcoming HM although he did say “ye’ll no forget the code fer the shoooowers It’s 1320 The Declaration of Arbroath when Scotland declared it’s Independence ye ken”. Great walks along the cliffs either side of the harbour with fantastic views of the gannets diving into clear waters for the fish. Good clean facilities. Anstruther, a drying harbour on the North bank of the Firth of Forth, a pretty little place which has everything one could need. The other fishing villages along this stretch of coast are just as well kept as Anstruther and walking between them kept me occupied for days. The ancient university town of St Andrews is a short bus journey away and well worth visiting. The berthing costs were one of lowest I’d encountered so I left the boat there for four weeks and travelled home by train. Good clean facilities – tell the attendant you are a visiting yachtie with a boat in the harbour or he will charge you – even for a wee pee! Stonehaven, grey and uncompromising to look at - it really is a Stone Haven. A fantastic natural setting, with the long arm of the outer wall of the harbour protecting the two inner drying harbours. The grey stone is replicated in the buildings of the town and gives the place a wonderful air of solidity and permanency. The romantic ruins of Dunnottar Castle on its headland a few miles South of the town is well worth a visit just to marvel at its position and also to wonder how it held out for eight months as Cromwells army “knocked it abart a bit”. To stay afloat you lie against the tall outer harbour wall, maybe even rafting up. The facilities are a bit basic, water, toilets, showers but don’t let it put you off – it’s a charming evocative sort of place – even got a first rate fish restaurant just along the quay. Whitehills, first port of call in the Moray Firth – you call up Bertie the HM when a couple of miles off and he gives you best advice about entry and when you get there he and another chap are on the pontoon to take your lines. He then gives you a welcoming speech describing the harbour, its facilities and impresses on you don’t fail to call him on his mobile if there’s any help you need. He then provides the free WIFI key and hands over what he describes as the welcome pack, security gate code, harbour bits and pieces and all about the town and its history and facilities - - - WOW ! Can’t speak highly enough about Whitehills, although it’s a small harbour – the welcome is fantastic, the people go out of their way to be helpful and I’ve never seen toilets, showers and laundry so spotless. And - joy of joy’s, the longest softest loo paper you could wish to apply to your person – no nasty short and shiny hard bog roll here! They’ve even got a reading room with books and armchairs so you can go ashore to a quiet area to read if you need to. Findochty, (pronounced Finechty) very pretty little ex fishing harbour now populated by local sailing boats on a set of drying pontoons. Visitors lie along the inside of the outer harbour wall and take the ground. Finechty village is unusual in that the houses are painted, giving the place a colourful appearance. Most of the cottages in the fishing villages along the coast are left in natural stone. There is a shop, public loo and a tap but no other facilities. There’s also no HM based here. Finechty is worth visiting just to soak up the atmosphere. In truth along this Moray Firth coastline you could choose several other small harbours to visit Portsoy, Banff, Portnockie, truth is once you turn the corner into the Moray Firth at Rattray Head they come thick and fast so guess you’ve got to draw the line somewhere. It’s a great coastline for exploring though. Findhorn, of all the places visited on the cruise North this is my favourite. It’s actually a large bay behind a series of sand dunes fronting the Moray Firth with a narrow entrance channel to one side. The entrance is tortuous with a shifting bar which the pilot book likens to the entrances to the Deben and Ore, so I felt quite at home. After the narrow entrance though the bay opens out and is quite glorious with views on every hand. South and inland are gently rolling hills, to the West pine plantations, to the North dunes, the Moray Firth and beyond the Firth the towering mountains of Northern Scotland in the far distance. The village backs itself into the Eastern shore of the bay, old stone buildings fronting the water and a series of rows of small single storey cottages arranged face to face down narrow grass or shingle tracks leaves an impression of what it must have been like as a fishing village. There is water for fin keelers to stay afloat on a mooring or two piers to tie up to but on the piers you take the ground. I chose the pier so I could walk ashore and I had only been there 20 minutes when a member of the RFYC came up, welcomed me and pointing to a magnificent three storey stone edifice on the shoreside and said that’s the club house and you can use facilities showers etc, there’s water on the pier and oh there’s no charge for visiting yachtsmen, here’s the code to get in if the clubs locked up. Later when I visited the club they even gave me their internet key so I could sit in the sun lounge fronting the bay, cup of coffee, answering my e-mails. It’s an enchanting place, which has a gentle alternative air about it with a welcome that’s motivated out of the fellowship of sailing rather than profit. I stayed several days and after speaking to a couple of RFYC committee members asked if I could present a Marconi burgee to hang on one of the vacant flagstaffs which decorated their entrance hallway, they agreed and presented one of theirs in return which I’ve passed to Murray with RFYC’s compliments. Caledonian Canal, almost too much to say about the scenery from quiet and pastoral to the outright magnificent. Turning the corner into Loch Ness for the first time and seeing this enormous body of water (and it’s not the sea) is breathtaking. Then seeing the depth sounder register around 190 metres and go blank because it can’t find the bottom is eerie – maybe Nessie is down there after all ! The peace and quiet of the wee Drumnadrochit harbour under the ruins of Urquhart Castle in Loch Ness on our first night in the canal was sublime. It was here I got my best ever sighting of a Kingfisher, I was still and looking over the Loch when this magnificent little bird perched within six feet of me and right in my eye line, I kept still and he stayed - it must have been about a couple of minutes – wonderful experience. If you’re worried about going through locks and lock gates on the Caledonian – don’t, because every bridge and lock is manned – they know you are coming watch out for you and help you through. My only regret and I understand it’s quite common for this April 2011 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk to happen is we had to motor virtually all the way through the canal. We did try to sail once as we found the wind for once coming from astern – out came the genny – we zapped up to 6kts quite quickly for about five minutes, then over the next few minutes the wind switched first from one side then the other, ahead, astern, port, starboard, we gave up and switched the engine back on. I’m told in mountainous lochs it’s something I’m going to have to get used to! Final leg to the West coast, at the end of the Caledonian the descent down Neptune’s Staircase towards Corpach basin was a real experience when you come out at the bottom and look back up the eight flights it’s remarkable to see how far down you’ve come. One more flight just before Corpach and we were in the basin to overnight before leaving the sea lock in the morning for the last leg of my summer’s lark. One of the enduring memories of the summer is standing by the side of the sea lock that evening – it was a beautiful clear sunlight early evening, looking round the bay that is formed by the head of Loch Linnhe, across to Fort William, then further round seeing clear to the top of Ben Nevis and knowing that tomorrow we would be heading past the red of the channel marker down the Loch and towards the West coast. The coast I’d explored with my Mother and Father when we lived in Scotland close to 50 years ago – it was quite frankly an emotional moment. The summer’s final destination was Barcaldine in Loch Creran roughly 28nm from the head of Loch Linnhe a passage which in a small sailing boat is very definitely controlled by the tides. Part way down the loch at Corran Narrows the tide runs at 6kts and when we got there our SOG peaked at just over 10kts. It was a spring and it was interesting to say the least to see as we went through the Narrows small whirlpools in the surface of the water that appeared left and right then disappeared just to reappear somewhere else! The entrance to Loch Creran is made on the flood, it’s a fairly narrow entrance and there’s a lot of water behind it in the loch – once inside things go a bit quieter and we soon made up to the moorings at Barcaldine Marine. A call ashore and the manager Martin came out took me ashore and showed me round – the decision made this was where Edal would overwinter. Four days later she was lifted ashore and I got the train home. Early May 2011 she will be lifted back in and the “larks” continue North of Ardnamurchan. There is more to this tale about preparation, musings on each leg of the trip, passage planning, people I met plus photo’s and a few (badly made - I’m no Dylan Winter) video’s on a Blue which is accessed by invitation. If any member of the club wants to access the Blue just send me your e-mail address to and I’ll issue an invite. David Lakin April 2011 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk th June Issue copy deadline: Sat 14 May 2010 Club Notes Commodore’s Notes Lets hope the balmy days we have enjoyed so far continue during the rest of the season. I can but say “Many Thanks” to all the members who turned out for the two working parties immediately before Neil Pembleton the start of the sailing season. The turnout on the first Commodore weekend was very impressive and so many jobs were completed that I wondered if there would be enough to do at the second one. I need not have worried, despite the Club Secretary same or even greater number of people on site, Murray managed to conjure up enough to keep everyone occupied. Consequently we have started the season with Marconi Sailing Club Ltd the site and clubhouse looking the best it has for many Disposal Notice years. I can only re-iterate my thanks to you all. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Club News Royal Wedding Pursuit Race & Street Party Elsewhere in the monohull fleet, Thomas Goode deserves a special mention. Thomas was to sail the Vago with his PURSUIT RACE dad – but at the point of launch Tony was afflicted with severe cramp which meant they could not sail. On Friday 29th April – once the church and balcony scenes Undeterred, Tom simply got into his Pico and raced that were well and truly over – a Pursuit Race was held at the instead! club in honour of the Royal Wedding. Flags, bunting and crowns abounded to mark the occasion which took place in The race however really belonged to the Sprint 15s. A a good breeze and disproportionately lumpy river. very close race ensued between Peter Richardson, Kevin Dowley and Eamonn Browne as they caught up and overtook each of the monohulls. The race tension increased as Pete managed to lose his tiller extension near the end of the race. This made for a very interesting last upwind leg and Pete rounded the last mark with Kevin Daley right on his stern. However, Pete managed to hold onto the lead for long enough to win the race. Prizegiving was conducted at the Street Party and we were particularly pleased to reward the cadets who had taken part in the race. STREET PARTY With a computer in the corner so we could watch the Royal Wedding over the internet – a team of volunteers transformed the clubhouse lounge into a venue fit for a ..well, Royal Wedding Street Party. Flags and bunting were also liberally distributed outside the clubhouse – including an extremely large Union Jack at the top of the club mast – which, I am informed, was visible from the main road! The Street Party took place in the evening after the racing – long tables were filled with club members and party food whilst another group of members cooked on the club BBQ outside. There was not a spare seat in the house! Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk MSC Ambition – a reference document to guide development The following paragraphs express the Board’s view of our key ambitions for the status, style and operation of the Club for the foreseeable future. This document will provide a reference point for the consideration of any plans that affect the future structure and direction of the Club. Status • We will be member-owned and independent • We will be recognised as the premier club in Essex for our style of • mixed fleet family sailing. • We will be recognised nationally (and in Europe) as a club that hosts well – run open events (national and international) and sends competitors to open events across a wide area. • As a consequence of all of the above and our own self-promotion we will be known as one of the premier sailing clubs in the UK Activity • There should be good training provision for all ages • The Club will promote a strong racing calendar for its major fleets, will encourage members to compete nationally and internationally and will seek to attract Open event activity. • The club will promote non-racing on–water activity for all members. • The club will actively promote formal and informal social activity for the benefit of active members and their non-sailing family members. • The Club will actively and exclusively promote wind-powered sailing activity in all it forms but will avoid the creation of harmful conflicts of interest (eg kite boarding). It will not provide a base for powerboat activity or Personal Water Craft (eg Jet skis etc). Presentation • Comfortable and high quality facilities for non-sailing social activity to include a dry lounge with capacity for 100+ and an adequate outside seating area. • Sufficient space on site to meet all our needs in terms of movement, storage, social activity, parking and camping commensurate with the size of the membership. • Consistent high standards of presentation and décor across the site that match the best commercial amenities • Full accessibility. • Sufficient undercover storage and maintenance space for club equipment in secure buildings that blend with the rural setting. (Commenced in 2009 and ongoing) • Good access to the water and easy access to the hard. • A high standard of handling equipment and full H&S compliance. • Changing facilities on a scale that matches the needs of the active sailing membership. (Achieved in 2010) Financial • Income from membership fees will underpin all our spending activity. • Additional income to aid and support development may come from the following: 1. Grant aid 2. Donations 3. Non-conflicting rent-producing commercial activity on 4. site (subject to planning and other considerations) 5. Members loans 6. Commercial Loans • It should be noted again that the latter two are dependent on sustainable levels of membership income. Membership • Membership should not fall below 400 members or rise above 550 members (as presently defined). June 2011 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk • Membership increases must be sustainable if project funding is largely or wholly reliant on such increases. • Overall membership numbers must be managed within the constraints of available common facilities (changing, toilet, parking, storage). • Individual fleet membership may also need to be managed in line with available fleet-related facilities. Style • Family-friendly. No restrictions to membership by boat class. Fee structure to encourage family involvement. Strong training and development support. Support for both racing and non-racing activity. • Self-help to the extent that members will be involved in routine housekeeping and maintenance (particularly in respect of their own storage areas, mooring facilities, boat recovery and movement). • Non-exclusive. Straightforward membership criteria, no fleet restrictions and a fee structure that can be described as affordable. • A management style that is positive, open and direct – built upon excellent communication with members, utilising appropriate modern techniques. Staff • A level and style of staffing commensurate with our needs, within our means and allowing the fundamental character of the club (as expressed here) to remain unchanged. Neil Pembleton (for the MSC Board) April 2011 After review of original document published by Chris Davies (for the MSC Board) January 2004 June 2011 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk “Protecting the waters of Essex” To All Members, Thank you, for taking your time to read this article. Let me introduce ourselves to you. We are the General Aviation and Maritime Unit for Essex Police force area. We are a small team of dedicated Counter Terrorism officers and cover all the maritime sites apart from the port of Tilbury and Harwich. We want to impress on you the importance of contacting us if there is something that you feel suspicious about whilst out on the waters around our coastline. You, ‘The Public’ are our eyes and ears and no piece of information that is sent to us will be overlooked or seen as trivial. We would rather have lots of information than none at all and will never be wasting our time. Project KRAKEN is a national initiative which has been launched UK wide. So, whether you travel to Cornwall or Edinburgh and wish to report something suspicious or that you are not happy with it is called Project KRAKEN. This is the neighbourhood watch of the marine world and this system is here for the long term. There have been local initiatives in the past but this is the first national project of this nature. So if nothing else, please remember Project KRAKEN if you see anything of a suspicious nature. This could be counter terrorism or criminal activity but if you don’t tell us we will never know!! Our leaflets have been left at your club; please take one and all our contact details are on it. We presently cover 78 general aviation sites and 66 maritime sites that we know of!! We would love to visit you more but there are only two of us unfortunately. We do what we can and if you need any further information we would be more than happy to pay you a visit. Regards, DC Jacque Howe DC Sean Adams General Aviation & Maritime Unit Counter Terrorism Division Essex Police Tele: July 2011 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Wayfarer Rally on the Orwell and Stour rivers, July 2011 THURSDAY 7TH JULY Dawn on Friday in Brightlingsea at the end of the Blackwater River brought a dilemma; one faced by seafarers the world over. Richard Higgs, Myrtle (my 40 year old Wayfarer) and I needed to be in Ipswich that evening for the UK Wayfarer Association rally, the weather however had other ideas. The wind whilst not feeling too strong in the shelter of Brightlingsea harbour was forecast to be a force 6 south westerly, 25 knots gusting 30 in the North Sea. We had two choices (if we were to make the rally), the first was to turn back up the Blackwater for a 3 to 4 hour beat against tide (and tow Myrtle), the second being to continue our journey, running downwind with tide. Neither prospect much appealed at 0700. The previous evening Richard and I had met at Marconi sailing club around 1600, loaded up Myrtle with clothes and provisions for at least the weekend and set off down the Blackwater for the short passage to Brightlingsea. We had planned for a full week of sailing, visiting some of the East Coast Rivers as well as meeting up in the Orwell at the Royal Harwich Yacht Club for the rally organised by Anne and Dennis Kell, and the lovely Emma. A force 4 on the starboard quarter and the last of the ebb ensured a pleasant and uneventful late afternoon sail. The harbour master allowed us to moor up for the night on the inside of his pontoon (negating the need to get a taxi to the shore from the mid-river visitor’s pontoon). Fish and chips from the not so local shop and a pint at the ‘Famous Railway Tavern’ set us up for the night; Richard in a land tent at the local campsite, me on Mrytle under the boom tent. The forecast was not looking too good for tomorrow but eh that would be another day. * Warning for those attempting to use the inside of the pontoon at Brightlingsea. At low water springs the pontoon sits on the mud whilst you continue to fall on the tide for another two feet. I awoke at midnight approaching low water to find Myrtle hanging off the mooring warps, oops! FRIDAY 8TH JULY I awoke at 0600 to find Myrtle somewhat embarrassingly floating 2m away from the pontoon, it now being high water and having loosened her warps somewhat excessively at low water the previous night, oops again! Neither Richard nor I fancied the beat back to Marconi sailing club; we knew from experience that it would be pretty horrible, cold, choppy and tiring. The wind did not seem that bad (in harbour it never does) and running down wind would reduce the apparent wind. Continuing our passage to the Orwell some 20 miles down tide and down wind seemed the best option, and so at 0730 we pulled out of the shelter of Brightlingsea harbour; full dry suits and sailing jackets, two reefs and the small jib flying. A short period of beating into wind got us out of the harbour and around the point at Lee-over-sands heading down wind on a near run. Past Clacton pier and then Frinton sea front, the wind picking up as forecast, waves 2m from trough to peak rolling along and over Myrtle’s starboard gunnels. By now travelling at some speed we were being over powered by 30 knot gusts, Myrtle rounding up to wind alarmingly. ‘Time to take the main down I said’ as we passed Walton pier, Richard nodded ‘just what I was thinking’. Turning to drop the main we felt the full force of the wind, a scary time but once back on course things calmed down, on jib alone we reckoned we were still doing some 3 knots through the water. Not fast enough unfortunately now to out run the waves and minutes later without warning a wave broke over the stern leaving a cockpit half full of water. Easy this sailing lark isn’t it? Rounding Walton Naze to port we headed across the Backwater entrance now with Harwich in sight. The wind and waves persisted until we finally rounded the harbour breakwater and in calm conditions we made our way into the Orwell; Felixstowe container terminal on our starboard and Harwich town to port. We moored up on the welcoming Halfpenny pier for a deserved rest at 1200, some 4½ hours after leaving earlier that morning. Both were extremely cold and it would be some 2 hours before we felt ready to continue our journey (most of it spent getting warm in the café on the pier). The Royal Harwich Yacht Club occupies an enviable position overlooking the beautiful Orwell River just short of Ipswich and some 8 miles up river from Harwich; Richard and I sat having a final beer on the grass outside the club house as darkness fell. Earlier that afternoon we had left the comfort of the café on Halfpenny pier and sailed up the river on a force 4 beam reach, passed the Yacht Club to port, under the bridge on the A14 and on towards Ipswich docks for a ‘look-see’. The return to the yacht club entailed the use of the outboard as Myrtle struggled to cope with the short tacks needed to retrace our course into both the wind tunnel effect caused by the bridge and a rising tide. The berthing master offered Richard the grass bank in front of the club house as a pitch for his tent, very decent indeed, prime views. Throughout the evening friends both old and new arrived, food and drink a plenty consumed, plans for the following day analysed in detail and salty tales swapped. A typical Wayfarer rally was beginning and we were really chuffed to have arrived under sail. SATURDAY 9TH JULY The East Coast north of the Thames comprises a series of rivers each travelling considerable distances inland and all running roughly parallel to the Thames itself; rivers such as the Crouch, Blackwater, Stour, Orwell, and Deben. Each is very tidal, varied in nature but essentially muddy, ideal for Wayfaring about. The Stour made famous by Constable’s paintings of a working river December 2011 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk whilst actually navigable for 40 miles in land, for all intents can be sailed only up to Manningtree some 10 miles from its mouth at the North Sea, The Orwell likewise with its all be it more recent industrial heritage runs from its junction with the Stour and North Sea to Ipswich. The weekend rally would see us sail both rivers; we were to sail down the Orwell on the ebb to Harwich, cross into the Stour and up on the flood before camping overnight in a creek on the northern shore. Leaving mid morning on ebb, 7 Wayfarers left the Royal Harwich Yacht Club, a brisk north westerly ensuring a fast passage down-river. The hamlet of Pin Mill (featured in the children's novel by Arthur Ransome: We didn’t mean to go to sea) quickly passed to our starboard and in the distance the looming cranes of Flexstowe’s container terminal soon announced our arrival at Harwich. Turning to starboard past Harwich and up the River Stour we now headed upwind, the wind strength force 4, with waves breaking over the top of the dinghies (in ‘The Green One’s’ case breaking into the forward bouyancy tank through a very large crack in the deck seams). Crossing into Essex we pulled the boats up the beach for lunch and some collected oysters. After lunch we sailed further up the Stour, beating energetically, eventually arriving at Mistley where a delicate bit of light wind short tacking and the ocasional running aground was the order. Returning to the Suffolk side of the river we passed the Royal Hospital School built by Greenwich Hospital to educate the children of Navy personnel. Our intention being to dry the boats out overnight at Holbrook Creek, required that we arrive bang on high water which we duly did. The evening meal was taken at the Baker’s Arms in Harkstead village following a nice half hour walk through the Suffolk countryside. Most people slept in their Wayfarers with their boat tents that night with some pitching tents on land. SUNDAY 10TH JULY Sunday morning was a very early wake up as high water was 0720 (remember we beached the boats at high water the night before). Boats can only get in and more importantly out of Holbrook Creek 30 minutes either side of high water, otherwise it would be a 12-hour wait! A lack of wind meant that the the boats paddled out into Holbrook Bay, anchored as a group in lovely flat calm waters and cooked breakfast. Becalmed with no wind it was a slow drift downriver to Harwich town. Myrtle got out her oars and showed the fleet what a determined Wayfarer could do; about 2 knots. Approaching Harwich the wind picked up nicely, just as well as we needed to avoid the 1030 Harwich to Hook ferry. We glided into the marina adjacent to to the Halfpenny pier and moored for lunch (tea, scones and ice cream to be exact) awaiting the turning tide. Some took the opportunity to walk around the beach and the historic town in glorious sunshine. Soon after lunch the tide turned and a sea breeze set in, the wind obligingly turning 180 degrees ensured another quick downwind sail on the flood this time up the Orwell. A north westerly on Saturday to a south easterly on Sunday helping us both ways, not often you can say that happens? Returning to Royal Harwich Yacht Club around mid afternoon, gave plenty of time to pack the boats away for the various road journeys home, There were fond farewells from each to all and of course many a well deserved thank you to Dennis and Anne for organising such a lovely weekend. Eventually though folk drifted away, ………. apart of course from one Wayfarer and her intrepid crew who still had many adventures ahead. MONDAY 11TH TO WEDNESDAY 13TH JULY Over the next three days Richard, Myrtle and I would work our way up to Woodbridge at the end of the Deben and eventually via a short stay in the Walton Backwaters sail back to Marconi sailing club. The south westerly wind that took us north turned kindly into a north easterly force 5 taking us speeding back south (see it happens all the time). A wild run down wind and tide to finish a journey which over 7 days and nights, covering some 135 miles would take in the full length of 4 rivers, a Backwater and a rally. Just about perfect. Many thanks to Richard for being my companion and for putting up with my rants and impatience, many thanks also to Anne and Dennis Kell for the excellent hard work they put into organising such a terrific rally. For the record, attending the rally were: Anne and Dennis Kell in Emma, W247 nomn Colin Wardell, Robin Broham, Cliff and Kay Poutney in Blue Moon, W6697 Graham and Tom Lawson in Skylark, W1004 Andrew and Dinos Ktenas, in The Green One Matt Sharman and Octavia Heath in Wild Lone, W773 Helen Ratay and Brian Hudson in Penelope, W6542 Richard Higgs and John Eardley in Myrtle, W7114 Author John Eardley, Oct 2011 December 2011 Navigans 7
