Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Retiring West After 32 years of teaching, the end of April was my final month as a Primary school teacher, having been eventually persuaded to retire by my Skipper…. the aim being to embark on some extended cruising. Time and length of day for such retirement ‘jollies’ weren’t the only things that were important; the weather was as well… but it wasn’t until later in June were we to realised that ‘crucial’ would have been a better adjective! Planning and research for a trip to the South and South West Coast of England was extensively worked upon. Christmas gifts of The Solent Pilots and South-West Cruising Guides were welcomed and avidly read by the Skipper. Many friends gave us the benefit of their local knowledge of the areas we hoped to travel. Naturally, E-bay was well used for purchasing Charts, [certainly to be recommended]. 21/5/11 Finally we are ready to leave, with house locked, cars sorted out and boat loaded…. a bit too much according to the Skipper! Alas, the first problem to arise was that the weather was due to be pretty dire for 2/3 days! We adopted a strategy of “..must go somewhere…”, so two intrepid sailors set forth for Brightlingsea to sit it out until we could cross the Thames estuary. After 4 days of winds force 5/8 we finally got away…. to the Orwell. This is, of course, the wrong direction for Dover/Ramsgate but the weather was clearly not going to abate so a change of scene was decided upon ‘come what may’ in the short weather window we were offered. 25 to 27/5/11 Wrabness, BBQ ashore with our ‘cruising in company’ companions Sue and Peter Arnold aboard ‘Last Dream’, relaxing and enjoying a red sunset. This did not follow the correct pattern as a gale warning for later was given. The 26th proved wet, windy and rough, we did get ashore briefly and discovered the new Community shop in the village – it’s great, well stocked with good quality groceries. Also at the top of the path to the village is a farm stall selling delicious pasties, quiche, fruit, jam and eggs - all in aid of charity. After a short walk curtailed by a thunderstorm we returned to the boat, gale warning immanent! So rough in the evening that the dinghy threatened to capsize so we dragged it into the cockpit and got the engine safely stowed. Phew… I felt seasick! The rest of the week we spent in the Orwell…at Pinmilll Picturesque walk along to the Clamp House, returning via the House Boats and The Butt and Oyster…lovely Aspall’s cider and Adnams! The new concrete walkway at Pinmill makes getting ashore much easier and less muddy. 28/5/11 Sailed to Ipswich in 22kwind. Loads of washing to do and is one of the less enjoyable aspects of cruising. It can take ages and needs some patience. You need to find an empty laundry room, have 2/3hrs. to spare and be ready for a fitness routine [considering the number of times you have to keep returning to move laundry between washer and drier] and hope that no one has done this for you by putting theirs in and jumping the queue. This is when ‘laundry rage’ can set in! The MSC Bank Holiday cruise to Ipswich (that we’d not expected to do) was great fun! Joining in with everyone renewed our spirits somewhat as did the promise of improving weather. The only disappointment was Manchester United losing to Barcelona…. but it was fun watching it with fellow fans at Ipswich Yacht Club. 31/5/11 Left Orwell at 0300. Very dark but interesting in Felixstowe Harbour - lots of lights. Daylight by the time we reached Medusa. Good sail across Thames Estuary making up 2hrs so pressed on for Dover 1300, wind 3/5 NW/W. 1/6/11 Dover to Eastbourne, set off 1200, pleasant 2/3 NW calm but not so after Dungeness as the wind increased to 5/6 SW, with wind over tide and really lumpy - kept falling off waves. Locked in 2000 only 1/2hr later than planned but wet and weary - huge marina…loos etc miles from berth! 2/6/11 Eastbourne to Brighton, sunny…Beachy Head spectacular - light winds. Concrete surround at Marina is rather ugly. Once in, can’t see the sea, which is useful when the Skipper persuades you that even though it sounds windy in the marina it’ll be fine when you get outside! 3/6/11 Sailed rapidly to Cowes, one reef in, 26k at times - great arriving in the Solent…marked by The Isle of February 2012 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Wight, Spinnaker Tower, Napoleonic Forts, Cruise ships and hundreds of yachts. All sights I’ve seen each summer for eleven years while taking 20/30 Primary school pupils on their school journey and now here was my chance to share my favourite places with just companions! Queen Mary 2 liner was immediately to starboard as we neared Cowes, getting abeam of her we double jibed! “Where are you going?’’ the Skipper asked - but I hadn’t done anything! The wind shadow from such an enormous vessel had caused this. Luckily he’d just re-entered the cockpit after taking photos. Immediately, the VHF sounded a ‘May Day’ – a very small gaffer in Osborne Bay just behind us had capsized! Other closer boats went to her rescue and the RNLI attended. Once moored at Shepherd’s Wharf, we chatted to the Lifeboat crew and they seemed to think an involuntary jibe had caused the capsize, so be warned of Cruise ships. 4/6/11 Cowes the yachting Mecca of the UK! We’re here – and so is the sun at last! Had lovely day wandering around shops, museum, yacht clubs and waterfront. Certainly to be recommended is to have lunch at the Island Sailing Club – most welcoming and a great view from the terrace of the Medina River’s traffic. Our berth was rather choppy and noisy opposite the Red Funnel terminal - amazing how many times 5 hoots had to used due to ignorant boat handling…not us!! We moved to an inner spot for the second night but it wasn’t quiet as the wind increased during the night. We decided shelter was needed for the next night. 5 to 9/6/11 Travelled further up the Medina away from the main marinas, boat yards and ferries to a beautiful spot called The Folly. Mid- river pontoons are close to shore and The Folly Inn! Also close by are Osborne House and regular bus routes. Berthed here for the next few days. We did a lot of walking and used the excellent bus services [free for 3 members of our party!] Ah! Osborne House. No matter how many times I visit it, Osborne House is special – a full day is needed to do it justice. From The Folly it’s a relatively short walk to the main entrance. Buses took us to Newport, Alum Bay, the South side of the Island and across the centre via Brighstone. The views from the top deck were superb. We ventured forth in a 40k gale to the Needles Battery, finding that keeping upright to be quite difficult! Never the less, a very interesting place. Suffice as to say the weather was still poor and quite wet at times. Thank goodness we’d invested in a cockpit tent…this proved invaluable during the whole holiday even though the Skipper thinks it makes C’est Moi look like a caravan! 9/6/11 Made a break for new surroundings, headed from The Folly to Newtown Creek. Pilot describes it as a pretty, quiet, anchorage. The creek lived up to its description. The entrance was quite tricky needing a lot of care following the pilotage instructions. Unfortunately we didn’t get ashore due to winds being force 5/6, picking up a mooring was difficult and anchoring out of the question. Certainly, venturing ashore in a rubber dinghy would not have been a good idea. Costs of marinas, moorings and anchorages on the South coast are higher than those on the East - we were ready for this but didn’t expect to pay The National Trust £16 for a night’s stay on a mooring. However, it was with regret that we didn’t return to go ashore as it was a very peaceful pretty spot. 10/6/11 Headed across to the Hamble for the weekend, as we were to provide our daughter Alice and her partner Damian with a base while they competed in a Firefly dinghy event at The Hamble River Sailing Club. At last, light winds across the Solent and a quiet drift…. but…looking across at Southampton, things were about to change. Black clouds like ‘ink’ loomed! An hour later we had torrential hail and winds 5/6 as we navigated carefully up the busy ‘car park’, which is the Hamble River! A gale forecast for the next 2 days somewhat spoiled the dinghy racing. Saturday night we booked in at The Royal Southern Yacht Club, an imposing building with grey-suited permanent staff manning reception. They made us feel most welcome, the only problem was that the pontoon berth we were given wasn’t normally used for visitors and we created a certain amount of consternation by our presence. We think we were given it in error…. Still, we felt quite special all weekend! A jolly Saturday night was had with the Firefly sailors –sausage and mash+ice cream for supper - raising money for charity and a big raffle in which we all won a prize. The Skipper won a 10yr old bottle of Malt….and it’s not finished yet (for those of you who would like to take note)!! 12/6/11 February 2012 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Rain all day –the UK had this across the country – washing needed doing so went up to Swanwick Marina - I got as wet as the two loads of washing I had to do with all the ’to-ing and fro-ing’ to the laundry – at least in a warm heated boat I dried out quickly. 13/6/11 Left for Lymington – due to meet friends – quite lumpy wind over tide in a force 5/7 but we made it to the Town Quay – sheltered here and near the old part of the town –a lot like being in the Netherlands. Intended to meet up with friends during the next 2 days then go up the Beaulieu and meet family on the 15th but weather altered that…. heavy rain and winds 5/7 kept us here ‘til 19th. During our stay we made the most of the beautiful New Forest surroundings with bus trips to Beaulieu and Christchurch and also walking along the coastline to Keyhaven. Nature reserves here are unique with a variety of birds. A fun diversion, part of Lymington Arts and Music week, was a rock concert in the grounds of the Congregational church! We listened to an excellent Police tribute band as well as a local Heavy Rock band! Never to young to rock…. even in retirement! Heavy rain brought our enjoyment to an abrupt end. However interesting the visits ashore may be, you can imagine that not continuing with our cruising was frustrating. Here in Lymington both Skippers decided defeat at the hands of the weather had to be considered and may be we’d have to return to home waters earlier than planned. 19 to 21/6/11 The plan to sail up Bucklers Hard and not just go on the bus was still on, so we left Lymington and moved in to the Beaulieu River. We split from our companions for a while, as they had to return home to attend to family business. They left their boat in Lyminton for a few days [at a very reasonable weekly rate]. The Beaulieu river entrance is interesting – similar to that of the Deben - careful pilotage is essential – we rolled our way in but once in the river it was idyllic – calm with wooded sides. Once berthed we enjoyed a lovely walk to Beaulieu…no rain for a change. I was hopeful we’d have a day at Buckler’s Hard Museum and a meal out at ‘The Master Builder’…also do the laundry…but no…it was not to be! The Skipper checked the outlook…winds increasing again – so sadly we had to make an exit from the Beaulieu – to Swanwick again 21to 23/6/11 Swanwick – enjoyed good value meal at the Spinnaker pub – relived Howard’s Way at The Jolly Sailor – got laundry done – walked around the Hamble river path to Warsash. Squally conditions made us think the ‘Pink’ ferry wouldn’t be running but the intrepid Ferryman came to fetch us, laughing at the thought that we’d gone out walking in such changeable weather! Back at Bursledon we visited the ‘Chandlery Barge’, a real education. Especially if you are renovating any craft built around 1930’s! 23/6/11 Returning home – definite! Decided to complete our Solent cruising by going to Portsmouth. Pilotage entering the harbour is not difficult but relies on lining up two high rise buildings – suffice as to say on our way we were caught in a squall that cut down visibility and left us running out to the Forts to find deeper water in 35k of wind! More settled weather after an hour or so. The rest of the weekend was fun visiting The Historic Dockyard – going across from the Gosport side on the Ferry. Saturday was The Round Island Race – winds of 5/7 expected- we did this two years ago but as we listened to calls on the VHF we were worried for the competitors. The coastguard had to stack up the ‘Pan Pan’s’ in preference to the ‘May Days’. Later when reading the Internet reports, sailors had experienced waves of 20 feet and Ben Ainsley described the Race as ‘extreme’ sailing! We decided this year was a good year to have given the race a miss. The Dockyard was fascinating. We split the visit into two days, ‘The Victory’ and a boat trip around the Naval Base followed by a special inter-services day, allowing us to visit HMS Daring (brand new stealth- designed warship), HMS Warrior (Victorian era), and the Mary Rose Museum - all thoroughly to be recommended. 26/6/11 Fog rolled in…. but hey… the sun came out and it was hot!! 27/6/11to2/7/11 Returned to the Orwell, via Brighton, Eastbourne and Dover. Taking a few days to explore surroundings. Ironically weather was on many occasions lacking in wind and quite dry! Eastbourne was a place I’d wanted to linger in on the outward journey but didn’t get a chance - now we had time and the weather. Got out our bikes for gentle peddling and sightseeing. Skipper had other ideas - we cycled all the way up Beachy Head! Completely …ackering! Worthwhile though - an amazing view from above the lighthouse. On arrival at the marina, Gordon and Cynthia (from MSC) appeared along the pontoon…coincidence - we enjoyed their company on the evening of the 29th. February 2012 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Dover was also somewhere I’d also missed visiting on route south. 1/7/11Climbed up to the Castle, it’s years since we’d been here but many features have been revamped. D-Day Operation Dynamo exhibition in the tunnels used during World War 2 was the highlight and inside the Medieval Keep locally made reproduction furnishings and artefacts now fill many rooms, giving an amazing atmosphere to the building. A whole day is needed here to enjoy the surroundings. Sun and zero wind filled the day – a treat…. may be summer is going to come! 2/7/11 Final day of Cruising West or now East …the best sail of the 7 week trip…. how ironic…left Dover 10:15 – Lavington 18:30 – tide all the way – wind 3/4 – listened to Wimbledon Ladies final in peaceful sailing conditions! Our Cruise has been an adventure – most enjoyable and opened up our travelling knowledge. Disappointing in many ways – maybe we should have stuck it out and been more patient waiting for the weather to change, but sailing is all about doing what you’re happy with and feel is within your capabilities. Returning South and West in future is something we’d like to do again. By Hilary Gardner ‘C’est Moi’ Answer to the Cruiser Knowledge was: False. Absolutely untrue, though it is a commonly held misconception. In fact, there are few cases when power must give way to sail. Examples where the vessel proceeding under power has right of way are - vessel engaged in fishing, vessel towing, vessel constrained by draught, i.e., it must stay in a narrow channel of deep water, vessel in a ship separation lane - such as the English Channel, etc. Also, if the sailing vessel is the overtaking vessel it must keep clear of the motor vessel. February 2012 Navigans 14

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk RACE OFFICER & CONTACT NUMBER RACE OFFICER & CONTACT NUMBER David BALL David KENNEDY Jenny BALL Nick MILLER Eamon BROWNE John/Caroline NICKALLS John BURGOYNE Chris KIRBY Peter CLAYTON Peter PLAYLE Martin HALL Andrew POTTER Lee HARRISON Howard ROGERS Julien HAMPSON John SALMON Richard HENSHAW Bryan SPENCER Dave HEWES Roger SMITH Gary JACKSON Peter TOVEY Steve MONKS Fenella MILLER Dave/Kate WILLIAMS Cruiser Fleet News – Cruiser Knowledge Answer Steer to port You are seeing the port light of a vessel ahead, and is about to pass in front of you from your starboard side. She is the stand on vessel and you must give way. Your best choice to avoid collision is to steer hard to port. In the same situation in a power boat or a sailboat on a port tack you would steer hard to port so that the two vessels pass port to port, but on a starboard tack you don't want to get caught in irons with another vessel head on. On another Tack. An elongated odyssey around Britain. TO HEAD SOUTH OR NOT TO HEAD SOUTH – THAT IS THE QUESTION. I’m not usually this indecisive, maybe it’s post operative stress after being under the surgeon's knife. (we’ll examine that in a bit more detail later) But give me a situation and usually I can weigh up the alternatives and come to a decision pretty quickly, this decision though is giving me some difficulty and I need your help. If you read my previous account of sailing up the east coast you’ll know end of summer 2010 we ended up (me and the boat) being lifted out on Scotland’s West coast in Loch Creran, just north of Oban where “Edal” (the boat) would overwinter before we turned south again in the spring 2011. Thing is - I’m still there. Sure, we got lifted back in but the siren call of Scotland’s West coast got to me and we spent the summer cruising in waters which OK can sometimes be a bit boisterous – plus it don’t arf rain - but and here’s the big BUT – when the weather’s “clement” it’s breathtakingly beautiful. It’s not that we’ve done loads of sailing because “stuff” at home during the summer of 2011 got in the way. Retirement what retirement – it just means for one’s children “one” is more accessible. We did though cruise up to Skye (just missing Malcolm Robertson who’d gone to Stornoway for the Tall Ships) plus two other short cruises and enjoyed them all enormously. I’d also discovered two things about cruising Scotland. First is, the tides are in the main pretty benign – it’s just those places where you get narrow gaps for all that water to squeeze through that it’s better to go with the flow, Kyle Rhea for example. Second is you are never far away from another stunning anchorage and even if the wind’s in the wrong direction for the one you’ve chosen there’s usually a sheltered one you can plan to get to. Oh - and a third – if it’s pontoons you prefer you can now pretty much day sail between them from Oban all the way up to Kinlochbervie, they do get a bit busy in July though. Put those “larnins” together and with all the places left to explore and you can start to see my dilemma - to stay another season or head south ? To stir the decision making pot for the jury and make the case for the defence (to stay in Scotland) here are a couple of cruising experience’s cut out of the Blue from last summer. AROUND ARDNAMURCHAN FROM TOBERMORY, WEDS 13TH JULY. I'd heard tales from fellow sailors of passages attempted round the fearsome Point of Ardnamurchan and how they or fellow rovers (they'd heard of) had battled for what (in the telling) seemed like days to get round the Point against the nastiest seas imaginable. Some (the tales go) even tried several times - each time turning back to the safe arms of Tobermory harbour. The tales said - what seemed like OK sailing conditions in the Sound became untenable when the Point itself was reached so it was with some caution I anticipated the "Roundin o the Point". In the event it was a "pussy cat" nothin to it - why was I worried - big brave sailor boy like me - easy peasy - nix - nuttin - doddle - why Well, best answer is the reason reputedly signalled by the March 2012 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk heavy cruiser HMS Cumberland at the battle of the River Plate when she was asked how she managed to get there so quickly - she signalled back - - - A N T I C I P A T I O N. Or to put it another way - planning. The pilot says best is wind with tide and stay 2nm off if there's a strong onshore wind of even a short duration. With an opposing tide very heavy seas build up 2mls offshore. There's also a strong inshore set on the ebb just south of the Point. For a first timer then my planning said - do it in fair weather with wind and tide in the same direction - so Wednesday the 13th it would be. After a couple of nights in Tobermory I was glad to be away - it was not that I didn't enjoy my stay, it was great but "Tob" as I heard it called is very much on the tourist trail and after a while the appeal palled particularly when a giant cruise liner put in, disgorging crowds of passengers along the front and pontoons. I also (and with my history this is very strange) felt at odds with the Scottish Piper who in dress jacket and kilt was employed to play Scotland the Brave and such tunes along the harbour for the entertainment of visitors. Now I absolutely love the pipes and after a couple of malts, Flowers of the Forest has been known to move me to tears but this seemed contrived and somehow unworthy - - but hey - what do I know, Edal on the Tobermory pontoon. the tourists loved it - and am I not a tourist in my own way ? The weather for the 13th was to be good and the wind light and variable, predominately from the south and west, HW Tobermory was approx 0526 and the tide off the Point was slack at roughly midday, turning north about an hour later. The distance from Tobermory to the Point is approx 11nm so planning at the usual 5kts, if we left about 1000 we'd reach Ardnamurchan at slack or with the tide just turning north. Our destination was to be Mallaig 36nm's away where despite its reputation as strictly a fishing and ferry port they'd recently installed extra moorings and pontoons to become "yacht friendly" and encourage rich yachties "tae spend in the toon “ Places to divert to were numerous, from Muck just 16nm from Tobermory, to the Isle of Eigg, Loch's Moidart and Ailort, Arisaig, Armadale, Loch Nevis and further up the Sound of Sleat, Isle Ornsay all pretty tenable in the forecast settled weather for next couple of days. So with plans laid and on a lovely summer morning we left Tobermory at 0940 bound for the north. The morning was delightful with clear blue sky and few white clouds, the wind was light and to maintain our passage plan speed the engine stayed on with the main up motorsailing to the Point. As we reached the Point and gradually came round to a more northerly course the wind increased slightly, moved aft of the beam and then onto the port quarter. The log entry for 1255 shows a course east of north having come round Ardnamurchan in very quiet conditions, making for the Sound of Sleat.With the direction and lightness of the wind, relatively flat sea Edal sails best under cruising chute - so up it went - engine off - the big red white and blue chute pulling us up to Mallaig on a sparkling sea through the most glorious scenery - bliss ! The lighthouse on the Mull shore just north of Tobermory, looking towards Ardnamurchan, By just after 1600 it was time to put Mallaig to the test to see just how friendly they were - so called the harbour by phone and a very nice lady answered but said "we're full". She apologised and said their new pontoons were now due to go in next week and all the moorings were taken - I could though lie outside a fishing boat against the wall if I liked. I pictured the scene of being wakened by a burly fisherman at three in the morning wanting to go to sea - me full of roast chicken, vegetables and red wine from my evenings repast and thought plan B should come into play. I thanked her for her time and looked at the alternatives. We had been making up the middle of the Sound of Sleat and the next potential place to overnight was either Loch Nevis or Armadale. I opted to call Armadale on the shores of Skye as it was closest and for leaving the following morning was right in the Sound. March 2012 Navigans 14

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Another nice lady said yes we've a mooring and as you're a "wee one" come close in and pick up one of our blue buoys closest to the shore and you'll have a quieter night. She asked the name of the boat and when I said Edal she said "Och you're in good waters here with a boat of that name, you're not far from Sandaig". I’d already plotted that Armadale was only 9nm from Sandaig where Gavin Maxwell wrote Ring of Bright Water and if the weather was fair I could land there and do a bit of exploring. By 1645 we'd arrived Armadale - sure enough a blue buoy close inshore was vacant we picked it up and it wasn't long before a chap came out in a launch and welcomed us. We were told the moorings were laid in the bay by Skye Yachts a charter business and they offered us diesel, water and advice about toilets, showers and the shops ashore. Water and diesel was not something we needed but he showed how they carried diesel on their launch in a bulk tank which had a pump so they could refill their yachts when they came back off charter without having to go ashore, The water was supplied by a long long floating blue pipe which the launch towed out to the boats in the bay to fill their tanks - ingenious. The overnight mooring cost was £12.50 which I guess for the west coast is pretty average. The evening went by in glorious technicolour, watching the ferry to Mallaig come and go on the same route Carole and I took when we were touring Scotland all those years ago in our old Rover 110. At least here I thought I'll have a quiet night and my stomach will have the peace and time to digest my roast chicken dinner without that imagined fisherman banging on my hatch in the early hours. I didn't have to be up early as Sandaig and Kyle Rhea were not far away and the fair tide to take us through Kyle Rhea started roughly 1320 - after a wonderful first day north of Ardnamurchan there was more to look forward too - - so to bed, and as Peter Dawson the old time baritone used to sing - - Rocked in the cradle of the deep, I lay me down in peace to sleep, Secure I rest upon the wave, And calm and peaceful is my sleep, Rocked in the cradle of the deep. PART OF A CRUISE TO LOCH'S SUNART, DRUMBUIE, ALINE AND ON TO OBAN, 23RD AUGUST TO 3RD SEPTEMBER. After a month at home -this time the outline plan was to go back to Tobermory and once there make a decision whether to go round Ardnamurchan again or cross the Sound of Mull to explore Loch Sunart. We left the mooring in Loch Creran at 0735 on Tuesday 23rd August roughly an hour after LW Oban it was a neap and there would be enough water for us in the entrance of the loch and not too much tide against us till we could get into the fair tide up the Sound of Mull. The sail to Tobermory was now familiar and the day opened out as fine with a light breeze, so for the bit out of Loch Creran and around the top of Lismore Island we motored, then as we shaped towards the entrance to the Sound of Mull we raised full sail. The passage completed in an easy seven hours for the 32km. When we first visited Tobermory the pontoons were packed and a call to the harbour master was necessary, this time there would be no such problem. Later in talking to the HM he said as it was now getting late in the season there was always a fairly dramatic fall off in the numbers of visiting boats after mid August - I thought "blimey" it would still be busy in popular harbours "Dahn Sarf". Met a fellow yachtie in the showers - as you do and fell into conversation - told him I was just starting a cruise and he said "oh it's a bit late in the season for that isn't it " Must say with the cautious nature of most sailors kicking in - I wondered if he knew something I didn't. I still hadn't finally decided where to go - so settling down in the cockpit after a good meal and with a glass of something I opened the excellent book published by CCC called Cruising Scotland to see what Loch Sunart had to offer. The book said most boats turn North round Ardnamurchan and miss the delights of Sunart - it described several lovely anchorages and the delights of Salen and Strontian - all in the relative safety of a 17 mile long sea loch - so I decided - exploring Loch Sunart it would be. Was I influenced not to go round Ardnamurchan by the "Oh it's late in the season” comments - well who's to say - all I know is the thought of lying to my anchor in the anchorages described in Cruising Scotland was very appealing and enjoying quiet nights on mooring buoys in Salen and Strontian had a strong attraction ! The distance between anchorages was also small making the passages easy (although that's true of a lot of the west coast) plus as I'd decided to stay in Scotland and overwinter, there was always next year for beyond Ardnamurchan - - so exploring Loch Sunart it would be. For our first overnight I decided to make for Loch Drumbuie which to describe to East Coast sailors is a bit like leaving Brightlingsea and overnighting in Pyefleet Creek except it's Into Loch Sunart with the entrance to Drumbuie about a mile about three times the distance at just over 5nm and a "tad" away hidden in the mist. more dramatic ! An easy day was in prospect - this is the way cruising should be - a good night's sleep, a decent breakfast at a reasonable time in the morning - an easy walk along the harbour to the supermarket to get final stocks for the larder - then March 2012 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk another cup of coffee in the cockpit before eventually setting off just after 1130. There was a good breeze as we left the left harbour - as soon as we had sea room the main went up and out came the genoa and we were sailing across the sound of Mull with a course to miss the rocks known as The Stirks just off the mainland shore. Half way across the wind piped up and it was obvious from the sudden drop in the light and visibility that there was more wind on the way - I reefed the genoa down to about a third and off Edal tramped for the far shore. The conditions on this day were perfect for her to fly, a stiff breeze, full main, third of the genoa and the relatively flat water in the shelter of the Sound. We tacked once in the Sound to come a bit further south to make absolutely sure we could be far enough away from the Stirks (and also because I was enjoying myself) then made past Auliston Point and into Loch Sunart towards Loch Drumbuie before the wind died away. Gradually the visibility improved as the sky lightened and the narrow entrance to Loch Drumbuie could be seen. The entrance at its narrowest is only about 120yds across and with steep hillsides on each side as you approach - on a murky day it looks forbidding. However it is deep and the sides fairly steep to with only one isolated rock on the starboard hand just inside the entrance. Once inside, Drumbuie is a delight almost completely surrounded apart from its narrow entrance it provides complete shelter. You can tuck into the corners to get away from the prevailing wind and sink your hook into good holding. We made up to the head of the loch and dropped the hook in about four metres of water. By the time we'd scouted the borders of the loch for potential anchorage spots, picked one and anchored the entry in the log says we were secured at 1320 only an hour and fifty minutes out of Tobermory. Drumbuie though is a world away from the hustle and bustle of busy Tobermory, it’s remote, no roads and as the skies cleared and the afternoon came on bright and sunny it showed itself as very beautiful. After a coffee and making sure Edal was secure - as soon as I could I took the dinghy ashore and did some exploring. Back onboard after a dinner of pork loins, steamed veg and a good red – replete, watching the sun go down - it was breathtaking - this picture gives an impression but really doesn’t do the colours justice. The shallow head of the loch as the afternoon comes on One of the great things about cruising Scotland is - on the water (providing you are about 100yds offshore) the midges don't get you. So with settled weather in a quiet anchorage you can leave the hatches open, light a light and read a good book till you feel sleepy enough to slip into your pit and sleep the sleep of the just. Plus, there are times and anchorages where, although you wake every so often - you feel secure, feel the light breeze on your face coming in through the open hatch above you, move slightly to stretch and in the seconds you are awake have checked out the sounds of the boat and know she's fine, then soon you are back asleep once more - and wake in the morning feeling good.. This anchorage is one of those and it's a wrench to leave but I've promised myself I'll come back sometime, for now though the rest of Loch Sunart beckoned. So there ladies and gentlemen of the jury you have the defence case for staying in Scotland one more year. In summary, we’ve hardly scratched the surface, there’s lots more to see, get the planning right and the cruising is easy, the scenery magnificent plus we’ve got a good yard to overwinter and for summer moorings and it’s not frantically expensive (as long as you pay up front for a year) The prosecution’s case for turning south is not so easily made and is made up of a few actual benefits and some emotional reasons. March 2012 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk OK the cruising is great in Scotland when it’s fair – but try sitting at home looking for a weather window to go sailing – there ain’t many. It’s a long way to go sailing (476 miles front door to boat) Travel costs are getting more expensive. The journey is tedious. If something goes wrong with the boat over the winter it’s a long way to go. I’m bustin to go South into the Firth of Clyde where I wus brung up ! I like the idea of progressing on my odyssey around the UK – do I want to leave that progress for another year? I’m really looking forward to sailing into Cardigan Bay to see my elder brother (we ain’t getting any younger) And believe it or not I’m starting to miss the muddy Blackwater and cruising home waters. And finally, members of the jury - the last point for the prosecution comes in the form of a tale about a hernia – almost “a tale of two hernia’s”. There I was in an Addenbrookes Operating Theatre, lying on the operating table, the surgeon who had examined me and drawn a large arrow on my skin with a marking pen down into my left groin (he said it was to make sure they opened me up on the correct side) was looking down at me with what I thought was a slightly manic grin. By his side was a very attractive lady anaesthetist who invited me to think glorious thoughts whilst she put me under - and at the foot of the table was a boy who looked about sixteen - I wondered why he was there. I remember looking up at the lights and thinking – “strewth in a minute or so these guys are goin to be cutting me open” and all I could think of was not the delightful lady anaesthetist’s offer but “oi I’ve got a lot of sailin to do – get it right guy’s” - - - slight panic, then oblivion. The sixteen year old boy came round later with the surgeon to see me in the recovery ward and said when he’d opened me up the repair he’d eventually had to make was almost the size of two regular hernia’s so I’d need to take it really easy over the next month – seems like trainee surgeons are a bit like policemen getting younger every year. Now, I’d not been in hospital since I was seven when I had my tonsils out and frankly I didn’t relish the experience and that moment before I’d dipped into oblivion had concentrated the mind about completing my odyssey before my ageing frame collapsed altogether. Bit of an emotional exaggeration for someone of 66 - but you know what I mean. So you see dear fellow members of Marconi (the jury) why I need your help and wisdom in coming to a decision – should I stay one more season in Scotland overwintering again then moving South in the Spring of 2013 or should I head South this coming season ? If you are able to come to a conclusion based on the above facts and emotional arguments and help resolve this thorny case please send your decision to I shall offer to Dave Ball to post the verdict of the jury (and their reasons, no names no pack drill) in a future Navigans but in the meantime - please, nothing comical - - - - - It hurts when I laugh ! p.s. The above infers no criticism of Addenbrookes they were very professional and most caring - particularly the lady anaesthetist. David Lakin, Sadler 26 “Edal” March 2012 Navigans 17

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Log – Entry for the Mamgu Trophy st The Mamgu trophy is judged by the Commodore and awarded annually for the best log submitted by 1 October for a cruise st commencing between 31 July of the preceding year and the closing date. If you undertake an interesting voyage (big or small) why not write it up and send it over to the Commodore, Neil Pembleton? In addition, if you would like to share it with fellow members through Navigans you can also send it to navigans@marconi- sc.org.uk The log below from Derek is, I believe, the first entry for 2012. Ed. A SAIL WITH Mona Newer members to Marconi Sailing Club may not know our club members, the Shaft family. They sailed several traditional boats from the club and loved going off cruising for weeks on end during the school holidays with their children, Laura & Jenny. Eventually they purchased Mona, an Alan Pape design 33ft Ebbtide, a traditional, steel, long keel boat. After another couple of years more at Marconi they sailed off into the sunset. Their travels were extensive, traversing the Atlantic, then the Panama Canal to the Galapagos Islands and across the Pacific to eventually end up in New Zealand, later sailing on to Vanuatu and Australia, returning to New Zealand another two years later and eventually putting their anchor firmly down in Opua, a village in the well-known beautiful Bay of Islands on the North East side of North Island. After living on the boat for ten years Mona required a MAJOR extensive and expensive refit, so this was completed a couple of years ago and now she awaited our arrival! The Bay of Islands is a New Zealand MUST DO activity. There are over 150 islands in the area and only one has habitation and that is not with any permanent buildings or residents. We had the pleasure to see it at its best and over several days 23rd January 2012. We met up with Malcolm and Helen at their lovely house perched on the top of a hill surrounded by a mangrove swamp a few kilometres outside the small town of Opua. The weather forecast for the week ahead looked really good, so in the morning we headed off to board Mona just a short journey into town. 24th January 2012. Opua is a stunning small harbour with clear blue water and a view across to Russell on the other side of the estuary. No Essex mud to be seen anywhere, just golden sand. Whilst Malcolm and Helen went out to their swinging mooring to get ready for us, Hilary & I had a walk around the village, stopping to look round the local chandlers! I was quite surprised to see that two stroke engines are still freely available there as the pollution concerns in Europe seem not to be of importance there, which seems quite strange knowing how “green” the Kiwis are. Malcolm duly arrived to pick us up from the pontoon and off we went to Mona. She looked wonderful gently swinging to the warm breeze. It was difficult to believe that they had sailed so many miles from Marconi to all those distant shores over ten years. There appeared to be some external additions since we had seen her last, but she still has the grace and elegance of a long distance cruiser. After stowing our gear in the forepeak cabin, we fixed a passage plan for the first day. The winds were light as we sailed away from Opua harbour swinging moorings. Out past Pahia where all the larger sailing boats are based we headed East towards Russell point and on to Takepa Point. Passing Waitangi on our port we could clearly see the massive flagpole that was erected to mark the famous Waitangi Treaty between the Maori and Kiwis. The buoyage is fairly intermittent as the water is so deep in the main channels. We had a lazy sail with the main and yankee, as the wind was light. Also remember that Mona is only 33 feet but weighs in at 11 tons so she is not a racing boat, but a safe, stable comfortable world girdler), wonderful as it was just so good to catch up on the last 10 years of news with Helen and Malcolm. Those of you that know Malcolm will know that he always has a number of hilarious and fascinating tales to tell about their experiences during their world cruisings, so we had numerous tales of their experiences from Vanuatu to Panama and beyond May 2012 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Our destination was Moturua Island that meant a turn to starboard as we passed Takepa Point and a pleasant reach along the Rawhiti Inlet to find a beach for the night. After perusing the weather forecast we found the lovely Otupoho Bay to the South of the Island where we anchored in about 5 metres of water. It was an idyllic situation where the crescent shaped yellow beach was bounded by rocky outcrops on the two sides. As this was the middle of the sailing season we expected it to be busy, but as Malcolm & Helen pointed out, there are so many delightful anchorages they are seldom busy. There was one other boat anchored closer in to the beach! A pleasant afternoon swim in the warm water gave us all a thirst and appetite so Malcolm got going with the barbeque that Mona now sports on her stern rail. A couple of Sundowners were enjoyed as Malcolm continued to tell us more amusing tales about their travels to all points of the globe. ‘Bay of Islands A Skm_, _ &) Cape Brett Asad ay Sf , EN a < — 45 » sf ‘pa 25th January 2012. After a quiet night some physical exercise was necessary so we hopped in the dinghy to go ashore. As mentioned previously none of the islands are really inhabited and so there are no facilities except for the occasional log drop toilet! Malcolm took on his official Role sporting his orange jacket, as he now spends time as a volunteer for DOC (Department of Conservation) policing the Islands’ vermin traps and talking to other visitors about the importance of conservation and keeping the Islands vermin and rubbish free. May 2012 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk For interest, animals like stoats and rats introduced by man only relatively recently, are a real threat to the native wildlife. There are several species of birds that cannot fly and thus are at the mercy of the vermin and pose a great threat. One specie has already been wiped out completely. The Kiwis are determined to keep New Zealand as natural as possible not only with the wildlife, but with trees and plants also. There are some controversial ways of achieving this and we saw evidence in several places of what is being undertaken by DOC to reach their goal. We climbed up the hills and walked through the bush looking at the most interesting plant and tree life. We could not name any of the plants or trees as we don’t have any of the species we saw in Europe at all. Need to buy a book of plants, trees and birds on our next stop! A few stops were necessary to cool down and admire the fantastic view of the many islands stretching into the distance. We could just make out Cape Brett where you can go out into the open Pacific and away from the Islands, but our plan was just to enjoy the Bay area. 26th January 2012. We weighed anchor in 32 degrees and full sunshine with a gentle SW force 3. Now we know why Mona was fitted with full awnings, to protect us from the sun, high UV in New Zealand, and rain if we have any. We turned north through a very narrow heart stopping passage between two rocky outcrops and out into the open sea for a good sail. Navigation is quite straightforward once you get oriented and also helps to have the chart plotter just to be safe. There was the necessary job of the holding tank that needed emptying and we had to be offshore in specially designated areas to do this, the sail was great. The aroma from the emptying tank was not quite so good though! A sail back south after rounding Urupukapuka Island to hunt for another bay was rewarded, but shock horror there were about seven boats already there! It was a huge bay so with plenty of room we dropped the hook again in Otaio Bay, all of us desperate for a swim. It also happened to be Pahia Race week – a bit like Burnham Week but with fewer boats- so there was plenty of activity with the racing fleet dashing between the islands spinnakers flying and they all made quite a spectacle as we watched them rapidly sailing by out in the main channel. Hilary decided to try her hand at a bit of fishing off the boat whilst the rest of us sampled a sundowner or two. Her persistence paid off eventually after much mickey taking and she landed a fish!! A Snapper by name and by nature, as it did get its own back because it bit her with its needle sharp teeth and even drew blood! Even more mickey taking! It was just big enough, as measured on Malcolm’s official fish measure, but the poor thing looked so sad we thought it better to return it from whence it came and toast to its recovery. Another bbq expertly cooked by Malcolm was enjoyed by all, sadly no fish course! Urupukapuka is one of the larger islands with several quite high hills and was inhabited (as most islands were) by Maoris many centuries ago. It is famous for its Greenstone. On our morning constitutional we came across a pair of archaeologists on a dig. They had discovered an old Maori settlement (Pau) which was most interesting, we climbed a hill to look at some old Maori water storage tanks and food storage pits. We also came across a number of American students doing some voluntary work, clearing undergrowth, maintaining pathways etc. They were camping on the island not far from where we were anchored. The camping is very strictly controlled and only on a temporary basis through the DOC The forecast was for it to be windy that night and the following morning so we went for a sail around the island and out to sea again to do our duty! Also as we were running short of drinking water and there is none available on any of the islands Malcolm decided he needed to make some! He has a relatively new toy that purifies seawater by high pressure and reverse osmosis. Unfortunately the engine needs to be run for this, so we motor sailed for a while. After tasting it to ensure the water had cleared any salt taste we left the watermaker to it. After a couple of hours it appeared we had made 70 litres or so, sufficient to last us during our stay. Anyhow it was very interesting to see the equipment and watch it all work as if by magic! We noticed many of the boats heading for shelter due to the forecast of gusts of up to 35 knots with the promise of squally showers. Malcolm found us a secure spot in Urupukapuka Bay for the night round the back of the island of Urupukapuka, where we were sheltered from whichever direction the wind chose to come from and indeed true to form the forecast was about as May 2012 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk accurate as in Europe and we had a very quiet night at anchor again with virtually no wind. There are no marinas or harbours only back in Pahia or Opua where there are any facilities for absolute protection. 27th January 2012. Our last day dawned a bit grey and blustery , so after a hearty breakfast we had a romping sail from Urupukapuka back to Opua. This was the kind of weather that Mona takes in her stride. Whilst the racing fleet were broaching and tearing spinnakers, we sailed on steadily without drama at a good speed. As we rounded the Takepa Point we spotted a white block of flats – a cruise ship at anchor- off Waitangi. It is a popular spot for these monsters to ferry their fare paying passengers ashore in small boats to the town of Pahia to spend their money on souvenirs. They only spend a few hours in this beautiful spot, but we were lucky to spend four days around the islands and be able to soak in the atmosphere and enjoy the magic of being on a small sailing boat and choosing where we wanted to go! A great sail back to Opua moorings and it was with sadness we left Mona to go back to Helen and Malcolm’s house where we were to spend another two days enjoying their company and visiting several interesting places. As we got in the car it started to rain! What an amazing place to visit and definitely a MUST DO if you plan to ever go to New Zealand. Derek Gardner Note: If you are reading this in Navigans it may be worth looking at the photos on the club website version as in colour you will better appreciate the wonder of the Bay of Islands May 2012 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk On another Tack. An elongated odyssey around Britain. Putting up with “the persistence.” You might remember my last missive when I made a plea to members of Marconi to sit on the jury considering my cruising dilemma of whether to stay in Scotland cruising it’s delights for another season or head south down the west coast to Cardigan Bay, to continue an odyssey around Britain. The case both for and against was I admit littered with emotional debating points - particularly the bit with me whinging on about my mortality after a hernia operation. How am I now ? – absolutely fine thank you – it’s amazing what they can achieve with modern surgery. From a distinct bulge in the left groin to now perfectly flat to match the other side – just a sizeable scar and no discomfort whatsoever apart from an occasional rather strange itch which my wife forbids me to scratch in public! The other points in the case saw the Marconi jury generate a consensus which could best be summed up as “well dunno really” as the voting was pretty much split – so as final arbiter I have had in the end to make up my own mind after of course consulting with higher authority. She, as a final discussion point said “Oh make up your own mind” – I always feel better after a consultation! Even as late as May when I launched the boat back into the waters of Loch Creran I still hadn’t made the final decision. It’s true to say my inclination was to head south, but- but- but I’d say to myself, you love Scotland, it’s easy cruising and there’s still lot’s to see. Before I launched I’d become even more hesitant about turning south when a rather upper crust elderly gent with a walking stick hobbled across the yard accompanied by his good lady wife and plonked himself on the tree stump I’d been using to sit on to polish the prop and engaged me in a cruising experience conversation. He and his wife it turned out had cruised pretty much everywhere, buying their latest boat (a rather nice blue hulled Vancouver Pilot 38) in the Med then cruising home before taking her to the Baltic for a couple of years then heading to Scotland. Here was a couple of great experience and modest with it - although they clearly could have been opinionated about their experiences they were just as interested in what I’d done and where I’d been and happy to share their knowledge to make another’s cruising easier. We talked for what must have been over an hour, it rained on and off but we didn’t notice such was the quality of the conversation. He asked where my home mooring was and when I said “the river Blackwater in Essex” he asked if I knew Mike Peyton who he said was a bit older than himself. I said most people on the Blackwater knew of Mike Peyton and his succession of ferro boats - I knew though he’d now “swallowed the anchor” as in his eighties his eyesight was failing. He said “oh no, I know Mike and he must be in his nineties because I’m 85! The thing about our conversation that kept coming back to me though was how this couple with such great cruising experience loved Scotland because of its scenery, easy distances between anchorages and despite the fact that the weather could sometimes be awful, often it would change in a moment and become glorious, they described it as “the best cruising ground in the world.” We had also in enjoying our conversation ignored the rain - something which perhaps in cruising Scotland you have to learn to do. After launching I thought I’d have a short cruise north to try to get to Sandaig for the silly emotional filming of Edal the boat at anchor in Sandaig bay where Edal the otter from the book Ring of Bright Water used to play – to be a remembrance for my dottage - - - but the rain, despite me trying to ignore it persisted, persisted and persisted and looked like it would “persist down” for the next couple of weeks, I also convinced myself there was important stuff to do at home - so home I went. Early June came and went and I genuinely got caught up in home stuff till one day the sailing bug crept up on me and bit me hard enough for me to make a decision. I’d phone the yard at Barcaldine and ask them what a year’s rate would be and if it wasn’t too expensive I’d stay. I was kidding myself of course I already knew I wanted to stay. The wonderful soft lilt of the nice lady in the yard office came over the phone “Och halloo David, I thocht you’d be phonin soon” - - am I that transparent I thought – well yes obviously. She worked out if I stayed for another year, that is summer mooring, lift out, pressure wash, winter storage, lift back in, then a month’s mooring next spring to sort things out it would cost (if I paid up front) the equivalent of £3 per day for the year - - so the deal was done. Most of the reasons for turning south had diminished in my mind - I’d recovered completely from the hernia op, the manic surgeon and the delightful lady anaesthetist were a distant memory, I’d bought an IPod on Ebay to download podcasts for easy listening whilst driving the long distance to Scotland and I’d convinced myself that the persistent rain was my friend. Maybe the first cruise of the season would prove if I was right or wrong to stay. AROUND ARDNAMURCHAN TO MALLAIG AND SANDAIG. Sunday 24th June the rough plan was to leave the mooring in Loch Creran and be at the entrance to the Sound of Mull roughly LW Oban at 1542 to take the tide up the Sound to Tobermory roughly 32nm. The following day get round Ardnamurchan to Mallaig 35nm, then onto Sandaig just a short hop of 10nm. After that I’d make the decision on next destination. The wind for the 24th was forecast at N or NW 9 to 11kts with gusts somewhere above that, with some clouds and rain – but hey this is Scotland so who knows. We left the mooring at 1228 motor sailing out of Creran and into Loch Linnhe. Once round the top of Lismore Island we switched the engine off and set the main and genoa. Soon over pressed, put one reef in the main and two in the genoa as the wind gusted off the top of the mountains on the Morven shore – it became quite a boisterous ride down Loch Linnhe. July 2012 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk A quieter period close hauled down Loch Linnhe. We turned the corner into Sound of Mull the wind came on the nose and bashing on another 12 miles to Tobermory didn’t seem like a good way to spend an early evening so we turned into Loch Aline just inside the Sound on the starboard hand and tied up at 1702 in sheltered water on their pontoons. £16.80 for an overnight stay including water and electricity seemed good value for a nice quiet secure berth for the night. Monday 25th we left Loch Aline at 0800 with a couple of hours of flood left to take us up the Sound. Motor sailed all the way and tied up in Tobermory and making for the showers at 1045 – 2hrs 50 mins later. Tuesday 26th – At Ardnamurchan the tide turned north about 0600 – it’s about 11nm to the Point depending on how much you cut the corner in settled weather. Today was to be quiet with southerly winds of 8kts – poss gusts of 17kts – so wind with tide. We left Tobermory at 0600 and were round the point two and half hours later. We motor sailed past the point and once round had one of those no wind moments before the wind set in again from the NE. We set the main and reefed genoa in 10 to 16kts of wind heading towards the Sound of Sleat and Mallaig. Coming round Ardnamurchan – Isle of Muck low in the middle of picture, the Mountains of Rhum behind and the long peak of Eigg to the right. July 2012 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Sails set towards Mallaig as the day brightens. Last time we came round Ardnamurchan heading for Mallaig we called them up and they announced “we’re full” this time, earlier in the season and with new pontoons in the harbour we expected a berth and sure enough there was loads of space – we arrived 1231 just 6hrs 26mins after a passage in which we’d seen a real mix of wind, rain and shine and some great sailing. The next couple of days though were forecast to chuck it down with that wonderful “persistent” nature that Scottish rain has – it was also due to be warm and humid so the midges would be out in force for my sojourn ashore at Sandaig and my new friend the rain was due to test me. The new pontoons in Mallaig Harbour on the grey morning before we left for Sandaig. Wednesday 27th - There was no hurry to leave - it was roughly 10nm to Sandaig and the tide would be with us most of the morning. Also I would have time to make friends with my new chum (the rain) as overnight I’d bent my mind to making the next couple of days as easy as possible so in looking at tonight’s destination I’d chosen Isle Ornsay as a perfect anchorage. Ornsay is just one nm across the Sound of Sleat from Sandaig and gloriously the pilot book said you can anchor in 3mtrs into deep mud – oh how my East Coast heart pounded at the word MUD – a friend indeed to help me defeat the “persistence.” The trip up the Sound of Sleat to Sandaig was a motorsail – leaving Mallaig at roughly 1130 we headed out into – in local parlance a “dreich” morning, grey, no real wind, rain slatting down. Despite the climate I felt rather elated and the closer we got to Sandaig a bit emotional. It’s daft I know at my advancing years to feel like this – but this after all is one of the reasons I’d come to Scotland in the first place to take my wee boat – the boat I’d lavished all that care and attention on (not to mention all the spondulicks) to the spiritual home of the otter her first owner had named her after. July 2012 Navigans 17

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Edal at anchor in Sandaig bay. If you’ve read Ring of Bright Water you may agree it’s a rather idealised book of its time - one man living in almost isolation creating his own environment and virtually taming a wild creature to live with all in the most romantic of settings. An idealised existence – yes – but something I suspect many would like to try to for themselves. On this grey misty rainy day, I was glad the day was the way it was, because it enhanced the romance of the place in a way that blazing sunshine couldn’t have – it made my visit with Edal more intimate and memorable. I found everything I wanted to record – the waterfall whose sound Maxwell said was his constant companion, the stone where his ashes are laid and the memorial to Edal the otter. Edal’s memorial. Romance though is one thing “Mudgies” as Para Handy would have it are entirely another – plus not having followed my own advice to “grease up” with repellent meant the little blighters on this nice humid day were out in clouds and having a field day feasting on me. So discretion being the better part – I departed on the dinghy back to my Edal gently bobbing to her anchor in the bay. Soon with the rain still “persisting” we had upped anchor and motored away from romantic Sandaig and were heading the short distance across the Sound to Ornsay to anchor again for the night. As the distance was small, engine on little more than a tickover we crept out of Sandaig Bay and two Dolphins (Porpoise ? I can’t tell the difference) surfaced several times near the boat – before we’d anchored they’d welcomed us in and were now seeing us out. I tried to photograph them but by the time I’d aimed the camera they’d gone - their presence though added to the experience and memory of the visit. The pilot book was right and the mud at Ornsay with four other boats at anchor, provided a safe and secure night. Although I’ve yet to experience more than half a dozen Scottish anchorages this has to be one of the best, not exactly dramatic but pretty in its own way quite large enough for several more boats and a good area of shallow water with good holding at its head. I ate on board, in the continuing mizzle, I left the rain to its own devices and watched a DVD on the lap-top, slept late, bacon butties for breakfast. As I de-rigged the riding light (it’s an all round LED plugged into a 12v socket) I mused on how in most of the anchorages I’d been into when I’d been up in the night for my usual visit to the porcelain in checking out all was well with the boat – how, most other boats don’t use riding lights – maybe I’m too much of a traditionalist but I don’t fancy sinking into sleeps oblivion without a nice bright light marking my presence – even if it’s just so I can say to the insurance company I’d rigged one. After several cups of coffee and a discussion with myself the plan now became to return to Mallaig after exploring Loch Hourn then following day a dog leg to the Isle of Eigg – then back south to Tobermory. July 2012 Navigans 18

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk We left Ornsay at 1150 made across the Sound towards Loch Hourn which the pilot describes as a fjord like loch with high mountains on every hand, best seen on a dark day with the clouds spilling off the peaks - - this was such a day and with a good stiff wind blowing directly out of the loch we tacked in and ran back out again after penetrating about five miles. Grey and forbidding Loch Hourn, photo doesn’t really do it justice – it was magnificent. We made out of the loch and miraculously the wind disappeared, the surface of the Sound became glassy and the rain stopped although it remained overcast as we gently motored the 10 or so nm back to Mallaig. The afternoon brightened as we approached and passed the entrance to Loch Nevis the twin sister of Hourn. I am told these sisters are known as “Heaven and Hell” clearly with its dramatic peaks Hourn is hell. Later in conversation with the harbour master at Mallaig he described how as a fisherman he’d worked “at the fishin” during the night in Loch Hourn and in foul weather when the wind screamed off the mountains it really did sound as if the hounds of hell were after you – having been there in dark weather I could believe it. Friday 29th June the forecast was for mixed rain and showers with a mostly southerly wind blowing from 8 to 14kts. The tide in the morning for going south would mostly be against us but if we were going to Eigg from Mallaig we would have some cross tide. We left Mallaig at roughly 1100 and into what was then a bright sunny morning with the promised southerly blowing well. The course to the anchorage on Eigg proved to be pretty close hauled and with some tide against us to the leeway meant we’d not make the anchorage in one go so we made as best we could on a long port tack before tacking across onto starboard making back towards the mainland. The little boat looks after herself well in these conditions and with one reef in the main half the genoa and the wind blowing consistently at 12 to 14kts sometimes more she fairly bowled along under Albert the autopilot with me just enjoying the scene and letting time slip by. By 1400 we’d got half way down the last tack towards the Eigg anchorage - I was digesting lunch and the midday forecast on Navtex which seemed to suggest a worsening of the weather overnight. Did I have a plan B if I didn’t fancy the Eigg anchorage – well not a planned one - but in this neck of the woods there’s actually several of them depending on direction and strength of the wind. If the wind was going to strengthen in the next couple of days though I’d prefer to be round Ardnamurchan and not in some anchorage waiting for quieter weather to get round. The south going tide at the point would start roughly 1600 and it would take me at least two hours to get there so south round Ardnamurchan it would be. An hour later and the day had distinctly deteriorated the “heavenly persistence” came on again and the wind got up more - so the second reef went in the main, she’s got cockpit reefing so fortunately it only took moments – then back on her feet and off we went charging for the point in 20kts of wind. It was at this “point” I started to think of all those nice pictures you see in “Cruising Scotland” all bright and sunny with light zephyr’s swishing you along – this was becoming distinctly different and I muttered “well this wasn’t in the brochure” if I complained to the Scottish Tourist Board maybe I could get some recompense – at this rate might amount to a pretty penny! I also thought of the tale of the seafarers of yore who in heavy weather if they happened to be carrying a female aboard would get them up on deck to “bare all” to the foaming brine and as if by magic the sea would die away. But dammit - I realised I’d left my female at home and even if I hadn’t I could just imagine the response to my order “Oi get forard and get yer kit off.” If any Marconi member is braver than me I invite them to issue such an order in heavy weather to their other half and let the rest of us know if it works! By 1600 we were about three miles off the waypoint for making the first change of course to start coming round the point into the Sound of Mull to pass about two miles off when the weather closed in and the mainland and its lighthouse disappeared as vis came down to what I thought was about half a mile. Time to plot – time, position speed and course just in case the vis stayed low all the way round and the plotter gave up. Cutting inshore blind in Scotland with all those hard rocks is not an option and with the weather the way it was it would be rougher inshore on the point - so staying a couple of miles off was the best option. With a recent position established and the turn into the Sound of Mull being deep and wide I’d got plenty of room for error if the vis stayed poor. Gradually as we came round the sea became quieter the lighthouse reappeared - the wind a little more towards the beam still at 18/20kts as we turned into the Sound - the rain still stair rodding - the little boat flew towards Tobermory the water fizzing away under her stern as she went. I found myself on this grey rainy windswept early evening, in the cockpit helming the boat, rain streaming off me - singing my head off and having a really great time - - strange this sailing lark. July 2012 Navigans 19

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk We left Tobermory following afternoon with the wind still high from the south and being twisted by the hills to blow up the sound of Mull we had a tacking passage in occasional rain for the 12nm back to Loch Aline where we again stayed overnight. The following afternoon saw us back on the mooring at Barcaldine in Loch Creran by 1402. Over these few days I’d had some terrific sailing and experienced some of the very different moods of Scotland. I’d come to terms with the rain - in future it won't bother me and I won't bother it - and being Scotland where, as the old gent had said – “you can see all types of weather in one day” - I'll just get used to treasuring the sunshine when it does occasionally appear. Thank you to Marconi members for helping with my decision making I know some are considering a trip north, I hope you found this tale encouraging if I can help with any info then its, David Lakin, Sadler 26 “Edal” p.s. Yonder lumes the Island, yonder lie the ships, With sailor lads a-dancing heel-an-toe, And the shore-lights flashing, and the night-tide dashing, He sees it all so plainly as he saw it long ago. Roving tho his death fell, he went with heart at ease, A dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe, Take my drum to England, hang it by the shore, Strike it when your powder's running low, If the Dons sight Devon, I'll quit the port of Heaven, And we’ll drum them up the Channel as we drummed them long ago. How many times have you tested your skills in the water fully clothed and with your lifejacket on? Do you carry a liferaft and if so have you ever experienced launching, inflating, getting into it and righting it should it be inverted? We have sailed for many years and have never done any of these things. The opportunity to do all of these was not to be overlooked when the opportunity arose. There was no time for politeness and graciousness as the person had to be mauled into the raft! We had a casualty with a broken leg (me) that had to be boarded. Some said it was better not to compromise the safety of the others inside the raft and to let the injured casualty float off to drown. He presented three trophies: Seamanship Trophy awarded to John Littlewood who sailed his boat, Crazy Suzy, to the aid of Mike Turner in Killara II, which suffered a failed engine in the Ipswich Marina, and was able to safely manoeuvre the disabled boat to its berth. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Minutes of the 2012 Fleet AGMs Combined Cat Fleets Annual General Meeting 2012 – 04/11/2012 Those present; Fenella Miller, Peter Richardson, Rob Clay, Carolyn Warren, Dave Hewes, Kevin Dowley, David Ball, Peter Tovey, James Tovey, Jenny Ball, Clive Shenton, Simon Plumb, Nick Pavitt, Sophie Hurrell-Smith, Tom Brooks, Neil Pembleton. Apologies; Steve Glynn, Tom Duckmanton, Andrew and Michaela Glynn, Rebecca Tovey, Lee Harrison. Simon Hey, Kevin Kirby, Liz Jackson, John and Caroline Nicholls, Steve Cleaver. Agenda: 1 OVERVIEW/STATISTICS FROM 2012 Discussion took place about the racing at MSC in 2012. Statistics show that the overall numbers of catamaran entries were down on last year. This was thought partly to be because the bad weather we have had throughout the season. The only person to have consistently entered all the races needed to count for a series was Jenny Ball. The question was asked “How do we encourage more to race?”. A lot of clubs having same problems. Dave Hewes asked for a change in the sailing instructions to allow a boat to enter rather than a helm, but it was pointed out that this would probably not be acceptable but consideration could be made to allow different configurations in the same boat(Dart 18 only ie. Uni rig- one helm or 2 sails- 2 crew) This would be taken back to the Sailing Sub Committee for consideration. It was observed that Wednesday evenings were consistently popular. This was thought to be because it was more family orientated and social, more relaxed. Clive suggested a series of pursuit races. It was also thought that the Cadets should be encouraged to join in with catamaran racing as part of their training programme, members of the fleets were keen to encourage the young people and would help them with starting skills etc if they raced with them rather than separately. Congratulations were also expressed to Jenny Ball for winning the helm of the year title, and for her constant turn out. It was agreed that there should be a Cat fleet “come and try racing day” making a direct approach to individuals to invite them along. It was observed that the Olympics has not made any effect on the numbers racing but the Open day most effective way for recruitment. Neil told the meeting that they had not planned to have an Open day next year. OPEN EVENTS AT CLUB Fenella summarised that there had been a number of successfully run Open events at the club involving Cats. These included the Sprint 15 TT, East Coast Piers Race, The Junior Cat Championship in association with UKCRA and the Dart18/Shear water TT. The exception was the Steeple Chase in association with Stone Sailing Club. This will not be run next year as Stone members were not keen to participate. The Sprint 15 association would like to come again next year and a date has been booked for 6th /7th April.2 nights camping has been applied for. The Dart 18’s and Shearwaters also said they would like to come back in the near future. Piers race report by Clive. Poor weather was forecast but 10 more entries than last year. The Fast Dinghies joining in was successful. There was a better on-the-day profit. £500 has been donated to the Essex Air Ambulance and £2,353.25. The Cirdan Trust have raised a further £12,000 so far on the back of the race. Next year the ECPR will be on 30th June. Thanks were expressed by Clive for the support of the cat fleet. JUNIOR CAT TRAINING Fenella told the meeting about the work that Lee Harrison was putting in to encouraging young people into cat racing. He has become the UKCRA Junior co-ordinator (that is: arranging catamaran training around the UK for young people up to the age of 16). We have 3 Dart 16’s which are RYA/UKCRA owned which are available for the use of any young person to use at the Club and which can be taken to other clubs for racing events. Peter Richardson is the bosun and responsible for their upkeep. TRAVELLING ACHIEVEMENTS Fenella pointed out that one of the reasons why there were not consistent entries in club racing was because a number of people have travelled to other events. These events include the Sprint 15 Nationals at which we had 8 boats. The Spitfire Nationals, The Tornado Nationals, Canvey Cat Open, Grafham Invitation Cat Open, and the Tornado Europeans. It was pointed out that those travelling were good ambassadors for the Club and the experience gained helps to improve the quality of sailing when back at the Club. Andrew Dowley has produced club stickers to be stuck on the sails of travelling boats. It was raised that those doing winter series’ and opens elsewhere including monohull dinghies should all have the opportunity to have these stickers on their sails. Contact Andrew if a sticker is required. 2 RACING: CHANGES PROPOSED FOR NEXT YEAR. Fen outlined plans for next year. It was suggested by the Sailing Sub Committee that because Bank Holiday Monday racing is poorly attended that there should not be any scheduled series racing, but to put in the “one off” races instead like the Pilots Cup, etc, depending on tides. It was suggested by this meeting that pursuit races could be put on at bank holiday Mondays. A vote of thanks was made to Kate Williams for working on next year’s programme and for being an excellent results secretary. We all wish Dave and Kate all the best in their new ventures in Cornwall. Jenny Ball has agreed to be Trophy co-ordinator. Peter Richardson will continue to obtain the club’s fuel. February 2013 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk 3 CLUB MATTERS: Neil explained why Terms of Reference for flag officers, fleet captains and sub committees have been defined in order to clarify the expected duties of each club official. Neil highlighted the Board’s responsibility and liability, and explained that they need to know what is going on at committees and so have requested that a copy of the minutes should be provided to the Club Secretary. A new membership data base being designed which will be more interactive. He also told the meeting that money would be tight next year amongst other things because of rising fuel costs. No major works to the club are planned for next year. 4 WORKING PARTIES 18th November- general tidying up prior to the Winter is planned. Activities will be dependent on the weather. 5 VOTING FOR 2013 FLEET CAPTAINS Fenella has stood down as Sprint 15 and medium cat fleet captain and Bekki Tovey has stood down as fast cat fleet captain – in order take over the running of Cadet Week. Fenella thanked Bekki for her help and support to the fast cat fleet. Fenella proposed Kevin Dowley as joint catamaran fleets captain and he was unanimously voted in. An assistant to help him is still being sought. Clive asked that a vote of thanks was recorded to Fenella for her work over the years with the Cat fleets and on other committees. 6 ANY OTHER BUSINESS Fenella raised the issue of support boat cover. There is a shortage of support boat drivers. It was suggested that all dinghy members should do support duties. It was also noted there is a shortage of race officers as well and more volunteers need to be sought. Kevin asked that the support boat co-ordinator needs to be made aware of what boats people sail so that clashes are not made next year (e.g. a cat sailor scheduled for Jack B driver on ECPR weekend). Clive: Explained why Top Cat was on the grasscrete next to the club - too wet on field. Peter: stated that it is good that junior cat training is coming to the club. It is an ideal opportunity to encourage them to race with cat fleets. Simon Plumb raised cadet fleet starts, there is discussion at the cadet committee for integrated starts with other fleets rather than their own start to give then better competition on the start line. Fenella added that there had also been some discussion about moving the cadets to the front of the starting sequence so that the parents could get on the water to race after sorting their children out. Dave Hewes is standing down as race equipment bosun. A new bosun is being sought. Neil summarised that he had heard a lot of positive talk today , especially in encouraging young sailors and in supporting other cat owners into racing but it was now down to us to encourage individuals. He acknowledges the tremendous support from cat fleet over this year and for the effort of everyone last weekend at the Dart 18/Shearwater Open. He expressed his thanks for everything we’ve done as a fleet in contributing to the club as a whole. Solo Fleet AGM 2012 Held on Friday 16 November 2012 Attendance: Steve Connolly, Dennis Dear, Ron Greygoose, Tim Halhead, Geoff Josey, John Nisbet, John Salmon (Fleet Captain), Roger Smith, Malcolm Stuart, Mick Taylor. Apologies for Absence: Bob Anderson, Martin Hall, Peter Playle, Bryan Spencer. Minutes of last meeting: Were approved. Matters Arising: The Fleet Captain reported that the proposals for changes to sailing format that were objected to, had been the subject of further discussion at Sailing Sub Committee and not implemented. The decision to recommend disposal of the Fleet Solo had resulted in it being sold during the summer. Fleet Captain: John pointed out that he had now completed two years of a one year commitment to fill this role, and now wished to stand down. He called for a volunteer to take over the role, but none was forthcoming. He advised the Fleet that whilst he was prepared to carry on for one further year he would definitely stand down thereafter. He will be working to identify his replacement during the year. The fleet unanimously applauded John for an excellent job over the year and thanked him for agreeing to carry on. Review of 2012 Sailing Season: Number of boats competing in all 3 points series was an improvement on the previous season primarily because of the two new members who joined us at the beginning of the year and were frequent competitors in the series. This more than balanced the reduced amount of racing of some of the older members. Fleet members commented that they thought the racing was good, and no particular issues were raised.
