Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Child Protection Policy Statement & Code of Practice MSCP16 - Issue 02 - 11/12/2012 Policy Statement The MSC Policy Statement on Child Protection is as follows: • The child’s welfare is paramount • All children whatever their age, culture, disability, gender, language, racial origin, religious belief and/or sexual identity, have the right to protection from abuse. • All suspicions and allegations of inappropriate behaviour will be taken seriously and responded to swiftly and appropriately. • As defined in the Children Act 1989, anyone under the age of 18 years should be considered as a child for the purposes of this document. Code of Practice The MSC Code of Practice on Child Protection is as follows: • The Club does not at any time act in loco parentis. Whenever activities are organised for the involvement and benefit of children it is on the clear understanding that their individual parents or guardians have responsibility for the care and safety of those children. All training and development activity for children carried out in the name of the Club will be carried out on the clear understanding that their individual parents or guardians are on site at the time and for the duration of that activity and are responsible for the care of their children at all times. • All training and development activity for children carried out in the name of the Club will be carried out only by individuals (‘Trainers’) who are known to and approved in advance by the Cadet Co-ordinator (supported by his or her committee). The Cadet co-ordinator will advise to the Executive in advance the names of all trainers to be involved in any training or development activity. • Trainers will not take responsibility for activities other than those training and development activities specified by the Cadet Co-ordinator and specifically will not have any responsibility for children at social events or non sailing related activity. • Anyone with a complaint about or suspicion of inappropriate behaviour towards children must inform the Club Welfare Officer immediately • Club officers in particular and members in general are expected to promote behaviour that minimises the risks of and opportunities for inappropriate behaviour towards or between children. The Licensing Laws will be properly and full respected in all regards, including those prohibiting the serving of alcohol to children. • Parents and guardians are reminded of their duty to care for children in their immediate control. It is desirable that parents and guardians, when on the MSC site, should be as aware of where children are and what they are doing as they would be in any other situation. Note to Parents – for general use. Marconi Sailing Club is a great place for children and their parents or guardians. The freedom, space, social ambience and shared activities all give a great feeling of well-being and security. However, this does not mean that parents and guardians should become inappropriately relaxed about their control of and awareness of the behaviour of their young charges. Parents and guardians are responsible for the behaviour and safety of their children at all times and should take appropriate steps to ensure that children are not exposed to inappropriate risk, either through their own behaviour or the behaviour of others. Parents and guardians should also give thought to the availability and accessibility to private supplies of alcohol that might be available on site during Camping Fortnight, for example. Experience shows that uncontrolled access to and consumption of alcohol by children can expose them to unnecessary risk. Chris Davies on behalf of MSC Board May 2006 Neil Pembleton, Commodore, on behalf of the Board approved amendments made December 2012 Reviewed by: Frank Burgess R.Y.A. December 2012 Reviewed on 11th December 2012 by the MSC Welfare Officer. To be reviewed after 4 years. Next review due December 2016 March 2013 Navigans 8

REVIEW OF SEASON 2012 CRUISER FLEET ACTIVITIES M FOSTER / G MALE (MF) The review started with a discussion on how the weather had affected the season along with mechanical problems with some of the club equipment (Mast Derrick). With the last cruiser being launched in September! The club was visited by the Colne YC which was a success – with the Colne YC wishing to make it a regular event. REVIEW OF 2012 RACING SEASON P WARD Fantastic season! See attached report from Peter Ward. ECPR REPORT C SHENTON Clive Shenton ECPR Chairman This year’s ECPR event was the Jubilee event marking 25 years. The whole club played their part in the event, culminating in it becoming an excellent Piers Race. Saturday weather was awful but 73 entries turned up – 10 more than previous year. Fast dinghies took part this year in the Colne Race – it was very successful. With no problems identified. ECPR is a charity event, with the charities being theCirdan Trust and Essex Air Ambulance. Revenue Streams for the weekend where – Raffle/Adnams Beer supplied free/entries/Sale of shirts. Biggest contribution is sponsorship organised by Cirdan Trust supported founded on ECPR - £15,000. The Cruiser Fleet had the main focus of the safety of the ECPR fleet – plenty of safety boats plus 18 cruisers mother boats spaced up the course – providing support and acting as spotters. Thank you to the Cruiser Fleet who provided the mother boats. Problems with 1 boat his year but it worked well and he was safely returned to the club. Cruisers that provided cover where provided with Sunhats as a thank you. th Next year’s ECPR date has been set for the 30 June 2013. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Camping Rules 2013 THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES. • All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight. • No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday • Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid. • Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members. • No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site. • No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site. • No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site at all times. • The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area. • All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present. • Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times. • Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc. • Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected. • Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non- camping members do require access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc. • Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are probably not paying much attention to traffic. • Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS. • The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed. • All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk There is plenty of time at low tide to visit Maldon and surrounding areas. For example most of the party went to Beeleigh Abbey Gardens on Saturday morning and were back before the tide cut off the causeway. Similarly on Sunday morning David and the girls had time to cycle to Maldon swimming pool and Jenny and Dave walked to the Queens Head at the Hythe for a quick pint and they were all back in time. Had we wanted to go out for the day we could have left the island in the morning and returned in the early evening. What you can do on such a holiday is obviously dependent on tides but low tide in the mornings and evenings served us well. Having suffered from noisy house parties when we stayed on Osea Island last year we really appreciated the solitude on Northey. There was something for all the generations; be it climbing into the tree house or sitting on the seawall watching the tide come and go. It was so near home and yet seemed so far away; magic. Definitely a ‘must do again’. Peter recruited and mobilised a good Proposed New Fee Structure for 2014 Introduction – The Problems. In Navigans last month I explained that a financial review undertaken earlier in the year has shown some adverse trends which will need to be addressed to ensure the future viability of our Club. Our fee structure has evolved over many years, is complicated and time consuming to administer and has too many loopholes which lead to loss of income due to fee avoidance. The other problem we face is one of demography. The age profile of our members is increasing and too few of our keen cadet members transfer into young adult membership. Possible solutions In a Club such as ours, where our only source of income is subscriptions & fees, there are only two possible solutions to the problems; either increase the fees & subscriptions or reduce expenditure. In the opinion of the Board and the Management Committee a reduction in expenditure would severely affect our ability to maintain and develop the Club and, crucially, would not produce sufficient funds to safeguard the future. Hence an increase in fees & subscriptions is thought to be the way forward. Objectives Our prime objective in introducing the new fee structure is to increase income. The new system will be simpler to administer and thereby close the loopholes in the present system. Another objective is to create a fee structure that is fair and reasonable and that keeps our fees in line with our competitors thus promoting recruitment. A fair fee structure will ensure that present members pay fees in proportion to the load their membership places on Club resources. Research The Board have carried out a comprehensive survey of 12 sailing clubs in our area and compared and contrasted our present fee system and the new system with that data. Membership categories Single full member – Our research shows us to be competitive at the present level and the 2014 fee will be marginally increased to £175. Family member (including couples). In all our research we are the only Club that sets family membership at the same rate as single membership and, of course, two or more people make greater calls on Club resources than one. For these reasons it is proposed to increase family membership to £210. This is still excellent value, especially for those families with children, and places us in a good position against our competitors. July 2013 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Retired single member and retired family member. To address the projected drop in income as more and more of our members reach retirement age, the retirement discount will be phased out over the next four years. In 2014 it is proposed that single retired members pay £110 and family retired members pay £120. Most of the Clubs surveyed do not give a discount to retired members. Those that do place restrictions on that membership. Young adult members – To address our demographic problem it is proposed to reduce the fee for this category to £40 to encourage our cadet members to transfer into this category on reaching 18 and to stimulate new recruitment. The age limit of this category will increase to 18 – 24. (To those that ask why we are reducing fees when the Club needs more income I say that we only have 11 young adult members at present and that, if this initiative doubles this number, then it has more than paid for itself). Junior members will enjoy a reduction to £30 a year. We don’t have any such members at present. Overseas and Honorary Life Membership levels remain unaltered. Senior life membership for a one off fee will cease. Members who already enjoy this level of membership will be unaffected. Boat Permit Fees Dinghies & cats – Single Full and Family members. The reduced fee for a second dinghy or cat will be discontinued. The fees of £120 for a dinghy and £140 for a cat will be inclusive of hard fees, summer and winter storage, trailer storage and apply to each boat owned by that member. To many members this will be a saving on 2013. Dinghies & Cats – Young adult members, Junior members. These members will enjoy reduced fees of £80 & £60 respectively for the same reasons given in the membership categories above. Sailboards make few demands on Club resources and a fee of £40 is proposed. Cruisers The reduced fee for a second cruiser will be discontinued. It is proposed that each cruiser will pay a fixed fee of £150 plus a fee of £12 per foot of length. These fees will include hard fees, mooring fees, winter storage, trailer storage, launching, recovery, travel hoist, tractors, winches, mast derrick, water and power. The effect of these fees will be to reduce charges to smaller boats with less desirable drying moorings and increase charges to larger boats with deep-water moorings and large trailers. Even at these increased levels our cruiser fees compare favourably with our competitors and are a fraction of the costs for comparable professional marina services. This is made possible by our well-developed “self-help” ethos and the fact that, thanks to the good stewardship of our Board and members over the years, we own our Club, land and equipment. Existing Loan Notes The Fee & Subscription discount given in lieu of interest on Loans to the Club will continue as before. Current status The proposals have the full backing of both the Board and the Management Committee. Next steps I believe that this proposed new Fee structure will achieve the objectives set out above and I commend it to you. On the following page is a spread sheet that presents the information I have explained above in another format. I invite you to study the information and understand what the proposal will mean for you and your family. Many of you will be agreeably surprised, others less so. Either way I invite your feedback by email on Clive Shenton Commodore July 2013 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk October Issue copy deadline: Saturday 14th September Committee Notes Commodore’s Notes I am delighted to be able to bring good news of the sailing kind to my Notes this month. Members will be pleased to hear that in early July we heard that we have been successful in our application to Sport England for a grant to purchase a new support RIB. My thanks go to Neil Pembleton, Michaela Dowley, Simon Elwell, Bryan Spencer and Sue Shenton, all of whom had a hand in the successful application. The grant is for £10,000 and the Club will be required to add several thousand to this amount. To get the best value for money the new RIB will be built during the winter and we can expect it to be in service for next season. Another successful East Coast Piers Race weekend has just passed into history. Blessed by a good sailing breeze on Race Day, all the competitors went home happy, including the crew of a Prindle who were towed back by one of the big RIBs. The ECPR was won by Grant Piggott in an F18. Grant was a Club member for many years and in his speech at the Prize Giving he said he had been trying to win the Race for 20 years and now he had won he could retire a happy man. He also presented the Bryan Piggott Memorial Trophy to the first Tornado home. Line honours went to Will Sunnocks in his hugely impressive M20 Vampire GBR1 who finished 23 minutes ahead of the next cat, but this was only good enough for sixth place on corrected time. Steve Glynn & Tom Duckmanton were first Club boat in a very creditable seventh place. I have great admiration for the crew of the Tornado Sport that won Line Honours in Colne Point Race, not only for their sailing abilities, but because it was crewed by Nicole Davy who is blind. The Race was won by Robin Leather in a Shadow X. Club members Michael Taylor & Peter Playle sailing an Osprey dinghy were forth in the combined list and we look forward to welcoming more Ospreys in 2014. Another Club member, John Pearse in a Sprint 15 was sixth. While the competitors were racing mother boats deployed, observed, reported and ultimately returned to the Club long after the Prize Giving. RO Mike Turner and OOD Simon Elwell led their teams on the Committee Boat and in the Bus. Much of the liquid product donated by Adnams was consumed in the bar; all the souvenir shirts were sold and the first prize in the raffle, a Wildwind Sailing holiday in Greece, was won by Nick Miller who immediately became the most popular man around as the holiday is for two. I am proud to lead a Club that is willing and capable of putting on an Event like the East Coast Piers Race. Around 100 members give freely of their time, expertise and energy to make the weekend successful. From mother boats to competitors, from Race Committee members to support boat crew, from the hard team to reception and many others, I thank you all. It is too early to say how much will be raised for the charities that the Race supports but early indications are that the out-turn will compare favourably with previous years. The after-glow from the Event was tempered somewhat by the news of the untimely death of Nick Dewhirst from Whitstable YC, a staunch supporter of our Race, organiser of the Forts Race and UK cat sailing in general. He will be missed. The week after ECPR the Club hosted a Solo Open Meeting which was well supported on a terrific day for sailing. Thanks go to John Salmon who organised the event, ably supported by Race Officer Jenny Ball and several more from the cat fleet. See fleet reports for the whole story. Now for a word about the new fee structure that I went through in detail in the last edition of Navigans. So far I have only had ten emails telling me what you think of the proposals. It’s not too late to email me on if you have something to say. I wish you all good fortune and good sailing this summer. Let’s hope that the weather co-operates with our plans. Clive Shenton Commodore August & September 2013 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Fleet Reports Dinghy Cruising UK WAYFARER ASSOCIATION, TWO RIVERS CRUISE, 1-2 JUNE 2013 Seven months of detailed planning, twenty miles of sailing and a successful crossing of dangerous sandbanks in the North Sea and there am I, standing on the Outer Crouch No.1 buoy trying to free Myrtle’s reefing line from where it snagged. Whoops, not really what we had in mind. A very long time ago the river Thames formed a delta which emptied into the North Sea across much of the east coast. Over time as man reclaimed the land from the sea with high sea walls, the now distinct Essex Rivers took shape; all parallel to the Thames and each running about ten or fifteen miles inland. The Blackwater and Crouch are closest to the Thames, separated by an eight mile wide stretch of mainly agricultural land, the Dengie peninsula. The intrepid Wayfarer sailors at Marconi Sailing club on the Blackwater had often talked about how it would be great to sail to Burnham-on-Crouch, a pretty town on the river Crouch; only some four miles away by car but some twenty seven miles by sea. Some had done the trip, others even there and back, most just talked about it. A UKWA cruise seemed the ideal excuse to just go and do it. Our intended passage plan The major problem (although indeed the secret to a successful passage) is that half way between the Blackwater and Crouch rivers out in the North Sea lies the Ray Sands, a series of sand banks which dry at low water and block your way. The trick is to pick a time when low water is around lunchtime, use the ebb in the Blackwater to get you to the sands, wait until the tide turns and gives you enough depth of water to get over the sands and then allow the flood to carry you up the Crouch to Burnham. The following day would of course be an almost reverse passage, this time using the ebb down the Crouch to get you to the sands before using the rising tide to carry you up the Blackwater and home for a well deserved beer. Easy eh! Well not really because we now throw in the weather. The prevailing wind being south easterly means that you are likely to face a long beat to windward at some point in the passage, either up the Crouch or up the Blackwater. In strong winds this could be very unpleasant and tiring, not to mention dangerous crossing the sands at near low water. In light winds (even with favourable tides) we would just not get there. Throw in a mixture of boats with unknown provenance and skippers with somewhat variable sailing abilities and there you have the typical UKWA cruise. In the days leading up to the cruise the forecast had been showing some but not much wind, this was a problem. In some ways we were happier with strong winds, we would just not go. At a previous UKWA cruise we had just day-sailed in the Blackwater in winds up to F7. Worst of all would be decent weather on the Saturday but no wind on the Sunday. In this case we would make the passage but were prepared as a contingency to trail the boats back from Burnham. Nine boats and nineteen sailors assembled for the 0800 briefing on Saturday morning to hear an unexpected forecast. It was going to be basically F3 Northerly for the whole weekend, giving us the prospect of a beat both down the Blackwater and up the Crouch and a nice run through the Ray Sands; the only tricky bit being a beat to windward on the Sunday as we made our way back northwards. No reefing required. August & September 2013 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Being in no hurry we managed to get all boats away by 0930 and set off down the Blackwater for the ten mile sail to Brightlingsea (our lunch stop). As predicted a nice beam reach, leaving the Thirslet spit buoy at leisure to port, past Bradwell to the starboard and finally making the short tack northwards towards Brightlingsea where we made a stop for lunch anchored at the Mersea Stone, a shingle beach on Mersea Island. Here we needed to wait sufficient time to allow the now rising tide to safely cover the Ray Sands. Brightlingsea for lunch Eventually we slipped anchors and headed due south, now on a dead run following a series of buoys which would lead us through the channel. We must have watched the final buoy (the Outer Crouch No. 1) for a considerable amount of time; these things however have a habit of creeping up rapidly if you day-dream, as I was. I noticed the buoy 20m dead ahead, made a slight shimmy to avoid it but in doing so Myrtle gybed, the sail came rapidly across and the reefing line snagged on the buoy (would you believe on a 4mm protruding bolt). Myrtle came to a halt. I had to climb on the buoy unhook the line and jump back on board as Myrtle dashed away (hoping nobody noticed). The sail into Burnham in the late afternoon sunshine with the wind on the beam was very pleasant indeed, winding our way through the multitude of moored yachts, past the posh sailing clubs and by the town quay with its pubs and ice-cream parlours. Finally we arrived at the marina, paddling, motoring, sailing and rowing to our berths for the night. Some camped on boats in the marina, others camped at a local campsite, and all met up for well deserved drinks and food later at the Anchor pub on the town quay. As promised we awoke to the forecast F3 northerly wind and after much moving of people, boats and camping gear we once again set off from the marina; an early start this time necessitated by a need to get back across the Ray Sands before low water. It was a beautiful morning’s sail in bright sunshine as we took the ebb down the Crouch. Leaving Burnham on Sunday morning Leaving the dreaded Outer Couch No1 buoy well to port this time, we turned north into the North Sea and once again across the sands. A long series of tacks into a northerly wind split the fleet even though we tried to keep together; the last of the boats August & September 2013 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk taking some two and a half hours to cross the Dengie peninsula before finally turning westwards into the Blackwater. The fleet assembled off Bradwell and headed for Thirslet spit where we anchored for lunch. On a rising tide the Blackwater spits don’t remain for long and as water lapped our feet we made a timely escape. As the land around us disappeared leaving us in the middle of the river, the last of our boats actually sailed directly over the spit we had so recently occupied. Lunch on the rapidly disappearing Thirslet Spit A short sail later and we were back at Marconi Sailing club, all safe and all accounted for. All that remained was more movement of cars and gear, a celebratory beer, fond farewells and a good night’s sleep. In the end we were really ambitious in our plans but lucky to be blessed with ideal weather, some excellent crews and great company. From all at Marconi Sailing club, our thanks go out to all who helped organise this cruise and particularly to those who attended and made it such a delightful fifty four mile cruise. WORK ETHIC News has arrived from an agent in the field (or more accurately, in the cruiser park) that the Great British work ethic is alive and kicking at MSC. The following photos were allegedly taken 10 minutes apart and demonstrate a tireless rate of progress ☺ Ed A TRIP TO SCOTLAND BY TONY WILSON. On 1st June Colin Leveridge and I started on a journey to Scotland in my boat Moontide to see and go over the Forth road and rail bridges.We had 1 month to do the round trip, so decided on as few stops as possible. The original plan was Lowestoft, Hartlepool, Amble and Port Edgar, but after 36 hours from Lowestoft we decided to stop off at Bridlington also. 1st. We started off at 06.10 and sailed to Walton pier (10.00)where, because of head wind, we took down sails and motored to Lowestoft arriving at 21.40. 2nd. Stayed at Lowestoft for the day, looked round the port,marina and town. 3rd. Leave 06.00 intending to go to Hartlepool. Headwind, so motor till 12.30 then sail. No headway so sails down and engine on at 14.30. Weather kind took forever to pass the wind farm. The sea was like glass in the evening and we passed a number of anchored ships in the Humber area. Morning came and as neither of us had slept properly we decided it would be safer to head for Bridlington and a proper rest. 4th. Arrived 12.15. Entered the marina and promptly went aground and had to ‘walk’ Moontide to a berth as the tide came in. Moontide is a bilge keeler and as the tide went out the outer keel went into a hole made by bigger boats so we found ourselves at an angle of about 30 degrees, so it was a case of letting the mooring lines off at intervals! Least said about the marina the better. 5th. Left Bridlington at 13.15 and passed a new wind farm, then the Steelworks at Tees side, a blaze of lights on the horizon, then arrived at Hartlepool in pitch darkness at 02.15. Now, Hartlepool has a light down a long tube to guide you in, but if you don’t see it you are confronted by a huge wall of blackness and we found ourselves heading for a blank wall of concrete. So a warning over the radio from the port control and a hurried burst of energy in reverse from my trusty Beta 16 and we were able to find the guiding light into the lock. 6th. After a rest went to see a Paddle Steamer and Square Rigger in a museum complex. Had lunch in a pub and we saw a Pound Shop. Now, I had been suffering with cold hands and needed a form of glove that would slip on and off easily, so £2 bought me 2 oven gloves. Perfect! When we made arrangements to leave Hartlepool, there was just a gentle breeze, but when they opened the lock at 19.00 to let us out, the wind was howling a gale and white horses came marching towards us. There was no turning back so on we pressed, heart in mouths, pulpit dipping under solid water, until we reached deep water when things thankfully calmed down a bit. We even had a lifeboat escort - don’t know when or why they appeared but they kept station way off to starboard until calmer water then with a cheery wave they were off to wherever they were going. The wind and sea soon calmed down and we were able to sail halfway to Amble before again using the engine. We saw, first time ever, a few Puffins skimming across the water. August & September 2013 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk 7th. Arrived at Amble 06.30 and had to wait a bit for enough water to cross the bar. Amble is my favourite marina. I wish it was a weekend jaunt away. 8th. 13.30 Leave Amble and motor overnight to Port Edgar arriving at 11.00. 9th. After a rest we walked to Dalmeny station and bought return tickets to North Queensferry so had a pleasant ride over the Forth Railway Bridge and back. Port Edgar is open to the River Forth but for a wall of floating tyres so there is no protection from the wash or wind, and of course the visitors moorings are the most exposed. But luckily a large ferry boat came and moored on the other side of our pontoon each night and gave us much appreciated protection. 10th. On Monday we took a bus ride to Edinburgh and went up Scott’s Monument in Princes Street, all 287 steps high, for a wonderful view of the City and then went to the Castle for the rest of the day. Had wonderful haddock and chips and peas in a pub, ( nice local beer too) on our way to the station and came back to Moontide by train. 11th. Tuesday morning we walked to and across the Forth Road Bridge then down to North Queensferry, had a cup of coffee in a nice café, then walked up a very steep hill to the station and had our last ride over the rail bridge. We left Port Edgar at 16.30. Sunny, no wind, then rain and headwind and arrived back at Amble at 13.00 the next day. 12th. Had to wait for the tide to lift us over the bar (again), had a rest then found a local pub with good food. 13th. On Thursday we had a bus ride into Newcastle and had a look at the bridges, walked over the Millennium Bridge and looked in the Heritage Centre where there was a young lady giving a beautiful cello recital. We then went over the Tyne Bridge, along the embankment and up to the Discovery Museum. This was a fantastic place, where they have Turbinia, the first turbine powered ship, and hundreds of model ships and boats and all kinds of electrical and mechanical machines and inventions and lots of things where you can pull and push levers and press knobs etc.. Unfortunately they closed at 4pm so back to the bus for our journey back to the pub for supper. 14th. 10.30. Leave Amble. Motor/sail for 3 hours then motor to Hartlepool arriving at 21.00. 15th. 06.00. Leave Hartlepool. Sailed for 8 hours then ran into thunderstorms all round us so sails down and motored in rain and wind up to force 7,dodging the black columns where the lightning was coming down. All this with Whitby Abbey on the skyline. Spooky. 19.00. Into Bridlington, thankfully still in one piece, glad to be on solid ground and ready for our fish and chip supper in a local fish restaurant. 16th. Went to York on the bus. Had a walk round and lunch then went to the Railway Museum for the rest of the day. Bus back to a feast on the boat. A thing we noticed now and on our previous visit was the number of flags of all sorts and sizes on the boats. I asked someone if there had been a carnival of some sort. No, he said. It’s to scare the birds! Apart from the ever present gulls there was a great number of Turnstones on the pontoons. A mass of them would run along in front of you and would only take off when they reached the very end. 17th. 09.00 Leave Bridlington Engine non stop. Tried jib for short time. No help. 18th. 10.00.Arrive Lowestoft. Have a rest then walk round the town, marina and port. Had Dinner at the Boat Club at the marina. 19th. Visited a 1960s trawler which is now a museum and had an interesting guided tour and general boating chat with one of the volunteers. 15.00 Leave Lowestoft. Light mist, no wind, calm sea. I become nervous of what looked like a tsunami wave on the starboard horizon, it was the only way I could describe it, but when it got nearer, it was no more than a line of foam about 2 feet wide and as it passed under the boat it was a dead straight line from horizon at the bow to horizon at the stern, to be followed a few minutes later by another. The mist turned to fog early evening and by 21.00 was thick fog and dark and very still. About 23.00 a light patch appeared on our port bow, it was the stern of an anchored ship all lit up. It was like passing a big block of flats with all the lights on. And shortly after we passed a buoy with a green 4 flashing light which suddenly appeared out of the fog on our starboard bow. Scary stuff. At 24.00 we were at the shipping lane so ran parallel till we came to a buoy then Colin radioed Port August & September 2013 Navigans 10

They said yes and requested a call back when we got to the other side, which we did with relieved thanks. As if to round off our trip nicely the fog lifted at about 01.00, dawn broke to a nice day and we got back to our mooring at 05.45. 20th. After a couple of hours there was enough water to go alongside the pontoon to unload Moontide of excess provisions, rented liferaft and dirty washing. Our trip was over. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Commodore’s Notes Autumn approaches but at least we can look back on an excellent summer. I hope you, like me, made good use of the weather and enjoyed your sailing. The Club has been particularly active over the August holiday period. Cadet Week & Camping Fortnight were a great success as were the Junior Cat Championships. The Kestrel fleet joined us over the Bank Holiday weekend and seemed to enjoy the experience. Our cruising fleet went on two cruises in company, one to the Orwell and Deben and another to Ipswich, both of which were well attended. The vigorous conditions experienced on the return from the Deben brought its own challenges. Club cruisers have also entered BJRC races with success and one of our number completed the Fastnet. May we have many more summers like it. I now need to return to the proposed new fee structure, amendments to which were emailed around all the membership in late July. The amendments were made in response to emails received during the consultation period. A specimen 2014 Membership Renewal Form follows so you can work out your Fees & Subs for next year. I think it is worth restating that the Board and Management Committee have three objectives for the new structure; simplicity, fairness and to increase revenue. Simplicity – to make the fee structure easy to understand, and thereby reduce administration and close any loopholes. Fairness – to ensure that the fees paid by individual members reflect the club facilities utilised by each member, and to some degree align our fee structure to local clubs which offer a similar standard of facilities. Revenue – to increase the annual revenue to enable the club to maintain its existing level of service, and to fund further developments as necessary. The unavoidable running costs of the club have risen steadily over the past few years, over and above the annual increase in fees, which has resulted in a gradual decline in the cash reserves held by the club. I have still only received 26 responses to the new proposals about a third of which are fully supportive. Twenty six is small proportion of a membership approaching 400 and I encourage you to send me any comments you may have to me at: - To further help your understanding of the new fee proposals I will chair a meeting at the Club on Sunday 27th October beginning at 14.00 hrs. My plan is to start by restating the objectives of the new fee proposals before throwing the meeting open to questions from the floor. Meanwhile enjoy the remainder of the season. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Club Secretary ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING – SUNDAY 1ST DECEMBER 2013 Elsewhere in this issue of Navigans you will find the formal notification of the AGM. It has essential information about resolutions and committee nominations. CLUBHOUSE SECURITY CCTV evidence shows that at all times of the day and night YOUR clubhouse is being used by strangers such as beach fisherman and casual visitors. The reason is obvious. Strangers know that the chances are that at least one of the outer doors to the clubhouse will be open for them to use or abuse as they see fit at any time. The solution to this is so easy. Always close the clubhouse after you have been in unless other members are using it; particularly during ‘off peak’ times. Take the trouble to check the other outer doors. It will only take a few minutes. Do not leave the clubhouse open because you are working somewhere on site and might want to nip back there from time to time. The answer to all site security is very simple and is just common sense. FLOOD GATES The Environment Agency requires that the flood gates must be kept closed from 1st September unless the hard is in use. Please shut the gates when you come ashore unless it is obvious that another member is using the hard. If in doubt, shut the gates. They can always be opened again. PARKING IN CRUISER PARK At this busy time of boat, boat hoist and trailer movements cars must not be left unattended in the cruiser park or the cruiser parking area of the cat park. Owners of cars in the cruiser parks must be available at all times and ready to move them at short notice. Do not leave your car unattended in the cruiser parks even if you are ‘only nipping out to the boat for 5 minutes’. CHAIRS ON THE SEAWALL Large numbers of chairs are being taken on to the seawall and left there. Please do not leave chairs on the seawall for somebody else to put away. BOAT DISPOSAL Members may recall that there were disposal notices in the last issue of Navigans for a Dart 15 and a Pico which had been abandoned on the site by ex-members. To bring you up to date, the Dart 15 owner reappeared on the scene and has sold his boat to a Club member. Hopefully we will continue to see this Dart 15 out sailing from Stansgate with the other Dart/Sprint 15s. The Club has decided to ‘adopt’ the Pico. After some repairs and replacements it will be available for MSC cadets and others to use. The disposal notices for both boats are therefore withdrawn. Many thanks to those of you who approached me to show an interest in these boats. ESSEX OUTDOORS, BRADWELL – VHF RADIO COURSES A recent advertisement from the Essex County Council sailing school at Bradwell informs us that from 1st January 2014 the VHF radio course and examination will be spread over two days rather than the one day as at present. This will mean an increase in time and, no doubt, expense. To cater for those who want to do the one-day course before the end of the year Bradwell are running VHF radio courses on 19th October, 3rd November, 30th November and 14th December. The cost is £100 per person including the examination fee. To get ‘chapter and verse’ on this and other courses offered at Bradwell please see the advertisement on the notice board in the Mamgu Bar. Bradwell may be contacted on or at Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: , email: Clubhouse We have had a number of non members using the clubhouse of late, mainly Fisherman during the night but some day trippers during the day. On most occasions, the clubhouse door is left wedged open with a block of wood or fire extinguisher. The only time that the door should be locked in the open position is when an OOD is on duty and then by using the correct key on the OOD key ring. October 2013 Navigans 6

aIuees Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Fleet Reports Cadet Fleet JUNIOR CATAMARAN CHAMPIONSHIPS The weekend of the 17th and 18th August marked the second running of the Junior Catamaran Championships hosted again in association with the UKCRA (UK Catamaran Racing Association) by Marconi Sailing Club. This year saw eight teams with ages ranging from 9 to 16 taking part in a hotly contended regatta all sailed in UKCRA owned and borrowed Dart 16 catamarans. Many of the teams this year determined to show the Multihull sailing skills have spent much of the summer brushing up on the extra skills needed compared to sailing a dinghy. Following the Saturday briefing where teams were allocated boats for the day. They were then faced with a forecast which saw the wind increasing throughout the afternoon from a pleasant force 15 to 20 knots, to a challenging 20 to 30 knots. The teams ranged from competent club sailors who have done some multihull sailing to top class Topper squad sailors who have done very little multihull sailing. Race 1 started with a pleasant 15 knots of breeze, but by the first windward mark it was possible to see the larger gusts pushing their way across the race course. David Nickalls and Ben Cross took an early lead and held this the whole way round, several other team got to grips with perfecting the technique of right a capsized Dart 16 and how to hand those challenging mark roundings. The race team quickly got Race 2 underway as the wind was building there were several more capsizes across the fleet, this time the two all-girl teams of Emma Crane, Abbie Wallace and Sophie Savill and Hannah Bard put in a great performance, but team Nickalls / Cross remained untouchable. With two races under their belt and the wind still increasing, the race team decided to cancel racing for the rest of the day, with the promised forecast for Sunday looking perfect. Sunday dawned, with near perfect champagne sailing conditions. The race team were quick to get the teams out sailing again swapping the boats around to ensure fairness and were able to complete 3 races in the morning and 2 in the afternoon. Emma Crane and Abbie Wallace quickly showing what she had learnt from the previous day with a very respectable second in race 3. Throughout the day there was some very close racing and all teams and positions changed dramatically right up to the finish lines with several occasions the leaders being pipped over the line, simply by missing a crucial tack in the strong tide. With the fight for 2nd and 3rd place coming down to the last race, Jack Collis and Becki Chapman only lost out to Daniel Nickalls and William Harrison as Becki lost her footing and was found swimming in the Blackwater, only losing a couple of places, but it was enough to knock them back down to 3rd on count back. At the prize giving a new perpetual award was presented, the "Dewhirst Award" This was presented in memory of Nick Dewhirst the UKCRA Chainman who sadly passed away in July. Nick's tireless work ensuring that catamaran sailing received the recognition it deserved among the wider sailing community, including the battle to reinstate a Multihull in the Olympics will be remembered for years to come. The boats made available by UKCRA for the event were again only available due to Nick's constant campaigning for the support at grass roots level of the sport to ensure that our up and coming junior sailors have the opportunity to try out the exciting world of catamaran sailing. Ray Ball Company Secretary Nav Sailing on board the Pioneer, Last of the Skillingers In early July, I had the opportunity spend three days on board the Pioneer – the last surviving Essex smack of her kind, based in Brightlingsea. I was accompanying a group of young people on a Prince’s Trust programme and - for the first, and probably the last time in my life – I actually got paid to go sailing! The Pioneer is very special. She is a 64ft Skillinger built in 1864 at Rowhedge, just up the Colne from her current home. She was one of a large fleet of Essex fishing smacks that dredged for oysters and scallops not just around the Essex coast, but further afield off the French, German and Dutch shores. Pioneer saw active service until the 1930s when she fell out of employment and was taken over by the East Mersea Golf Club who cut out most of her deck to build a shed on top. In 1942, she was towed to West Mersea and sank soon after. She remained in the West Mersea mud until 1998 when she was salvaged by a group of professional enthusiasts with sound financial backing that went on to form the Pioneer Sailing Trust. She is now wonderfully re-built, fully rigged and fully employed providing adventurous trips for school children and young people who would otherwise never have the opportunity for such an experience in their lives. Additionally, the Pioneer Sailing Trust has a thriving marine workshop in Brightlingsea which employs apprentices in the now re-emerging boat building industry. The Trust specialises in the restoration of historically significant craft and also the production of beautifully lined coastal rowing vessels. For our particular three day voyage, we originally planned to head up the coast and into the Orwell. However, after crashing into lumpy seas off the Colne Bar with the wind on the nose, a number of the young people began to feel the effects of sea sickness – and that was whilst the wind was still with the tide! Judy, the Skipper, therefore decided on plan B which was to run back into the Blackwater and smoother waters. The young people quickly recovered and threw themselves into all the duties on deck. After a very pleasant sail, we fetched up off Osea Pier for the night and watched the sun go down in very familiar tradition to those of us at Marconi! The next day, the crew arranged for the young people to learn how to row and to tie knots whilst we waited for the tide to become more favourable. I was in full Cadet week flow teaching the bowline and banging on about rabbits, holes and trees when the mate told me with great consternation that the word “rabbit” was never said on board, because it was bad luck. He was unable to explain why. I wonder if anyone else is able to tell me? Google and Wikipedia explanations were not very convincing!!! We spent the rest of the day beating down the Blackwater getting plenty of practice with all that is involved in tacking a proper boat (bit more complicated than my Sprint 15) and then moored up for the night at the end of the Mersea entrance, by the Nass beacon. We then took the young people ashore to stretch their legs and to buy some essential provisions (we had run out of sugar for their cups of tea) and enjoyed watching all the West Mersea cadets tacking their way back home at low water. On the final morning, we aimed to head off early – but although we had a good go at creating a new Pioneer channel, we had to concede defeat and go and have breakfast whilst we waited for the tide to rise. We then had another great beat along the October 2013 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk length of the Mersea shore before reluctantly turning into the Colne and heading for the mooring. We then spent a couple of hours cleaning and scrubbing Pioneer so that she looked like new for the next group of people lucky enough to come on board. If you are interested in finding out more about Pioneer – there is a short book called “Pioneer, Last of the Skillingers” published by Jardine Press in 2004 and written by Rupert Marks and other. The Pioneer Sailing Trust is always keen to hear from schools or groups who think their young people would benefit from a trip on board. They can do day trips or residential for groups up to 10 young people plus 2 team leaders (in addition to the Skipper and 2 crew). I would certainly recommend it to anyone. Ed. “Like doing Everest without Oxygen” A classic yacht competes in the 2013 Fastnet By Tom Anderson Duet is a 50ft gaff-rigged yawl with an unashamedly beautiful and elegant shape, designed by Linton Hope and built in 1912 in what proved to be the zenith of the Edwardian long summer. Classic Boat readers might recollect an article on Duet by Peter Willis in last year’s “Centenarian of the Month” series. She is on loan from the Courtauld family (see below) to the Cirdan Sailing Trust (cirdantrust.org) which now uses her for sailing expeditions, particularly for disadvantaged youth groups but also wounded service personnel and the Duke of Edinburgh award scheme. She is a remarkably well-travelled boat, and her most recent expedition was a circumnavigation of the UK to celebrate her centenary last year, with assorted groups doing legs of the journey. Continuing this expeditionary spirit, she was entered for the 2013 Fastnet race although it was felt that despite Duet having won the MCA and ASTO “Sail Training Vessel of the Year” this particular event might not be suitable for non- sailors so the crewlist was opened up by race skipper David Cannell to a few fortunate individuals who are connected to the Trust. She certainly was an incongruous entry into the Fastnet. There were a record number of entries, and almost all the 350 boats taking part were modern racing machines – their ultra-light carbon-fibre hulls and Kevlar rigs were manned by sunglass-wearing crews in matching, uniform kits. Something of a contrast to our teak on oak frames, weighty spars, traditional sails and crew of Corinthian harlequins, let alone the warm mahogany and brass that welcomes you to her saloon below (and the Baby Blake)… Perhaps because we rather stood out, many people who were otherwise unconnected with Duet and the Cirdan Trust followed our progress enthusiastically on http://fastnet.rorc.org/2013-fleet-tracking.html. They may have been occasionally bemused by our track but our course was heavily dictated by wind and tide as we saw them, which gave us some incredible sails but also some very frustrating moments. After the start, we struck out into the Channel, thinking that we might get a better breeze out there, unfortunately (inevitably) it was the other way around and we were almost becalmed for two days, and flushed backwards and forwards by the tides. It was some consolation to hear that these fickle zephyrs also frustrated the fastest boats on their return as they were stuck in sight of the finish at Plymouth. As we passed the Scillies the wind had freshened into a steady westerly, so we punched up to the Fastnet on one tack, pounding through a confused chop as the Irish and Celtic seas met. We were beating into some lumpy water through the Irish Sea as we watched other competitors go past us on their reciprocal run home and were also looking forward to a fast sail back to the Scillies, which would have been a good broad reach if the wind had stayed west. Unfortunately, we got around the Fastnet and the wind promptly changed north-westerly so having gone around the rock and found the turning mark (laid to separate the boats coming towards and away from the rock) we were not able to aim straight at the Scillies as it would have been a dead run and it wasn’t worth risking a crash gybe in heavy seas and growing wind. This was a tough moment for all the crew as we realised that the best course we could lay would be south which would add miles onto our track, rather than the direct south-east route that all the other competitors had been able to take. We were aware that there was a deep low working its way across the Atlantic and the wind and rollers steadily grew as we gybed towards the Scillies. This gave us some very fast sailing – albeit nerve-wracking – as the swells lifted the counter and October 2013 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk swung us towards crash-gybe territory. Lots of fighting the tiller, trying to find a balance between going dead downwind on the straightest route home and going too far off the wind and risking the gybe. As you can imagine on a classic yacht with no winches every rig change and sail adjustment required extra crew on deck; whoever went onto the bowsprit to unhank the genoa or yankee would get plunged unceremoniously into the sea at some point whilst the rest of the off-duty watch fought to get sails up, down and tied away. All kit went slowly from damp to wet, although we had an afternoon of sun somewhere west of the Scillies so the deck immediately transformed into a Chinese laundry as socks went back from wet to damp. Duet was worked pretty hard, but we didn’t break anything that couldn’t be jury-rigged with a bit of imagination and some quick splicing from one of Duet’s permanent crew, Alex Carpenter. The genoa ripped a cleat off, so we used a pulley system to take some of the pressure off the sheet which was useful but another thing to remember when we tacked. The bowsprit’s tack downhaul snapped so a beefier one was put together. The genoa itself also took a bit a battering but nothing too terminal; just a small tear and some stitches pulled out. Our boathook disappeared somewhere south of Ireland. Bumps and scrapes for the crew but nothing that couldn’t be overcome by a cup of tea and another sail change to take your mind off the fresh bruises. A few salient facts picked out from the log show that we raced over 800 nautical miles, and did over 30 sail changes, as well as a couple of reefs (one of which was completed in a F7). The main was obviously used throughout the race, albeit reefed and shaken out a few times; we also used the mizzen, mizzen staysail, jackyard topsail, working topsail, staysail, genoa, yankee and No1 jib. Phew! Just in case the crew of 7 were feeling too relaxed, the bilges required 11,300 pumps and there was also a very jolly 20 minutes spent using buckets to empty the bilges while we were wallowing mid-channel. Duet is a deeply elegant Edwardian lady, but she does have a leaky bottom. Having said that, our speed is mentioned several times in the log at around 9 knots, but according to the GPS we topped out at about 11 or 12, which is pretty good going! However, it wasn’t all hard work and the log shows high levels of morale throughout the race with several mentions of lunch and the 4th Ashes test, a description of the weather as “lovely”, and (a slightly relieved) “England sighted!!” as we saw Blighty re- appearing on the horizon… We saw plenty of dolphins, usually in pods of about 6 animals. Although I have to admit that my ridiculously limited zoological knowledge doesn’t stretch to an ability to identify species, the ubiquitous Google tells me they were probably one of the genus Delphinus. We saw a very nonchalant sunfish splashing along in the Channel, and a small, curious-looking, long-nosed garfish was swept onto the deck as we thundered downwind towards the Scillies. It was probably as surprised to see us as we were to see it, but our miniature Poseidon was returned to the briny without further incident. During the quiet night watches there was ethereal bio-luminescence which complemented some very clear night skies, giving us several stars to steer her by. During the final run in towards Plymouth the wind strengthened, and blew F7. Big rollers, 3 or 4 m high, were sweeping in and toppling over themselves in a roar behind us. We had our only ‘all hands’ call about 30 miles from the finish to put in a double reef and dropped to the No1 jib. Difficult with the wind behind but with the indefatigable energy of Gavin Taylor, Duet’s regular skipper and with the finish so close no-one minded by then, although we were all pretty pooped, as you can imagine. We had a great welcoming party on the pontoon when we arrived. About 30 people, led by David Cannell’s family, had turned out and their generous champagne and boisterous hallooing was much appreciated; especially as it was blowing a gale with horizontal rain and we finished about a day after everyone else, thanks to our little wind-induced detour west of the Scillies. I think Duet had become something of a talisman for the rest of the fleet, and there was lots of clapping and cheering from the other boats in the Plymouth Yacht Haven. We had a good supper in the nearest hostelry and then dropped, soggy and drained, into bed. We later admitted to each other that we had woken ourselves up during that first night ashore, in anticipation of a whispered “wake up mate, you’re on watch…” We must thank all those who supported us before, during and after the race. There are too many to name individually but many people have given generously to support the Cirdan Trust, which uses these donations to provide bursaries to groups who would otherwise struggle to experience the challenge and teamwork required on board a sailing vessel. One of the things that surprised us, and the Cirdan team, was the number of sailors who were proudly following Duet’s progress as a classic in what is a very modern race, posting supportive comments and maintaining a positive online commentary on a variety of sailing websites and blogs – thank you all. The 2013 Fastnet was certainly a rigorous test for boat and most importantly, crew. It would have been a real bonus to have competed more strongly but the weather has a vote and it went against us so we were delighted to have finished, even if it was behind Jolie Brise! It was a genuinely remarkable experience. Duet’s gear has not been modernised, and there are no nautical mod-cons such as winches so any rig adjustments require gruntwork. One of the crew described it by saying “doing the Fastnet on Duet is the equivalent of climbing Everest without oxygen”, which (with apologies to any readers who have climbed Everest) feels about right. I would strongly recommend trying to do a long-distance race if an opportunity presents itself although during the race you will ask yourself why you volunteered and after the race you will have to face mystified faces in the office when trying to explain what you’ve been up to during your hard-earned summer holiday. By the way, if you see Duet, or the other vessels in the Cirdan Trust’s fleet (Queen Galadriel, a Baltic trader, or Faramir, a purpose built sail training ketch) on the water do give them a wave – they deserve it! Duet was built in 1912 and is believed to be Britain’s longest serving sail training vessel. Since she began this role in 1960 she has sailed more than 250,000 miles and provided a sailing adventure for more than 8,000 young people. Her involvement with the Courtauld family began in 1931, when the arctic explorer Augustine (August) Courtauld was virtually buried alive under snow in Greenland but kept himself together by designing a yacht which would turn out to be Duet. He was a member of an expedition investigating the possibility of an air route to North America via Iceland and Greenland which involved taking regular weather readings through the darkness of the Arctic winter. October 2013 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk They established a weather station up on the Greenland ice cap which was to be manned by relays of two men at a time. Unfortunately, one of these relays was delayed by atrocious blizzard conditions and arrived with rations much depleted and insufficient for two men to stay the winter. Rather than allow the recording of the weather to lapse August insisted on volunteering to stay and man the station alone. He was there for five months, cut off with no communication to the outside world, the last six weeks of which he was actually trapped and buried in his tent under the snow with only a breather pipe for air and running out of food and fuel. During his entrapment two plans occupied his thoughts, the first to marry his future wife Mollie and the second to design a yacht. He was eventually rescued and after his safe return to England and his bride-to-be, scoured the country looking at boats for sale, until he found one at Burnham-on-Crouch which was so similar to the one he had mentally designed, that he bought her. He renamed her Duet in honour of his forthcoming marriage to Mollie. They lived in Essex and brought up their six children in that magnificent county. August, who served on the County Council and as High Sheriff of Essex, sailed Duet until 1955 and died in 1959. His widow, Mollie, subsequently married RA (later Lord) Butler and they continued to live in the house where Christopher spent his childhood and where Mollie eventually died aged 101. August’s son Christopher inherited Duet and in 1960 co-founded the Ocean Youth Club, making her available for young people to enjoy the experience of sailing. Although on loan to the Cirdan Sailing Trust, Duet remains in the ownership of the Courtauld family who came over from France as Huguenot refugees in the 17th century, originally setting up as silversmiths in London and subsequently in Essex as textile manufacturers. Ray Ball Company Secretary Pam Davies I am saddened to write that Pam Davies died on 11th September having been ill for some time. Together with husband Dick and children Gill, Corrina and Huw, Pam was an active member of MSC in the 1990’s and, through family and friends, never lost touch with the club. A service of thanksgiving for her life was held at St Mary’s Church, Great Baddow, on the 4 th October. Many of her friends from the sailing club were present. I first met Pam when she was Jean Fluke’s galley helper one Sunday just after the Davies family had joined Marconi. Getting stuck in like this was typical of Pam’s sense of duty and service. Pam was not an avid sailor herself, but she would accompany Dick for ‘jollies’ on his Dart 15s “Di-Pa” and “Cold Feet”. Back ashore, Dick and Pam forged many firm friendships with fellow members that continue to this day. Just over a decade after I first met the Davies clan, Gill and I were married and I was privileged to have Dick and Pam as my in- laws. I, like so many others, can testify to Pam’s generosity, hospitality and sense of humour – all of which were second to none. During 2013 Pam remained active despite her illness, and visited Stansgate several times. She took great joy in watching grandchildren Becky, Ruth, Jamie and Megan take to the water on my Dart 15 one evening during cadet week. She will be greatly missed by all who knew her. David Ball NSSA Regatta 2013 In 2012 two MSC cadets joined many others at the NSSA regatta in Weymouth, enjoying a great week of sailing. This then sparked the idea to take a team from MSC to the 2013 NSSA regatta in Bassenthwaite, Cumbria (Lake District). John Nickalls took on the role as Team Manager and started the many emails to organise the trip. In total 9 cadets were keen, with parents and brothers tagging along too. I (Richard, brother to Matthew) joined Caroline and John as Team Managers for MSC. The awkward task of transporting boats was sorted, sweatshirts printed, tents packed, sailing bags overflowing and cars crammed to the roof, the long journey to Bass was upon us. The MSC team comprised of: John & Caroline Nickalls – Team Managers Richard Dixon – Team Manager David Nickalls – Laser Radial Dan Bard – Laser Radial Gemma Clarke – Laser Radial Beth Spencer – Topper Sophie Savill – Topper Dan Nickalls – 420 Hannah Bard – 420 Crew Olivia Duckmanton – Topper Rookie Fleet Matthew Dixon – Pico Rookie Fleet Matthew has written about his Regatta: Sunday, We left early on Sunday morning, on our way to the NSSA, which was being hosted by the sailing club of Bassenthwaite, in the Lake District. First we had to pick up Beth from the Boreham interchange, and then we carried on our very long journey up North to Bass. Behind us we had a 420, which belonged to the Nickalls. After our 6 hour journey, which included a lot of sleeping, we arrived at the sailing club to unload the boats and met the Nickalls family who had only just arrived. After unloading we rigged the boats to make sure it was all ready for the week’s regatta. Then we drove the short distance to the school where most competitors will be staying on the school's playing field. The first step was to put up the big marquee in our allocated slot,(R – thanks to the MSC member who offered this for our trip to Bass, it was used daily and invaluable to dry our kit November 2013 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk and sit under) whilst the Mums went shopping for lunch. David decided to try flying with Beths tent rather than help put it up, he didn’t get very far! After dinner served in the school canteen, we had the main briefing in the sport hall of the school, where we learned more about what we would be doing over the week. I was entered into the Rookie fleet which is aimed at sailors who hadn’t sailed away from their home club, in a Laser Pico. We then played games as a team before heading to bed ready for the weeks sailing. Monday, After having breakfast at the school we then travelled the short distance by car to the sailing club. We rigged our boats, and then each separate fleet (Laser, Topper, Handicap, and Rookie) had a briefing in the marquee at the sailing club. Today being the first day of racing many of us were nervous not knowing what it is going to be like sailing somewhere different. Then the fleets launched one at a time, in order to not cause chaos in the 3 slipways that were available to us, although we were lucky that we were right next to one of the quieter slipways so could launch easily. Each fleet had its own race course. The Rookie fleet was close to the shore so didn’t have that far to go, our course was a triangle shaped, the Handicap had a windward leeward whereas the topper and Laser had odd shaped, but wasn’t obvious from the shore. Each lunch was provided as a packed lunch delivered to us. After the afternoon sailing we ventured back to the school to shower and get ready for the evening entertainment. Tonight’s was a talk by Virtual Rigger who showed us some video footage and pictures of the days sailing. Tuesday After another morning briefing to the Rookies (which was very quiet), we had a rather uneventful days sailing due to the severe lack of wind on the lake. After the days sailing, and dinner we had an invitation to a game of rounders against the other teams. This was made a lot more interesting by the fact that the rain had made the field extremely slippery, and so there were many occasions where a runner slipped over on the mud, with the most spectacular example being when somebody from the other team ran a rounder and finished it off by falling backwards and sliding into one of their teammates lining up to bat. Wednesday Today, we had something different which came in the form of the Mount Haes event. Sophie and David were chosen to represent Marconi in the race, which took place in Topper Xenons The race format was similar to the Football World Cup. To progress to the next round they needed to come in the top 2 after 3 laps, but unfortunately they only managed to come third, however this was still a very good result as David and Sophie had never raced competitively together. Also, there were two other events that were being held, which was a Topper race, which Daniel and Hannah did, and then there was the all-comers race, which everybody else did including adult. Richard and Beth sailed the 420, I sailed the Pico with Olivia and David (who had finished racing) & Dan sailed their Lasers. This again was unfortunately met with an even bigger lack of wind than on Tuesday, with an Oppi passing many boats which started 5 minutes before it. This resulted in a very late lunch. After the sailing and dinner, we went on a scheduled walk up a nearby mountain. We met at the sailing club on what was advertised as an easy 1 hour walk. In the heat of the summer evening it wasnt easy and I soon drank all my drink. The view from the top was amazing and you could see the lake we were sailing on and also the view far into the distance. After returning to the school we dived into the canteen for a well-earned supper of bread with jam and hot drink before retiring to our tents for bed. Thursday Thursday was a disaster day, we had been using John and Richards cars to transport all of us from the school to the sailing club, unfortunately his car broke on the way to the club (R – the flywheel went, AA Tow truck booked for Saturday!). Everyone had a great day sailing until the afternoon when we found out the 420 was been protested over a minor incident in what was their best race. After the sailing and ferrying all of us in Johns car back to school for dinner, we went for a walk around Cockermouth, which was the nearest village to us. The town has a statue for William Wordsworth which we discovered, and it was made famous of the flood that happened in 2009, which was above my head! John then started our Prize giving giving us each a NSSA Bassenthwaite Mug and Mint cake (that had been to the top of Everest) and also our virtual prize (as the real prizes were in shops that had shut!) Mine was a loud hailer, I was the quieter member of the MSC group! Friday On friday, I managed to come 1st in both the races of the day which I believe was down to the heavier winds, which I was used to instead of the light winds we had been having for the rest of the week (R – it was really down to the excellent sail training given by John!!). These results along with the re-positioning of previous results and gaining another discard, I managed to jump unexpectedly from sixth place earlier on in the week to finish the Rookie Fleet in second place. Once we were all off the water we got the boats loaded up on the road trailers ready for the journey home on Saturday. The prize giving in the evening was at the sailing club in beautiful sunshine, overlooking the lake. My name was November 2013 Navigans 6

However instead of an AA man we got piked up by a local company for the first leg. He then took us to a very busy services, which barely had enough room for us to manoeuvre around for the changeover to an actual AA truck. Most of our return journey consisted of us sleeping, being interrupted by the changeovers, which there were 3 of in total. I really enjoyed the NSSA event in Bassenthwaite and would recommend it to anyone, it is friendly and you get to sail against people of the same ability. Richard Dixon Team Marconi in Ibiza At the end of September 3 Marconi teams travelled all the way to the sunny island of Ibiza to take part in the 2013 Tornado World Championships. T415 Michaela & Andrew Dowley T431 Steve Glynn & Tom Duckmanton T424 Lee & Paul Harrisson The World Championships were scheduled to be over 6 days with the practice races starting on the Sunday. We arrived in Ibiza on Friday evening with Steve, Debbie and the trailer coming off the ferry on Saturday morning. Saturday turned out to be a boat building and testing day, we rigged in the harbour so had to sail the boats over to the private, sandy beach where they would be located for the rest of the week. Lee had done an excellent job of finding an apartment which was situated just up from the beach. The 7 of us had a nice home for the week. Sunday's practice races had to be cancelled because there was too much wind outside of the harbour. In the evening it was the opening night with traditional local dancing and formal ceremony where we carried the Union Jack through the town to the marquee and were presented to the sponsors and crowds. Monday morning came and we could feel a reasonable breeze from the is beach, there was certainly going to be more outside the harbour wall and onto the race course. Looking back it was probably the windiest day of the week. Steve and Tom managed a couple of fantastic swims, the 2nd wasn't their fault as they had a port/starboard with a German team who didn't give them the right of way. The second day saw similar conditions and it was questionable as to whether the breeze was above the 25 knot limit, the race committee seemed to think it wasn't but they were super keen to get the races completed. It was Andrew and Michaela's turn for a swim on Tuesday, a sudden gust downwind after going round the windward mark with the leaders put us out of the race because the mainsail popped out of the mast track. Luckily we made it back out for the 2nd race. While all the swimming was happening Lee and Paul were finishing all of the races and were putting together a good series of results. Wednesday was the lay day and perfectly timed after two windy days. It wasn't just the wind we were recovering from after a heavy night and a road trip across the island to the infamous Ibiza night spots for some of us. Wednesday evening we were lucky enough to be able to visit the exclusive Blue Marlin Beach Club who were a main sponsor of the event for dinner and drinks. November 2013 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk On Thursday morning the wind had swung round and was now coming from the East bringing some big rolling waves around 2.5m high. Waiting round before the start was very uncomfortable with the boats being thrown up and down. The first race of the day turned out to be carnage with lots of swims and breakages across the fleet which included Michaela, Andrew, Steve and Tom unfortunately! The race committee decided that one race was enough for Thursday and send the fleet limping back to the beach. Friday was a complete different story with very light winds which continued to drop all day, unfortunately the waves were still present which made it very hard to get the boats moving, although the Olympians and Pro's didn't do a bad job of it, more practice is needed for us club sailors. Saturday and the last day had came around very quickly as it always does when you're away from work and in beautiful sunny place. Fortunately there was more breeze on Saturday with between 7 and 13 knots at different times during the day. The race committee got 3 races in to make the full quota for the week. With only 1 discard from the 10 races there wasn't much we could do about the races we didn’t finish, final positions for team Marconi were: Michaela and Andrew – 21st Lee and Paul – 24th Steve and Tom - 30th Importantly we all learnt new things about our boats and what to do in different conditions to make the boat go faster. Now we've all got the bug for competing at this level the next World Championships are in Perth over Christmas and New Year 2014/15, watch this space…. If all goes as planned at the AGM, the Club will have a new Commodore who will create several “firsts” for the Club, the most important of which, in my view, is that Michaela will be the first of the next generation to take on the role. I wish her, the new Executive and the 2014 Management Committee all good fortune with running our Club. I am certain that they will take good care of the legacy and bring fresh impetus to planning for our future If there has been a vote in favour of the proposed new fee structure at the AGM then a vital “foundation stone” has been well and truly laid and the Executive & Management Committees will be able to plan for the future with confidence. However if the proposed new fee structure has been voted out by a majority of those present at the AGM then the immediate and most important problem will be to ensure that the Club can meet its bills in January and remain solvent. This will call for quick and decisive action and I hope such an early “test of character” for the new Commodore has not become necessary. For my own part I will be returning to the back benches as a Vice President and ECPR Chairman. I wish to thank my fellow directors, Company Secretary Ray Ball and all members of the Management Committee for their advice, hard work and unanimous informed support during the last seven months while we have plotted a course through the difficulties facing the Club. Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: , email: Fleet News Dinghy Cruising DINGHY CRUISING GROUP - SUMMARY FOR 2013 The dinghy cruising group held a programme of local and away cruises throughout 2013. We sailed from the MSC every month from March to October on the first Saturday of the month. The only cancellation was in November - yesterday - when the forecast wind was too high. In the event we walked to Stone, past an idyllic scene with calm water and warm moderate airs - but it did get windy later. We ended the day with a most enjoyable meal at the Fox and Hounds in Cock Clarks. Two high points were our cruises on the South coast and from MSC to Burnham. In May we trailed boats to the Solent and camped and launched at Eastney, sailing through Langstone Harbour, round the top of Hayling Island and down through Chichester Harbour to Bosham and back - leaving the boats overnight at Sparks marina at the very tip of the Island - some of the roughest sailing we have done. We were joined by Andrew and a friend from the Shadwell sailing club, a frequent fellow- adventurer. In June we hosted a UKWA event at MSC, sailing round the Dengy peninsular into the Crouch, camping in Burnham and returning the next day. In John Eardley's words : Saturday morning saw 9 boats and 20 people assemble at Marconi for a little return trip to Burnham on Crouch (4 of our boats; Myrtle, Blue Moon, Nirvana and Samphire) and 5 visiting. A northerly F3/4 wind and fine conditions ensured a swift beam reach down the Blackwater, followed by a beaching at Brightlingsea’s Mersea Stone for a lunch stop whilst we awaited the tide to rise in the Thames - we were to cross the Ray sands drying channel no earlier than LW+2 (1500). A due southerly course took us across the sands and we picked up the flood up the Crouch and into to Burnham. Great early evening sail followed by a short paddle/row/motor into the yacht harbour. Lots of transferring people and gear between marina and campsite, and then an evening meal in the Anchor hotel. We woke to a similar forecast on Sunday morning, more movement of people and gear; for some a stop off at the local café for a full English. A northerly F3/4 in bright sunshine gave us a beam reach down the Crouch on the ebb, before once again crossing the sands and heading northwards; a two and a half hour close-hauled but pleasant hack. The welcome rounding into the Blackwater, followed by a quick lunch stop on a rapidly disappearing spit, and we were soon back at Marconi and saying our fond farewells. 54 miles in total, not bad at all. For both major cruises we are indebted to John Eardley and Cliff Pountney for the organisation. It is good to combine with other clubs, extending the network of likeminded sailors. Our local sails have been up to Maldon, down to Mersea and all points in between, stopping of for picnics on the spits and inlets around the estuary. Cruises are generally of between 3 and 10 boats, with 6-20 people, but we are able to mix and match, taking as many or few boats as the conditions warrant. We are planning a similar programme for next year and would welcome anyone interested in joining us. Colin Wardell December 2013 Navigans 4
