Ray Ball Company Secretary Changes to VHF SRC course from 1st January 2014 Do it now on 15th December 2013 if you need it! The RYA are about to change the procedure for VHF SRC courses and assessments. In a nutshell the current system where one is trained and assessed on the same day by the same assessor in a one day course will be replaced by the need for an independent assessor and an increase in the study time to 10 hours minimum. There will also be an increase in the cost of the RYA fee for the issue of the certificate from £30 to £60 to cover the assessment and this will need to be paid at the time of booking. The fine detail has yet to be worked though by many schools and an online course is being prepared by the RYA as an option but the assessment will still need to be done in person at an RYA Training Centre. In short it will cost you more and take longer after 1st January 2014 Therefore members considering doing the SRC in the near future will find it in their interests to get this under their belts before 1st January. Bob Wale is running a course on Sunday 15th December 2013 and will run at MSC if this is requested. Courses can be booked and paid for on the Yachtwise website at www.yachtwise.org and the fee remains at £60 for the course/assessment which includes a light lunch. The RYA fee of £30 for the issue of the certificate is separate and is payable on successful completion. I have seen that Bradwell are also offering courses in December if mine is not suitable for you although they are more expensive. You will need this certificate if you charter or go abroad and it is a legal requirement in the UK so there has never been a better time to get this done if you need it. December 2013 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk February Issue copy deadline: Saturday 17th January Club Notices Commodore In this initial edition of 2014 Navigans I am writing for the first time in Commodores notes. For those of you who do not know me, I have been a member of the Club for about 20 years (I started young!). I learnt to sail at Marconi during cadet weeks many years ago and have gone on to tutor for a number of years. I currently sail a Tornado Sport but can also be seen out and about on a laser or support boat. I have served as a Rear Commodore for the past 4 years so have a good idea of the workings of the Club. I have personally gained a huge amount from MSC over the years - fun, friends and even a husband. I assure you that I have the very best interests of the Club at heart both in the present and future. I thank you for your support for all the resolutions passed at the recent AGM, including those affecting the new fee structure. This new foundation will provide stability and allow the Board and Committees to effectively plan for the future of the Club. We welcome the return of Pat Shaw to the Board along with Graham Cross, both of whom are filling Rear Commodore positions on the Board of Directors. Winter sees a relatively quiet time of activity and I wish those competing at winter series elsewhere and flying the Marconi flag the best of luck. You will all be shortly receiving an invoice for membership and subscriptions due on 1st January for payment by 31st January 2014. Please bear in mind that the information on the invoice is only as accurate as the data held on the club membership database. To ease the burden of the Membership Secretary I ask that you return fees as soon as possible along with any amendments to your details. Finally I wish you all a happy and prosperous new year and look forward to seeing you both on and off the water. Michaela Dowley Commodore Ex-Commodore’s Notes I am sure you will see that the minutes of the AGM are published in full elsewhere in this edition and you will have read, or heard on the grapevine, that the new fee structure was approved by a 97% majority. I would like to thank all members that turned out to support the Resolution. I remain certain that the new fee structure will create a firm base from which to build the future of the Club. That future is now entrusted to a new Commodore and to the 2014 board and management committee. I know they will do a good job. I would like to re-visit something that you will find tucked away in AOB, that of the lifting of age restrictions on OODs. It has been our practice to exempt members over state retirement age from OOD duty. But, now that almost a third of our members and rising come into this category, it is no longer feasible to continue with this exemption as it puts excessive burden on other members. So don’t be surprised if OOD maestro Keith White contacts you next season. I send you all my very best wishes for the festive season and look forward to seeing you out sailing in 2014. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Blackwater & Colne Open Sailing Series (BCOSS) Q: What is it? A: It's about encouraging large fleet participation in sailing events on the Blackwater & Colne estuary. After the success of the 3 x events in 2013 all clubs on the Blackwater and Colne have agreed to participate in the 2014 events and include them in their sailing calendar. The fun events attracted large fleet numbers last year, making a spectacle on the river and giving rise to great publicity opportunities for the clubs involved. At Marconi we're looking to build on that success and hope that members will join in the sailing activities and make crew spaces available on their boat to introduce potential cruiser members to our club. The events will have a relaxed format for those simply looking for a fun day on the water and will allow those more competitive sailors to let off a bit of steam. Each of the events has a social aspect to it, and at Marconi we'll be hosting a BBQ, cricket match, and other shoreside activities on the evening before the sailing event. We've had many visitors to this social over the past few years, but many of our own members have been missing out, so get this one in your diary, it really is going to be a great weekend. Richard Roberts BCOSS LH Series Champion of 2013 receiving his Trophy from Clive. Credit: Peter Ward DATES: Event 1: Sunday 8th June (organiser Marconi – SC) 10:30am start from Thirslet Buoy. With a Saturday evening BBQ & games, trot boat provided both days, breakfast in galley on Sunday morning. Event 2: Saturday 5th July (organiser Mersea Joint Clubs) 10:00am start from Nass With a Saturday evening garden party on the WMYC lawn, live music, games and supper. Proceeds to Packing Shed Fund Event 3: Saturday 19th July (organiser Colne – YC) 10:00am start S of Molliette. With a Saturday evening supper and prizegiving in the Colne YC SERIES FORMAT: The series will be conducted in the form of 3 x long course races for White Sail, Short handed, Family Crewed, Local Handicapped and IRC rated boats. It's aim is to encourage large fleet participation in sailing events on the Blackwater & Colne estuary. HOW TO GET INVOLVED: I'll be adding info to navigans, the club notice board, and the website over the coming months but contact me if you'd like to discuss the events in more detail. Cheers and have a good winter. I'm off to polish my bottom! Peter Ward. January 2014 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Honorary Treasurer, Sue Shenton, presented the Financial Statement up to 31st August 2013. Questions on the Honorary Treasurer's Report: Referring to the Financial Statement, Kevin Kirby questioned the apparent discrepancy in the information on the bank loan for 2012 and 2013. Sue Shenton explained that detailed accounts were not available for 2012 only an overall figure. Detailed figures were available for the end of the 2013 MSC financial year and are reflected in the Financial Statement. Bruce Hood asked whether the current Bank Loan had an interest rate collar, possibly transferred from the previous ‘purchase of club’ loan which he recalled did have a rate collar (as explained by the person responsible for the financial presentation at that time). Bruce then briefly explained that a collar (also called an interest rate swap) consists of a defined pair of ceiling and floor limits for the variable rate. A ceiling is advantageous in times of higher than expected interest rates and conversely the associated floor is disadvantageous in times of lower than expected interest rates. Since we are in a protracted period of the low interest rates what appears to be a decision not to continue with a collar is proving to be a wise one. Sue Shenton replied that she was not familiar with the term but could confirm that the interest rate is variable, although there was an option to fix it if it thought appropriate in the future. Bruce then pointed out that one simple measure of financial stability, often used in business, (together with the cash reserve figure) is to look at the ratio produced by comparing the loan total variable rate interest charges i.e. £17.7K (re Financial Report Page 4) with the net annual surplus i.e. £20K (thus 1.1 which is adequate/good). This gives a useful indication of the amount of generated liquid cash likely to be available to absorb future rising interest rate charges that may occur. In his opinion this is more meaningful and useful than the £227K Total Reserve figure (i.e. owned Embedded Equity, excluding cash reserve) based on Tangible Asset Valuations. Sue thanked Bruce for his input and confirmed that the suggestion will be considered. Graham Cross stated that if the Club has bad debts these could be offset against corporation tax. Sue Shenton explained that most financial losses were due to members not renewing their membership. Acceptance of the report and the Annual Accounts to 31st August 2013 was proposed by John Nickalls, seconded by David Ball. Carried overwhelmingly with one vote against and no abstentions 4.4 Sailing Secretary's Report The Sailing Secretary, Jenny Ball, presented her report. Date of AGM 2014 – 23rd November 2014 R D Ball Company Secretary. 4th December 2013 Commodore’s Report to the 2013 AGM I will now give you my report which I will read so that it can be transferred verbatim into the Minutes of this meeting. Sailing I am delighted to tell you that Marconi Sailing Club has been active in its core business of providing facilities for sailing to its members. I believe we have discharged this objective well and that the Club has had an excellent year’s sailing helped no doubt by some unusually good weather. ECPR I will leave the detailed report on sailing activities to the Sailing Secretary, but as I was ECPR chairman (again) this year, I will report on that Race. Back in late June all the different sections of the Club pulled together when we staged our “signature” Race for the 26th time. Good conditions enabled the full course to be run with a minimum of incident. Although entry numbers were down on last year we were able to donate £400 to Essex Air Ambulance and £2,100 to the Cirdan Sailing Trust who also raised a further £12,000 sponsorship on the back of the Race. My grateful thanks go to every member who helped in any way, especially the crews of the mother boats & RIBs that make it possible to control the risks inherent in the Event. Cadets Our cadet fleet has gone from strength to strength this year, building on the firm foundations laid by Bryan Spencer and propelled onwards by the driving force of John Nickalls and his willing team. Not only have the number of training sessions increased but numbers attending each session have also. All this is in addition to our successful and long running Cadet Week. RYA Affiliation We have continued to build strong links with the RYA with regular visits from area co-ordinators whose practical advice has been helpful and instructive. We have also received valuable advice from the RYA Legal Department. Sport England Grant Although not directly connected, I am sure our close RYA relationship was instrumental in our successful application to Sport England for a grant to purchase a new RIB to support our sailing. We are required to add match funding to the grant and an order has been placed for delivery in the New Year. My thanks go to the three or four members who pooled their efforts to complete the lengthy bureaucratic process of the grant application and to the procurement sub-committee headed by Andrew Dowley. Training Centre During the year we took a decision to become an RYA accredited Training Centre. Again, much form filling is required and this process nears completion. Meanwhile I am pleased to report that we have appointed a Chief Instructor in the shape of Pat Shaw and he is in the process of gaining the formal qualifications necessary. We have also appointed Bob Collins as the impressively titled “Training Centre Principal”. The intention is to be ready to train Club members to PB2 level by the start of next season. Shoreside Self-help The Club’s only employee is Joan, our cleaner. All other work at the Club is done by our members. Whether it is Launching & Recovery of moorings or cruisers; cutting the grass; maintenance of buildings, site or plant and equipment; it is all done by members. This enables the Club to offer our members (particularly our cruiser members) excellent facilities at lower cost than anything comparable elsewhere. January 2014 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Our tight budget dictated that we only carried out one Capital Project this year, the new mast derrick. Much of the work was undertaken by Club members thus keeping costs down. A large amount of the work is carried out by the slightly inaccurately named “Wednesday Gang” led by Murray Bates. Inaccurate because at mooring, launching and recovery times elements of the Gang work up to five days a week. In addition the Wednesday Gang have brought the new meeting/training room into service and I hear that the long term project to provide a Club launch for use as a Committee Boat nears completion. One of the pleasurable duties of the Commodore is to select a member who has given outstanding service to the Club and present him or her with the Commodore’s Trophy. This year I have selected a long term member of the “Wednesday Gang” who is always around working hard and giving good advice. As an example, just recently he was on hand to rescue a Club sailor who was drifting mastless towards Bradwell having ventured out in a Force 7. I am certain he is fully deserving of this award and it gives me pleasure to ask – Colin Leveridge – to come up and collect it. Management positions In several ways it has been an unusual year. It has been a year of mid-term resignations from key positions in the Club management structure, one of which was my co-option as Commodore back in April. Both the Cruiser Fleet captain and the Sailing Secretary were unable to continue due to pressure of work and I am grateful to Roger Camp and to Dave Russell & Jenny Ball for stepping forward at short notice to fill the voids so successfully. Business of Board and Management Committee I will now attempt to summarise the main thrust of business within the Board and management committee since the last AGM. Safety. Two different events have led us to give particular attention to Safety: - The accident some 20 months ago to the mast derrick and new RYA Legal advice which was published in autumn 2012. This has led to a “root and branch” review of all our safety systems with greater emphasis on the assessment of risk and the updating of our written Codes of Practice. I am particularly grateful for the work of Andy Samuel and Ray Ball who led the process, but many other did their bit as well. Developing and updating of our systems to respond to the RYA Legal advice is well advanced but there is still work to be done, especially with regard to the Club’s duty of care to children entering Club Races. I acknowledge the hard work, drive and diplomacy of Michaela in the Board’s dealings with the RYA Legal Department and to Dave Russell, Jenny Ball and the sailing sub-committee to whom much of the work of implementation has fallen. The process has not been easy; some members have taken the attitude “we have always done it like this so why do we need to change” and “we are a sailing club why do we need all this bureaucracy”. I think we have made progress in changing those entrenched attitudes and I also say that any company in the business of providing the facilities and services that we do, must keep up with changing legislation or face the consequences. Proposed new Fee Structure The other main thrust of Board and Committee business has been the proposed new fee structure. This is a summary of the many historical, current and future problems that led us to embark such a major undertaking. 60 year old fee system. Our existing fee structure has been evolving for the 60 years the Club has been in existence. It was not updated when we bought the Club from MASC some ten years ago, nor since. The current system is very complicated to administer and defies all attempts to use software to ease this burden. The system has loop-holes that lay us open to both avoidance and evasion esp. with regard to dinghy/cat winter storage payments. The Cruiser Park is not immune either. There are several “custom & practice” unofficial discounts and underpayments in operation which do not form part of any fee system past, present or proposed. These unofficial discounts have encouraged a situation where over 30 cruisers did not launch this year and did not pay a mooring fee. Our existing By-laws and fee structure did not anticipate this situation and the only rate we have been able to apply for summer storage is the second boat fee that was only ever intended to be applied to dinghies and cats. The impact on Club finances does not need further explanation. On a mitigating note, the Board does have the discretion to adjust cruiser fees when a member hits hard times, for example serious illness. However few cases of the “no mooring but still storing” cruisers come into that category. Basic imbalances between dinghies & cruisers. Our practice over many years has been to apply a “percentage across the board” approach with increases to Fees. This has meant that any small imbalance set-up many years ago has been magnified. Based on our research the Board believe that a large imbalance exists between the fees we charge to dinghies and those charged to cruisers. Dinghy/cat fees are amongst the January 2014 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk highest and cruiser fees amongst the lowest; a trend that cannot be fully explained by the “self-help” ethos within the cruiser fleet. Demographics Our membership is ageing as “baby boomers” reach retirement age and nearly a third of our membership is now in this bracket. When this category was instigated all those years ago nobody had foreseen the rise in the active life-span we “oldies” enjoy today. Unfortunately the discount we have offered for retired members is unsustainable. We have another problem at the other end of the age range. We have a thriving Cadet Training scheme but, after we have spent 10 years imbuing our youngsters with a love of sailing, few Cadets transfer into Young Adult membership. Families Although we have separate membership categories to differentiate between single and family members, as long as I have been a member, we have charged the same amount for each, thus keeping the single membership artificially high to sustain the low family rate. No other Club appears to have a similar practice, indeed many charge for each cadet member in addition to their parents. Revenue The Board and Management Committee are also alert to the need to generate more income to put the Club on a better financial footing for the future. This will be covered in more detail in the Hon. Treasurer’s Report. The Board and Management Committee have considered all the above problems, complexities and unfairnesses and reached the conclusion that they can only be addressed by the introduction of the proposed new Fee structure which is before you in Resolution 2. I urge you to vote in favour of acceptance. Thanks I would like to thank everyone who has given his or her time, resources or expertise to help the smooth running of the Club. I particularly wish to thank my fellow Directors for their support, enthusiasm and tenacity. They have attended and contributed in full at often lengthy Board meetings; all fully motivated by our joint objective to ensure the present well-being and future existence of our Club. We have one director, Rear Commodore Bryan Spencer, who is reluctantly stepping down from his role after several years. Bryan’s job takes him out of the country often and unpredictably but nevertheless he has been fully committed and determined not to become another mid-term casualty. Bryan will join me in the ranks of Vice Presidents next year. I thank him on behalf of you all. I must express my admiration and thanks to our Company Secretary, Rall Ball, for the immense work he does for the Club. He is a totally motivated, tireless and deeply knowledgeable “backroom boy”. He is the glue that holds the Club together. Thank you Ray and please look after yourself. The future There is every reason to be optimistic for the future of our Club. The new fee structure will be a solid foundation to build on. Doubtless there will be challenges to come but, with a strong Board supported and advised by an equally strong Management Committee, I firmly believe that the Club will be able to meet and overcome any challenges that a changing world can throw at us. Marconi SC Sailing Secretary Report 2013 Good morning everyone and it is my pleasure to present the Sailing Secretary Report for 2013. Given we are a sailing club, and a very active one at that, this is the best AGM report to have to present - however, it also presents some challenges – so I am going to start with two apologies. Firstly, I have endeavoured to cover the full range of sailing activities in 2013 but if I have missed something out – I am sorry. Secondly, an enormous number of people give up their time to support the wide variety of sailing activities that we all enjoy. Again, with apologies, I am not going to try and name everyone as I will only miss people out – but a huge thank you to you all. 2013 has been another very busy year for sailing activity across the club. In addition to individual sailing activity, the Cruiser Fleet organised a number of passage cruises this year to Brightlingsea, Heybridge, Tollesbury and Ipswich followed by the Orwell and Stour. The weather was mixed for some of the passages but the longer passage to Suffolk at least benefited from the positive summer when it arrived. A number of successful social events were also arranged including the Fitting Out Supper, a visit by Colne Yacht Club and the Cruiser Fleet AGM – all of which required the Bar Managers to do a full restock afterwards. Thanks go to Mark Foster, George Male and Roger Camp as Cruiser Fleet captains during the year. The Cruiser Fleet were also actively involved in racing with participation in East Coast Gaffers, BJRC, local regattas and offshore races. Among those who had successes in these events were Nick Hillman, Richard Roberts, Tom Clayton, John Littlewood, Dave Onyons, Peter Ward and their respective crews. Peter Ward and his crew also successfully completed the Fastnet which is a tremendous achievement. Thanks go to Peter for co- ordinating cruiser racing activities. We would also like to register a particular thanks to the many cruiser fleet members who supported the East Coast Piers Race and made this important event so successful – the safe running of this event depends very much on this support. Windsurfing members continued to be very active this year – and, as ever, were seen to venture out when the rest of us had retreated to the clubhouse to drink coffee. Some of the windsurfers have also entered into the world of cat sailing – presumably for when the wind is below a Force 6 – and they are welcome additions to those fleets. Dinghy cruises took place on the first Saturday of every month from March to October and continued to be very well attended. Local cruises ranged from trips to Maldon and to Mersea and all destinations in between. In June, Marconi hosted a visit from the UK Wayfarer’s Association with a passage cruise round to the Crouch, camping overnight in Burnham and returning the next day with a stop off at Thirslet for lunch. In May, the fleet travelled even further afield, trailing their boats down to the Solent – launching at Eastney, sailing through Langstone Harbour, round the top of Hayling Island and down through Chichester Harbour to Bosham and back. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk BLACKWATER & COLNE COORDINATED CRUISER EVENTS Q: What is it? A: It's about increasing participation in cruising. A group of cruising sailors from almost all the clubs on the Blackwater & Colne got together at the end of the 2013 season to see if it might be possible to organise joint events in 2014. The basis of the idea came from the fact that most of the clubs were organising cruises to the same destinations, so why not pool and share the organisational effort, whilst many of the clubs were turning out very small numbers on their cruises. Also, some clubs were only organising 'stay local' cruises whilst some of their members might have liked to cruise in company to cross channel ports. Two coordinated cruising events were decided upon and organisers came forward. These events now appear on the cruising calendars of many of the Blackwater & Colne Sailing Clubs. Any member, from any sailing club is very welcome to participate in any of the events. They are not races, they are most definitely cruises, but there could be fun prizes awarded by the organises. Information on how to participate will be circulated later both through navigans, on the club website and through the website of the Blackwater & Colne Open Sailing Series. Here's some info to whet your appetite. If you'd like to chat about the events than Peter Ward is the Marconi contact (Yes I know he's a racer, but these are definitely not races, Peter just has more info about them as he was one of the originators of the idea). May Bank Holiday Weekend Rally - Pursuit Date: Saturday 24th - Monday 26th May 2014 Organiser: Mel Daniels (WMYC) Rally Start: All Blackwater & Colne participants will rally at the Nass Beacon on Saturday morning 24th May. Rally Format: The rally will be conducted in the form of a pursuit. All participating boats must complete the registration form in the weeks prior to the event so that each boat can be allocated a start time. Individual clubs can use the event to award their own trophies and points. Boats will sail leaving Bench Head to port and North Eagle to starboard and will take their own finishing times at Harwich breakwater. The slower boats will start at least an hour after high water, which gives them time to get to Harwich just as the flood starts, and allows upriver boats to get to the Nass in time for their start time. Berths have already been booked for our sizeable fleet to enter Shotley marina on completion of the passage and these will be allocated to participating boats along with their start times. Entrance to the lock will be staggered, so that inside rafted boats are in position before their outside neighbours enter the marina. We're expecting a big turnout for this event. Saturday Evening in Shotley: The rally will hold an informal BBQ ashore at Shotley so boats participating in the rally should take along their own food, wine, seats, portable BBQ's and stands for the BBQs so as not to burn the grass. No doubt there will be other impromptu activities to keep everyone amused whilst the wine flows. Sunday & Monday : There will be a mini cruise organised for those rally participants able to stretch their time away from the Blackwater & Colne beyond the weekend, and more details will be available as we firm up the planning of this element shortly. One possible option is to cruise up to Lowestoft, whilst those needing to return to home waters can do so on Monday. Ostend Rally 15th August 2014 Date: Friday 15th August 2014 Organiser: Robin Impey (Colne YC) contact details to follow. Rally Start: All Blackwater & Colne participants will rally at Batemans Tower at - O400hrs - on Friday morning 15th August. Thursday Night at Brightlingsea before the Rally: Moorings will be available at Brightlingsea for boats arriving on Thursday evening. A water taxi / trot boat will be available on Thursday evening to deliver crew to and from the pontoon for a rally briefing in the Colne Yacht Club. Rally Format: The rally will be conducted in the form of a passage in company. It's aim is to provide support for everyone in the fleet wanting to hop across the channel for a summer adventure. Radio communication will be positively encouraged, so those with little experience of channel crossing can seek advice and support from the fleet members around. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Doreen Kirby On behalf of the family, I would like to say a big "Thank you" to all the Club members who attended Doreen`s funeral at the Southend Crematorium then afterwards at the reception held at the Chichester. Plus of course the many cards, letters, emails etc. of sympathy. The comments I made at the reception i.e. A LOVELY LADY - HER WONDERFUL SMILE - HER CONCERN Were comments made by her friends, I only repeated them - thank you so much Derek Kirby Happy Morning in Barbados Mike Duckmanton reports on the latest escapades of the yacht “Happy Morning” and her crew in the Caribbean… Ed We are sitting on the beach at the Babados Yacht Club resting after an action packed couple of weeks. We left Rodney Bay St Lucia on Friday 11 Jan to sail across to Barbados. The trip across was our worst. Two friends of David Onyons members of the Maldon Little Ships Club (MLSC) David and I are all experienced helms and we had a new friend with us who had never sailed a boat before although he had owned river boats back in the UK. The wind has been strong around St Lucia and Barbados for several weeks which has increased the wave heights so we had a rough crossing. Fortunately we were able to take it in turns to be ill or steer the boat. We finally arrived and anchored at Port St Charles Barbados at 4-30am and managed to sleep until we were able to visit customs and book ourselves into Barbados. During the trip one of David's friends stated that out of all his ocean experience including the Atlantic twice this was he worst ever trip. Later that morning we continued our journey to Carlisle Bay and anchored off shore at the Barbados Cruising Club. We rested for the next few days visiting Bridgetown to sight see and do some shopping and meeting up with friends at the Club where we had met and sailed against them. Other friends of David Onyons and his girl friend had travelled directly to Barbados. Unfortunately one friend Bill who sailed with us last year had travelled out a week before and had an unfortunate accident. He was found in the sea face down and unfortunately died. This has put a cloud over our adventure this year. We took part in the regatta on Friday 17th, Saturday 18th and Sunday 19th. The courses were on the west side of the island in waters which were much calmer than the seas on the east side. We managed an overal 2nd in our class but because there were only three in this class we looked at the times of other racing boats and were pleased with our overal performance. Monday 20 January was a rest day and a day for getting Happy Morning ready for the race around the island. On the day of the race, 21st January, we were up bright and early so we could load the crew on board. Our crew was made up with David Onyons Captain, myself first mate and foredeck, David Harris main trimmer, Simon Onyons genoa trimmer, Ian Gaskell 2nd genoa trimmer, Graham ex pilot and GP now our navigator, one ex Mount Gay Rum girl Belinda weight on the rail. Two crew members didn't turn up but we were lucky a Canadian Leon was standing on the shore and asked if he could join us, and it was sooner obvious he was an experienced racing sailer and now a new friendship is begin to form. We headed off northward to round the island clockwise. Along the west coast the conditions were very good, but that changed as we sailed round the north end avoiding reefs, no short cuts here. Turning south on the east side we had approximately 3 hours of hammering into Atlantic waves and strong winds. At east point we had to maintain a southerly course until clear of more reefs. At this point fast boats which started after us this being a form of pursuit race, came past, Idea a 70 footer and also a Volvo 70. You could hear their sheets groaning as they were eased as we all started to bear off and head west along the south coast. More reefs to avoid on the south west corner of the island and then a long run to the finish. The tall Hilton hotel near the finish line was a welcome land mark. Then the finish, and we had successfully and safely completed another Mount Gay Rum Round Barbados race. Congratulations amongst the crew and promises to do better next year. No rest the next day we were off for a Safari ride in a jeep around the island followed by the evening party and prize giving. This year year most of us were in bed before 1-00am. Simon Onyons had to get back to family and work so we have started to loose crew. Tomorrow Saturday we go and log out of the island with Customs etc and Sunday up early for the 18 hour or so trip back to St Lucia. For now another rum punch and enjoy the cool weather, yes the weather here is not as warm as usual. Mike Duckmanton February 2014 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Continuing Tale Of A Slow Meander Round The UK (part 1 of 2) THE "LARKS CONTINUE" OR "THE LEAVIN O BONNIE SCOTLAND" SUMMER 2013. It had become a bit of a tussle - stay or go - stay or go, still so much to see in Bonnie Scotland - this self centred debate swung back and forth until eventually I could stand it no longer and as we say in the "Sarf" "I ad a word wi me self". Look - I said, although you aren't getting any younger you are still relatively healthy and once you get round (the UK that is) if you want to come back you can - you've done it once you can do it again - blimey - look at Malcolm Robertson he does it nearly every year ! This seemed to settle the debate although the healthy bit struck home when I discovered a lump in my neck and on visiting the doc - she unhesitatingly referred me to Addenbrookes (again !) where the consultant said "oh we'd better cut it out there's a lot going on in the neck you know". A couple of scans latter there I was for the second year running being marked up with felt tip to ensure they applied the blade to the right part of my anatomy. I did start to wonder after being under the knife last year for a hernia op if these visits to Addenbrookes were to become an annual event as I gradually fell apart with age - but hey ho ! All this of course somewhat b - - - - -ed up my timescales to get South to Cardigan Bay in a nice leisurely way possibly detouring to Ireland along the way but let's look on the bright side - it was a very happy old sailor who received the news that what they excised from my person was nothing to be worried about and was just a fatty lump - and as they said at the time "better out than in". Nothing but praise for Addenbrookes - all done on the NHS with superlative care both in practice and care of the individual - in the four clinic's I attended didn't wait more than 10 minutes beyond my appointment time and on the day of the op the consultant even phoned home to my wife to say "he's OK and all went well but as we operated late in the day he's a bit dozy we'll keep him in overnight, pick him up tomorrow". She said" he's alway's like that anyway but ok, thanks for phoning". So what with all that going on little "Edal" wasn't launched till 21st June - and sat on her mooring at Barcaldine till the op on 11th July so we didn't leave our Scottish home of the last two seasons till 22nd July. The plan was to get to Aberdovey in Cardigan Bay were my brother lives - to lift out in a small boatyard across the river at Ynyslas - pronounced "Inislas". The passages between Barcaldine and Aberdovey would (all going well) be day sails - potential ports of call and distances would be as follows, Easdale - overnight at anchor, distance from Barcaldine 21nm. Crinan canal - overnight at Cairnbaan roughly half way through, distance 13nm to entry of canal. Tarbert - East Loch Tarbert, marina with pontoons, distance 10nm from canal exit. Larg's Marina, distance 23nm. Troon Marina - distance 17nm. Girvan - harbour with pontoons, distance 20nm. Glenarm, Northern Ireland - old harbour with pontoons, distance 41nm Bangor - marina with pontoons, distance 22nm. Arglass - old harbour with pontoons, distance 35nm. Peel on Isle of Man - pontoons in harbour, distance 34nm. Port St Mary, Isle of Man - berth against harbour wall, distance 12nm. Holyhead - marina, distance 46nm. Porth Dinllaen - anchorage, distance 28nm. Pwllheli - marina with pontoons, distance 33nm. Aberdovey - harbour wall or visitor buoy, distance 29nm. You can see - no great long tiring passages in any of the days - fitting with the ships established principles of sailing being fun, visiting new places, tieing up in the evenings for a decent meal and a glass of red, enjoying a good book in the cockpit, maybe stay a day or two if it's nice - all hopefully after a light zephyr has breathed on the sails to keep to the skippers immaculately prepared passage plan. Minimum distance to be covered at sea 384nm, not including the Crinan canal, nine land miles in length. Would be singlehanded most of the way except for the legs between Troon and Peel where John another aged sailor would join me for the trip across to Northern Ireland then down the Irish Sea. There's also at least nine destinations where if the forecast looked inclement for a few days I could go home quite easily. In practice I went home twice once because of "home stuff" to do and once because the It was a beautiful early morning as I left the weather looked poor. head of Loch Creran and the moorings. BARCALDINE TO EASDALE 22ND JULY. The ebb to take me south would start after HW Oban at 0610 and it was with a sad heart I dropped the mooring line in Loch Creran - what larks I had had going from here round Ardnamurchan to those wonderful anchorages in points north - but for now - here's to the new. February 2014 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The wind was forecast to be light so motorsailed main and engine low rev's out of the loch and past Oban - with tide keeping our SOG respectable, we had covered the 21nm to Easdale by 1040 - 4hrs 18 minutes later. If you know this neck of the woods you might ask why Easdale and not Puilladobhrain as a destination - everybody wants to go to Puilladobhrain don't they ? Well I just fancied, particularly if I never come this way again the more "gritty" attractions of Easdale and it's industrial past. You wouldn't think it now but once this was one of Britian's biggest quarries for slate, shipping it all over the world from it's pier in the narrows between Sail and Easdale islands and for a West Midland "Black Country Boy" a bit of industrial heritage is just the thing for a bit of exploring ashore. The Island, hollowed out by the quarrying into huge square pits, flooded by "The Great Storm of 1881" which all but ended quarrying on the islands and wrecked the local economy so that now the wee Edal (middle of Pic) from Easdale Island, slate remnants in foreground - ruined pier to right. squares of hooses facing each other across their communal greens are inhabited by a mix of locals and holiday homes. It's an evocative sort of place with a nice little local museum and scatterings of it's industrial past. There's also a wonderful community centre so the locals obviously think a lot of their "hollowed out" island. We (Edal and me) had picked up the only visitors buoy in the bay between the islands and after my history lesson ashore settled down to an evening meal and some planning for the easy passage to Crinan early tomorrow. CRINAN TO CAIRNBAAN IN THE CANAL, 23RD JULY. It was a peacful night at Easdale - another early start at 0648 to make sure we had the ebb to get through both Northern entrance to Easdale. Sound of Luing and Dhorus Mhor - know by the locals as "Big Doris". There's loads written about both of these so I won't go on - but safe to say it needs planning for tide and safe water. As it dawned the morning was overcast and "driech" grey, grey, grey in a way that only the "hielans" can sometimes be. Little wind, smooth surface to the sea until the narrow channel by the lighthouse appeared and the surface became troubled, smooth here, wee whirlpools there, tiny wavelets over there and patches of bubbling water which twitched the boats steering and had me correcting to keep her on the straight and narrow as we sped at over 8kts SOG past the lighthouse and into the Sound. Completely on our own in a rather wierd quiet grey morning - on the boat no noise, little movement - almost like standing still, till you looked around and saw how far we'd come from the lighthouse. Passing by the Gulf of Corryvreckan, as we approached Dhorus Mhor the morning brightened, speed had slowed in the wider waters of the Sound and after a slight change of course to head towards Big Doris - the speed increased again as Doris sucked us in then spat us out towards Crinan. Little whirlpools on the water as we approach the lighthouse on Fladda. Inner harbour at Easdale The entry into Crinan is a personal milestone for this is one of the canals Dad had some responsibilty for when we lived in Scotland over fifty years ago, canals don't really change that much and whilst I couldn't remember every detail - it looked pretty much as I remember it. February 2014 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk We were in the sea lock by 0912 having left Easdale at 0648 - 2hrs 24minutes for the 13nm distance. It's when you get into inland waterways that you start to understand why people cruise there - no tides, little wind effect, easy slooooow pace if you want it. The challenge though if you singlehand is the locks - particularly going uphill. Unlike the Caledonian where the locks are all operated for you the Crinan maintains a thing called "assisted passage" which means if you go through short handed they will operate the locks for you and take your lines unless they see you going through with a couple of other boats who being yachties all muck in opening gates etc - the staff will then stand back and let you get on Edal in Crinan sea lock with it. At least though one way or another you know you will get some help so just have to figure out a routine of handing up your bow and stern line, keeping the boat steady in the lock and getting the lines back ready for the next time. I had two 15mtr lines which I'd used in the Caley - put a loop secured with a bowline at one end of each rope made them off fore and aft with the ends draped over the lifelines. As I came into the lock the loop on the end of my boathook for the stern line was passed up to a willing helper and dropped over a bollard - brought the boat to a halt shortened the stern line then went forward to pass up the bow loop and stood by to shorten either line as she went up in the world - it worked pretty well. I just made sure I was last boat of three going into the lock - felt under less pressure that way and stayed away from the turbulence of the sluices as the lock filled. Going downhill was much easier - Bollards on your eyeline, with the boathook you could slip the stern line over as you went into the lock - the bow line passed ashore to a helper then sit on the coach roof with both lines in hand as she went down. Night's berth at Cairnbaan, toilets and showers nearby - it's all downhill from here ! Edal in the basin at Ardrishaig waiting for the sea lock into Loch Fyne. David Lakin February 2014 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk th Minutes of Cruiser Fleet AGM 16 Nov 2013 Apologies D Gardener, R Hadley, L Smith, F Burgess, A Samuel, A Davison M Turner M Bates Introduction Roger Camp explained that Mark Foster had stepped down as fleet captain mid season due to pressure of work and that he had taken over in the interim but was happy to stand. Review of 2013 Brightlingsea some dodgy cider was consumed. Heybridge saw terrible weather, wind and rain but it dried out for the barbecue. Tollesbury contrasted with lovely weather and good swimming. Ipswich 18 boats enjoyed the maritime festival which was lively with good fireworks. This was followed by a good week on Orwell and Stour. Brightlingsea. Only 2 boats made it due to awful weather. Review of Racing Peter Ward reported a busy season. Club boats participated in East Coast Gaffers, BJRC, local regattas and offshore EAORA and RORC. MSC successes; Nick Hillman 1st in Penny Hole race, 1st East Coast race and 3rd under 25ft in Maldon regatta. Richard Roberts and Tom Clayton 1st Frday night series and Doctor Shield. Richard Roberts had considerable success in BJRC. 1st MSC boat in BCOSS series and series winner. John Littlewood 1st MSC boat in passage race. Dave Onyons won Steeple Bay trophy. Peter Ward and crew won Buckley Goblets race in EAORA and completed Fastnet with Derek Brown, Tom Clayton, Rorie Ash and qualification assistance from Mike Turner and Andy Fowler. Election of Fleet Captain, Vice Captain and Race Officer Roger Camp, George Male and Peter Ward elected. Moorings Plea made to prepare moorings for inspection on pallet with anchors facing forward left and right, ground chain in middle and chain piled on top to facilitate laying out on hard. Peter Clayton reported no breakaways this year. As most come from chafe on mooring strops these should have protection. Light chain protected by tube is ideal. He explained the moorings allocation as, when members leave everyone else moves up the row. He stressed that the wearing of bouyancies for mooring duty is essential and a supply is available. Winter Storage, Cruiser Park, Haul out and Launch List. Neil Pembleton has been cruiser park co-ordinator for the past 5 years and is now standing down. Sue Arnold as new co-ordinator made a plea for people to ensure that their boats are clearly identifiable during the lay up in order to compile effective records. Peter Clayton talked about effect of the storm and advised that recommendations for the future will be discussed. Scrubbing Post Richard Roberts should be contacted for bookings. It was suggested that in addition a list also be kept on the board in order for people to make effective planning. Similarly the mast derrick needs to be prebooked. Tractors and Equipment The club now has a pressure washer available to speed up procedure. All equipment will be out of action during Jan. Chain, Anodes, Boots and Gloves. Frank Burgess has an ample supply of chain, anodes and shackles available at cost price from January. Also safety wellies. ECPR Peter Clayton to recruit. Must have a radio that works on M2 and preferably a mobile. Clive Shenton reported that the event this year sailed the full course in good weather and generated £2100 to Cirdan Trust on the day and £400 to air ambulance. Very successful event and Clive thanked all mother boats. Next year 6th July Security No major thefts but some petty vandalism. There is a growing problem with letting non members in. Fisherman frequently use the site and may have access to club house if it is not shut. Be vigilant. Mast derrick had 120 feet rope cut off it. Hose fittings taken off hard. Bar Opening Lizzie was thanked for running the bar on Sundays. Derek Gardener suggested a programme for organising bar opening on Friday evenings when tides are favourable and suggested some supplementary ideas for the light evenings. He will organise a rota and Bob Godbold volunteered to run the bar one Friday a month. 2014 Programme Sat 15th Feb bowling evening at Chelmsford Sat 26th April Fitting out supper 24th 25th 26th May Brightlingsea . Bank Holiday weekend. HT 21.30 with barbeque at St Osyth 7th 8th June Colne YC visit. BJRC Race with barbeque 14th/15th Heybridge Watercress run. 5th/6th July ECPR 12th/13th July Tollesbury. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk April Issue copy deadline: Saturday 15th March Club Notices Commodore I am pleased to report that in early February we took delivery of our new support boat, part funded by a £10k grant from Sport England. Hopefully by now you will all have received your 2014 membership packs which are full of useful information, including the 2014 sailing programme. Michaela Dowley Commodore Club Secretary CONDITION OF FIELDS The wet weather continues at the time of writing and our fields are getting more waterlogged. (We are still better off than some sailing clubs which have been under several feet of water.) Until the fields dry out please be extremely careful where you take your car. Bogged down vehicles make a mess of the ground, leaving ruts that people will be tripping over all season. Don’t think you are safe because you have all-wheel drive. 4 x 4s on soft ground just dig four holes instead of two. It is hoped that the fields will have dried out by the start of the season but after one of the wettest winters on record that cannot be guaranteed. Please park wisely whilst the ground is so soft. If you need to get your boat past the cordoned off areas please contact Murray Bates ) in advance. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Dinghy/Catamaran Park Space Allocation Process If you are buying, selling or changing a dinghy or catamaran dinghy, it is in your interest to follow this process so that you can be contacted in an emergency about your boat and to avoid the possibility of being charged for a boat which is no longer your property. To this end please ensure that your boat is located in its allocated position. The record on Medusa is the Master Reference List of all dinghies and catamaran dinghies registered with the Club. Dinghy Park spaces are given an identifier of DP followed by three numeric characters and similarly Catamaran Dinghy park spaces using CP for the initial characters. These locations correspond with physical locations at the Club. The Master Reference List on Medusa is maintained by the Membership Registrar, Dinghy and Catamaran Dinghy Park co- ordinators using the process below. SPACE ALLOCATION FOR NEW MEMBER AND NEW BOAT(S) 1. Membership application received by Membership Registrar who checks information and creates the Boat record assigning a Z**nnn space location. 2. Membership Registrar contacts the relevant Park Co-ordinator and requests the space allocation. 3. The relevant Park Co-ordinator assigns the space and informs the Membership Registrar. 4. Membership Registrar updates the space location on the Boat record 5. On completion of the membership acceptance process, Membership Registrar informs the member of the space location(s) and member is free to bring the dinghy(ies) and/or catamaran dinghy(ies) to the Club to store in the assigned location(s). SPACE ALLOCATION FOR EXISTING MEMBER AND NEW BOAT(S) 1. Member notifies Membership Registrar of details of the new boat who checks information and creates the Boat record assigning a Z**nnn space location. 2. Membership Registrar contacts the relevant Park Co-ordinator and requests the space allocation. 3. The relevant Park Co-ordinator assigns the space and informs the Membership Registrar. 4. Membership Registrar updates the space location on the Boat record 5. On payment of any additional fees etc. Membership Registrar informs the member of the space location(s) and member is free to bring the dinghy(ies) and/or catamaran dinghy(ies) to the Club to store in the assigned location(s). RE-ALLOCATION OF SPACE ALLOCATION FOR AN EXISTING MEMBER AND EXISTING BOAT. 1. Member discusses and agrees with the relevant Park Co-ordinator the re-location. 2. The relevant Park Co-ordinator informs the Membership Registrar of the space being vacated and the new space location. 3. The Membership Registrar amends the Boat record to show the new location. 4. The Membership Registrar confirms the change to the member and the relevant Park Co-ordinator. SALE/TRANSFER OF BOAT FROM ONE MEMBER TO ANOTHER MEMBER. (SEE CLUB BY LAW 3.1.4 AND 3.1.4.1) 1. The selling owner informs the Membership Registrar of the sale providing the details of the new owner. 2. The Membership Registrar confirms that the buyer has paid the relevant fees. 3. The Membership Registrar uses the “Transfer” facility in Medusa to update the Seller and Buyer Boat Records Records 4. The Membership Registrar confirms the transfer to both members, the relevant Park Co-ordinator and the Honorary Treasurer, who will refund any fees as appropriate. SALE/TRANSFER OF BOAT FROM ONE MEMBER TO A NON MEMBER. (SEE CLUB BY LAW 3.1.4 AND 3.1.4.1) 1. The selling owner informs the Membership Registrar of the sale providing the details of the new owner. 2. The Membership Registrar seeks confirmation from the relevant Park Co-ordinator that the boat has been removed from the Club site. March 2014 Navigans 5

The record is not deleted so that the history remains remains on on the the Medusa records. 4. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Continuing Tale Of A Slow Meander Round The UK (part 2 of 2) EAST LOCH TARBERT AND LARGS. 24TH AND 25TH JULY. Came out of the sea lock at 1201 into a good 8 to 12kt southerly breeze - which after a quiet time in the canal - was just what the doctor ordered ! It would mean tacking back and forth across Loch Fyne to get to Tarbert but who cared - we could sail and we only had 10nm to go. Arrived and tied up on the pontoons at Tarbert at 1525. What made the sail down Loch Fyne memorable though was the appearance of Waverley coming out of Tarbert on her way up Loch Fyne. No walk down memory lane for a child growing up in Glasgow in the 1950's could exclude the memory of a trip "doon the watter" on The "paddlers" Waverley and Jeanie Deans or later on the first Queen Mary. We went on both Waverley and Queen Mary - Mom, Dad and me from the Broomielaw in Glasgow at different times over the years to Tighnabruaich and other ports of call in the Firth of Clyde - these delightful old boats provided an escape to paradise for thousands of Glaswegians every summer down to the delights of the beautiful Kyles of Bute and sometimes further. The old Queen is lying mouldering in the Medway awaiting funding to restore her - but here is Waverley still plying her trade and as beautiful as ever. The old Queen will hopefully be restored she's a historic ship in being one of the worlds first passenger ships to be turbine driven and of course for famously having given up her name to Cunard for the later big liner to be called Queen Mary (she became QM2) then regaining her original name when the Cunarder was laid up in America. As nice as Tarbert was I was keen to go the following morning as I had a further date with memory lane and a Knickerbocker Glory in Nardini's Cafe at Largs. The tides in the big waters of the Firth of Clyde and where Loch Fyne widens are fairly benign the only part where I wanted to go with flow was the last part of the passage between the Cumbraes and the SP co a mainland so we left at 0938 which would allow us the last of the flood up to Largs. The day was bright and we had a good breeze until we turned round the southern tip of the Isle of Bute where the wind died and it started to rain. In fact it was very odd because the surface of the sea became very still, wind died, but it absolutely bucketed down for about 15 minutes , greatly reducing visibilty until between the Cumbraes. From the Lakin family archive Mom and me at Tighnabruaich the old Queen Mary in the background around 1960. Motoring on through Cumbrae Pass Waverley again hove in view - this time bound for Millport, for an old girl she certainly gets about. There is a little sideline to this story apologies if you've heard it before - but when Carole and I bought Edal, we'd made the offer, it had been accepted and we knew she was ours - her previous owners kept her at Wolverstone on the Orwell - we walked down the pontoon the better to view our new boat and to marvel at her lines - like you do - and with our backs to the river talking, after a while I heard this beat, beat, beat of the noise of her paddles coming back to me from over the years and without turning round to look I said to Carole - I know that's Waverley - and sure enough it was. We'd covered the 22nm to Largs marina in a little under five hours arriving at 1432 and found the marina a big impersonal rock wall of a place - can't actually put my finger on it but I just didn't like it - the guy's in the office were fine, the toilets and showers were too - wasn't too expensive - maybe it was all the jinormous boats - but then I've been in places with them before - strange - just didn't like it. So decided to move on to Troon next day which mean't I had to walk into town to Nardini's for my Knickerbocker Glory that afternoon - I can hereby say Nardini's did not disappoint the KG was fabulous. March 2014 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Nardini's in Largs is somewhere, everybody but everybody who visits Largs over the years would eventually gravitate to - to sit in the Art Deco spendour and sample the delights of their ice cream or just "tak a wee scone tae their efternoon tea". I only got my KG back then if I'd been a very good little boy but today I felt I deserved it again after all these years. Sitting in Nardini's the years between seemed insignificant and my overwhelming feeling was of being happy were I was - like being at home - despite the 50 or more years between visits - I also felt grateful - grateful for the parents who brought me here and for the love and memories they gave me. I could be accused of being a soppy old sod ! TROON 26TH JULY. This next leg, small though it was at just 17nm and under four hours duration seemed a bit of a watershed. Most of the way round (the UK) there'd been a "voyage of discovery" excitement to each days passage. Since entering the Crinan canal emotionally, because of my family history it had been in the familiar territory of "memory lane". Like most people I'm very happy with the familiar and would not have missed the days of retracing childhood steps. The "memory lane" phase though sort of dulled the tingle of excitement that can be had when venturing into pastures new - now though I would be moving south and starting out of the Firth of Clyde of my childhood. The passage to Troon was initally a slow motorsail then a brisk sail with full main and genoa of 18nm which brought me into Troon harbour by about 1445 - aaah this is more like it ! An old harbour with a very sheltered marina in it's far corner - a "comfy" sort of place. Here I would stay till August 5th when John would join me for the passsages south - I would use the time by doing a few remedials on the boat, finish off my book and then spend some time at home. It had only been five days since leaving Loch Creran, it seemed longer, I hadn't come very far south but the difference in the time to get home compared to being north of Oban couldn't be more different. The train to Paisley 30 minutes, bus to Glasgow airport 35 minutes, Easy Jet to Stansted about an hour - ok you have to wait around in the airport but when I came back to the boat I left home about half six in the morning (I live about 30mins from Stansted) and was back on the boat just before midday - terrific ! My cockpit reading by the way in these five days was Admiral Sandy Woodwards memoirs of the Falklands Task Force - quite revealing of the internal emotions of an outwardly hard bitten commander as his men die around him and what a close run thing the campaign was. One small tale which would interest men from Marconi was of the British warship HMS Brilliant. She left Gibraltar with a Marconi man still on board (having been kidnapped) working on the Sea Wolf weapons systems radar - this man, David Brean was described by the captain of Brilliant as having a deep working knowledge of missile computer technology. He became on the trip south to Ascension and then on to the Falklands a key part of the warships team despite being a civilian. In the defence of the landings at San Carlos Water, Brilliant's Sea Wolf wiring was damaged and at night as Brilliant was going round to King George Bay to insert an SAS team David Brean got to work to rewire and reprogramme Sea Wolf. At length and I quote from the book, he said to the Captain "we have a problem with the radar antenna up the mast" without a thought for the knifing wind and the cold rain not to mention Mr Brean was not in the Navy the Captain said "better get up there then" David Brean apparently gulped then said "OK Sir and proceeded to go up the mast in the middle of the night to fix the antenna - - "first class man" said Captain Coward "best after sales service you can imagine" The following morning morning HMS Brilliant reported one of her Sea Wolf systems completely operable again and that the man from Marconi was working on the other. Although it was gripping stuff I would not finish the book before going home and I would not pick it up again till the longer passage to Holyhead from the wonderful Isle of Man - an island beloved of the TT enthusiast Murray Bates - in the next episode of "Continuing Larks". David Lakin March 2014 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk May Issue copy deadline: Saturday 19th April BLUES AND BLUEGRASS BAND MAY17TH (open pay) EVENING Club Notices Commodore By the time you read this edition of Navigans the season will be well under way - I hope as many of you as possible manage to get out on the water this year. Don’t forget the sailing sub committee have put together a packed sailing calendar this year with something to suit everyone. Hopefully you will have all seen the handy guide to sailing at MSC, a real must read for members old and new to find out what Club organised activities are on offer throughout the year. One of our first events includes the Sprint 15 Open on the 12th-13th April - anyone with a Sprint 15 is encouraged to register for the event. Volunteers are also needed so if you are able to assist with race box, ‘trolley dollies,’ support boat crew, bar staff etc… please get in touch with Kevin Dowley, Cat fleet captain. Date for your diary - Saturday 17th May - MSC Open Day. This is when we open the gates for visitors to see what a wonderful Club we have. We need your help promoting the day and spreading the word, with posters available soon. An open day requires a huge number of volunteers, from welcoming at the gate to taking visitors out for a sail and helping with the evening BBQ. Please let Graham Cross, Rear Commodore Events know if you can help out. There is camping available and of course the bar will be open! Moving away from sailing, I would like to thank to all those who turned out to the recent working parties in early March - this year the weather was on our side and we managed to get a huge amount done both inside and outside. Apologies for the slightly sad note to finish on but many of you will have seen that Tony Benn, our Club President since 2001 sadly passed away on 14th March 2014. You will find an obituary in later pages of this edition of Navigans. A letter of condolence has been sent to the family on behalf of MSC and you will be pleased to know that a Club representative has been invited to attend the funeral being held at Westminster Abbey on 27th March. Michaela Dowley Commodore Tony Benn Tony Benn died aged 88 on Friday 14th March at his home in west London. He had been President of Marconi Sailing Club since 2001. The Benn family have been our friends and neighbours ever since the sailing section of Marconi Athletic & Social Club moved to Stansgate from Heybridge in the late 1960s. No doubt newspapers, magazines and historians will devote many column-inches to the life and career of Tony Benn but the notes below attempt to illustrate the connection between the name of Wedgewood Benn and Stansgate. Tony Benn (until 1973 Anthony Wedgewood Benn) had a long if controversial parliamentary career lasting from 1950 to 2001. He stood down from Parliament in 2001 “to spend more time on politics”. Those who are old enough will remember him as ‘the reluctant peer’ when he inherited the title of 2nd Viscount Stansgate from his late father in 1960 (William Wedgewood Benn, 1st Viscount Stansgate). At that time peers could not renounce peerages and April 2014 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk remain in the House of Commons. The passing of the Peerage Act in 1963 allowed Tony Benn to be re-elected as an MP. The title of Viscount Stansgate still exits and is inherited by his eldest son Stephen who is now 3rd Viscount Stansgate. Amongst his ministerial positions Tony Benn was Postmaster General (1964-1966). At that time I was a teenage trainee technician on the GPO (Post Office Telephones). I like to think that it gave him added confidence in his role to know that a youthful Ray Ball was on his team! I and other Club members met Tony and Caroline Benn at Stansgate many years ago. They were a very pleasant couple. At that time he was a minister and asked for permission for a helicopter to land on our field to pick him up the following day. Ray Ball Club Secretary STONE WATERSPORTS CLUB – EUROPEAN SKI RACING CUP – 26/27 APRIL IMPORTANT NOTICE FOR ANYONE SAILING PAST STONE THAT WEEKEND Stone Watersports Club will be hosting a European Ski Racing Cup meeting on the weekend of Saturday 26th and Sunday 27th April. The main racing will be on Sunday 27th April between 10:00 and 14:00 but there will be boats and skiers out practicing at other times. The racing will take place in the main channel which is why the event has been organised for early season. There will be safety boats around the course and Nigel Harmer the River Bailiff has been consulted. The ski racing boats are seriously fast and the dangers to comparatively slow moving sailing boats crossing the course are obvious. If you are in the area please be advised and directed by the safety boats. We have a good rapport with Stone Watersports Club and they are very good at avoiding arranging events on ECPR weekend so please cooperate with them if you happen to be sailing in the area. As far as MSC racing is concerned we have the Figure of Eight Race and Spring Points 7 on the Sunday neither of which need go anywhere near Stone. EARLY SEASON WARNING As I write this the sun is shining, the tulips are out and spring has (hopefully) arrived. After the rain we have had this winter it is guaranteed that the water will be wet but also, on a more serious note, for the early part of the season at least the water will be very cold. It takes the water a long time to warm up. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius. Even if it is warm ashore make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the wind chill. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm which is not only safer but more fun. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk THANK YOU ALL! Splitting into two groups made a real difference, allowing us to focus on the needs of different sailors, very positive. The new grant-aided RIB (‘Greygoose’) was a great asset for the training. In the morning, Bryan helped Group 1 to have a think about the conditions (wind and tide) and how they'd affect the sailing. Then they rehearsed 'how to tack' on the shore (thanks to David for his great help :-) ). Sometimes it seems easier not to bother with dagger grip, 'superman' and changing hands after tacking... but it really will make a big difference as the wind gets up, or as you want to sail faster. And remember, in a boat like a Pico you ALWAYS tack facing forwards. Then Group 1 went out and practised their skills just off the hard. Group 2 crossed the river (wasn't the tide strong?) and sharpened their technique: some focused on gybing, and others on improving their upwind sailing. Remember, upwind sailing ('close-hauled') is all about pulling the sails in close and pointing the boat so that the sails just completely fill with wind (don't flap at the front). If you can do this, then (if it's at all windy) the sail will make lots of sideways 'tipping' force which you will have tobalance with your weight. To do this, you need to get your feet under the toestraps, get your bum up on the side of the boat, and probably even lean backwards ('hike out')... and then you need to steer the boat carefully (small tiller movements) so the boat doesn't tip up too far but the sails don't start to flap. This takes practice to do well! And if you find you're having to sit in the middle of the boat to stop it tipping (or 'heeling') towards you, then probably you haven't sheeted in enough, or you're pointing into the wind. Have a look through some of the lessons from previous sail training sessions to see some other clues :-). They're here:http://www.marconi-sc.org.uk/61E54/Members_Area/Cadets/Sail_Training.aspx In the afternoon we did some racing, over a very short course just off the hard... I hope you enjoyed it! A key part of racing is the start, and it was great to see how much your starts improved as we went on. Graham very kindly took some video with the club’s new RYA-helped GoPro camera, which we watched for a while in the training room. I'll put some clips on Dropbox and send out the links to everyone who put their email address on the registration forms, enjoy! That's it for now... next session is Saturday 3rd May (only 2 weeks' time), and there's camping at the club that night. The weather will OF COURSE be warm, sunny with a lovely breeze*... see you there! (* Probably) John Nickalls MSC Cadet Coordinator Cat Fleet The season is now under way. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk LAierrTM Sprint 15 Marconi SC Sprint 15 TT - 12th/13th April 2014 In unprecedented mild weather for April, 17 visiting sailors joined 6 of Marconi SC’s finest for the first Traveller event and first Sprint 15 TT event of the 2014 summer season. Saturday morning started with promise of a consistent breeze that did not disappoint as the day went on. Along with the rain staying at bay for all three races (although the weatherman did promise sunshine throughout!) the over-cast conditions were good for competitive racing in April. In Race One, the majority of the fleet opted to start on port with one or two boats on starboard creating an interesting dynamic on the start line, that resulted in many boats getting a poor start. The two Sport mode boats, Kevin Dutch and Paul Grattage battled it out between them all the way round the course with the rest of the pack led by Stuart Snell, Jenny Ball, Chris Tillyer and Dave Ball chasing behind. At the leeward mark, the fleet split to different sides of the river for the upwind leg which was against the tide – resulting in multiple changes of positions within the fleet. After three laps, Kevin finished just seven seconds in front of Paul – but on handicap Paul Craft took first place and Jenny Ball took second place, with Kevin and Paul taking third and fourth respectively. Down the pack, increasing breeze caught a few boats of guard resulting in a few unplanned swims! Race Two saw the breeze easing off; again with the majority of the fleet on port dodging those boats that chose to start on starboard. The ebbing tide had strengthened, combined with the drop in breeze making rounding the windward mark a bit more challenging for a number of boats in the fleet and a few mishaps occurred! Kevin Kirby had a near perfect start which gained him an early lead, chased by Dave Ball and Stuart Snell, in amongst the two Sport boats. At the leeward mark, the fleet again split for the beat enabling Erling Holmberg and Jenny Ball to gain ground over the fleet leaders; a great tactical choice by both boats. After a closely fought second lap, Kevin Kirby held on to his lead, closely followed by Jenny Ball and David Ball in second and third place. By Race Three, the wind had shifted favouring a starboard start at the outer distance mark. Kevin and Paul struggled to pull clear of the fleet to start with, but on the second lap, with increasing wind favouring the Race Mode boats both managed to pull out a clear enough lead to put in a first and second on handicap. Jenny Ball, Dave Ball and Paul Craft came in third, fourth and fifth. After nearly five hours of exhilarating racing, the fleet and safety boats returned to shore for a well-deserved slap up dinner, a few (too many?) pints and a chat over the racing in the bar. Sunday morning saw the weatherman’s predictions came true – glorious April sunshine greeted the fleet as they stirred into consciousness. Along with the solar rays, a decent breeze rose throughout the morning, presenting near perfect conditions for the now legendary long distance race around Osea and Northey Islands. The Race Officer set the usual figure of eight course around the two islands, with an additional lap round Osea Island to ensure a proper long distance race given the favourable wind conditions. The fleet set off in a good breeze and with a fair tide but shortly after the start, the wind began to be more fickle with patches of light winds and stronger winds lasting throughout the whole race. Dave Ball led round the turning point at Northey Island followed by Stuart Snell and Jenny Ball, with a gap to Pete Richardson and the rest of the fleet. However, on the run back past Osea Island, the wind filled in bringing the Sport boats and Pete Richardson and Chris Tillyer up to the front of the pack with a tightly fought leg to the turning mark. By now the tide had turned, making for a tougher beat against the tide back past Osea Island. This leg saw Paul Grattage extend his lead over the water and the front of the fleet spread out with Stuart Snell taking the lead for the una rigs. Stuart maintained his lead to take overall race win, with Paul Grattage second on handicap and Dave Ball and Jenny Ball in third and fourth respectively. After a very enjoyable weekend of racing, Jenny Ball took the overall win with Paul Grattage in second and Kevin Dutch in thi rd. A big thank you to everyone involved in organising the event and to those who travelled from all over the UK to take part in the first event of the season! Jenny Ball May 2014 Navigans 7
