Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk July Issue copy deadline: Saturday 14th June Club Notices Commodore I hope many of you were able to come down and enjoy the Open day held on 17th May. Having had a chance to reflect on the day I have to say how immensely proud I am of how we put the Club on show, and I think visitors and Club members alike had a really great day. Graham Cross and team did a fantastic job of co-ordinating everything but I am always amazed at how well the Club can pull together to make things happen so smoothly – thank you to all involved. To start with the event was widely advertised and the site was well prepared – it looked clean, tidy and well maintained. There was something for everyone with sailing, Pimms, bouncy castle, kids activities plus a great evening of food and entertainment. All comments I heard from visitors were positive – 'such a friendly place', 'everyone is so nice', 'what a great Club.' I am pleased to report that in May MSC finally received formal confirmation that we have achieved RYA Training Centre Status – you should see our new Training Centre flag regularly flying at the weekend. Watch out for more news on upcoming power boat training courses. I’ve been asked to mention the sterling efforts of Mick Richardson who has worked recently to fix our sewerage system. Mick has spent a number of weeks on a Wednesday getting up close and personal with the system and has installed a new sludge pump allowing us to get back up and running. Efforts well above and beyond the call of duty – thank you Mick! Michaela Dowley Commodore Club Secretary LIFEJACKETS – USELESS UNLESS WORN Transferring to and from a tender is probably the time when yachtsmen are most at risk; particularly in the MSC moorings which can be choppy and subject to a fast tide. A recent incident served to illustrate this risk and the need to be wearing a lifejacket. The member involved was unlucky to end up in the drink but fortunate that he was seen and an MSC RIB was covering cadet activities nearby and other help was at hand. This may not always be the case particularly if sailing midweek. Take care when doing familiar tasks which you have done dozens of times without mishap before. (By the way, when did you last check/service your lifejacket? Does it hold air for 24 hours, if automatic is the actuator in date and the CO2 bottle intact and not corroded? Instructions for servicing lifejackets are usually displayed on or in the jacket.) KILL CORDS – USELESS UNLESS USED PROPERLY Nearly all outboards whether big or small are now fitted with kill cords. Please use your kill cord attached to your person and not attached to the boat. ADDERS Adders have been seen on site. There is nothing unusual in this; we have always lived with them and them with us. However care is needed when on site particularly in long grass or when feeling under a boat or cover. Children should be warned. Obviously if a snake is seen it should be left alone. VISITORS Members are reminded that ALL visitors to the Club must be signed in the Visitors Book. The Visitors Book is kept with the other MSC documentation at the far end of the upstairs lounge. Members are also reminded that any visitor is only permitted to visit the Club three times in any 12 month period (bylaw 1.1.13.3 refers). If they like sailing from Stansgate that much they are welcome to apply for membership. ‘REGULAR’ VISITORS Following on from the above, if you bring a visitor regularly to the Club perhaps to crew on your dinghy, catamaran or cruiser that person must apply for membership. June 2014 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The main source of revenue for the Club is membership fees and subscriptions. It is by ensuring an adequate income that the Club can pay its bills, maintain the existing facilities and provide improvements. It is only fair that all people using the site pay their fair share for the enjoyment of the facilities provided. These facilities, of course, include the upkeep of the approach road and the site itself. STANSGATE ROAD JUNCTION I find that turning right out of Stansgate Road towards Steeple is a worry due to the hedges and the speed of the traffic. The introduction of a 40mph speed limit may have helped a bit. The hedges mean it is necessary to partially pull out into Bradwell Road to have a sufficiently clear view to the left whilst at the same time hoping to hear any traffic approaching from the right. I have written to Essex County Council Highways Department to ask that they arrange for the hedges to be cut back on the left to provide a clear view and that the height of the hedge on the right be reduced so at least the tops of cars and the heads of motorcyclists can be seen. This was done a few years back to good effect. My letter would be reinforced if other members also wrote to ECC. The address is: Essex County Council Highways County Hall Market Road Chelmsford CM1 1QH Alternatively problems can be reported on the Essex County Council Highways website. DISABLED SAILING AT HANNINGFIELD – HELPERS REQUIRED The authorities at Hanningfield Reservoir have given permission for disabled sailors to sail on the reservoir between 11:00 and 15:00 on Wednesdays and Thursdays from April to August inclusive. A clubhouse and a small fleet of sailing boats have been provided. Safety cover is provided by an inflatable boat with an outboard engine. Assistance is required shore side to help rig the boats and get the disabled sailors afloat and ashore again. Willingness to get wet would be helpful but no doubt there are other jobs to do where you can keep your feet dry. Crew is also required for the safety boat and volunteers with RYA power boat or safety boat qualifications would be particularly welcome. The sailors are all experienced so teaching is not a requirement. Several of the Crouch clubs are providing volunteers but extra help is always appreciated to spread the load; so the organisers are appealing to Blackwater clubs. Bryan Spencer Marconi Sailing Club, Medusa and Dutyman My apologies as it may have been better to have had this in the last Navigans before implementing DutyMan but I failed to get it into David Ball in time. You will be aware that the Club took the decision to invest in the use of proprietary software for its membership database and selected the Medusa system provided by Sailing Club Software for this purpose. One factor influencing that choice was the availability of a linked system which is Dutyman also developed by Sailing Club Software. Dutyman enables the Club to create its duty rotas, such as Support Boat, Race Officer and OOD, and make them available for all Club members to view. It allows members to confirm that they will be available for their duties as well as being able to swap duties between each other, at the same time informing the person with overall responsibility. It is expected that the ability for all Club members to view the rota including any changes will allow Race Officers, OODs etc. to know who has confirmed that they will be available and reduce the administrative load on the Club volunteer responsible for controlling the rota. It may be that you are concerned that the Club has made your data available to a third party. This is not the case. Sailing Club Software simply provide the software, technical expertise to develop and maintain the systems and the data storage medium. Each club using the facility is set up in its own rights and has its own database. There are various different levels of access to the system all under the control of the Club. In our case Medusa can be accessed by myself and Mike Turner as Administrators having access to all the features, members of the Board whose access does not include those features associated with the technical areas of the system, and currently David Clarke who has access to the Duty Planning Module. Limited data from Medusa is downloaded to DutyMan under our control without any involvement of Sailing Club Software personnel. Within DutyMan I am the only person with access to all the facilities at the present time. Access for the ordinary Club Member such as you is limited to viewing the rota simply showing the dates of events and the people scheduled for the duties. In addition you can view your own profile data (taken from the Medusa system) but not other peoples’ although using the Directory feature you can view their email address and telephone number. In the case of those who are scheduled for a duty, they do see the email address and telephone number on the rota of others scheduled for duties. June 2014 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk In addition, you as an individual can limit the data visible to other members, even to the extent of not being visible on the directory, as explained in the email notifying you that we are using DutyMan. For your information the email addresses dutyman@marconi-sc-mail.co.uk and administrator@marconi-sc-mail.co.uk are used exclusively by David Clarke and me respectively. They are not associated with any person at Sailing Club Software. I can appreciate that the wording in the email, which is coded into the system, can give the impression that Sailing Club Software or Dutyman are involved in the day to day operation of the rota on our behalf but can assure you that is not the case. So where from here? Please log on and take a look at the rota even if you are not a Support Boat Driver or Crew. Please confirm that you can do the duty as soon as possible so that everyone can see where we may be short of Support Crews. If you are a Support Boat Driver or Crew and cannot do your scheduled duty, please arrange a swop with someone else scheduled to do the same type of duty, and follow the instructions to make the swop on the system. If you need to swop with someone doing a different type of duty, such as a Greygoose RIB Helm swopping with a Marconi RIB Helm, you will need to email David and myself to make the change for you. This is necessary as we have set up the system to ensure that only those authorised by the Club can be allocated to the correct boats but it treats each RIB as a separate entity. Although the system allows you to simply indicate that you cannot do a duty, please make every attempt to arrange a swop with someone else and put it on the system. It is only by doing this that the Club will benefit from the potential of the system to reduce the administrative load on the Support Boat Coordinator and for the Race Officers/OODs to view an accurate list of those in support boats during their duty. After an initial “Bedding Down” period, we will be extending the system to cover the Race Officers later this year but OODs will probably have to wait until next year. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Peter Richardson and Kevin Kirby took the overnight boat from Portsmouth to Caen leaving a 3 ¾ hour effortless drive to Carnac on the superb French roads, Jon Pease took the more ambitious route via Dover/Calais leaving an 8 hour drive although he was still there for registration Wednesday evening! Carnac, in The Morbihan region is a fabulous chic seaside resort with fine restaurants, wonderful shops and beautiful safe beaches, Carnac yacht Club is one big catamaran club, geared to youth training and a lot of support from The French sailing system looking at the number of SL16’s and Twinx boats lined up. The first days racing commenced Thursday afternoon and the fleets were split in to 4 classes;F18’s, all other kite boats, Dart 18’s and our class of Sprint 15’s, Hobie 14’s,and Twinx 2 man youth boats so swelling our fleet to 27.The wind was Force 6 gusting 7 offshore so you really didn’t realize how windy it was until you got 500 yards from the shore but having seen sever al cats blown over on the beach before launching we had a rough idea what to expect. It seems it’s not the race officer’s decision weather to race or not, it appears if he can get on to the committee boat its sailable! After a very uncomfortable sail out to the start line in heavy seas (it made wind over tide off M mark on a windy day a stroll) Kevin and Peter decided with 3 more days racing in front of them that a swift return to the beach was in order. To his credit Jon stuck at it and although he had a swim carried on to finish the first race, in the event it was the only race of the day, all the other class starts were abandoned due to the many capsizes putting the substantial fleet of rescue boats under considerable strain. Day 2 dawned bright with a F3 / 4, but having lost a day the fleets paid for it with 4 races back to back in short about 7 hours on the water so by the time we got back to the beach the complimentary drink and croissant was very welcome. Day 3 was a long distance race, some 40+ miles for the fast cats which included a 20’Phantom, a carbon curved boarded foiling catamaran (a smaller Americas Cup look a like but with a crew of two) which was out of site of the chasing pack of Tornados, F18’s and Vipers within 2 legs. For the slower fleets there was a shorter 22 mile course all in all similar to our Piers race. Our three helms decided to have a day ashore taking in the sites and giving Liz and Fenella a well deserved day off from carrying and fetching our trolleys. Day 4 was the final day with no starts after 1pm allowing everybody to get finished and packed up. The wind had dropped to a 2 /3 but we were left with a difficult chop which made for some frustrating sailing at times but it brought to an end some fine sailing in a lovely location. The prize giving was conducted in a typical French enthusiastic manner with our class being won overall by Brian Phipps who not only supports us so well as the UK distributor attending all major events, showed us that he has lost none of his sailing skills to become the 1st European Sprint 15 Champion, runner up was Stuart Snell the current National Champion, Kevin was 6th, peter 7th and Jon a well deserved 17th in a very competitive fleet. The Sprint 15 fleet was singled out for a special mention by Carnac Yacht Club being a new fleet to EUROCAT, purist sailing at its best with just a main sail and taking the top 10 places in our Class, easily recognizable around the park in our light blue tee shirts organised by Jon for the fleet and supplied by our very own Dave Clarke. The Sprint 15 association would like to double the number of entrants for EUROCAT 2015, we have within the class Cheryl Craft who runs her own travel company and arranges everything, all the little hitches have now been ironed out, there is a lovely EUROCAMP site a few minutes from the beach so if you are interested keep an eye on the association website or speak to me. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk August & September Combined Issue copy deadline: Saturday 12th July Club Notices Commodore With the season now in full swing there has been a huge amount of activity at the Club with more to come in the next few months. The introduction of ‘Friday Free 4 Alls’ has been a great success with over a dozen boats attending each session, many of whom are new members or members wishing to gain confidence in new or different boats. Many thanks to Jenny Ball, Dave Russell and the Sailing Sub for making these happen. If you are interested in taking part see the sailing programme for future dates. Sail training and the newly formed ‘Oppi Club’ have gotten off to a roaring start this season with over 40 different cadets getting involved so far. This is all thanks to the great work of John Nickalls, Fee Barnes and team. With the cadets often the largest fleet out racing on a Sunday and with cadet week just around the corner, the future of the Club looks as bright as ever! Marconi were well represented during May at EuroCat, one of the biggest European Sailing events. 3 of our Dart 15’s travelled to Carnac in France to race, with Kevin Kirby taking 6th place, Peter Richardson 7th and Jon Pearse 17th in a very competitive fleet - see the MSC website for a full write up. We’ve also seen some great results from Marconi boats in recent cruiser races including BJRC, EAORA and the North Sea Race. Again, full details are available on the website. We’re into the best part of the year now with big events such as ECPR, Cadet Week, Camping Fortnight and a number of Opens almost upon us. I hope you all enjoy the summer of sailing and remind you to please observe Club rules - they are there for a reason. Please respect other members of the Club by keeping all dogs on leads, signing in visitors and keeping the site, including changing rooms tidy for us all to enjoy! Michaela Dowley Commodore Club Treasurer PLANNED REPAYMENT OF MEMBERS’ LOAN NOTES As you are no doubt aware the club is required to repay the membership loan notes by 2023. Loan notes have been refunded for all members who leave the club and request repayment. However it is necessary to spread the remaining repayments over the next 9 years at about a rate of £12000 per year. If you would like your loan note to be repaid, please will you contact the Club Treasurer (email address below). If there are sufficient volunteers for repayment to meet the planned figure for this year that will be helpful. If there are more volunteers than required, the club will repay on a first come, first served basis. If there are not enough volunteers, the terms of the Loan Note scheme require that the club should put all loan holders’ names in the hat and draw out the required number for repayment. Contact Email Address: . Club Secretary DOGS During the recent camping weekends at least three members had unpleasant and frightening experiences with dogs off leads. One member was confronted in the dark by what was described as an angry, barking dog running free. The owners were nowhere to be seen. The member felt distressed and intimidated by the incident. This is unacceptable and should not happen. People come to the Club to relax and indulge their interest in sailing. There is no way that inconsiderate dog ownership should be allowed to interfere with that. The majority of dogs that come to Stansgate bring a responsible adult with them and are no trouble but clearly some do not. If you bring your dog to the club make sure it is kept on a lead (bylaw 10.5.1) and does not interfere with the enjoyment or, in some cases, the safety of other people. All members, including other dog owners, will appreciate your consideration. Thank you. Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: July 2014 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk October Issue copy deadline: Saturday 13th September Club Notices Commodore A short note from me in this bumper edition of Navigans. Both Navigans and the Club committees take a well deserved break during August to enjoy the peak of the sailing season so please read this issue for all the summers news and events. It’s a busy time at the Club with cadet week, camping fortnight, summer cruises and a number of other events already upon us. Enjoy and stay safe whatever your summer sailing involves. ECPR weekend was another resounding success, albeit with slightly reduced numbers. Initial feedback from competitors has been excellent and the date for the 2015 event has been set for 12th July – get it in your diaries. A huge thank you and congratulations to Clive Shenton and team for putting on such a well organised event. Of course this year’s event was made even better by the ECPR winners trophy being taken by the MSC team of Mitchell Glynn and Andrew Dowley! Marconi continues to be well represented further afield – some highlights include a team of cadets entering the NSSA championships and a number of cruisers taking part and doing exceptionally well in offshore races. Michaela Dowley Commodore EAST COAST PIERS |XiRACE East Coast Piers Race and Colne Point Race 2014 I am pleased to report another successful weekend for our premier open event of the year, the East Coast Piers Race (ECPR) and Colne Point Race (CPR). The weather was benign, perhaps a little too benign, on the day of the big races while the Saturday series produced more capsizes than I have seen for many years. In a growing trend as more dinghies enter, this year the shorter CPR had the greater number of entrants than its Big Brother the ECPR. While CPR ran its full course, Race Control had one decision to ponder in the gentle winds, which led us to turn ECPR at Clacton. I am particularly happy to report that Line Honours, first Tornado home and overall ECPR winner trophies were won by Mitchell Glynn crewed by fellow Race committee member Andrew Dowley in a bravura performance. It is only the second time that a Club boat has won the Race. Another headline performance in a generally good showing for Club boats had Jenny and David Ball claiming third place in their Spitfire. Mark Bunyan and Andy Bunyan sailing Sprint 15s were first and fourth with the intervening places occupied by ex-member Simon Plumb and Barry Peters sailing Dart 18s. The 49er easily won Line Honours in the Dinghy Race with the International 14 not too far behind, but overall winner, as last year, was Club member Mike Taylor in his Osprey. In a “just for fun” PY calculation Mike would also have beaten all the cats in the Race on corrected time. My thanks go to Peter Clayton and all the Club cruisers who turned out as Mother boats and Matriarchs (M&Ms) to provide essential safety cover for both Races. Coordinated by Roger Camp at Colne Point these boats and their crews provide invaluable service enabling Race Control to keep close tabs on all competitors. This was especially helpful when one of the backmarkers set course for the Crouch. The good efforts of the M&Ms would count for little without the front line RIB support provided by Club RIBs crewed by members but I acknowledge our friends from Stone, Bradwell Outdoor and Brightlingsea who joined the support fleet to give a high degree of cover both in numbers and quality. Many thanks to you all. Malcolm Stuart & crew in Jack B were once again placing and recovering buoys at each end of what is a long day for them and many others in the support fleets. Shoreside organisation is equally important in a large event such as this and I acknowledge and thank Murray and Mick for preparing the site & the buoys as well as bossing the hard; Dave Russell & team for scruiteering and beach-mastering and not least, all my family especially Alex who manned reception, calculated results and organised the Prize Giving. After our usual Race Officer, Mike Turner, was injured in June, I took on the RO role which meant I spent most of the day on the committee boat where I was greatly helped by Leonie Golding, Linda Chaplin and more family members Dan, Sue and Marian. My thanks go to Bryan Spencer, Julie Hawkins and Leonie who picked up the mantle for the Saturday races. They were helped by Mike & Maggie Boreham who combined their usual Sunday role of running the leader-boards with the noisy Saturday job of firing the cannons. Auguest 2014 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Joining OOD Simon Elwell in the Race Control BUS this year was our Commodore who, having only previously seen the Race from the competitors viewpoint, confessed to be greatly impressed by the level of activity and commitment of the team which included regulars Barbara Davies and Ray Ball. Another safety feature of Race Control, are the spotters who are based on the Matriarchs where they gather information and pass it to the plotters in the BUS. My thanks go to Fee Shaw who led the process and to the spotters, some of whom had exciting RIB rides to and from station. Finally I wish to thank the core members of the Race committee who meet regularly for some eight months a year to organise Race weekend. Andrew Dowley; Roger Davies; Kevin Dowley and Ray Ball. Keith White OOD Co-ordinator email Fleet News Solo Speak As we move into the best of the summer weather there have been some good developments in the fleet. Firstly, we had our first trial of the new short race format in June. This is following up on the RYA recommendation that our fleet racing would be improved by having shorter races, and more of them, in a day. The Sailing Sub Committee agreed that we could try this on selected Summer Points Sundays by having an earlier start for the first Solo race such that we finished in time to join in with the normal 11-o-clock start procedure for a second race on a back-to-back basis. This worked a treat and we are very grateful to the Race Officer, John Nickalls, and the support boat crew who turned up early to enable this programme. All taking part agreed that this format was more enjoyable than the normal programme so we are hoping to trial it again in August. The other good news is that we have a new member of the Solo Fleet. He is Geoff Springett who made his racing debut in July. The more people racing, the more enjoyment for everyone, so if you have a Solo come and join in the fun. If you do not have one, we can provide boats that can be borrowed, provided that you are a competent helmsman. Just contact me in advance to set up a chance to experience the joy of Solo sailing. A quick reminder that our Solo Open Meeting is coming up shortly (7th Sept) so please support this event if you have a Solo as we need maximum number of Club boats on the water. John Salmon Solo Fleet Captain Cruiser Fleet Our next cruise is to St Katharines dock and the River Medway commencing Saturday 2nd of August for one week. The list is now on the club notice board. On 23th August we have our annual cruise to Ipswich for the three day bank Holladay weekend. Bob Godbold is organising the marina and a list will be appearing on the notice board shortly. Colne Point Race had started 20 minutes later in light winds; this became a drift between Bradwell and Colne Point with only the tide to help. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk November Issue copy deadline: Saturday 11th October Club Notices Commodore Welcome back from the summer break - I hope each and every one of you has managed to make the most of the fair weather and wind over the summer and took part in the huge number of activities on offer at MSC over the past few months. I have a number of positive messages for you in this edition so I have endeavoured to keep my notes as brief as possible! I am pleased to report that following in the footsteps of his late father Tony Benn, Stephen Benn has accepted our offer to take on the role of President of Marconi Sailing Club. Stephen is the eldest son of Tony Benn and continues to be our friend and neighbour at Stansgate. Many of you will have seen the new launch/committee boat moored just off the hard - the Tony B. The Tony B is named in honour of our late President and a formal naming ceremony is due to take place shortly. I must also acknowledge here the number of members who have worked tirelessly over the past few years to restore the Tony B to its current state. Following in Navigans are a number of reports from our packed events calendar over the summer. Please take the time to read about the huge amount of activity that has been going on over the summer months. Highlights include a visit from the Chernobyls Children, the National Schools Sailing Regatta, Cadet Week 2014, successful cruiser racing, topper traveller event, solo and kestrel opens plus dinghy and cruiser cruises. Cadet week was yet again a huge success with over 80 cadets taking part this year- thanks are due to the organising team headed up by Dave Clarke, Bekki Tovey and Chris Kirby. They even organised the perfect weather! I am also very pleased to be able to tell you that as of 11th September, MSC was accepted as an RYA Champion Club ‘with flying colours.’ A formal presentation will take place at the Dinghy Show in March 2015 - so don’t forget to book your tickets. Thanks are due to Lee Harrison for leading this initiative, which means that the club will have access to advanced training and RYA resources. I would like to thank the sailing sub committee and social secretary for their efforts over the summer. We have had a packed calendar with a huge number of successful events. I would particularly like to thank Jenny Ball for the weekly update initiative to let us know about ‘sailing and other activities at MSC,’ which we all receive by email. It’s amazing just how much is going on at our club! For interest - a recent return of information to the RYA has given us cause to look at our membership demographics which I am happy to report are very healthy. As of the beginning of September we have 392 memberships which totals to 774 club members - 144 of these classed as ‘junior.’ Finally, and very importantly - in this issue of Navigans you will find the notice of AGM which is being held on 23rd November 2014 and nomination forms for election to the club committees. Marconi Sailing Club only functions because of volunteers fro m the membership who give their time to keep the club going. I encourage everyone to strongly consider standing for posts on the Club committees. These positions are not fixed to ‘the same old people every year’ and we welcome new members and fresh ideas. As well as the Board and Management Committees, there are a number of sub committees that play vital roles within the Club structure. If you think you have the skills and importantly some time to give to the Club then please get in touch to see how you might be able to help. CLUBHOUSE SECURITY A member who was on site late on the last Sunday of Camping Fortnight after everyone else had gone home found, in his words, ‘every door and window in the clubhouse unlocked and open’. I will therefore repeat the note I put in Navigans last year about clubhouse security. It’s YOUR clubhouse and YOUR money that would have to be used to put right any damage. CCTV evidence shows that at all times of the day and night your clubhouse is being used by strangers such as beach fisherman and casual visitors. The reason is obvious. Strangers know that the chances are that at least one of the outer doors to the clubhouse will be open for them to use or abuse as they see fit at any time. The solution to this is so easy. Always close the clubhouse after you have been in unless other members are actually using it; particularly during ‘off peak’ times. Take the trouble to check the other outer doors; it will only take a few minutes. Do not leave the clubhouse open because you or other members are working somewhere on site and might want to nip back there from time to time. Everyone entitled to be in the clubhouse has an access card so closing the doors is not going to cause problems for legitimate users. The answer to all site security is very simple and is just common sense. FLOOD GATES The Environment Agency requires that the flood gates must be kept closed from 1st September unless the hard is in use. Remember that on at least one occasion last winter the flood gates prevented the site and the ground floor of the clubhouse being flooded. Please shut the gates when you come ashore unless it is obvious that another member is using the hard. If in doubt, shut the gates. They can always be opened again. PARKING IN CRUISER PARK At this busy time of boat, boat hoist and trailer movements cars must not be left unattended in the cruiser park or the cruiser parking area of the cat park. Owners of cars in the cruiser parks must be available at all times and ready to move them at short notice. Do not leave your car unattended in the cruiser parks even if you are ‘only nipping out to the boat for 5 minutes’. There is a very real risk of damage. Keith White OOD Co-ordinator email Fleet News Solo Speak SOLO OPEN MEETING 2014 Our Solo Open Meeting was held on Sunday 7th September when twenty helms signed on including five members of the Marconi fleet. The pre-race briefing was held in the club house when the course was described as a triangle followed by a sausage and the position of the buoys was highlighted. High tide was given as 11:45 and 5-8 knot winds were forecast with a committee boat start. Each race would be three laps with shortening of the course a high possibility. The scene was then set for races mid-river between the Steeple shore of the Blackwater and Osea Island. First Race - There was great enthusiasm in the fleet, dinghies bunched together racing for the line as the count down concluded and the hooter sounded. As a great number of boats were over the line, too many to distinguish, a general recall was sounded. While the fleet was regrouping and the countdown restarted rain lashed down but dinghies sped off in a clean start into the first triangle of the course. The boats rounded the leeward mark and then passed through the start gate with Ewan Birkin-Walls leading Steve Ede and Mark Maskell. The weather improved, although there was mist and cloud but the rain had stopped. At the end of the first lap Steve Ede had taken the lead from Ewan Birkin-Walls and Chris Mayhew moved from fifth to third place. Committee boat members shouted encouragement to Marconi sailors: John Salmon (Fleet Captain), Roger Smith, Mike Taylor, Bryan Spencer and Gerry Kamstra. Towards the end of the second triangle the shortened course procedure was initiated. The leading two boats crossed the line within a hair's breadth of each other with the third boat only just behind. The order had changed again, Steve Ede first, Mark Maskell second and Ewan Birkin-Walls third. Second Race - Now the tide was ebbing fast so the leeward mark was repositioned closer to the committee boat. The course was the same. This time it was a very clean start. There was close racing at the front of the fleet, first and second had changed places to give Steve Ede the lead at the end of the first lap. Some skilful boat handling and buoy rounding saw the first four boats pull away from the rest of the fleet. With the course shortened to two laps, at the end of the race, Ewan Birkin-Walls finished first, a good distance from Steve Ede, who was second, closely followed by Mark Maskell in third. Third Race - Due to the light airs it was decided to run the third race without going ashore for lunch but it was now sunny. The tide continued to run out strongly and to accommodate the low water the buoys and the committee boat were moved. The race was about to start, with the countdown under way, when it was decided to postpone as not only was there no wind but most of the fleet were too far away from the start line. Although this was frustrating the boats floated calmly while the helms chatted. When a light breeze eventually blew it was fluky in direction which necessitated moving the buoys yet again. A new course was set and sixteen boats were at the start line. Unfortunately, like race one, many were over the line causing another general recall. October 2014 Navigans 7

Kevin Dowley Cat Fleet Captain Cadet Fleet CADET WEEK 2014 Over 78 Cadets took part in Marconi Sailing Club's annual Cadet Week last week to enjoy 6 days of fun and training on the River Blackwater. The club caters for sailors of all ages and experience levels and tailors the tuition accordingly. This year a number of new members took part for the very first time, after having signed up to join the sailing club after its successful Open Day back in May. Non-members were also welcomed to join the fun. To kick of the week, everybody took to the water on the Monday morning to sail in some challenging winds to familarise themselves with sailing, which for many was their first time. In the afternoon cadets were invited to take part in the Capsize Drill, a permanent fixture of all Cadet Weeks which teaches important boat righting skills for the remainder of the week! On Tuesday and Wednesday the groups separated in to different fleets which allows the volunteer Marconi tutors to provide specific training and guidance in smaller numbers. Lighter winds ensured everybody was able to enjoy a full day on the water. Osea Island was the destination of choice this year for Thursday's long distance race where the Cadets competed against each other with a staggered start from the club's based in Steeple. The stronger winds proved too much for some with a number of boats ending up capsized, however the training that was given on the Monday certainly gave people a chance to put in to practice what they had learn to right the boat again! After enjoying a picnic lunch on the South Western area of Osea, the fleets convened again to commence the second race of the day, against an ebbing tide for the trip home. After another eventful summer of sport with the Brazil World Cup and the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, event organisers decided upon the them of "Countries of the World" for Friday's fun day. After a morning of Pico Water Polo and Dinghy based Basketball the groups joined together after lunch to take part in "The World Class Competition." Cadets split in to different country groups to help assist "Captain Graham Cross." of the World Navy who had become stranded on Osea Island with his fleet of 12 Laser Picos. Working as a team, the cadets had to find their respective country flag and the pieces of the boat that had been scattered across Osea Beach to help Captain Cross rebuild his fleet and sail back across to Port Marconi. After each group had re-assembled their boats, they had to sail back across the river with up to 6 people in each boat - which for anybody who has sailed a Laser Pico is not the most comfortable experience! Pole position for the event went to Team France. The Cadet Regatta was held on Saturday with the beginner groups and advanced sailors being catered for separately. Race Officer Jenny Ball set two races for the Regatta with only the advanced cadets taking part in the afternoon race due to challenging conditions and stronger winds. October 2014 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The week was rounded off on the Saturday evening with a prizegiving event and thank you BBQ for all the volunteers and helpers. Follow up sail training days are expected to be held for the remainder of the season and next year to help the cadets further improve their skills ready for next year's Cadet Week! Chris Kirby NSSA REPORT This year NSSA was held at Downs Sailing Club in Deal from 20th July to 26th July 2014. The Marconi team (or should I say macaroni as we were known by the other competitors) included David Nickalls in a Laser Radial, Rowena potter and Jack Wardell in 4.7 Lasers, Daniel Nickalls and Hannah Bard in the 420, Sophie Savill, Olivia Duckmanton, Jason Clarke and myself in toppers and Sam Featherstone and William Richardson in the Comet Duo. We came back with a selection of fantastic results, for example Hannah and Daniel’s 4th, Jason’s 7th and jack’s 13th. Well done everyone! The start lines were very busy with up to 80 boats in each fleet. It was certainly a difference from Marconi but it gave us chance to improve our confidence and skills when starting. Unfortunately we were unable to sail on the Tuesday due to the large shore breakers. This was disappointing but allowed us to spend the afternoon relaxing on the pier while eating very fast melting ice cream. Of course, the sailing was the main part of our trip, but I believe the camping and the evenings activities brought us closer together as a team. Sports evening saw Sam win the tabletennis and the Marconi rounders team get to the final without playing any games as the other teams didn’t turn up. I would like to share some of my memories from the week:- Dinghy Rope as a perfect changing room, climbing frame and somewhere to store our sailing gear. Thanks Andy for letting us use it, sorry if it still smells! The very steep beach was shingle which was fun to roll the boats down, but after five hours sailing it was hard work trying to get them back up again. Luckily there were lots of people around to help. We also managed to get one of the teams flags but forgot to give it back. Opps! Getting our funny prizes on the Friday from our team managers, John and Rhiannon. Lastly, thank you to everyone one who was involved in getting the team to deal and making sure we had an exhausting but amazing time. I know that the general view is ROLL ON NEXT YEAR! Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Report Porpoise Sightings Harbour Porpoises have been spotted in the Blackwater (off Colne Bar). There have only been a small number of sightings on the East Coast, compared to lots on the West and North coasts of Britain. To see a list of sightings of whales, dolphins or porpoises, or to report a sighting, go to: http://www.seawatchfoundation.org.uk/sightingsform/ Robin Bromham (Wayfarer Samphire) Extreme 40 Sailing Series August Bank Holiday saw the return of the Extreme 40 sailing series to the UK for some spectacular close quarters racing in Cardiff Bay. For those who are not familiar – Extreme 40s are cats which are a scaled up version of something between a Tornado and a Spitfire – complete with asymmetric kites. They are 40ft long so they can fit into a container. They are very light and very fast and can do up to 30 knots. They also fly hulls, pitchpole and capsize (and crash) which makes for good spectating and film footage so long as no-one gets hurt. Some of the world’s top sailors have been attracted to the series which sees 10 – 12 teams competing at 8 events around the world. More recently, it has become part of the training and recruitment ground for America’s Cup teams. As such, this year’s teams include JP Morgan BAR skippered by Ben Ainslie and Emirates Team New Zealand skippered by Dean Barker. Former Marconi SC member Mark Bulkeley is on board with Red Bull Sailing Team. Additionally, teams are required to have a crew member who is either female, under 25 or an amateur sailor so it is becoming a great training ground for new talent. A core element of the Extreme Sailing Series is that it is accessible to public spectators – as opposed to other events which take place offshore. The venues are, therefore, chosen to support this and the race courses are very tight and compact – particularly for boats of such size and speed. Cardiff Bay is a perfect setting – an enclosed sailing arena and anywhere the spectators stood around the bay gave them a perfect view of the racing. The official spectating area was freely accessible to the public. Corporate and hospitality clients got the opportunity to go on board the boats during each race as Guest Sailors (subject to weather conditions) – which is a pretty unique opportunity! The format is multiple races each lasting around 10 minutes and the race marks are about the same length apart as our club marks. The finish line is shorter than the club start line and was just off the harbour wall in full view of the spectators. Additionally, the sailors are often around the public spectating area as they attend race briefings etc and were very open to requests for photographs and autographs – even when about to go off racing. The atmosphere is very accessible and family friendly. Having followed the series on the web and Youtube for some time – I decided to sign up as a volunteer for this year’s event. Over the three days I got to help guest sailors get into sailing gear, ambush members of the public with leaflets and information they may or may not have wanted and on the last day, I was in charge of the finish hooter and the big clock that counted down to each start! We were able to attend the skipper’s briefings and try to overhear the redress hearing between Team New Zealand and SAP. We were lucky enough to get out on a RIB to watch two of the races and, thanks to the rainy weather, some guest sailors did not show up so we got to be Guest Sailors for the final race of the series! I was lucky enough to be assigned to Red Bull so got to sail with Mark Bulkeley again – I reckon the last time that happened was 25 years ago in a Mirror ……. And – as some of you may know, I am a massive fan of Team New Zealand so rounded off the weekend with a picture with my all time hero Dean Barker! The Extreme 40s are at Istanbul, Nice and Sydney for the remainder of this year – and the series will return again next year with an event in the UK (Venue and dates to be confirmed). See www.extremesailingseries.com for info and some great footage. I can highly recommend going along for some or all of the next UK event – it is refreshingly geared up to the fans and if the breeze is up, it is fascinating viewing for anyone, even a non-sailor. I also bumped into a number of sailor friends – either October 2014 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Mike Smith 1929 - 2014 LT.CMD. M.A.H. SMITH (SCC) R.N.R M.B.E. In 1959, aged thirteen, a school friend suggested that I ‘try’ the Sea Cadets. Yes, I thought, a sailor’s suit would be irresistible to attract the girls, as I cycled from Billericay to Brentwood one summer’s evening. This was the first time that met Mike Smith; He was a young C.P.O. Instructor, having recently come out of the Navy where he had served as a P.O. Telegraphist / Yeoman. This would explain why anyone making a faux pas with their flags was firmly corrected by him! Unbeknown to me this was the beginning of a life long association with sea cadets and with Mike Smith, who became my instructor, mentor and then to lifelong friend. In the early 1960’s he built a heron dinghy in his garage and I could only marvel at his carpentry skills. It wasn’t long before he was teaching many of us to sail on the River Crouch, in the Heron. Mike’s drive and enthusiasm for Youth work took up nearly all his spare time and he was soon promoted to become the Commanding Officer of Brentwood unit. Following a disastrous fire in the old unit it was due to Mike’s motivation and the aid of his highly qualified committees, as well as the parents and friends that the new unit was built in 1966. Alongside this construction he also instigated and fulfilled his dream of a Boat Station on the River Crouch. There must be many hundreds of people who have fond memories of weekends and weeklong courses afloat at the Boat Station, learning to sail. I recall one occasion when we were both examining candidates afloat in the Walton Backwaters; each of us in a 16 foot six open dinghy , with six cadets in each . One candidate froze on the mainsheets! The boat slowly heeled over to 90 degrees and Mike in equally slow motion entered the water with his clipboard held aloft and was heard to say ‘You’ve failed son!’ After more than the usual period of ten years in command, Mike was promoted to District Officer, for the eleven units in Essex. His enthusiasm and leadership was then transferred to all these units and he was greatly respected throughout the area. Mike’s commitment to youth work was recognised, in June 1980, when he was awarded an M.B. E. which he proudly accepted at Buckingham Palace; not that this altered his down-to-earth attitude to life. It was about this time that his serving Sea cadet career was coming to a conclusion. He then devoted his time to management committee work with the Sea Cadets as well as becoming a member in the Royal Naval Sailing Association, sailing under the blue ensign. Mike’s love of boats meant that he bought a succession of small craft, in varying states of repair, and was always at his happiest using his restorative skills to make the current project sailable; until the next acquisition appeared. Working for Marconi ,at this time, he decided to join the M.A.S.C. and M.S.C. and many of you will know that he always had time for a yarn and a joke or two. Those of us that went aboard his boat were never allowed to leave without sampling his ample supply of rum and hospitality. His presence of 33 years, with the M.S.C., has been and will continue to be felt within the club not least because of the various projects that he undertook. He instigated and designed the Dell Bar, now the Managu bar, where club members meet and socialize today which he built and equipped almost single handed. We will all be aware of Mike’s love of dogs and he rescued more than I can remember. I have fond memories of many of them, not least Hobi. This dog was well known at the sailing club; he also loved boats but more than that he loved jumping off of them! Many was the time that Mike was seen chasing after Hobi, in a dinghy. But the frustration of ‘first catch your dog’ resulted in Hobi being confined to terraferma . Mike told me that his claim to fame, in his opinion, was that in 1940, as a spotty schoolboy, he organised a petition to start a Sea Cadet unit in Brentwood. The list of names he collected was treated seriously and as a result 1941 saw the inaugural meeting of Brentwood Unit Number 52. The one thing that upset him, as the first member, was that his name was not the first in the ship’s books. Smith will never be first in the register. At that time the corrugated iron building was being used as a Soup kitchen and subsequently shared its use with Unit Headquarters. Interestingly the new unit, still in use, was built on the original site. Mike loved sailing and was seen sailing a week before his death. At the grand age of 85 years, I can think of no greater tribute or inspiration. Graham Cross Rear Commodore Fleet News 420 Open Residential Class Training at Rutland The 420 is a great boat to sail: it's challenging, with a traditional symmetric spinnaker and a much more tunable rig than many other boats... and it goes really well in a breeze. Hannah Bard and I, and Jack Collis with Jack Wardell, seized the chance to join 4 days of 420 Class Training up at Rutland Water (the week following the Laser Inlands). It was a residential course, staying in the clubhouse bunk-rooms with all the other sailors. The group was very friendly and got on well; most of us were in Yr 11, with some as young as 13 and up to 18. After a hot breakfast (three hot meals a day!) Hannah was delighted that each day started at 8:15 with a warm-up / fitness work for an hour, then we had a briefing on the day's topics. Boat handling was covered, including trim/balance etc., roll tacks, roll gybes, spinnaker work and double tacks; other sessions included rig setup, race tactics, starting skills, team racing and many others. The 13 boats were coached (often in separate groups) by three top-end coaches (Steve Irish (470 Olympic coach), Tom Mapplebeck and Sam Brearey) so we had great inspiration as well as feedback on all our faults! We had two on-the-water sessions each day, with the final debrief usually finishing after supper around 7:30. Overall it was a great 4 days: Rutland was perfect, it was great socially and we had a lot of fun learning a lot about high performance sailing. Thanks to everyone! Dan Nickalls December 2014 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk MSC at Laser Inlands The number of Lasers sailing at MSC is rising, and looks set to rise further, so we thought it would be interesting and fun to take up the challenge of the Laser Inlands at Rutland on 25th - 26th October. We sailed in different fleets: Dan in the Radial (with 103 others) and David in Standard rig (with 43 others); with the 4.7s, there were nearly 180 Lasers on the water, sailing off the same line but with inner and outer loops to keep us reasonably separate. It was windy! Finding a good slot on the line had to be balanced against getting clear air and staying out of trouble. Loads of boats capsized (including us) in the strong gusts. It was impressive to see the leaders sailing radical angles downwind, including by the lee, to take advantage of shifts and the waves that had built up at the bottom end of the enormous reservoir. The weekend was exhausting, but we learnt a lot and could clearly see the difference between the top sailors and club racers. We're looking forward to the next chance! Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: Ron Greygoose As this edition of Navigans was going to press we learned with deep regret that Ron Greygoose had passed away in Broomfield Hospital on Saturday 15th November. Ron had been a member of the Club for many years. The records of the early MSC days are incomplete but records from 1970 onwards show that Ron occupied the following positions in the Club: Sailing Secretary 1971 & 1972 Vice Commodore 1975 to 1977 Commodore 1978 to 1980 Vice President 1981 to 1992 President 1992 to 2000 Solo Fleet Captain 1982 to 1984 This is truly a remarkable record of service to the club and until fairly recently, although no longer sailing himself, Ron was still prepared to take his place in the race box as Race Officer. Ron compiled the Club History with pictures for the MSC website which is well worth reading. The Club was pleased to name the new RIB Marconi Greygoose after Ron; which was a fitting tribute to his years of service to the Club and now a fitting memorial. Above all Ron was a true gentleman in every sense of the word with a smile and a friendly word for everyone. His passing is a great loss to those who had the pleasure of knowing him. Our sympathies go to Ron’s family and friends at this sad time. Ray Ball December 2014 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Saltmarsh 75 – An alternative way to see the River! Saltmarsh 75 is a long distance event which (as its name suggests) covers the 75 miles of sea wall from South Woodham Ferrers, through Fambridge to Burnham, turning left along the Dengie peninsular to Bradwell, along the south bank of the Blackwater to Maldon, then along the north bank past Tollesbury and finishing in the village of Salcott. And you do all that in a weekend. And some people are mad enough to run it – although you can also walk it or even enter as a relay team. As many of you will know, walking along the sea wall by the River Blackwater or Crouch is one of life’s great pleasures and over the past few years, I have walked virtually the entire route albeit in much smaller chunks. I therefore recognised some of the challenges that the Saltmarsh 75 organisers warn you about – eg. that stretch between Burnham and Bradwell, the weather, the terrain and the psychological challenges of seeing your destination quite close as the crow flies, but having to walk a lot further as the sea wall twists and turns around various creeks and inlets. I knew that I would not be able to do proper 8 hour training walks as I was sailing every Saturday and Sunday in the run up to the event in early October. I also noted how many competitors had dropped out after the first day at last year’s event. But I decided to give it a go anyway with the target of at least completing the first day. I did not manage to convince Dave to join me – but I did sign him up as my pit crew for the day. The start was at Marsh Farm at 8am on Saturday 5th October and I was pretty apprehensive – Route Map rsh 75 Sal Saltma although the organisers could not have been more friendly and welcoming. After a short safety briefing, the walkers set off and you could quickly see those who do this type of thing regularly and who roared off into the distance – leaving me, predictably, somewhere near the back. The runners set off at 9am – so caught up and overtook the walkers by mid morning. The weather was glorious and it was a lovely walk through a safety checkpoint at Fambridge, past Bridgemarsh Marina, through Creeksea and round Burnham Marina to the next checkpoint for a quick lunch stop. 14 miles down, 24 to go…… Pe The next stretch was 13 miles from Burnham to Othona (Bradwell) which is one of the most isolated walks you can do in Essex – plus the forecast was for the weather to deteriorate significantly. About an hour into this leg, the wind swung from southerly to a strong north westerly and it poured with rain. Unhelpfully, this was as the walk turned northwards along the Dengie peninsular – meaning three hours directly head on into cold, driving rain. One of the advantages of sailing is being used being soaked to the skin and walking around all day in wet boots – which is just as well. Even so, I got very, very cold and by now my legs and feet were tired and sore. However, I decided not to risk stopping because of the cold and ploughed through the whole four hours from Burnham without a rest. Unexpectedly, I started catching up a lot of the groups of walkers who had taken rests and who looked pretty miserable – clearly not sailors! Dave met me at Othona with some welcome additional jumpers and food! I wrung out my socks and boots as best I could. A number of walkers had got so cold and miserable that they decided to call it a day at Othona – including some who had managed the whole event last year. I was not inclined to give up although I was so cold, I could not do my boot laces back up and I was getting concerned I would not be able to complete the walk before the 9.30pm cut off. Helpfully, the rain cleared and it was a beautiful walk in autumn evening sunlight to the next checkpoint at Bradwell Marina where Dave was kind enough to meet me again with a steaming mug of coffee! December 2014 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk At the start: The next stretch was 4 miles from the Marina to Stone Sailing Club. Night fell during this stretch and it was an extremely dark walk!! By this stage, I was having to stop every few minutes because of muscle pain in my right hip so I was also not particularly quick! The last stretch was from Stone Sailing club, through to Marconi, along the access road and then across the fields to finish the day at Steeple Village Hall. Dave met me at Marconi and then escorted me along the sailing club road to the footpath. He then drove round to the Village Hall and walked along the path to meet me for the very final stretch. This moral support was very much needed by this stage. I staggered to the last checkpoint at 9:30pm which was the safety deadline for finishing. I could barely walk but I was really pleased to have finished the 38 miles – particularly after the challenging weather! The following morning – my left leg was OK but a blister underneath my right foot and muscle pain in my right hip meant I was in no fit state to do another 37 miles. I opted to go sailing instead because at least that involved sitting down! After sailing – Dave and I drove round to Salcott to see some of the participants finish the overall event and give them heartfelt congratulations on managing to finish both days. It was also an opportunity to thank the organisers for a very well run and friendly event. If you are into ultra running or a challenging walking event – then this is definitely the event for you. Local, well run and straightforward from a navigation point of view – with the added bonus of fantastic views of two beautiful rivers. If covering 38 miles a day is not for you – then I would still recommend that you dig out an Ordnance Survey and go for a walk along any stretch of the seawall that takes your fancy – it will be a lovely day out. APOLOGIES Derek Kirby, Russel Hatherleigh, Peter Ward, Mike Cutmore, Andy Samuel, Lewis Smith, Keith Murray, David Payne, Julie Bloomfield, Frank Burgess and Mike Turner. 2. REVIEW OF 2014 24/25/26 May 12 boats went to Brightlingsea and enjoyed a BBQ. 14/15 June Heybridge. 14 boats again enjoyed a BBQ and watching England lose in the pub. 12/13 July Tollesbury 12 Boats went and 24 attended a meal in the clubhouse. Thanks to Bob Godbold. 13/14 September 12 boats went to Brightlingsea and had a meal at Winkies. 3. ECPR – CLIVE SHENTON. The objective of the Race is to run a flagship national event to benefit visiting and Club sailors alike while raising money for sailing related charities. There was a slightly reduced number this year due to clashes with other events although there were still 55 entries. The financial outcome was better than last year: - £2,300 to Cirdan Sailing Trust £400 Essex Air Ambulance These amounts included selling of liquid products donated free by Adnams and shirt and programme sponsorship from Mark Foster’s company AM safety specialists. Sponsorship raised by Cirdan produced a further £9,500 including a generous donation from Kevin Kirby Ltd. Safety is the important factor and once again the cruiser fleet greatly contributed to the safe running of the Race with our cruisers acting as mother boats and matriarchs under the direction of Roger Camp on the water and Simon Elwell on-shore as OOD. Peter Clayton was in charge of recruitment. Mike Turner was not able to do his Race Officer job due to having suffered a sailing related accident and he was missed. As a memento of the Race every cruiser that took part on Race day is eligible for a stuff bag with the same design as this year’s shirts. Next year’s Race 28th June 2015. 4. REVIEW OF RACING AND PRIZE GIVING REPORT– PETER WARD In his absence Sue Arnold read Peter’s report and Roger Camp presented the prizes. 2014 saw success for Marconi’s Cruiser racers in local, regional and international fleets. With the club being named in RORC reports throughout the season and member boats achieving podium finishes in local handicap and IRC races the clubs profile as a cruiser racing club is being raised. Ian and Laura Ivermee and the Woozle Hunter crew won the East Anglian Offshore Racing Series in Class 3 and finished in 2nd place overall, They were the only boat to complete all races in the series and won outright the Thames Estuary Race, Pattinson Cup and Houghton Cup. Their list of trophies and awards from 2014 is quite extensive and can be seen on the Marconi website. McGregor IV skippered by Derek Brown and Peter Ward completed a demanding Royal Ocean Racing Club campaign that saw their team which included Tom Clayton and Rorie Ash, finish fourth in the RORC series overall and second in class. They also completed the 700 miles Round Ireland Race finishing in 10th place and 4th in class. Closer to home Andy Ellis and the crew on Caroline, were winners of two races in the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee series and finished 3rd overall in the 9 race series, whilst in the same series Richard Roberts team sailing Blue Moon came 2nd overall in the highly competitive IRC class. The Marconi Cruiser Cup race which is part of the BJRC series and the Blackwater & Colne Open Sailing Series, saw 27 boats come to the line. The Cup was won by Barry Ely sailing Poohstick from the Blackwater SC. Towards the end of the season 9 Marconi cruisers participated in the Barts Bash event. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk CRUISER RACING DEVELOPMENT In the last season through my involvement in the clubs management committee I became aware that the club has an ambition plan. The plan has been in place for a number of years and many of the developments we have seen i.e. opi club, new rib, support boat containers, changing facilities upgrade, barn e.t.c. can be linked back to ambition plan objectives. On the plan are statements relating to racing such as: Status We will be recognised nationally (and in Europe) as a club that hosts well – run open events (national and international) and sends competitors to open events across a wide area. As a consequence of all of the above and our own self-promotion we will be known as one of the premier sailing clubs in the UK Activity The Club will promote a strong racing calendar for its major fleets, will encourage members to compete nationally and internationally and will seek to attract Open event activity. With regards cruiser racing, there have been a number of small initiatives and achievements by club members that help the club towards achieving its goals, but this has mainly been unplanned and coincidental. There are clear signs that Marconi are becoming recognised as a cruiser racing club locally for a number of reasons, and this provides us with the opportunity to build our reputation further. We are a long way off being one of the premier cruiser racing clubs in the UK, but I’d like to think that we could become in the very near future, the premier cruiser racing club on the Blackwater, if not Eastern region. When cruiser racing issues have been discussed at both the sailing sub committee and management committee meetings in recent years, there has always been enthusiastic support and I am in no doubt that any development plan that we might put forward for cruiser racing, will receive support and encouragement from these committees. A meeting has therefore been arranged for existing members with an interest in cruiser racing, to discuss topics that might be used to formulate a development plan for Marconi cruiser racing. Topics for discussion might include: Club Members only racing. Increasing numbers of Marconi boats in races. Cadets racing on Cruisers. Marconi cruiser racing Open Regatta. Club owned Keel Boat Fleet Acquisition. Promoting a Marconi Offshore Open Race. Attracting Racers to join from other clubs. The meeting will be held in the bar at 2pm on Sunday 11th January. I look forward to hearing your ideas. Peter Ward Cruiser racing Rep Club News Welcome To New Members We are pleased to welcome the following new member. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk But Ron’s passion was dinghy racing. When I first came across him in the early 1970s he was one of the helms in the very strong Enterprise fleet that Marconi had at that time, competing in Club, Area, and National championships. He subsequently moved on to a 420 with daughter Louise as crew, and briefly a Laser, before buying his first Solo in about 1980 when I also joined the Solo Fleet. Ron and I must have been racing each other in Solos for at least 25 years, and he was one of the people who gave me the most help while I was learning to sail the boat. Ron was always prepared to give help and advice to anyone who needed it, sometimes in a very practical way. John Nickalls recalls an early encounter:- My first memory of Ron is of the day when he stepped-in, as rescue crew, to stop me making an even greater fool of myself in my Laser in a big wind-against-tide off the club. After my umpteenth capsize he leapt unbidden into the water and sailed the boat home for me while I was motored back to the club. As one would always expect of Ron, it was just the right thing to do. The Solo fleet members have endless recollections of Ron going back through all those years, many relating to how he seemed to be able to coax the best performance out of his boat with the minimum of effort on his part, while the rest of us were straining every sinew. His sailing style somehow matched his personality – an undemonstrative character whose quiet manner masked a thoughtful and resolute will to win. His sailing prowess is reflected by the many times his name appears on our Club trophies. In all those years of competition on the water, or ashore for that matter, I cannot remember Ron ever using bad language or even getting really annoyed about anything, though there was the odd occasion when he shouted “starboard” quite forcefully. Ron was always a keen supporter of the Solo Fleet social events, and our other excursions, which included some long week- ends cruiser sailing on the Solent and East Coast. The photo attached records one of them. Where so ever Ron went to sail Mary was always there, doing enough worrying for all of us. Malcolm Stuart recalls an occasion when he and Ron were both capsized in heavy weather at Stansgate and struggling to right their boats. The support boat went straight past Solo Fleet Cruise on the Solent Nov 1991. Malcolm to attend to Ron, and Malcolm swears it was because Mary Back row: Geoff Josey, Ron, Malcolm Stuart had a word – no proof ofcourse. Front row: Martin Hall, John Salmon In white is the hired hand I don’t think anyone derived more pleasure from dinghy racing than Ron, particularly on the Blackwater that he loved, and I know how much it hurt him to part with his boat when the physical demands became too much. Even then his loyalty to the Club remained undiminished, and he always took a keen interest in Solo Fleet and Club activities, joining in our social events. He remained on the Race Officer roster through to 2014. His memory will be cherished by members of the Solo Fleet, and I’m sure by many other Club members, as there are so many happy times to look back on. Before the meeting started John Salmon said a few words about Ron Greygoose who had passed away on 15th November 2014. The Commodore then invited the meeting to sit quietly for a short time to remember Ron and other absent friends. 1. Apologies for Absence Apologies for absence were received from: Dave Payne Wendy Dowley Jonathan Pinnock Dennis Gilbey Alan & Carol Clark Geoff & Margaret Josey Malcolm Yeoman Tony Ferguson David St Pier Roger Davis Nick Tovey Peter Tovey Rebecca Tovey James Tovey Nick Miller Michael Miller Chris Burrows Derek Gardner Mervyn Muggs Robin Lovett Chris Kirby Roger Camp 2. Minutes of the 2013 AGM The minutes of the 2013 AGM were accepted as a true and accurate record, proposed by Neil Pembleton, seconded by John Salmon. Carried unanimously 3. Matters arising from the 2013 minutes. At the 2013 AGM Simon Elwell had asked about access to Club sailing dinghies. This was to be addressed by the 2014 board. The Commodore informed the meeting that Pat Shaw had taken the lead in bringing all the Club sailing dinghies up to a good standard. The fleet had also increased by the purchase of two additional sailing dinghies and a beginner’s sailboard.
