Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk 2014 Commodore’s Report - Michaela Dowley AGM 23rd November 2014 I will begin by commenting on the main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season. Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board, and for the previous financial year has comprised six directors: Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing Graham Cross - Rear Commodore for events Sue Shenton - Treasurer Myself, Michaela Dowley - as commodore I am managing director and chair We welcomed Graham and the return of Pat to the Board this year both of whom have hit the ground running and ensured a balanced representation across the fleets at Board level. Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of the administrative burden of the Club. The Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like to extend thanks to all who take the time to serve on the main and various sub committees to enable the Club to continue to thrive. I would like to review with you the subject of memberships and fees - the new fee structure voted in this time last year had been the subject of much debate and I must extend thanks to Clive Shenton for steering the Club through a difficult yet essential process. As a reminder, the introduction of a new fee structure had 3 aims: 1. Simplicity - bringing in a fit for purpose, sensible charging system 2. Fairness - to address the basic imbalances between dinghies and cruisers 3. To generate more income - accounting for our aging demographic I am delighted to report that at this point in time, there are 400 members of Marconi Sailing Club. This compares to 399 at the same point last year. This stands us in a very positive position in light of the following facts: 1. We are holding our own at a time when clubs in our local area see membership numbers declining. 2. Some considered that the new fee structure would drive members away and this has simply not been the case. 3. The demographic of the membership is encouraging in that 25 of our members are young adults and 152 are families. 4. The Clubs financial position is sound - the details of which I will leave to the Treasurers report. However I will say that the Club is in an improved financial position as a result of the new fee structure. This will allow us to invest in capital improvements and maintain our site and facilities. This past year has seen the embedding of our new membership system, Medusa and the use of dutyman which is software that allows the coordination of support boat and race officer duties. As with all new systems there have been some teething issues but I thank all the administrators who have made the systems work for us. As many of you are aware, unfortunately in March of this year our Club President, Tony Benn sadly passed away. Tony Benn had a long, if controversial Parliamentary career spanning from 1950 - 2001, when he then became President of Marconi Sailing Club. The Benn family have a long history with our Club both as friends and neighbours and I am pleased to say that Stephen Benn, Viscount Stansgate and eldest son of Tony has agreed to be our next President. Later in the agenda you will have the opportunity to vote Stephen in as an honorary member of MSC and as President. Moving onto sailing, and without treading on the toes of the sailing secretary, I have to say that 2014 has seen a new breath of life come into the sailing calendar. Thanks to innovative thinking from the sailing sub committee, we have seen the introduction of a number of new activities on offer - all designed to encourage members who are perhaps less confident on the water or wish to hone their skills. I have to add sincere thanks here to Jenny Ball who has again continued to demonstrate her commitment to our Club. Jenny proposed and implemented initiatives such as the Friday free for all sessions, revised the sailing programme to incorporate more popular styles of racing and has been instrumental in driving an increase in dinghy sailing participation. She is also the mastermind and author behind the sailing activities emails that grace our inboxes weekly. Like me, many of you were probably unaware of the extent of all our activities. So Jenny, thank you. Turning to cadets - the future lifeblood of the Club. Cadet week, in its new format was yet again a tremendous success. Sail training continues to go from strength to strength and this year has seen the addition of ‘Oppi Club’ aimed at our members as young as 2. January 2015 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk It is here that I would like to take a moment to recognise the contribution of John Nickalls to the development of our cadets. John has worked tirelessly over the past few years particularly in driving sail training with an incredible 409 individual cadet sessions delivered this season. This year John has also been involved in coordinating other events and activities such as the National Schools Sailing Regatta, a visit from the Chernobyls Children, cadet week and encouraging our cadets to participate in external events such as team racing, training days and fleet regattas. Of course these activities all involve a team of people, but nothing happens without strong leadership and John has been at the forefront each time. Ensuring our young members enjoy sailing and feel part of the Club is how we protect its future so I would like to invite John up to receive our new trophy awarded for outstanding commitment to Marconi Sailing Club. The sailing secretary will cover the various opens and training events hosted at Marconi this year, however I will report on the East Coast Piers Race. The ECPR attracted 55 entries in 2014. This slight reduction compared to 2013 is accounted for by clashes with other big catamaran events and is in fact an excellent turnout given that many other regattas have seen quite drastic reductions in entry numbers. Once again the cruiser fleet contributed to the safe running of the race. Mike Turner was missed as race officer after an unfortunate accident put him out of action, and thanks are due to Clive Shenton who stood in. Our financial outcome was £200 better than last year and the total donation to the Cirdian Trust was £11,800 with £400 going to the Essex Air Ambulance. The highlight perhaps is that for the first time a Marconi boat took both line honours and first place in the ECPR. Our cadets have been active in attendance at the National Schools Sailing Regatta, various training days and competing in the topper and laser fleet circuits. Here I would like to award the Mamgu trophy to Beth Spencer for her excellent write up of the team Marconi experience at this years NSSA regatta. The dinghies, catamaran and cruiser racing fleets have also travelled the length and breadth of the UK and even into Europe to and beyond to compete and fly the MSC flag. I would like to reflect on one particular race where there was an incredible achievement for an MSC crew. The Round Ireland Race is run by Wicklow Sailing Club every two years. The 2014 Race attracted 36 starters including McGregor IV from Marconi. The crew included Marconi members Peter Ward, Tom Clayton and Derek Brown with a number of other members involved as delivery crew. The Race is a course of 704 nautical miles and the Race instructions are very simple – leave Ireland to starboard. Any crew completing this course has exhibited seamanship of the highest standard. McGregor IV finished 2nd in Class and 10th overall in a time of five days 11 hours 18 minutes and a few seconds. For this achievement I ask the owner and skipper of McGregor IV Peter Ward to come forward to receive the Seamanship Trophy. Hosting opens and large events have been supported by access to the Tony B and our new support boat which took to the water in February of this year. Marconi Greygoose is a 5.5m rib and is the result of a successful Sports England grant. She took her maiden voyage on a cold February morning and has since supported a number of events and training sessions. It is very poignant at this time to say were pleased to name the new rib Marconi Greygoose after Ron. This is a fitting tribute to his years of service to the Club and is now a fitting memorial. The Tony B took to the water late this season and is named in honour of the late Tony Benn. This has been project over a number of years, with all renovation work carried out in house, mainly by the Wednesday gang. The Tony B has a number of functions, serving as a support to mooring parties and also as a committee boat. As well as on the water, there have been many shoreside activities and developments. MSC is ‘on the map’ more than ever before thanks to our new website, open day and numerous publicity opportunities with regular articles in yachts and yachting and the local press. We have also seen improved links into the RYA with Marconi now recognised as a Champion Club and RYA training centre. In May, the club held an Open Day as part of the RYA Push the Boat Out event to show off our club to prospective members. A combination of detailed planning, publicity and good weather resulted in a fantastic turn out on the day. Cruisers, cats and dinghies provided 100 individual sailing trips whilst the children’s activities and Pimms Tent were very popular onshore. Followed by an evening BBQ and social, it was an excellent day for new and existing members alike. 11 new members signed up which was a great result. Thanks to Graham & Jayne Cross and the army of volunteers who made the day possible. Social events in general have been a huge success this year with a number of new ideas and wider participation. Events have included Morris Dancing, Bands, theme nights and quiz evenings to name a few. Social events have helped to drive up the revenue generated by the bar - so I thank you all for helping on that front. The bar has also been open more frequently this year, often on a Sunday to help hydrate members after a days racing or working around the site. We all know serving behind the bar can be a thankless task. Although not purely for her barwork, it is here that I would like to award the Commodores trophy to Lizzy Sammons. Amongst other jobs, Lizzy has run the bar nearly every Sunday both on and off season, helped to paint the clubhouse and has been heavily involved in the restoration work to the Tony B. I am told that on occasion Lizzy has been known to walk from Canvey Island to Rayleigh in order to catch a lift to the Club on a Wednesday. In light of her huge commitment to the Club I would like to invite Lizzy to collect her award. In my opinion she is a truly deserving recipient of the Commodores trophy for 2014. The statement is also available in the members area of the MSC website under AGM Information. As Finance Director of Marconi Sailing Club Ltd, I present a financial summary along with the accounts for approval by the members. The accounts as distributed to the members are set out in the prescribed format ready for submission to Companies House and to HMRC on pages 1 to 4 of the attached document. INDEPENDENT REVIEW The accounts have been reviewed by John Bird, Chartered Management Accountant (former member and Treasurer). INCOME (TOP HALF OF PAGE 4) Overall income from subscriptions and fees stands at £141801 (£147651 less Member Loan Discounts of £5850) as against last year’s income of £124651 (£131026 less Loan Discounts of £6375). This is mainly as a result of the revised fee structure, as the level of membership has remained broadly same, currently standing at around 400 members. Surpluses on the bar, social events, camping fees, open meetings, Cadet Week and other activities has increased to £15541 (last year £14821). Overall therefore the club’s revenue has increased to £157342 (last year £139472). EXPENDITURE (LOWER HALF OF PAGE 4) Spending has been slightly lower for sailing activities (down £32), although this is a misleading figure given that there was a significant decrease in expenditure on rib fuel. Spending on club and precincts was down by £2595 but this was due to the late January 2015 Navigans 18

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk presentation of accounts by various suppliers which will now be met in 2014/2015. Social and publicity showed an increase of £622 due to the setting up the new club website essential both for the benefit of members and the attraction of new members. There was a decrease (£1969) in administration expenditure which was brought about largely by income received from RYA training now being carried out by the Club. NET SURPLUS (BOTTOM OF PAGE 4) The club’s surplus before interest and tax was up at £69218 (last year £48885). This increase is partly due to expenditure planned for 2013/2014 which was not actually incurred before 31 August 2014, and includes contingency amounts for major repairs to the approach road, potential insurance claim and refunds for boat fees payable in December each year. As the end of the financial year falls on 31st August, and subscriptions and fees are not due until 1st January thereafter, it is essential to ensure that club retains about £30,000 in the bank account to meet unavoidable expenditure for those five months (September to mid-January) where little or no income is received. One of the three aims of the revised fee structure was to produce a small surplus which could be put to minor capital projects improving the club infrastructure and/or as seed money to be used to secure a Sport England Inspired Facilities grant of up to £50,000. The club continues at present to benefit from the historically low interest rates in the repayment of its development loan, but we need to be prepared for an increase in interest rates probably within the next financial year. (0.5% increase would amount to an increase of at least £3000 p.a.) Corporation tax unfortunately shows an increase arising from the increase in income. The Board are investigating ways in which corporation tax can be reduced. The final surplus was therefore £40500 (last year £20092). BALANCE SHEET (PAGES 1 TO 3) There have not been any significant changes to the balance sheet during the year and the overall Net Asset Value of the club improved to a sound £319026 (last year £278526). This is approximately £798 per member! It is worth drawing members’ attention to the following areas: Capital spending (note 2, page 2): This has been fairly low this past year with the purchase of the new rib (£19394) which was supported by a £10,000 Sport England Grant. However the club infrastructure will require some significant expenditure e.g. internal roadways, galley refit, boiler system, hard and pontoon, main gate etc. National Westminster and Members' loans (notes 4 & 5, page 3): The balance outstanding on the long term bank loan has reduced from £412251 (2013) to £392404, a repayment of £19847. Repayment of £11,000 has been made against the membership loan which now stands at £116,500. The club's long term finance therefore is £508,904. When considering this figure members should compare it to the fixed assets total of £826,702 shown at the top of page 1. Essentially it is saying that the club's equity in all of it property and assets is now 38.4%. This represents a significant achievement since the members bought out the club 2003, especially in light of the developments undertaken. BUDGET FOR 2014/2015 The Board receives detailed monthly budget reports where the income and expenditure to date is compared against the annual budget, which enables the directors to closely monitor the club’s financial progress. The annual budget for 2014/15 was drafted in July, discussed and agreed with the main budget holders, and ratified by the Board in early October. As Treasurer I have a very detailed and comprehensive picture of the club’s finances which informs future planning. I am pleased to be able to report that the club’s financial position is sound. The cash reserves together with the proposed moderate increase in subscriptions will enable us to address over the next two years some of the more urgent projects such as the internal roadways, maintenance of the approach road, maintenance of existing club boats and purchase of additional, improvements to safety and security, essential upgrades to the Clubhouse and Club equipment. We are looking into the possibility of gaining a Sport England Inspired Facilities Grant of £50,000 for capital improvements to the Clubhouse, and our chances of success will be enhanced if we can support our application with some capital funding both in cash and in kind. Finally I would like to extend grateful thanks to Mike & Rosemary Turner for their assistance with the receipt of the income payable to the club, and to Simon Hey for his assistance with outgoing payments and administration of PAYE. Unfortunately for the club, Simon is moving up north and will no longer be a member. I would like to thank him for the years of service given to the club, and wish him every good fortune in his new home. Sue Shenton, Finance Director. January 2015 Navigans 19

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Marconi SC Sailing Secretaries’ Report 2014 AGM 23rd November 2014 Good morning everyone and it is my pleasure to present the Sailing Secretary Report for 2014. I am pleased to advise that 2014 has been another very busy year for sailing across the club. I will endeavour to do justice to the range of activity but I apologise in advance for anything I may have missed. With support from the Board and Management Committee and encouragement from the RYA, the Sailing Sub-Committee set out to enhance sailing participation during 2014. There were four strands to this: 1. continue improving the club’s sailing equipment and capability 2. support activities to recruit new members; 3. introduce some new activities to encourage wider participation 4. make our sailing activities more accessible for existing and new members to join in We were fortunate this year to have some welcome additions to our sailing related equipment. The new RIB, part funded through a grant, has been a valuable add to our support cover. The club has recently bought a new Laser and Topper thanks to proceeds from Cadet week and a generous individual donation. And 2014 saw the launch of our very own purpose built Committee Boat – the Tony B – which was officially baptised at the Helm of the Year event. A big thank you to the many people involved in making these projects happen and continuing to build our sailing equipment and capability. This was also our first season as an official RYA Training Centre which means we can now deliver RYA accredited power boat training – thanks to the efforts of Bob Collins as Principle and Pat Shaw as our qualified instructor. We have taken this opportunity to train club members to RYA Powerboat standards and Bob and Pat will continue to expand this offering going forward. The club was also awarded RYA Championship Club status this year in recognition of the club sail training and racing activities. Thanks to Lee Harrison for co-ordinating this with the RYA. In May, we supported the Open Day which Michaela has already covered – with cruisers, cats and dinghies providing 100 individual sailing trips, alongside the shore based activities. With new or recent members in mind, we introduced Friday Free4All evening sailing sessions. We provided safety boat cover and offered support for people who wanted to build on their sailing skills or just go for a sociable evening sail. These sessions were very well received and with the galley providing an evening meal after sailing – it was pretty much the best way to start a weekend! Based on the popularity of Wednesday night pursuit races – we also included some Sunday pursuit races to encourage people who prefer racing from the hard. Both of these formats will be continued next year. We also reviewed the communication of sailing activities in the club. The year book and website continue to be the main source of information about club activities. However, they do not necessarily explain what a particular sailing activity is or how to get involved which might deter some members from joining in. We therefore introduced a Sailing Information leaflet to supplement the year book – by explaining how the different activities work (eg. dinghy cruises, cadet training, cruiser events, club racing etc) and who to get in touch with to find out more. In a similar vein, we also introduced the weekly email to remind people of upcoming sailing activities and encourage people to join in. We hope members have found these to be positive additions to club communications. And we have had plenty of activities to talk about in the weekly emails! The Cruiser Fleet organised a number of passage cruises including Brightlingsea, St Katherine’s Dock, Ipswich, Tollesbury and the Watercress Run to Heybridge. Annual social events included the Fitting Out Supper, visit from Colne Yacht Club and Cruiser Fleet AGM. On the racing side, Woozle Hunter netted 14 trophies in the East Anglian Offshore Racing Series including winning their class and coming 2nd in the overall series. Caroline and Blue Moon posted consistent top 3 placings in the BJRC races and McGregor IV competed in the Royal Ocean Racing Club Series coming second in class and fourth overall amongst an international fleet in what is a very challenging series. Congratulations to Ian Ivermee, Andy Ellis, Richard Roberts, Peter Ward, Derek Brown and their respective crews. Thanks go to Roger Camp as Cruiser Fleet Captain and Peter Ward as Cruiser Racing Rep. We would also like to register a particular thanks to the many cruiser fleet members who supported the East Coast Piers Race and made this important event so successful – the safe running of this event depends very much on this support. Dinghy Cruises continue to go from strength to strength with cruises on the first Saturday of the month from March to November and taking part in the UK Wayfarer Association Rally over the late May Bank Holiday weekend. The dinghy cruise schedule for next year is being expanded with cruises in January and February and the introduction of some weekday cruises – so watch this space! Thanks to Colin Wardell and the team for co-ordinating the cruises. Windsurfing members continued to be very active this year – and, as ever, were seen to venture out when the rest of us had retreated to the safety of the clubhouse. The windsurfing fleet have been successful in recruiting new members and the club has recently purchased some windsurfing equipment to encourage people to give it a go. See fleet captain, Nick Miller if you are interested! The Cat and Dinghy racing season comprised a full schedule of Spring, Summer and Autumn Points Races, Bank Holiday Series, Wednesday night races and one off races. It would be remiss of me not to report that, with the exception of Wednesday night races, participation in racing was down this year vs last year. We are not unique in this and some of it is due to individual January 2015 Navigans 20

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk circumstances – but it is an area that we will review to see if we can improve racing participation next year. Nevertheless - we had a total of 221 fleet race starts over the course of the season – with very few races cancelled due to wind or participation. We will celebrate this season’s successes with a short Prizegiving after the AGM – we would appreciate if everyone could stay to support that. The club hosted a number of events including the East Coast Piers Race which Michaela has already covered, Open events for Sprint 15s, Solos, Kestrels, Toppers, Junior Cats and the Dart 16 Nationals. Marconi members also represented the club at the Sprint 15 Nationals, Tornado Nationals, Grafham Cat Open, Maylandsea Bay and Thorpe Bay Winter Series – and we will be represented this Christmas at the Tornado Worlds in Perth! Marconi was also well represented at the Barts Bash – an event involving 600 clubs around the world in memory of Andrew Bart Simpson, Olympic Sailor and to promote the Andrew Simpson Sailing Foundation. We joined forces with Stone, Blackwater, Maylandsea, Bradwell Cruising Club, Goldhanger and Harlow Blackwater Sailing Clubs to put on this event over three race courses. 54 Marconi cruisers, dinghies and cats took part raising over £1000 for the charity – many more club members were involved as support boat crews and race support and we also organised the Guinness World Record witnesses! It was a wonderful event and the sight of 200 boats racing together on the River is not one that any of us will forget in a hurry. And last, but definitely not least, Cadet sailing activity has continued to go from strength to strength. Cadet Week saw around 80 Cadets and adult learners take part in another full week of sailing, racing and fun activities. The long distance race saw well over 100 club members decamp to Osea for a picnic lunch in superb weather. The week ended with the annual Cadet Regatta with 42 competitors turning out to race in 25 boats. Around 60 helpers provided tutoring, support boat cover, launch and recovery and general support to ensure the Cadet week was a success. Our thanks go to Dave Clarke, Bekki Tovey and Chris Kirby who headed up the Committee which organised the week. Thanks also to David Nickalls who ended his term as Cadet Fleet Captain and has now passed the baton on to Beth Spencer. In addition to Cadet Week, the cadets have been busy through the rest of the year. John Nickalls co-ordinated 8 very well attended Sail Training days throughout the season supported by an army of helpers. Attendance ranged between 12 and 40 cadets split into two groups so training could be tailored based on experience levels. This was supplemented with the new Opi Club run by Fee Barnes for cadets who may not feel quite ready to join in the sail training – providing a welcome addition to our training provision. Further afield - John Nickalls and team again co-ordinated a group of our Cadets to attend the National Schools Sailing Association Regatta event in July. Marconi Cadets also performed very well in the Barts Bash, Eastern Region Topper Event, Topper Nationals, Junior Cat Event, Laser Inlands – and David Nickalls and Sophie Saville are this year’s Dart 16 National Champions. In addition to the people I have already mentioned, I would like to thank the remaining Fleet Captains, John Salmon, Kevin Dowley, Tom Brooks, Rob Bard; the bosuns Dave Clarke and Colin Leveridge for keeping the support boats in good working order and Tony Goode for maintaining the race marks. Additionally, John Burgoyne, Sally Wilson, Dave and Jemma Clarke have ensured that Race officers and Support Boats were rota’d, that results were calculated and trophies organised. Whilst this is just a whistlestop tour of 2014, I hope it does justice to the full range of sailing we have all been involved in. I am pleased to confirm that arrangements are progressing well for the 2015 sailing schedule. We again have a full range of events planned across the season and across all types of sailing. I look forward to seeing you out there. Jenny Ball Sailing Secretary January 2015 Navigans 21

MSCP54 Issue 2 Employment of Contractors by Members 16/01/2015 1. Introduction This Code of Practice covers the employment of contractors by members at the Marconi Sailing Club site. This Code of Practice MUST be followed when any contractor is employed by members to work on their boats or equipment. It is recognised that members may be assisted by relatives and friends when working on their boats and other equipment, who receive no financial remuneration. In such cases it is the member’s responsibility to ensure their safety and well being. Under no circumstances will the Marconi Sailing Club, its officials, employees and other Club members be held responsible for any injury incurred by any person working on a member’s boat or other equipment. At all times any equipment supplied by the Marconi Sailing Club may only be used under the supervision of an Authorised User and in accordance with the appropriate Code of Practice. February 2015 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk 2. Definitions Club Member: - Any individual member or group of members of the Marconi Sailing Club. Contractor:- Any person, company or organisation employed by a Club member to carry out work on the member’s boat, trailer or any other property for financial gain. 3. Member’s Responsibility 1. To ensure that the contractor is given a copy of this Code of Practice. 2. To ensure that the contractor has current Third Party Public Liability Insurance (minimum recommended amount £5,000,000 Five Million Pounds). 3. To ensure that any equipment supplied by the member for the use of the contractor is safe, correctly installed and fit for purpose. For example that any ladder is adequate and suitably fastened to the boat. 4. To obtain the agreement of the relevant Board member if the contractor will be using any Marconi Sailing Club equipment. (Contractors are expected to use their own tools and equipment as far as possible. This benefits the contractor who knows their own tools and equipment and minimises the use of MSC equipment. However it may be necessary to use MSC equipment, an example would be the mast derrick, where it is impractical for the contractor to supply their own.) 5. If MSC equipment is required, to make the necessary arrangements with an authorised user of the relevant Marconi Sailing Club equipment to attend at a mutually convenient date and time. The contractor and others may assist but only under the Authorised User’s supervision. 6. To ensure that they or their representative (who must be an MSC member) is present at the Club at all times when the contractor is on site. To record all such times in the MSC Log Book which is kept in the upstairs lounge in the Clubhouse including any damage/incident occurring. Any damage to other members’ property must be recorded in the logbook and reported to the owner of the property as soon as possible. Similarly any damage to Marconi Sailing Club property must be recorded in the logbook and reported to a member of the Board. 7. To ensure that the clubhouse and site are securely locked when the contractor leaves the site. 4. Contractor’s Responsibility 1. To comply with this Code of Practice. 2. To furnish to the Club member a copy of their current Third Party Public Liability Insurance (minimum recommended amount £5,000,000 Five Million Pounds). 3. To ensure that any tools/equipment they supply and use on site are fit for purpose and used in a safe manner. 4. To only use Marconi Sailing Club equipment in the presence of the Club member and a Marconi Sailing Club authorised user. 5. To ensure the safety and well being of any other persons on site who may be affected by the activity. For example ensuring that adequate shielding is in place to protect others when arc welding etc. 5. Member’s and Contractor’s Joint Responsibility 1. To act at all times with due regard to current Health, Safety, and all other relevant legislation. 2. To record any Dangerous Occurrence, Accident or other situation in the relevant documentation in the Club House. Completed sheets must be sent to the MSC Safety Officer. 6. Example of contractors record entered in MSC Log Book Date Time Club Member, Contractor Name, Comments contractor on Boat Name, Address, Club Equipment used, Authorised & off site Tel. No. Tel. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk April Issue copy deadline: Saturday 15th March Club Notices Commodore Welcome your March 2015 edition of Navigans. At the recent RYA dinghy show at Alexandra Palace, Marconi were presented with our RYA Championship Club Status. As a Champion Club we can look to enjoy the support and help of the RYA in achieving our aims in youth training and development including advice and support from our local RYA High Performance Manager. Thanks are due to Lee Harrison for driving forward this development with the RYA. I would like to update you on some applications for external grant funding that the Board of Directors have been working on over the winter months. In 2013 we were successful in obtaining a £10,000 Sport England Grant for a new safety boat - the Marconi Greygoose. In February 2015 we submitted a second application for £10,000 towards a rowing gig. The rowing gigs are built by the Pioneer Trust, based in Brightlingsea where young apprentices learn the boat building trade. We were fortunate enough to have a rowing gig on site during camping fortnight in 2014 where a number of our members showed an interest in rowing and had a go themselves. There is a very active gig community on the Blackwater and we believe the gig will be a great asset to the Club, allowing more people access to activities on the water. We hope to hear soon if our bid has been successful. We are also in the process of compiling an application for the Sport England Inspired Facilities fund. This is a fund where awards of up to £50,000 are made to aid in the renovation and modernisation of local sports facilities. Marconi SC will be submitting a bid to support the development of a permanent covered area over the patio at the rear of the Club, plus a viewing platform or veranda extending from the clubhouse towards the BBQ area which incorporates a secure storage area beneath. These are exciting projects, which will allow us to improve our training facilities and enhance the experience for members. However, these projects are dependent on the success of our grant application. The deadline for applications is at the beginning of June 2015 so I hope that we will have more news to share with you towards the end of the summer. You may have seen recent emails regarding the cat and dinghy parks. I would like to thank Jenny Ball and her team who have taken on the mammoth task over the winter of reconciling our membership database records with boats in the parks. It is absolutely essential that all boats in the parks can be identified for a number of reasons, one of which is to ensure that all fees have been paid. Please take note of the information contained in the emails and ensure that your boats are clearly labeled with your information. I would also like to remind you that the Spring working parties are scheduled for the Sunday the 8th and Sunday 15th March - please do support the Club by attending to help get us ready for the new season which is now rapidly approaching! Frank’s chain store is open every Sunday until the end of April, although if you are making a special journey, it might be best to ring him beforehand on either or . He has stock of ground and riser chain, shackles, anodes and rings. I believe he also has a couple of second hand moorings for sale. Whilst we are talking moorings, a personal plea from the telehandler drivers - would people please have the slots of the pallet (the bit where the forks go in) facing the road or accesses point with the anchors on the bottom stocks towards the telehandler. The ground chain should be on top of each anchor with the riser on the ground chain. This should be topped off with the mooring buoy. This makes it easier to pick up the pallet and pull out the mooring for inspection on the hard. WORKING PARTY 8TH MARCH @ 09:30 We have a club working party on Sunday 8th March starting at 0930. Pete Ward Solo Fleet SOLO FLEET BOWLING EVENING As you may remember from previous reports the Solo Fleet are keen bowlers (well once a year). So eight, with three supporters, descended on Madison Heights Bowling Centre in Maldon on Friday evening February 20th. As usual we played two games with a snack in between. All bowlers, including the two ladies, showed real skill in the first game and although there was one bowler well ahead, the scoring was very close. There was a good choice of snacks which was served on a long table to take all eleven of us. This was very much enjoyed . The snack must have fired up some people for they seemed to have their eye and arms co-ordinated (if that’s the right expression ) afterwards. This resulted in some good total scores. The first lady was Julie Spencer (214) and she was awarded the trophy and a bottle of wine. I think it may have been a little overwhelming for the men as Julie’s score was 13 higher than the highest man. That was Mick Taylor (201) (presented with trophy and wine). Next was Dennis Dear (187) followed by Geoff Josey (175). A good night was had by all, with the supporters sitting by the two lanes adding their encouragement. Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc-org.uk Social News WINTER DINNER DANCE REVIEW The new venue this year for the Clubs Annual Dinner Dance, proved to be a success! Over 100 people began the evening at the Orsett Hall, by enjoying a cocktail reception listening to concert harpist, Danielle Perret playing a selection of popular music for all tastes. I do hope that Clive Shenton, who won a raffle prize of a (model) combine harvester, appreciated the Wurzels playing "I've got a brand new combine harvester" as he walked back to his table!! If anyone has any further constructive comments, please contact me at . I really want to build this event up and encourage as many members as possible to enjoy, what really is a great evening out of wetsuits and buoyancy aids! Sorry for those of you who weren't able to get tickets this year. There was quite a waiting list of hopeful people. Tickets sold out relatively quickly. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Marconi Sailing Club CAMPING RULES – 2015 THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES.  All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.  No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday  Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.  Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.  No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.  No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.  No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site at all times.  The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.  All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present.  Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.  Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc.  Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.  Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc.  Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are probably not paying much attention to traffic.  Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.  The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.  All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk May Issue copy deadline: Saturday 19th April Club Notices Commodore I write this as the season is just getting underway with a busy first weekend of racing and mooring laying. Given the chilly temperature around 15 boats took part in the first Spring Points racing - lets keep it up! Early March saw 6 of our members qualify as RYA racing coaches during an intense 2 day course held at MSC. They broke boats and battered their bodies in freezing temperatures but are now well placed to deliver even better coaching and instruction to some of our advanced cadets and others in need of a bit of advice. Congratulations and thanks to John Nickalls, David Nickalls, Fee Barnes, Tom Clayton, Lee Harisson and Andrew Dowley. Membership packs were also distributed in early March where you can find all the useful information you need for the year. The sailing information guide for 2015 has been sent via email but can also be found in the members section of the website - a must read for members new and old! Keep an eye on the new MSC website for regular updates on club activities. I wish you all a safe and happy season. See you on the water. Michaela Dowley Commodore Club Secretary EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius. On sunny spring days it is easy to be fooled but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim. Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the wind chill. There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm. WATER HEATING The boiler has until now been operating 24/7 summer and winter. To economise on the use of gas the boiler has recently been fitted with a timer and it will only be on at times of anticipated need. There will obviously be a period of trial and error while the system settles in and achieves a balance between economy and the need for hot water. Please be patient while this is going on. Further information will be provided at a later date. Avy" Nearery| Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Cadet Fleet MARCONI AT THE 420 INLANDS After a balmy trip to Rope Runners for the cadet social last weekend, this week’s weather was just the opposite at Rutland Water for the 420 Inlands. A strong, gusty north-easterly, 4-6C and intermittent rain from threatening grey skies set the scene for a challenging weekend for Hannah Bard and Dan Nickalls. With easily the oldest boat and sails (leading to the class association’s dusting-down of a little-used ‘grandfathering’ rule!) in an intensely-competitive fleet (with squad selection at stake, and with personal on- the-water coaches at the top end), the scene was set for some challenges. Whilst Dan and Hannah didn’t win the event (by admittedly a significant margin) they had a great time (especially after they’d defrosted). They came away with some really good learning experiences (including an understanding of the dramatic difference between how you start in top-end 420 and Laser fleets), some stories of success (a great improvement in first beat performance was one of them) and a firm belief that you can keep a positive attitude and enjoy yourself even when any sane person would find the going very tough. Great to see the Marconi flag flown again on the circuit, especially with our new Champion Club status. John Nickalls CADET SOCIAL MEET UP TO ROPE RUNNERS On the afternoon of Sunday 8th march, the cadet fleet went to Rope Runners for two hours of adrenaline, excitement and competition. We got kitted up in our harnesses ready for the unknown. There were six courses, two bottom, two middle and two top, the hardest being the top right. So it was unsurprising that most of us went for the hardest courses first, a bit of competition came through here and a large amount of screaming. I was the only one who had been before, so I thought I would find it easy, but on the first course Olivia Duckmanton and I went on (the hardest one of course) and I got stuck. Left hanging for a while was not just painful but very embarrassing, especially as my legs were too short to reach the platform. It was certainly funny for everyone else who stood there laughing at me. I believe that I will never live this down now…. that teaches me for being so cocky. Along with the course there was a climbing wall, which a few of us (Jason Clarke and Dan Nickalls) took part in. It was neck and neck all the way to the top of the wall but with Dan’s advantage of height he was able to reach the bell first, taking the win. Within the Marconi cadets the fan drop was very popular. It involved jumping off of a platform to the floor. Our youngest participant was Alex who landed on the ground with a great smile on his face. He seemed to be the bravest throughout the whole afternoon, questioning those who didn’t want to do certain courses, asking why they were so scared. It was a very enjoyable afternoon that allowed us to all catch up before the sailing starts. Hope you all had a great afternoon, see you soon. March 2015 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Edal's continuing meander around the UK summer 2013 Troon to Isle of Man. Apologies to one and all but it's taken me a while to get round to updating this continuing tale but there's been a lot going on - particularly 2014 on the sailing front - more on that later. Previous logs detailed how we set out Spring 2010 up the East coast through the Caledonian, spent two seasons and three winters on Scotlands West coast then turned south in 2013 through the Crinan Canal into Firth of Clyde and in this episode are about to leave the Firth bound for Northern Ireland. We'd made it to Troon harbour in the south of the Firth by 26th July when I decided to spend some time at home before getting back to Edal on the 2nd August. TROON TO GLENARM. The marina at Troon is just one of those places that feels "comfy" - set behind it's old stone harbour walls which still has some trade and fishing plus the high speed ferry that berths on the outside of the wall. Maybe it's this mix that makes it to my eye's "comfy" I was always a bit happier with a bit of industrialisation and mix of different craft plying their trade. Coming up the East Coast the mixed harbours of Lowestoft, Wells, Grimsby etc were much more interesting than harbours where it was just leisure craft. The other thing I really like about Troon is it's transport links - getting back from home in deepest Essex to unlocking the boat hatch took just about five hours - I could hardly believe I was in Scotland and back on the boat in such a short time after the 11 hour drives I'd previously done to get back to Loch Creran north of Oban. Before I'd got back to Edal on the 2nd I had been communicating with my soon to be crew John about where and when he should join. The favourite seemed to be our next port of Girvan but it seemed the wind direction and strength would not be kind on the 3rd to allow me to get there. Come the 3rd and I did actually leave and started beating into a wind over tide but after a couple of hours I felt discretion was the better part and turned back and berthed again in Troon. Interestingly it's only the first time I've ever turned back after setting off and on reflection I think it was the best thing to do as it was not so much the conditions in beating into the sea but what I'd face when I got to Girvan as it has a shallow entrance which by reputation could cut up rough. Let John know I would be another day in Troon and he said - "no worries I'll come to Troon anyway and that will give the weather another day to go down". So in the event we left Troon together on the 5th in a light clement wind on which we sailed and motorsailed the 20nm to Girvan. The entrance to Girvan is shallow and best entry is 3 hours either side of high water - high water on the 5th was 1204 so last entry would be about 1500 - we left Troon at 0728 and were in the harbour at 1203 just about high water. Roughly four and a half hours for 20nm a pleasant easy trip. Girvan is another old harbour which the local authority has spent money on in the hope of improving both the environment and local income. There are super new pontoons with electricity and water and a very welcoming harbour master who can't do enough to help. The only negative are the facilities - at the time of our visit they were "public" and only opened restricted hours so if you wanted to leave early as we did, the "facilities" would not be open. The HM said as visiting craft numbers go up they expect to be able to justify building dedicated loo's and showers but at the moment they were "spent out". Despite this I'd recommend using Girvan as a passage port - in clement weather it's easy to get into and a very welcoming place. Edal on the new Girvan pontoons. Girvan beach and southern breakwater of harbour entrance - Ailsa Craig on horizon. The next day was to be a milestone passage leaving Scotland and across the North Channel bound for Glenarm in Northern Ireland. The North Channel has a bit of a fearsome reputation particularly in bad weather, when you look at a chart of Ireland and the Irish Sea you can understand why. As the tide floods a huge amount of water in the Atlantic squeezes in towards the land between Scotland and Ireland then turns 90 degrees south and squeezes up even more to rush into the Irish Sea down the North Channel towards the Isle of Man - so it's best to plan to go with the flow. As we would be crossing the channel, most of the time we would be across tide with a couple of hours at the start of the passage with tide against. Passage distance to Glenarm is just short of 41nm so at our usual plan speed of 5kts the crossing should take a little over eight hours. Girvan high water on the 6th August was at 1245 and we could leave three hours before but in consultation with the harbour master he said with our draft we could get out much earlier at 0800 so eight to leave it would be. Leaving then would mean we would punch the weak tide in the remainder of the Firth for about three hours before we got into the stronger tide in the channel and I wanted to take the strong tide more on the beam so the plan on leaving Girvan was to head south of the March 2015 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk straight line to Glenarm. The tide in the main channel was calculated to be 2,2kts going to 4.6kts when it went north so we needed to use it if we could but certainly we didn't want any part of it against us. The forecast said the wind would be in the south with a touch of west at 12/16kts for the entire trip so if the plan worked we would be a little slow to begin with but as we shaped more for Glenarm we should get a cracking sail. In owning Edal I'd done a fair few passages to get where we were now - but I can't remember one which came together and provided such a brilliant passage - this one was my highlight in owning her. We cleared Girvan harbour just after eight and motorsailed for a couple of hours as we were just off the wind and to make more south before gradually in the next hour coming round further west to make a course just south of our line direct to Glenarm - I wanted to be south of the line so we had the option of ending with tide to our destination. Before we left Troon I'd rigged the new No3 instead of the big genoa as it sets much better than the reefed 150% genoa and with a few tweaks to iron out the wrinkles (suggested by John) as we came onto the long tack of five hours towards Glenarm the little boat picked up her skirts and flew. The day was mostly bright with scudding white clouds - the wind stiffening to middle teens often higher, boat well heeled, autopilot steering we sat in the cockpit drinking coffee, eating, chatting, occasionally tending the boat and just enjoying the thrill of a sailing boat going so well. The only slight "jar" in the day was a minor disagreement with the crew about the course being kept as I still wanted to be with tide to our destination so we didn't have to punch it into Glenarm - but as is the way of these things it was soon forgotten as the excitement of going so well continued. Some shore side folk may wonder what all the fuss is about it's only a big piece of plastic being blown by the wind - but sailing and it's different experiences good and bad - stir the soul and this day was one of the best. Geoff Pack the old Yachting Monthly editor said in one of his last articles before he died "there is just nothing like getting your old boat sailing as best she can" I couldn't have put it better. We made it into Glenarm and were tied up at 1628 - eight and a half hours for 41nm not bad for a wee boat with a 20 foot 6 inch waterline. Glenarm was delightful - easy entrance - an old harbour with new pontoons and a welcoming HM both of the skippers on board would recommend it. We ate on board with a few glasses of wine before a walk then bed anticipating after such a great day the passage to Bangor tomorrow. Glenarm Harbour GLENARM, BANGOR, ARDGLASS THEN ONTO THE ISLE OF MAN. The next few days would see us covering shorter distances in very mixed weather although the forecast was in the main for fairly light winds. The plan was to make for Peel on the Isle of Man by day sailing south down the coast of Northern Ireland to Bangor, then Ardglass before striking out for Peel across the Irish Sea. Our next port would be Bangor only 24nm away and on the 7th August the tide would start south from 0620. The wind would be light so we would motorsail. With such a short trip we could afford to have a bit of lie in so agreed to leave about 0830. In truth after yesterday there was nothing spectacular about a motorsail down the NI coast there are a few hazards - - a cluster of off- lying rocks known as The Maidens and inshore of them the Hunter Rock. There is a lighthouse on The Maidens and the Hunter is marked by a North Cardinal at it's seaward end with a clear channel between them - we chose the channel rather than stand out to sea and go round. Just south of them is The Isle of Muck which if you are relatively close in the pilot warns it looks like you can go inside between the Isle and the mainland but don't as there's a drying causeway so we passed outside about a mile off. Leaving the Isle behind we were soon in Belfast Lough and several big ships came and went as we made the six nm from Black Head to the marina at Bangor, arriving at 1210 - only 3hrs 40min to complete the passage of 24nm - the tide had rushed us south. March 2015 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk After Troon, Girvan and Glenarm all relatively small harbours with pontoons - Bangor seemed massive, friendly enough, very nice facilities, everything you could want, a very good passage port but for me lacking in character. Leaving following day would be interesting as to get to Ardglass we had to pass through Donaghadee Sound between the mainland and Copeland Island and it's one of the places where the tide rushes through so you have to "go with the flow". The south going tide on 8th August would begin about 0651, we had 34nm to reach Ardglass and just under 5nm from Bangor to reach the Sound. We left just on the turn of the south going tide following a larger boat out of the marina who also turned to make for Donaghadee Sound - - - it's always reassuring when you see another sailor executing the same plan as you! The Sound although appearing quite wide has a fairly narrow buoyed channel which shallows then doglegs south to avoid a series of rocks called the Deputy Reefs. Both boats were rushed through on the south going tide, our companion with her longer waterline out distancing us quite easily. The remainder of the passage was an unremarkable motorsail on a mixed weather day, a little rain mainly overcast but sometimes a little brighter. It was also unremarkable due to my habit of preferring to be well off the coast to clear any off-lying dangers. Down this part of the NI coast if you stay well in there are quite a few and you'd be dodging in and out to miss them - I prefer to set a good long distance between waypoints so we can relax and just manage the boat. Arrived Ardglass just after 1300 having left Bangor 0651 just over six hours for 34nm another fast passage for such a little boat showing the power of the tide and Edal's speed using the Bruntons propeller to motorsail. The entrance to Ardglass and it's small marina is easy to get into and the town and harbour much more my cup of tea - with a working fish quay and modest boats on the pontoons - we were to stay here two nights due to some higher wind forecast next day. The elderly Harbour Master with his gentle Northern Irish accent was helpful and welcoming and at £21 per night with electricity, water, and showers was good value. The village and it's main street echoed it's past as a fishing village with grey fronted houses and small shops, some modest pubs and an excellent fish and chip shop where we dined one early evening. John also found himself a little local pub where he could satisfy his long held need for a couple of pints of draft Guinness on the island of Ireland. The dogleg entrance to Ardglass harbour at low water - it goes down a long way in these parts During our one day stay we fell in with a couple on a 30ft Jeanneau a boat we'd spotted leaving Bangor over an hour before us previous day - they cruised the Irish Sea from their base in Holyhead and when the wind had blown through were headed back there following day. For a time I was tempted to ask if we could sail in company with them as Holyhead was where I intended to eventually make landfall back on the mainland. I dissuaded myself from asking them though as if I never pass this way again I would be sorry to have missed what I'd been told by Murray Bates about the delights of The Isle of Man. When we got to Peel I was very grateful to have made the decision - would not want to have missed seeing the IOM. Friday 10th August we left Ardglass 0629 to make the 32nm to Peel a simple passage gradually losing sight of the Irish coast astern then seeing the bulk of the IOM come up ahead. It was a misty start gradually brightening but remaining overcast. We sailed most of the way and were tied up in the harbour by 1328, seven hours for the crossing. The approach to Peel harbour is easy with it's large outer mole protecting the gate to the inner harbour which only open certain times to allow boats to enter and berth on protected pontoons. The object of the gate (it also has a companion bridge) is to retain the water in the inner harbour so the boats and pontoons stay afloat - before the gates were installed most of the harbour dried. We were approaching at one of these opening times and after calling up the Port of Peel they advised we could follow an old gaffer into the harbour. As we passed through the entrance the HM called out our berth number and gave us directions to the bottom of the harbour. March 2015 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Aerial picture of Peel harbour. My immediate impression of Peel was - I loved it - here was an old port surrounded by it's town a busy bustling sort of place unspoilt by new developments, with a wonderful mix of different craft - - the Old Gaffers were visiting on their Round Britain adventure so they with their varnished spars, bowsprits and bunting made the old port look very gay. The tourists thronging the quaysides and going in and out of the shops, cafes and restaurants added to the bustling scene - it was wonderful just to find a seat at a waterfront cafe and watch the world go by. The harbour is very sheltered from the weather and an ideal place to leave the boat for a time. John and I had been considering best place to get home from and after looking at transport links - this was to be the place - we would both fly, him to Northumberland me back to Essex. A conversation with the Harbour Master said he was happy for me to leave the boat there for up to a month if necessary and he would keep an eye on her. In the event I would be away for just about a fortnight - it was a sad to say goodbye to John at the airport - he had been a good companion - in truth though we weren't fully compatible shipmates there were things he did and said which sometimes grated on me - probably due to us both being skippers on our own boat and having slightly different personalities - his glass always half empty, mine always half full - so although grateful for his companionship I would be happy to be back on Edal on my own. Sunday 12th saw us both flying home - I would be back on Saturday 17th to continue my protracted "lark" round Britain. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Tie a knot in your mainsheet so the boom can't go out more than about 80°. (Then tie another knot in case the first comes undone!) Flatten your sails as much as you can before you set out: kicker, cunningham / downhaul and outhaul all on tight Upwind: Hike hard to make sure the boat can keep moving If you can't keep the boat flat, let the mainsheet out until you can (but keep pointing close-hauled). Be ready to react quickly! Bearing away: This is the most tricky bit, and caused most of the capsizes yesterday. As you come up to the windward mark: o Ease off your kicker so the sail twists and the boom rises a bit (this can be tricky on a Pico  ) o If you can, lift your daggerboard to about halfway Then KEEP THE BOAT FLAT as you steer smoothly away from the wind around the mark, easing the sheet out as you go. Keeping the boat flat is really important, otherwise it will just turn back into the wind and you'll have to start again. As the boat accelerates, the rudder will get much more sensitive, so steer smoothly and firmly. Finally, as you approach downwind sailing, the tipping force on the boat will suddenly disappear: you need to be ready to get in towards the centre of the boat to keep it flat (and the right way up...). We did the first few races of the 2015 'Sail Training Series' at the end of the afternoon session. Success mainly meant getting round the course without capsizing (or capsizing fewer times than others), but we saw a variety of results and some excellent, fast sailing. We'll take all the results forward to an end-of-season celebration! Well done yesterday, everyone who sailed should be very proud about their performance... it was solidly windy and very gusty, and we saw great sailing and great determination. Well done!
