He was finally amused! Edal's Continuing Meander Around the UK Isle of Man to Aberdovey. I've always found flying exciting, even the interminable waiting in airport lounges hasn't been able dull the excitement of the take off, watching through the window and the landing - the smaller the plane the more exciting it is. I was lucky with the choice of the IOM to leave the boat - the small regional carrier Flybe has a route from the local IOM airport direct to Stansted. The small modern pencil thin twin engine turbo props, they fly have much more personality than the bigger "cram em in" Boeing or Airbus beloved of Ryanair and Easy Jet, for a smaller plane there even seems a bit more leg room. With the blades of the props whirring these terrific wee planes whisked me home then back to the island for the 18th August. Peel and it's harbour is one of those places I'd found that I didn't particularly want to leave but the itch to get going was setting in. There were things to do though so the remainder of the 18th and all of the 19th was used to run through a check of Edal, going to the supermarket to revictual, fill with water and diesel and sit and plan the next couple of passages to get to Holyhead after looking at the weather forecast. The tides around the IOM can be complicated but I'd found a very good tidal chart compiled by local sailors which explained very simply rates and directions hour by hour. I was headed for Port St Mary 15nm away at the southern tip of the island to overnight then make the 46nm crossing to Holyhead. The weather would be fair on the 20th for a passage to Port St Mary so because the inner harbour at Peel is not all states I left the inner harbour on the evening opening of the gate and bridge as the sun went down and picked up a visitors buoy in the outer harbour to spend the night. The critical bit of the passage is to time arrival at Calf Sound a narrow channel between the main island and the Calf of Man where the pilot warns you of dire consequences if you get it wrong. Even going with the tide it warns you will encounter a standing wave just past the middle of the sound - it cheerily goes on to say "don't worry it's short lived - just plug on till you're through". The night on the buoy was not one of the best due to continual swell rolling the boat so I was glad to get up before first light and motor out of the bay bound for Port St Mary. The tide turned south in Calf Sound close to 0400 and we'd got roughly 11nm to go to get there so with tide to punch we motorsailed south. The light came on as we sailed south on a moderate sea with some grand sights of the IOM's coastline. Dawn at Bradda Head with Milners Tower and the houses of Port Erin just starting to show. Calf Sound was exactly as described - - going with the tide it was a "pussy cat" till the standing wave I would think about a metre high, it had a slight trough in front of it then disturbed water behind - swung Edal about 30 degrees off course - she corrected immediately in answer to the tiller like the great little boat she is and we were through. The remainder of the passage was very quick as the tide pushed us through the Sound and on to Port St Mary - we stood off the entrance calling the harbour, got no response so headed in to try and find a berth inside the outer breakwater so we could stay afloat. Once inside we found only one other sailing boat a 40 footer, who sailed later that day - we berthed against a ladder on the wall just in front of her and behind two rafted fishing boats. May 2015 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The wall at low water it was pretty big! Port St Mary proved to be delightful - the kind of place it's enjoyable just to meander around - a mix of old and new and judging by some of the houses built on higher ground looking back towards the Calf of Man some expensive ones too. The harbour consists of an outer and inner harbour - the inner dries completely and just about two thirds of the inside of the outer wall has sufficient water to keep a yacht afloat at low water. This outer wall though is enormous and must over the years have withstood many a gale so even with the forecast increase in the wind for tomorrow plus it was from a direction the pilot suggested would not find it's way into the harbour - Edal was safe enough or so she seemed. We would stay two nights allowing the forecast wind to blow through then the plan was to leave early morning on the 22nd. The harbour master called round to pick up his dues, offer friendly advice about the showers and toilets in his building at the shoreside end of the wall, getting water to the boat and the shopping up the hill in the town - all very pleasant. The facilities were a touch agricultural but worked just fine - I always carry a pair of Croc type open plastic shoes for showering anyway as I don't like walking in bare feet in places where the local fisherman and public also go - - nothing against Fisherman it's just I've seen too many cleaners in public loo's using the same mops on the showers as they use on toilet floors. First day after arrival passed pleasantly meandering around, good meal with red wine on board in the evening - - and as the evening came on listening to wind on the other side of the wall getting up. After another short walk and peer over the wall a t the crashing waves on the boulders on the shore - retired to the foclse and the land of nod. High water was to be around midnight and it must have been about 11.30 when I felt Edal bounce hard off the wall - too hard for comfort - so I leapt up and went on deck to see what was happening. There was a swell coming round the end of the wall rippling up the wall getting to the end of it then bouncing off the wall under the harbour masters office which was at 90 degrees to the wall we were on then rippling back down. These two waves incoming and outgoing meeting at different places on the inside of the wall was making life unpleasant and potentially dangerous if it got worse. I figured out it was High Water that was causing the problem because when the tide came off by about an hour possibly two the incoming waves wouldn't bounce off the wall under the HM's office they'd just dissipate on the shelving beach underneath the wall. In the meantime if I shortened the lines Edal wouldn't have so far to bounce onto the wall she'd be held steadier and with every fender I'd got would come to no harm as long as I tended the lines as the tide dropped. About 2am in the morning the waves coming both ways down the wall had stopped the motion was more regular and lessening as time went by. I lengthened the lines to allow maximum drop of tide and by about 2.45am was tucked up in the focsle again. Guess the lesson learn't was - if you're coming to Port St Mary and tie up against the wall in the outer harbour and there's a bit of a blow be prepared to tend the boat at high water. I reckon it was blowing about a six anything higher than that ask the HM if you can go into the inner harbour even if you have to lean against the wall it would be better than bouncing off the outer wall. Following days high water it was still blowing and same thing happened but in daylight it doesn't seem as bad and tending the lines easier - - that night the 21st it happened again but as the wind was dropping didn't last as long so sleep wasn't too interrupted. I wouldn''t want to remember Port St Mary for this unpleasantness because in a way it was my own fault for berthing there and because Edal can take the ground I could on arriving have asked the HM if I could go in the inner harbour or even a buoy although that in open water would have been potentially boisterous. This rippling effect down the inside of the wall must be a known local thing to happen and no one even the HM walked down the quay to warn me. I though prefer to remember PStM as a delightful place with pleasant walks somewhere I'd visit again in passing this way - but learning from my experience. The wind as forecast died away overnight leaving behind a sea fog which was forecast to lift by midday. The passage to Holyhead was 46nm and I'd learned from the skipper of the Jeanneau we'd met in Ardglass that best plan approaching Holyhead from the north was to be at a waypoint 1nm West of the Skerries latest with an hour of ebb remaining to get into Holyhead. He warned that the tides around the top of Anglesey were very strong and need to be respected. This was to be a passage in open water no big ship routes (except closer to Anglesey) just maybe an occasional fishing boat so setting off in a pea souper with so little traffic about would be a little less bit daunting - - I do hate fog though. We left bang on 0945 after making sure I'd switched on the AIS and nav lights, looked out the foghorn and basically started to keep a sharp lookout. Gradually as midday approached the viz improved till about 1500 it was perfectly clear. There was little wind throughout the passage, we motored all the way and for a milestone passage back to the mainland it was unremarkable. May 2015 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The only notable bit were the clearly troubled waters around The Skerries it was obvious in a gale at springs this would be a difficult place to be - we made it through easily - the impressive bulk of the biggest breakwater in the kingdom came up over the horizon and we were tied up in the marina at 1820. Nine hours fifteen minutes for 46nm God bless you Messrs Beta and Brunton! Impressions of Holyhead - generally good, very impressive all states harbour, decent well protected marina with good facilities and protected by it's own wave screen heavy pontoon. Mind you the outer breakwater must protect the harbour and marina from all but the most awful weather - you don't realise the sheer size and scale of it till you're inside - it's enormous! Built to protect the ships plying their trade between mainland UK and Ireland and part of the infrastructure built to link Ireland to London by train line. The town is fairly ordinary, nice enough with all the shops you'd need to revictual but has a slightly down at heel air about it. I suppose at the height of it's use as a crossroads town when probably everything going backwards and forwards to Ireland passed this way particularly before the container trade took over and the railways lost business to road freight it would have had a more prosperous air. I would though recommend it as a passage port and as a place to spend a couple of days - which is exactly what I did. The Old Gaffers had reached Holyhead and there was also a festival of sail taking place which gave the waterfront and marina a gay and lively atmosphere - people to talk to and boats to see. Holyhead harbour, marina front left with a ferry leaving the terminal top of picture. I would leave on Sunday 25th after three nights having thoroughly enjoyed Holyhead bound anticlockwise round the top of Anglesey. Aberdovey my final port in this seasons sailing was now within striking distance, there were only twonotable navigation hurdles to jump - the first to round The Stacks of Anglesey's north coast - the other to plan a safe passage through Bardsey Sound on the end of the Lleyn Peninsula. At the Festival of Sail I had a discussion with one of the local lifeboatmen and got sound advice about best time to round The Stacks - the planning for Bardsey Sound could wait as I was bound first for an anchorage on the south west coast of Anglesey in the lee of Llanddwyn Island an anchorage known as Pilots Cove famed in these parts as not to be missed. The plan then was for a short hop to another "not to be missed" spot called Porth Dinllaen, before going through Bardsey and making for Pwllheli my final port before Aberdovey. We left Holyhead in the dark at 0430 motored out under the massive breakwater and turned to port and set sail for the first of the Stacks 4nm away. Clearing South Stack lighthouse at dawn, effects of Sailing down the Anglesey coast Pilots Cove in the different water flows shown in the surface of water. distance anchor locker open, anchor ready. We reached the anchorage in just under five hours after covering 22nm a delightful sail all the way made easy by following sound advice from the Holyhead lifeboatman. The anchorage which is quite large is open on the eastern side towards Caernarfon and to the west is in the lee of the Island with a small cove and sandy beach just off where we were able to anchor. We were one of only four boats at the start of the day, by roughly midday there were 10 boats of different types at anchor and May 2015 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk the afternoon although pleasant was spoilt by speedboats and jet ski's making in and out of the cove to the beach creating an uncomfortable wash as each unthinking idiot went past. By 1700 the Neanderthals had gone home, peace reigned the waters quietened and I began to see why Pilots Cove is rated as an anchorage. I rowed ashore to explore the island and the row of preserved pilots cottages looking across open water to the mouth of the Menai Straits. If you come this way I recommend this lovely place just do as I saw several boats do - anchor further in away from the mouth of the Cove to avoid the continual wash at the height of the day. After a very quiet night awoke to a misty morning with the sun behind the mist promising to burn off the mist before midday. To give it a chance and because we only had 12nm to reach Porth Dinllaen we had a lazy breakfast, another walk ashore then deflate the dinghy, before raising the anchor at 1123. There was no wind the sea being like a mill pond we motored slowly in the mist - the vis about 500 yards. We arrived PD at 1412 and in the offing called up the HM (as the pilot recommends) to ask if he had a buoy we could use - no answer - so approached and asked two or three folk on boats or on a buoy if they knew of one we could use - "no sorry mate" came back the answer. Virtually all the boats in the bay were speed or small fishing boats with just two or three small sailing boats so perhaps I was seen as something of an interloper. I did pick up a buoy but within 15 minutes a speedboat came up with four people on it and I heard in a Black Country accent I'm familiar with "Oi yowm on muy moorin n arl need it in a minit - yowl need ter cleer owf" - - so "cleer owf" I did and anchored beyond the moorings at the end of a row of fishing boats. I'd forgotten that although I was in Wales this part of the world because it's one of the closest bits of coast to the West Midlands is populated by Blackcountrymen and I can recognise the accent because I'm one of them! Despite the "warm" welcome from the locals I enjoyed the scene and settled down to read and occasionally take in the scene. I ate on board and settled into my bunk early as tomorrow we would need to leave by 0600 bound for Pwllheli and to get there we would need the tide through Bardsey Sound. It would be 32nm to Pwllheli and 15nm to Bardsey Sound the last significant tidal gate of my seasons sailing. We left at 0548 into a quiet grey morning motoring towards the end of the Lleyn Peninsula. Approaching Bardsey Sound - The Lleyn to the left Bardsey Island to the right. The tide in Bardsey Sound rushed us through and like several of these narrow channels we'd been through before we saw disturbed water on either side which in a gale of wind and at the wrong time of the tide would create very difficult conditions. After clearing the Sound we were able to sail using full main and all the No 3 pretty much all the way to the entrance to Pwllheli marina some 17nm. We were tied up in the marina and kettle on at 1205 - just over six hours for 32nm. I like arriving somewhere midday after an early start it gives you options - - after settling the boat down, bite to eat, sign in with the HM you can either go wandering or have a snooze - - I had a snooze. The other thing about big marina's like Pwllheli is just the enjoyment of mooching around the pontoons looking at boats and what struck me about this marina was the number of motor boats, some of them pretty big. There were a lot of sailing boats but in these waters unless you're a racing sailor going out for the sheer joy of a bash round the cans - once you've done the local day sails there's not much left. These waters have a lot of restricted harbours, big tides and important tidal gates - so for someone who wants to see more and go places - say from here to Ireland I can start to see the attraction of a motor boat that can do more than 10 knots and also why there's so many of them in Pwllheli. Expensive way of getting about though, price of diesel being what it is - but then with the number of West Midlands accents I heard wafting up from plush saloons I was developing a picture of the archetypal motor boat owner in Pwllheli being a Brummie factory owner having as Harry Enfield would have it "Considerablay mowa monay than yow". I liked "Poofheli" - as a town and a marina there was no "side" to it and despite my caricature of motor boat owners all the one's I met were down to earth and friendly. We arrived on the 27th and would not leave till the 30th partly to let some wind blow through but also because I liked it. The 28th was spent going by bus to Porthmadog a town where my wife Carole and I spent a holiday with our parents - in the late 70's. It was a bit of a treat for us to spend a week all together there - sadly none of the old folks are with us now - so the week is a fond memory. Porthmadog was just as I remembered it - almost a one street town, railway station at the end of it with the little steam train still taking trippers over the cob. The drying harbour looks pretty much the same and by it's side the complex of apartments where we spent our holiday - I even found the flat we stayed in. May 2015 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Porthmadog harbour nearly all dries with just a pool further out - the entrance dries completely and entrance for one and a half metres depth is restricted to an hour either side of high water, despite this there's quite a few boats in the harbour - it's a pretty place to wander. There's also a decent little local museum to while away an hour or so with a talkative gent who will provide a potted history of the town. How the cob (causeway) was built to reclaim the land beyond it and how that (by accident he says) improved the depth of water in the harbour so bigger ships could get up to the town and that meant the quarries in the mountains started using Porthmadog to export slate by boat. First a track was laid across the cob from the quarries and gravity brought the trucks down and Welsh Cobs dragged them back up - then steam engines came and made the horses redundant. The steam trains run for the tourists to this day as the Ffestiniog Railway and it's quite evocative to see the little train crossing the top of the cob with plumes of smoke puffing out of it's funnel as it moves across the flat land towards the hills. During the previous weeks I'd been having a conversation with the Harbour Master at Aberdovey my final destination about when I should be expected so he could allocate a buoy in the harbour. I phoned him again on the 29th to say although there still seemed a fair bit wind I'd like to make it across the 28nm of Cardigan Bay tomorrow the 30th. My main concern was not the strength of the wind but whether it's direction would affect the viability of crossing the Aberdovey bar. The forecast said it would be blowing SW 5 occasionally 6 and the HM said crossing the bar at the time I advised would be fine as it was flooding. This would be my final passage of the season and it looked like it would be a boisterous one as I would be heading more or less SW - but it was only 28nm and even tacking with that wind should take me no more than six hours. High Water Aberdovey would be at 1628 there would enough water three hours before so approach and entry could be made at 1328. I planned to leave at 0800 provided the wind didn't get stronger - and that would provide an ETA of roughly 1400 with two and a half hours of flood into the Dovey left. I suppose we all have a benchmark passages completed in the past that guide our decisions on to go or stay - I have two - the first a singlehanded 42nm from Lowestoft to Harwich the second with Carole from Harwich to Brightlingsea both against a SW F6. Although shorter the one with Carole was more memorable because keeping the boat at Brightlingsea we always phoned the HM when we knew we'd be back. I'd phoned the Harbour Master at the time, one Bernie Hetherington to say "Bernie we'll be back tomorrow" - Bernie said "you do know it's blowing up don't you - is Carole with you" I said "yes she is" he said "Wow the Wallet with over 20 knots of wind against you - that's my kind of woman!" On both of these passages Edal coped well and we realised she not only coped but if we handled her properly she revelled in it - - reefed down, cracked off to the correct angle off the wind she flew. dipping to the troughs, spray everywhere - but flying. So I was quietly looking forward to the beat across Cardigan Bay tomorrow. We left as planned at 0800 cleared the marina breakwater and set a course under two reefed main and all the No3 for the West Cardinal that marks the end of St Patrick's Causeway a part drying bank that blocks the direct passage across Cardigan Bay from Pwllheli. After 12nm once we reached the West Cardinal we would turn more SE to another Cardinal marking the end of the shallows of Sarn-y-Bwch before turning a little further East for the run in to Abedovey - that was the plan anyway. In setting out the wind was more like F4 occ 5 we made good progress for the first hour but as the wind piped up we made more leeway and after a further half an hour it became clear we would not make the first Cardinal on this tack. The wind (according to the instruments) was now blowing regularly over 20 knots and I didn't fancy short tacking down the course in the sea's we were encountering so decided to put in a long enough tack that on the next one we would be sure of reaching the Cardinal. We tacked back up towards St Tudwals Islands and as we approached their southern shore the VHF burst into life - - - Edal Edal Edal this is Holyhead Coastguard, Holyhead Coastguard. Checked all ok on deck and bounced below to the VHF - - "Holyhead Coastguard this is Edal over". They instructed a working channel and advised the HM at Aberdovey wanted me to give him a ring as he was concerned to discover if I was OK and was still planning to come into Aberdovey. I said everything fine and I'd contact him but not sure of mobile signal so could they confirm with him I'm still on the way - agreed and signed off. I was able to phone him on the mobile and he said great I'll come out for you and guide you in over the bar - - - I thought WOW what a service! Later when I got into Aberdovey and was ashore having a conversation with him it all fell into place about why he'd called the coastguard. First off - his VHF was "on the blink" so he couldn't call me himself - secondly - he was watching me on the Marine Traffic AIS website - he saw me come out of Pwllheli for an hour and a half then suddenly turn for St Tudwals and got a bit concerned because he knew the wind was rising (he's a lifeboatman) so decided discretion being the better part to call Holyhead to contact me. So in my beat across Cardigan Bay I was being watched - - and if this event tells me anything it's that May 2015 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk in any boat I own I will have an AIS transponder and in making a passage in anything other than clement weather I'll tell somebody I've got AIS - so hopefully they can keep an eye on me. After the conversation we tacked back onto the more southerly course and made towards St Patrick's cardinal which as the wind was still strengthening we reached in double quick time. By now it was blowing between 24/27 knots and in beating down to the cardinal I reefed the No3 to about two thirds - we took several waves over the sprayhood - still the little boat coped admirably. In rounding the cardinal we took the wind further towards the beam and a couple of white tops came into the cockpit and it became clear we were going far too fast and would reach Aberdovey bar far too early - so we needed to slow down. The main already had two reefs in and was well down it's track so I reefed the No3 further to a scrap - Edal slowed and she just rose with the waves making her way slowly to the next cardinal and on to Aberdovey. The day had been grey and overcast some driving rain but mainly dry and it took some time to pick out the line of houses on the Aberdovey shoreline - the offlying safewater buoy came up and as I picked out the first of the channel markers there was the harbour master in his twin hulled boat waving to me to follow him in. I was glad he was there because in the remaining waves over the bar the channel buoys were difficult to pick out. As we came into the pool at the jetty the water was quieter with sufficient room to drop the main and I could look round to see my brother and his wife on the jetty waving like "billy oh" to welcome me in. The HM pointed out a buoy in deep water which I picked up and would be Edal's home for three weeks before I took her across the Dovey estuary to Ynyslas Boatyard to be lifted out for the winter. We had covered the 28nm in six hours and five minutes from Pwllheli pontoon to switching off the engine after picking up the buoy in Aderdovey - pretty good for a little bilge keeler. My brother told me later he'd encountered the HM on the jetty before he'd come out to guide me in and apparently had said "it's rough out there today but he seems to be doing OK". With this comment in his mind when I'd got in and the HM had got back to the jetty my brother concerned asked "is he all right" the HM replied "when I got to him he was laughing his head off - it looks like he's had a great time out there" and so I had. Edal against Aberdovey jetty before going across to Ynyslas boatyard. I didn't know it then but this short passage would be one of possibly three or four which would live with me long after Edal was sold - why ? - I think it's just to do with the whole thing about boat ownership and sailing - - the trust you build with your boat particularly sailing on your own, one you know every inch of and repays every moment you spend in getting her ready for sea. Getting to Aberdovey was also important in being able to spend time with my brother, we come from a family of five siblings, a sister and four brothers and we'd lost our elder brother earlier in the year and we'd felt his loss greatly. His loss was making us realise that time spent together was becoming more precious so it would be wonderful to welcome my brother onto Edal before leaving Aberdovey in the spring, setting off again on our "lark" around Britain. David Lakin May 2015 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk July Issue copy deadline: Saturday 14th June Club Notices Commodore Our open day held on 16th May was another great success. Many thanks are due to the army of volunteers, headed up by Graham Cross who helped us to make the club a friendly and well-organised place to visit. Over 80 visitors came through the gate with 84 individual trips on the water taking place. We’ve had some great feedback and already have 8 new members as a result of the open day. Welcome to those new members receiving their first copy of Navigans! It was also a lovely day for our members as all fleets really pulled together during the day and enjoyed a social event with BBQ in the evening. As you know, membership is our only real source of income so it is vital to the future of the Club that we proactively look to grow our membership - please keep supporting events such as open days in the future. The East Coast Piers Race and Colne Point Race, the biggest event hosted at MSC is also just around the corner and takes place on 26-28th June. This year the race committee have introduced a third course - ‘the Bradwell race,’ which is aimed at dinghies for whom the 27 mile Colne Point race is too far. We hope to see an increase in the number of fast dinghies taking part in the race so please spread the word amongst people you know who might be interested! The ECPR is a fantastic event and I would encourage everyone to be involved whether by racing in the event, spotting from a mother boat, crewing support boats or just being around on race weekend. Camping is available and there is live entertainment on Saturday night. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk IF YOU HAVE ANY DOUBTS ABOUT BOAT PARKING PLEASE ASK RATS & ADDERS We share our bit of the Essex countryside with the local wildlife. We need to be aware of rats and adders. I have written about adders before. If we leave them alone everything should be fine but all members, especially children, need to be aware of them particularly in long grass where they may not be seen or when reaching under boats. Rats will occasionally be seen running round the site. Care should be taken particularly with standing water for example in boats or on boat covers. Rats urine can convey Well’s disease so standing water and puddles may be contaminated. Cuts and grazes should be covered to minimise the risk of infection. DOG POO (again) We are still getting complaints about dogs fouling the site and owners not clearing up after them. Club bylaws require all dogs to be on leads. That way they are under control and not a nuisance to members and other dogs. Also you know where you dog has been and what it has done. If you allow your children to take your dog for a walk make sure they are willing and equipped to clear up after it. UPSTAIRS TEA BAR & SINK (More moans – I get all the good things to write about!) When the bar was removed from upstairs there was a strong argument to retain a sink, kettle and a supply of mugs in that corner for members to make their own hot drinks and soup when the galley is not open. Unfortunately some members are abusing this facility by leaving mugs and the sink in a dirty and frankly quite disgusting state. The facility only remains remotely useable because a few members roll up their sleeves from time to time and clean up. There is no one else to clear up after members. It is not on the cleaner’s list of jobs to wash mugs left by members; she has more than enough to do and anyway why should it be necessary?. If you use the tea making facilities please clean up after you. Simples! Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk Cadet Week 2015 – Important Registration Information With Cadet Week fast approaching there will this year be some changes regarding the registration process. Registration for ALL up-front on the website (Cadets, Tutors, Support Crew) Payment to be made up-front Deadline Wednesday 1st July In previous years, the Cadet Week application form has been available to complete on the Club Website which allows you to fill out participant information and also indicate a preferred t-shirt size. Whilst this is helpful to get an up-front idea on numbers it has also created a bottle-neck during the Parents Briefing with a bombardment of cheque-writing and money counting on the day. For 2015, we are asking ALL participants of Cadet Week to register up-front. This would include Cadets, Tutors and Support Crew. By asking everybody to register, it will better help the Cadet Committee forecast and budget for the week. With this in mind we are also asking that parents pay the balance for the week up front. This should ultimately reduce the time that everybody will need to spend at the Cadet Week briefing and ensure that the correct t-shirt size is ordered. By the time you read this, the application form should be live on the website which will give instructions on how to pay. There will be two options – either cheques made payable to Marconi Sailing Club with a return address or by bank transfer. The deadline for Online Registration is Wednesday 1st July. If you miss the deadline for online applications – don’t panic. You will still be able to register at the Parents Briefing on the evening before the beginning of the week where cash and cheques will be accepted. Sadly we will not be able to guarantee the exact shirt size of your choice and whilst it would not be our intention, cannot guarantee the same registration fee for those who have registered in advance online. The ECPR is a 48 mile course to Walton and back for catamarans. The CPR is a 27 mile race open to catamarans and fast dinghies. For the first time this year, in addition to the above long distance races, we will be staging a shorter Bradwell Race for fast dinghies (PY 980) or faster. The course for this Race will be from the Club to the Bradwell gate off Whymarks beach, back to the Club then to Thirslet and back - some 13 Nm. It is thought that this Race will attract keen dinghy sailors for who would find the 27 mile Colne Point Race overlong. The course is almost entirely within the shelter of the river that can be closely monitored by Race Control. Because of the less arduous course the Race Committee, with Board approval, has decided to relax our age restrictions for the Bradwell Race such that one crew must be over the age of 16 on the day of the Race and the other over the age of 14 years. As with the longer races, a parent/guardian’s signature will be required for any crew under the age of 18 on the day of the Race. For more details go to website: - eastcoastpiersrace.com The ECPR weekend is the biggest event in the Club’s calendar and it is made possible, not only by Club members entering the Races, but by the many members from throughout the Club fleets who volunteer for duties both on land and on the water. Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc-org.uk Arthur Hodges Arthur Hodges was a dedicated member of the Marconi Club from a time when the wooden clubhouse was located where the Ribs are now garaged, and those lucky enough to own a wetsuit had to buy the flat pieces of rubber and hand tape them together at home. For 30 years from the mid-1960s sailing at the Marconi Club was his passion and there are still plenty of faces around from both the dinghy and cruiser fleets who will remember him. It is with regret therefore that I have to inform you of his passing on April 28 at the age of 87. Arthur started to sail in a Mirror but it was in the then burgeoning Enterprise and Solo fleets that he enjoyed his best racing and he travelled with club members to several national championships. Maybe his Police background made him rather a hard taskmaster as a helm and on one occasion Stephen jumped out of an Enterprise mid race to swim back to the clubhouse much to the joy of the spectators on the bank. Some of you may recall the Police regatta’s held at the club at that time. Once the racing became too much Arthur moved into the cruiser section owning the Westerly Centaur Viridia which still resides at the club. There were plenty of stories of high, and sometimes becalmed, seas as he and Irene regularly crossed to explore the European coast. Although failing health forced him to reluctantly move away from sailing he had plenty of interests including vintage motorbikes, cars and antiques to keep him busy and active until the end. It is the family’s intention to scatter his ashes in the Blackwater, this place he loved so much. Jeremy Hodges Anyone Fancy a North Atlantic Cruise? I am planning a trip of the North Atlantic in “Antigua Kiss II” (Dufour 40 Performance) – if I can find like minded people to accompany me! Leaving autumn 2015 to spring 2016. June 2015 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The cruise would be split into four ‘legs’:- Leg 1 – UK to Las Palmas. With a stop over in Madera (time permitting) Leaving mid September, arriving approx mid November. Don’t want to leave it too late to cross the Bay of Biscay! Leg 2 – Canary Island to Barbados / Saint Vincent. (Via Cape Verde Island if you prefer!) Leave Canaries mid November arrive mid December. Fly home for Christmas! The boat will be left in a Marina if you want to stay aboard. Leg 3 – Caribbean cruise / Bermuda. Starting early January with a gentle cruise to take in St Lucia, Martinique, Dominica, and Leeward Islands and possibly up to the Virgin Islands (or anywhere else ‘en route’ you fancy!). From there we will head to Bermuda, arriving early March. I then need to fly home for my daughters eighteenth and twenty-first birthdays! Again, stay on the boat if you want to! Leg 4 – Bermuda to UK – an epic sea voyage! (We may take a short rest in the Azores). Leave Bermuda early April and arrive home twenty days later – (or thirty days if we stop over in the Azores). Route and timing is flexible and can be planned to suit you (within weather and current parameters). You will be expected to arrange your own travel to and from the boat, and pay a small contribution towards your food on board. You should also have your own wet weather gear and life jacket with crotch strap and spray hood. I will require at least one other person, preferably two – you will each have your own cabins. Assuming three people on board, we will run a four hour watch system – four hours ‘on’, four hours ‘on stand by’, four hours ‘off’. We require two people on board to satisfy the insurers (myself and one other). Some previous experience of small boat cruising is required. If you are interested in doing the whole trip, or just a ‘leg’, please contact Roger Gibson, on or , or drop by Antigua Kiss at the far end of the yard for a chat. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk October Issue copy deadline: Saturday 13th September Club Notices Commodores Notes Welcome to this bumper, summer edition of Navigans. We have had a busy few months at the Club and many events are coming up soon. Hopefully many of you were able to be part of this year’s East Coast Piers Race, either by competing or volunteering on motherboats, support boats or with land based roles. Once again the event was a huge success and we had lots of great comments about the Club, how well organised ECPR is and how friendly and welcoming our members are. Many thanks are due to Clive Shenton and his organising committee who have worked tirelessly throughout the year to run such a successful event. Entry numbers were well up on previous years, lots of money was raised for our charities (Cirdan Trust and Essex Air Ambulance) and we had a record-breaking weekend of bar sales - so thanks to all for contributing. It was also great to see 4 Marconi boats in the top 10 results this year too! John Nickalls and team have been as busy as ever with sail training, which continues to be well attended. We welcomed a return visit from the Chernobyl’s Children group in early July - this event was covered by the local press and further details as always can be found on the MSC website. Thanks to all who supported this visit. Cadet week and camping fortnight are just around the corner now. Just a reminder that this is the only time during the year where camping spaces must be pre-booked. Please make sure you have registered for your place at cadet week online. Online payment is also now an option for cadet week. As an update on our grant funding applications - our rowing gig is currently under construction and we expect to take delivery towards the end of the season. Unfortunately we will not have our gig for camping fortnight but we will have a loan boat on site so please make use of it and have a go. Our Inspired Facilities grant where we have applied for £75k of Sports England lottery funding has now been submitted and we await notification of a decision, which is expected sometime in September. I wish you all a lovely summer of sailing whether it is cruising, windsurfing, racing or training. Please remember that we have a number of social events planned over the summer and it would be lovely for more members to take part and join in the fun. Michaela Dowley Commodore Management Committee CRUISER WEBSITE PAGES Over recent weeks you will no doubt have seen that the Marconi website has been further enhanced with additional cruiser related pages. This very comprehensive information that has been compiled and developed by Peter Booth over the past 6 months, illustrates our facilities and the self-help nature of our operation extremely well and serves as an excellent promotion of our facilities to potential new members and visitors to our website. The Marconi Management Committee, on behalf of the club members, would like to thank Peter for the sterling work he has done on this. If you haven’t seen it, then take a look, it’s evolving all the time, so if you have some photos of a recent cruise, race, or just some cruiser news, send it to Peter, we’re sure he’ll be able to use it. MSC Management Committee EAST COAST PIERS |Xi|RACE East Coast Piers Race & Colne Point Race Weekend 27th/28th June 2015 The last weekend in June saw the Club put on the ECPR weekend for the 28th time, and what a weekend it was! Good weather was in the forecast all week and this may be one of the reasons why we enjoyed an entry of 76 boats, some twenty more than last year and the best for some years. The weather did not disappoint, unless you count the rain during racing, but most competitors I talked to welcomed the cooling effect. The Race committee decided to run three races this year. As well as the traditional ECPR and Colne Point Races (CPR) we offered a shorter dinghy race which we called the Bradwell Race. Colne Point and back can seem daunting in a dinghy and the offer of a shorter alternative brought double the dinghy entries this year, albeit, in a sort of “group decision”, all the dinghies entered and successfully completed the CPR in the good sailing conditions. August & September 2015 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Another “first time this year” was the Race Committee’s decision, made several days in advance, to turn the Race at Clacton Pier due to the considerable obstacles between Clacton and Walton caused by beach re-charge works. I did not hear anyone who questioned the decision and Race Control got everybody out and back safely so I guess we made the right call. I am very pleased to report that Line Honours in both Races were taken by Marconi boats; Nick Miller sailing his foiling Moth in the Colne Point Race and, for the second year running in the ECPR, our Commodore Michaela Dowley helming and husband Andrew crewing their Tornado Sport. About 45 minutes into ECPR you would have got long odds on this result because that was the time it took Will Sunnucks in his foiling White Bear cat to get to Clacton Pier. On the Committee boat we had barely finished our post-start cup of tea; but the beat back did not suit White Bear and they finished well down the pecking order. Each Marconi boat was pipped into second place on corrected time by Samuel Curtis & Benjamin Clegg from Brightlingsea SC sailing a 49er in CPR and Simon Northrop & Sam Van Barker sailing a Nacra F18 in ECPR. Full results on eastcoastpiersrace.com. The Prize Giving was held with competitors sitting on the seawall in warm sunshine while our OOD Simon Elwell officiated and the Bishop of Bradwell and his wife presented the prizes and drew the raffle. The Bishop was full of praise for our event and for our support of Essex Air Ambulance and Cirdan Sailing Trust. Another feature of this ceremony was the number of competitors who grabbed the mike to thank us for running a great event. One such was a Dart 15 sailor who, with four other D15’s, had sailed from Seasalter SC Whitstable on Saturday only for his mast to fall down at Bradwell. He was rescued and towed in by Kevin Stubbs in the big Dive Club RIB we had on loan for the weekend. The last ticket drawn for the raffle was one bought for Derek G who phoned in his purchase from points east. Derek and Hilary now have an extensive wardrobe of ZHIK sailing wear. All of this good news and good feeling would not be possible without the small army of Club members who give up sailing time to organise the event in its many facets. Although I have never sat down and counted everyone involved I am certain at least 100 members contribute in some way. To each and every one of you I say thank you – I am most grateful for your support. I cannot name everyone here but would like mention some: - Peter Clayton and all the mother boats and matriarchs who help us provide a unique level of support boat cover. Andrew Dowley working closely with Dave Clark who recruited outside RIBs and coordinated club RIBs. Thanks also to all the “usual suspects” who turned out to crew the RIBs; Jack B and Trot Boat. Andrew also took on publicity, sponsored the shirts and picked up printing costs via his company Dinghy Rope and was my very able deputy. Roger Camp – Safety Coordinator afloat and Colne Point Matriarch. He also ensured the BUS had a VHF that worked. The Race Control crew led by OOD Simon Elwell + Mike & Maggie B. and Ray Ball as radio operator. Murray Bates – Hardmaster, site manager & deputy OOD + the Wednesday Gang. Roger Smith RO & the committee boat crew, Leonie, Noreen, Rod and Malcolm. Spotters led by Abbie Russell. Scrutineers led by Dave Russell. The Race committee who each took a slice of the organisation: - Michaela – Bar & all-round Board support; Kevin – Trophies, Bar and catering; Tom Brooks – entertainment, dinghy liaison & publicity; Ray - our secretary, sounding board and “sweeper” ensuring we forgot nothing. Wendy Dowley who, by providing First Aid cover, enabled us to avoid the cost of employing outside professional services. Alan Brown who answered our (muted) call for help when the PA failed and came up trumps. My Family, Sue, Marian, Alex, Dan and Ros for Reception, Results, Race Treasurer, Committee Boat and their undying support 12 months a year. All competitors who enter the Races. It would all be for nothing without you. And finally anyone I have forgotten. I know you are out there and I thank you even though my powers of recall have let me down. Sorry. ECPR weekend has always been a charity event and this year the signs are that this will be a good year for the “bottom line”. We have enjoyed major sponsorship once again this year from Adnams who provided copious quantities of ale and lager FOC which meant that anyone buying a pint was directly contributing to charity. We are also very grateful to Tristan Hutt at ZHIK for donating a large quantity of excellent quality sailing clothing which formed the backbone of the raffle prizes. £50 vouchers from Dinghy Rope and Fox’s Boatyard completed the excellent list on offer. Please put 10th July 2016 in your diary for next year so we can do it all again. Clive Shenton Race Chairman August & September 2015 Navigans 3

Michaela and Andrew Dowley Steve Glynn and Tom Duckmanton John and Caroline Nickalls Jenny and David Ball David Hitt and Paul Crick Peter Richardson and Fenella Miller Nick Miller Next Year - 10th July 2016 Kevin Dowley Cat Fleet Captain Roger Camp Cruiser Fleet Captain Club News Chernobyl Children’s Lifeline Marconi Sailing Club (MSC) on the Blackwater estuary played host Wednesday to twelve special youngsters from Belarus, giving them an unforgettable lifetime experience, which for many of them was their first time on the sea. The children: six boys and six girls aged between 8 and 13, are on a one-month recuperative holiday organised by the Chernobyl Childrens Lifeline charity and travelled with a doctor and interpreter. They have all been patients at a Childrens’ Hospital near the ill-fated Chernobyl nuclear power plant, where local communities continue to be affected by health problems thirty years after the nuclear disaster. All the children visiting are being treated for Leukaemia. Their time in England enables them to enjoy uncontaminated food and fresh air, whilst experiencing wonderful activities thanks to the generosity of organisations such as Marconi Sailing Club. The club’s young cadets did a fantastic job of entertaining their visitors with a warm welcome despite the poor weather on the day. Strong winds meant they could not go out on sailing dinghies as planned, but instead, under the gaze of curious seals popping up for a peek at these young visitors from afar, they all laughed as they bounced and rode the choppy waves on MSC’s fleet of rescue boats to visit Thirslet Spit; a seashell and sand bank only accessible at low tide. There they whiled away the day searching for shells; looking in awe at stranded jellyfish (“Medusa!!!!” in their language); and paddled in the shallows. All against the backdrop of the beautiful Essex coastal landscape so utterly different from landlocked Belarus. The rising tide eventually forced them to board the boats August & September 2015 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Club Notices Commodores Notes Welcome back from the summer break - I hope you all managed to enjoy some time out on the water in the sunshine. Following in Navigans are a number of reports from our packed events calendar over the summer. Please take the time to read about the huge amount of activity that has been going on over the summer months. Highlights include another visit from the Chernobyls Children, the National Schools Sailing Regatta, Cadet Week 2015, successful cruiser racing, topper traveller event, various opens plus dinghy and cruiser cruises. A number of reports are also available on the Club website. Although over for this year, Friday free-for-alls and Wednesday night racing have been well supported and have given an opportunity for more relaxed racing and sailing to members. Look out for more of these sessions next season. Cadet week was yet again a huge success with over 80 cadets taking part this year. Thanks are due to the organising team headed up by Dave Clarke, Bekki Tovey and Chris Kirby. The second week of camping fortnight followed with a number of organised social sailing trips - many thanks to Jenny Ball and team for organising. Plenty of our more adventurous cruiser and dinghy members have been participating in regattas outside of MSC and achieved some excellent results, most notably the recent Fastnet race. We have had plenty of successful social events over the summer, which have been well supported so thank you to all involved. The annual winter dinner and dance is due to be held on 30th January 2016 - it’s a great night and an opportunity to get dressed up! Tickets are selling fast so make sure you order yours today. Michaela Dowley Commodore Club Secretary ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING – SUNDAY 29th NOVEMBER 2015 Elsewhere in this issue of Navigans you will find the formal notification of the AGM. It has essential information about resolutions and committee nominations. There is also a nomination form. FLOOD GATES The Environment Agency requires that the flood gates must be kept closed from 1st September unless the hard is in use. Please shut the gates when you come ashore unless it is obvious that another member is using the hard. If in doubt, shut the gates. They can always be opened again. The gap in the seawall is vital to our club but is a privilege not a right. We must be seen to be doing the right thing by keeping them shut which as well as meeting EA requirements also protects our club and our neighbours. PARKING IN CRUISER PARK At this busy time of boat, boat hoist and trailer movements cars must not be left unattended in the cruiser park or the cruiser parking area of the cat park. Owners of cars in the cruiser parks must be available at all times and ready to move them at short notice. Do not leave your car unattended in the cruiser parks even if you are ‘only nipping out to the boat for 5 minutes’. There is a very real risk of damage to your vehicle and inconvenience to others. Roger Camp Cruiser Fleet Captain Cadet Fleet NSSA YOUTH REGATTA 2015 REPORT This year was the third year that Marconi have sent a team of sailors to the National Schools Sailing Association Youth Regatta – an event open to all under 18’s ranging from World Champions to ‘rookies’ who have never done an event like this before. This year the event was held immediately before Cadet Week at Rutland Water and over 300 sailors took part from across the country. The week began with very windy conditions and ended with very little wind, however over the week all the fleets went out and completed a good series of races, providing a challenge for us ie all. Unfortunately, as well as wind we had rain. % And, unlike the wind, the rain lasted beyond Wednesday, making for some less than ideal camping conditions through the week. i The Regatta was split into three Laser fleets, a Topper fleet, two Handicap fleets and two Rookie fleets. Our team was 11 strong at the beginning of the week, but was sadly reduced to 10 early-on when Will succumbed to a bout of Yellow Fever*. Each evening brought its own entertainment, including a sports evening (we were dodgeball stars) and construction challenges (until someone ate all the marshmallow ‘glue’). The team did incredibly well, posting three third-place series results. The whole team (those who didn’t pull a sickie) were very pleased with the turn of speed they showed in their week’s sailing; however even an amazing lack of speed, such as Jack’s consistently protracted consumption of his dinner, was celebrated by many of our competitors. On behalf of the whole team and myself I would like to give a massive thank you to John Nickalls, the organiser of our team and our main Team Manager, and also to Clare Clarke and Caroline Nickalls who shared the week as our female Team Manager. Thanks also to Susana Collis and her mum Marion who were ready to stand-in when we had some paperwork challenges. I know the team and I thoroughly enjoyed this year’s NSSA Youth Regatta, for the evening events and the whole social scene as well as the sailing. We’re losing a couple of team members as they go to university, so anyone who might want to come along next year to Great Yarmouth, speak to me or John. * Brought on by an earlier vaccination Daniel Nickalls October 2015 Navigans 6

Ray Ball Company Secretary MSC Rowing Gig ‘Elettra’ MSC will soon take delivery of our new 24ft East Coast Rowing Gig, to be christened Elettra. Purchase of the gig is being supported by a Sport England grant. Some members will already have seen or ventured out in Matchless, a similar vessel loaned to us for the 2014 and 2015 cadet weeks. When Elettra arrives we’ll be looking for members to crew it for recreational outings, training and racing against other clubs. If you are interested please get in touch with Peter Clayton. She is being built by ‘Harker’s Yard’, a boat building facility developed and run by the Pioneer Sailing Trust that provides apprenticeships and work experience for young people wanting to enter the marine industry. Working on real projects in a real working environment, apprentices learn the skills needed to work with a variety of materials on a range of craft. Apprentices also take part in sailing activities aboard the restored sailing smack Pioneer, where they further their understanding of water craft and gain teamwork and communication skills. Based on a traditional 19th Century design The East Coast Gig provides people of all ages and abilities with an opportunity to get on the water. The construction is a coldmoulded wooden boat which takes 4 rowers and a cox. Coastal rowing is a fast-growing sport which is based on local community clubs and provides healthy outdoor exercise and an opportunity to socialise and compete. The first clubs around the East Coast have been formed and races are underway. Peter Clayton visited the yard just before Cadet Week and reported that Elettra is now off the plug and turned the right way up sitting on her keel. The next stage will be to bond the floor in and work up fitting thwarts and then gunwales, before the hull can then be removed from the cradle for painting and final finishing. The photos here show how she is shaping up. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Woozle Hunter Fastnet Bloggy Thing. Kept by the Galley slave Laura Dear diary, Well, as mid life crisis go, this is a doozy!! I have been coerced into competing in the Fastnet Yacht Race! 611 miles non stop to Ireland and back, on a 33 foot tub, with 5 males and no shower!!!!! Bonkers. Must be hormones!! Hope there’s G+T involved :) Sunday 16th August 2015 09.30. Fastnet Race day. Beautiful sunny day. At least there’s no rain for now ... unfortunately there’s no wind either !! Heading for the start to check in - orange storm & tri sails ready to hoist for inspection. A few boats around & Fastnet marker buoys in place. All checked in. Starting to get busier. God there are a lot of boats out here and this is just a few of them ! Some of the mono & multi hulls are mahoosive !!! Now total chaos. Race boats, Media boats & ribs buzzing around between the yachts, getting in everyone's way ..... but .... no wind !!! Start no 1 is the multihulls .... and they're off .... but unfortunately can't go anywhere. Wind speed zero!! A couple more class starts. All going nowhere. Then it's the turn of class 4. We are around 10 minutes from the line at the start , and still 10 minutes from the line 20 minutes later!! Drifting backwards occasionally then inching forward. Time for a G+T? Yeah right !! Cuppa T is as close as it gets! Finally a poof of wind and we're off. Absobloodylutely amazing racing amongst this many yachts. Around 370 racing yachts, plus media boats, press boats and sightseers on the water, not to mention the Isle of Wight ferries and ginormous car carrier heading right through the middle of the fleet! Overtaking a few boats, with a serious close encounter with an idiot on port tack (we have right of way) asking if we mind if he cuts us up!! Idiot !!! Cap'n Ian informing him in very few words what we think of him. I think we frightened him away as he avoided us after that!! Heading for the Needles. Loads of fun missing all the other boats and having giant yachts within feet of us. Round the Needles and head for Portland Bill. First night. Very little wind which keeps dying. Good for us, but not so good for some of the others. Pass a few boats during the night including the classic yawl Argyll, owned by the comedian Gryph Rees Jones. Night watch is amazing. A hundred or more yacht lights all around us. Changing from white to red or green as we pass them. Fastnet day 2 Dear diary, Day 2. A little more wind and Gryph sails past us again. Bastard!! The watch system is working well. 4 hours on deck helming ... 4 hours on standby then 4 hours asleep - ish !! Boat behaving beautifully with only the odd failure. Compass light died which makes night time racing a challenge. But we're up to that. Doesn’t affect me as we discovered I can’t read the instruments at night anyway !! Oooops !!! Spinnaker up. Let's see if that helps. Keeping the spinnaker flying by will power whilst laying on deck sunbathing (master at work !!), we overhall another sigma 33, Polished Manx who is flying her code zero sail. Doesn't help her as we sail past (very slowly) ! Wind picks up a little as we pass Eddystone lighthouse, with a sightseeing detour tack of course !! Dinner cooked and another boat heading directly for us! How inconsiderate. Unfortunately they have right of way so we have to miss them! All that sea out there and we pass within 3 feet. Night watch again. A stunningly clear night with stars that seem to go on forever. A little more wind now as we approach the Lizard. Over 7 knots!! Wow !!! The boat has a tail like a comet made of phosphorescence. 1.30am and we have visitors !! A pod of dolphins has come to play.They are outlined in phosphorescence and leave a trail of lights so we can watch their progress through the water. Fantastic. I love night watch !! October 2015 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Fastnet day 3 Dear diary, Wind speed 1.6 knots !! Lots of boats going nowhere really slowly. We have caught McGregor during the night and our position on the leader board has improved. Bacon butty time to celebrate. Drifting gently on a millpond sea towards Wolf rock lighthouse with the occasional puffs of wind rippling the surface. 3 knots now. Wow!! 11 am and visitors again. A pod of around 20 dolphins have come to play. Swimming around and under us and jumping right beside us. Putting on a show just for the Woozle boat. They stay for quite a while showing off their prowess before heading off. Best moment so far & a very happy crew. A little more wind now. Heading directly towards the rock ... though long way to go still. McGregor, in front of us this morning made a strange decision to tack and stayed on it too long. Now 8 minutes behind us!! Yay :) Created a culinary masterpiece for dinner. Smoked sausage & tomato pasta with melted cheese on. Was inhaled by the crew! On watch & helm from 22:00 til 02:00. The weather changed hugely from smooth sailing to 20kt winds. Very lively. Decision to change the headsail at 2.30am in the wind & rain. Get called back on deck just after I got into my ‘damp’ sleeping bag. A pretty nasty time in 25kt winds. Unfortunately had a little accident when the boom whipped unexpectedly across the cockpit and the main sheet smashed me in the face. I now look like Ian has landed me a tuppenny one ! Oh well. Racing wouldn't be right without bruises . Fastnet day 4 Dear Diary! The weather this morning is 25kt winds, rain & big waves. So much for genteel sailing !! Oh well ... Woozle surfing :) !!!!! Still got dolphins escorting us though. Brilliant !! The boat looks like it has been in an explosion! Wet gear everywhere! Over on our sides so doing pretty much anything is very hard. Clothes wet ... bedding wet .... cushions wet!!! Heading towards the rock now. Hope to see it shortly. Land Ho! I can see Ireland. Finally the rock is in sight. Yay! Wind pretty light but we're getting there. No we're not !!!!! Wind has died. Lots of boats milling around the rock all trying to round. Time for freshly baked garlic cheesy bread methinks :) The dolphins are still with us though. I think they fancy Winnie the Pooh ! 5 hours and many tacks later ........ and we've finally rounded the Fastnet rock. Hoo - bloody - ray. And the tide has taken us back round again!!!! What! !!!!!!!!!! Right. Now rounded the rock for the 2nd time and headed for Plymouth at a nice genteel 5-6 knots. Ok! A nice 5-6 knot wind has mutated into a manic 20 - 25 knot howler !! Crossing the Celtic sea on our sides whilst being smashed violently by big waves is losing its appeal fast. Fastnet day 5 Dear Diary 18 hours later and we are still being smashed through the sea by 20kt winds. How this little boat stands up to this abuse I do not know. Massive crashes every few seconds as we are hit by big waves. 2 reefs in the main and another 4 am headsail change!! Why do they always wait til I get in my sleeping bag before they call me back on deck !!! The foredeck in this weather is not a nice place to be. The whole day spent on our side crashing along. Everything in the cabin is wet and 2 of the lee cloths to keep people in their bunks have failed meaning we are 2 bunks down. Tried to nap in the fore-cabin!! Bounced repeatedly between the cushion and roof!! Ian D's food pouches for dinner. Taste amazing. First hot food for a while. Crew has been living on snacks for a some time. People sleeping where they fall, fully dressed and still wearing wet weather gear. I have been wet down to the skin for 2 days now, and seem to be wearing 4 pairs of trousers!!. Not pleasant. 10pm and time for my 4 hour night watch. Wind still 20 knots and big waves. Total blackness. No lights. No stars. Nobody within sight of us so no lights to follow. Sailing by instruments then. Aah. Houston we have a problem !! I still can't read the instruments at night!! Bugger. Back to helming the old fashioned way. If if flaps - pull it .... If it stands up - push it !! Yee hah. Sailing by feel. 3.5 hours later and still on the helm ... and .... unbelievably still right on course with no instruments. Go me ! Knackered tho. Need sleep. Fastnet day 6 Dear Diary, October 2015 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Still wet! Still trucking along. Passed Lizard point at around 8 am and heading for the finish. About 48 miles to go. Wind has dropped a little so both reefs taken out the main and back to the big headsail again. Attempting a bit of boat clean up. !!!! Fighting a losing battle there. It can wait til we stop now. We are all in desperate need of a shower and clean clothes but have reached the stage where we really don't care. If a layer starts to smell, I put another one on top !! We can't smell each other so who cares! The finish line is getting closer. Considered putting up the kite ... but .... watched a Sigma 38 put theirs up and get repeatedly splatted. Maybe not then. Less than 10 miles to go and still can't see any land it is so murky. We know it's out there somewhere ! The crew has been mainlining Haribo and are high as kites on sugar and E numbers! They are getting rowdy & there seems to be a party going on in the cabin!! Lots of 'singing' (either that or someone is getting murdered) and 'dancing'! In a Sigma 33 !!!!!! 5 miles to go. Still no land visible! Beginning to doubt the navigator !!!! He still insists it's there. Hmmmm drunk maybe!! Must be too many wine gums. 2 miles to go ..... and ..... We can see land (well, slightly darker murk!) Yay. 1 mile to go. Land is beginning to actually look like land. We can see the lighthouse on the starboard end of the finish line. Me on the helm with repeated instructions not to hit it from Captain Woozle & the rest of the crew!! Thanks guys! Really helpful!!! An insane man in a manic dinghy buzzes up and starts photographing us. Hands us his business card and buzzes off. Bonkers. All crew on deck with the champers ready!! Yards to go. Clock ready to take our finish time ...... and ...... we cross the line ! Finish siren from the light house. Cue shouting, champagne spraying and the odd tear !! We bloody did it. A crazy bunch of Woozles in a tinpot Sigma 33 completed the Fastnet against 340 other boats. Many of them up to 100 feet long and crewed by professionals. So as the 4th slowest boat in the whole race, we didn't disgrace ourselves. Now we head for our berth and find out our position ........... and beer. Lots of beer!! Declaration ...... Beer ...... The best shower ever ...... and the results. 188th overall out of 340 boats! Our little Woozle boat has beaten 150 other boats ! Bloody amazing. So proud. We also came 31st in our class of 72 boats and 10th in IRC4b. And we won the Sigma class trophy. Not a bad result for a bunch of loony's in an old tub!! And so the celebrations begin !!! Beer and wine are free and things get messy .... especially once we meet up with the crew of Mcgregor IV. I seem to vaguely recall being up on a table at some point!! Nah, I wouldn’t do that !!!! But a good night was had by all. The brilliant Woozle crew: Mad Cap'n Ian ~ Galley Slave Laura ~ Nav Man & Air Guitar Ian ~ Cabin Boy Musto Man Abraham ~ Chief Tart & Skivvy Stuart ~ On Board Entertainment & Tart in training Jamie !!!! “It will be fun” he said!! “You’ll love it” he said !!!!! And you know what ...... he was right :) October 2015 Navigans 10

A member’s responsibility does not just end when the deal is done (bylaws 3.1.4 and 3.1.4.1 refer). Members’ gate cards are personal and must not be loaned to others; for example to a non-member who may want to gain access to work on the boat that they have just bought. If a non-member has bought a boat on site and wishes it to remain at Stansgate for a relatively short time they may apply to the membership secretary for short term membership. They will be granted short term membership for a length of time and for a fee which will be agreed in advance. If a non-member buys a boat at Stansgate and wishes to keep it at the club permanently they may apply for membership by completing and submitting a membership form. Copies of the form are kept in the clubhouse and are also available on the MSC website. If they have purchased a cruiser they should speak to the moorings secretary. Buying a cruiser from a member does not automatically mean that a mooring will be immediately available. There is sometimes a waiting list especially for deep water moorings. If they have purchased a dinghy or catamaran they should agree a dinghy or catamaran park space with the membership secretary and the appropriate boat park co-ordinator. All dinghy and catamaran park spaces are allocated to particular boats and members. It is essential that all information is kept up to date when boats change hands. Contact details for all club officials will be found in the yearbook or on clubhouse notice boards. OPERATION OF CLUB BOATS AND EQUIPMENT For information for new members and a reminder to older hands, there are detailed codes of practice and instructions for most activities at Stansgate from procedures for a flood alert to the operation of machinery. It is essential for the efficient and safe operation of club boats and equipment that users are familiar with the guidance. If you have a support boat duty, do read the guidance notes. Even if you have driven or crewed on support boats before it is worth reading the latest version of the relevant notes; they do get updated from time to time. Winches, tractors, mast derrick and boat hoists also have their own codes of practice and user guides. Please read them. Their relevance to the operators of the equipment is obvious but it is also useful for boat owners to be familiar with the codes of practice. You will have a better understanding of the operation of the equipment, which is satisfying in itself, but also appreciate the operators’ point of view and the codes of practice under which they work to ensure the safety of all involved. A paper copy of the codes of practice and user guides is kept in the clubhouse but you can also familiarise yourself with them at your leisure in the members section of the MSC website. Go to Members Area/Document Library/Operating Procedures. A document index may be found in document MSCP01. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Well done to everyone who’s joined sail training this year, it’s been a really enjoyable year and you’ve all been brilliant to go sailing with. We’ve had a bit of everything, from fully-reefed windy days to calm drifters, and from wonderful planing reaches to spectacular broaches. But most of all I’ve been hugely impressed by the positive attitude everyone has shown, as well as the level of control shown by all the sailors – every time the groups have stuck together and tackled the challenges positively and effectively. And it’s been a real delight to see everyone crossing the start line in a group as the hooter goes! (Above all, we’ve seen more deliberate backward sailing than accidental!) Oppi Club has been great for the little ‘uns, with games in the Cadet Hut and then some excellent sailing in the shallows in the Oppis. Thank you Fi, it’s been fantastic! Of course nothing can happen without our many helpers driving and crewing RIBs, allocating boats and counting them back in… and running the galley! So thank you to all of you! And a special thanks to Bryan for all his advice and for taking one of the groups out each session to help them develop their skills, as well as to Dave for all the behind- the-scenes work keeping the club boats on the water and upgrading them. On Saturday it was lovely to be able to recognise several achievements over the season: thanks to Dinghy Rope and the RYA for some fantastic prizes! As well as thanking those who supported sail training really well and recognising those who made some great progress, we celebrated a few new things this year: six of our cadets deservedly gained their RYA Start Racing certificates, and we congratulated the winners of the inaugural ‘sail training race series’. And so to the future… we’ll be reviewing this year’s sail training and making plans for the future over the winter, and I’d be really pleased to hear any suggestions. Then with a bit of luck we’ll get a chance to do some team racing at RHS over the winter. I’m sure there’ll be a cadet social in the early spring to kick-off the 2016 season and we’ll be back on the water probably in April (when, of course, it will be warm and sunny, and the tide will be perfect). Have an excellent winter! John Nickalls Cadet Co-ordinator Daniel Nickalls Club News MSC Rowing Gig ‘Elettra’ Another update on the MSC Rowing Gig….. it has arrived! Stay tuned for more information. Neil Pembleton The Ten Commandments of Sailing (according to Liam Thom and with apologies to William Fawcett) This recently appeared in the Sprint 15 Association magazine written by Shanklin member Liam Thom – who has kindly given us the OK to share in Navigans. Commandment 3 and 8 rang particularly true for us in Marconi too! Jenny Ball Commandment 1: Everyone shall present themselves at the place of meeting quietly, suitably clothed and in good time. Anyone who uses sail or oar to propel their craft steadily to its destination is better than those who use a motorized contraption. Anyone who uses any manner of engine or machine, except as a necessity, is an abomination. Commandment 2: Everyone shall first salute and speak words of comfort to the flag officers and safety personnel, knowing full well that they have hard work to perform. They shall then count the boats and examine them with great joy but in a quiet manner. They shall then likewise cheerfully salute their friends. Those that shall say that the day will be a bad sailing one, or in any manner, endeavour to prophecy evil is an abomination. Commandment 3: It is acceptable that those of experience shall, at all times, give explanation and encouragement by word and deed to all young persons, so that sailing may continued on the water from generation to generation. Those who think they know, when they know not, are an abomination. Commandment 4: Everyone shall remember that the water they pass over is not their own property. Whosoever uses not due care and consideration is an abomination. Commandment 5: Those who talk loudly or who fly a hull unnecessarily are an abomination. Those who wear an apron or mackintosh on wet days or who use any other device for making a mountebank of themselves, or in any way cause inconvenience to any boat or sailor is an abomination. Commandment 6: If it be possible, let every true believer abstain from all meat and drink, save only such as is necessary to sustain life. Let the whole day be kept as a special fasting and strengthening of the mind for the sail. In the evening, they shall partake of suitable meat and drink and on the evening after a good day, they shall have a special allowance. Commandment 7: Those who, of their own free will, go home before the race is finished or who is displeased with the day or who is not fully uplifted, joyful and thankful of the day is an abomination. Commandment 8: Whosoever takes to the water on a personal watercraft is an abomination. May their dwelling become desolate and their possessions a desert. May their mind be filled with bitterness and their body with pain. Commandment 9: November 2015 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk RACING PROGRAMME – PETER WARD A successful season for Marconi cruiser racing, saw club boats racing locally, inshore, offshore and travelling to participate in regatta’s and other events, as well as our inaugural Autumn Series from the club line. Blue Moon was the highest finishing Marconi boat in the BJRC series. 2nd in IRC and 4th in BJRC handicaps. Woozle Hunter was the highest finishing Marconi boat in the EAORA offshore series. 2nd in class 3 and 4th overall. In the Fastnet Race Woozle Hunter was 1st Marconi boat finishing in 188th position in a fleet of 309. Nearer to home Caroline finished 4th in class at the prestigious Ramsgate Week and in the Marconi Autumn Series where 6 boats competed with a further 4 in the Barts Bash event, 4 x boats were still in with a chance of winning come the medal race. Unfortunately the wind failed, which saw Woozle Hunter and McGregor coming out on top in IRC and local handicap although Blue Moon only lost out on 1st overall due to count back. Throughout the Autumn, at times we had more people wanting to sail at the club as racing crew, than we had spaces available and every boat that sailed was fully crewed almost all the time. The series has resulted in 7 x new members joining the club and as a club, we are looking at ways of increasing the number of boats representing Marconi in local races. For 2016 we have indications that there will be two further race boats joining us, also fully crewed. We now have a ‘crew pool’ therefore any owner who would like to start, or get back into racing, we have crew available looking for boats to join. In 2016 Marconi will once again be represented in EAORA offshore racing, as well as the BJRC inshore series. A complete race schedule of dates will be available after the BJRC AGM which is to be held next week. Over the winter we will be running a series of ‘Racing Rules’ workshops in the bar, and will be organising a sail measurement day upstairs in preparation for rating certificate renewals. On the 2016 calendar Marconi will be organising an Open Spring Regatta, which will include a team challenge. The event will see the fleet on a passage race weekend to Brightlingsea 21-22 May and will include a race in the Colne on Saturday before a social event in the Colne YC. Then on the 4-5 June two further races will take place at Marconi, with visitors from other clubs joining us for a prizegiving dinner. The team challenge will be scored on teams of 3 x boats. One of the team classes will require a team to include 1 x fin keeler, 1 x twin keeler, and one boat less than 28 feet. If you’d like to get involved in the event, or you know your mooring will be vacant on the evening of 4th June, then please make it known to one of our racers. And finally, a request for your assistance. As cruiser racing is developing at Marconi’s we need to increase our ‘support team’ capacity to allow us to organise and run our events, and through them increase our profile as an active racing club, which in turn will attract new members. We are therefore looking for a member with a racing background, who currently doesn’t race, who would be interested in receiving training so that they can act as a race officer to help us to run our events. Anyone interested in joining a race crew, looking to start racing, or able to assist as a race officer should contact Peter Ward. Roger thanked Peter for all his hard work over the year.
