Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk  As a consequence of all of the above and our own self-promotion we will be known as one of the premier sailing clubs in the UK Presentation Our ambition for MSC is for the development of the club and its facilities to a level that will equal the best in the sailing sector. By this we mean that we will have:  Changing facilities on a scale that matches the needs of the active sailing membership and to a standard that equals the best commercial gymnasia.  Full accessibility.  Consistent high standards of presentation and décor across the site that match the best commercial amenities.  Comfortable and high quality facilities for non-sailing social activity to include a dry lounge with capacity for 100+ and an adequate outside seating area.  Sufficient undercover storage and maintenance space for club equipment in secure buildings that blend with the rural setting.  Good access to the water and easy access to the hard.  A high standard of handling equipment and full H&S compliance.  Sufficient space on site to meet all our needs in terms of movement, storage, social activity, parking and camping commensurate with the size of the membership. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk > Marconi Sailing Club Ltd 2015 COMMODORE’S REPORT - MICHAELA DOWLEY Welcome all to the 2015 Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting. This report will comment on the main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season. Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board, and for the previous financial year has comprised six directors: Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing Graham Cross - Rear Commodore for events Sue Shenton - Treasurer Myself, Michaela Dowley - as commodore I am managing director and chair I hope you agree that this group of people provide a balanced representation across the fleets within the club, and we are fortunate that the Board membership has remained the same for 2 seasons, which has allowed some consistency to develop. Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of the administrative burden of the Club. Although it is only a small part of the job, I’ve only recently discovered that Ray dislikes writing minutes. Given that including this meeting Ray has produced more than 35 sets of minutes since the last AGM, I would like to offer him by most heartfelt thanks. I can report that the Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like to extend thanks to all those who take the time to serve on the main and various sub committees. There are also a huge group of non-committee members who work behind the scenes; some drive tractors, some drive databases, and some drive support boats or write our Code’s of Practice’s. Without these people, their time and their resources the Club simply would not function. Moving on to membership, I am pleased to report that our total membership currently stands at 401. This compares to 400 last year and 399 the year before. So I think we can say a clear trend is developing! 9 new members joined us as a result of our successful open day back in May of this year, 7 of those being family memberships. As well as a great success in recruiting new members, the open day was a brilliant opportunity for all fleets in the Club to come together for an excellent day both on and off the water. You will see under resolution 4 that membership subscriptions and boat fees remain largely unchanged from last year. This is a reflection of the Club’s sound financial position, and the fact that the bank of England base rate remains at a record low. There are minor fee increases to the retired categories. This is in line with the plan to phase out the retired discount altogether, however it is worth noting that the increase this year is below that of the planned increment. Trials of an online membership renewal process are planned for next year, and I hope to be able to give you more information during the course of the year on this initiative. I would like to extend my thanks to Peter Booth who has worked hard over the past 6 months on moving us forward in this area. Two other top agenda items for the Board this year relate to the MSC ambitions document and a Sport England Inspired Facilities award. You should have sight of 2 pieces of paper relating to these initiatives at this meeting. I plan to address each of these separately under the first items in AOB so as to not detract from the main Commodore’s report. Next onto sailing, and firstly I would like to welcome Tom Clayton who stepped in as our new Sailing Secretary this year and has hit the ground running with the support of the out-going secretaries, Jenny Ball and Dave Russell. Without stealing Tom’s thunder I will report on some of the major activities and achievements this year. I will start with cruisers and it’s been a busy year for MSC boats racing in external competitions. Of particular note is the participation of Woozle Hunter in this year’s Fastnet Race. For her very entertaining account of Woozle Hunters race, we would like to award the Mamgu trophy for best log to Laura Ivermee. Laura is a fairly recent recruit to the cruiser-racing scene and is incredibly enthusiastic. I’ve been told that she’s often seen trimming the spinnaker with one hand whilst photographing the fleet with the other. As Laura isn’t here today I’m sure she won’t mind if I read the first snippet of her Blue: ‘Dear Diary. I have been coerced into competing in the Fastnet Yacht Race! 611 miles non-stop to Ireland and back, on a 33-foot tub, with 5 males and no shower!!!!! Bonkers. Must be hormones!! Hope there’s G+T involved’ - so surely that’s worth a read if you haven’t already! On the topic of cruiser racing, it would be remiss of me not to mention the recent inaugural cruiser autumn series. I had the pleasure of presenting the awards a few weeks ago and it was great to see such a large and lively group of people enjoying this new initiative at the Club. It’s certainly added a new dynamic to racing at MSC and livened up those cold autumn Sunday’s. This series was only possible due to the inspiration and drive of one individual. For this reason I would like to award the Barograph trophy for outstanding commitment to Marconi Sailing Club to Peter Ward. We’ve had a busy year cruising in both dinghies and yachts. Colin Wardell’s group of dinghies have continued to sail monthly and are even set to make a trip out next weekend when most of us will be tucked up inside with the heating on. Our cruisers have been on a number of organised group trips which looked like great fun from the write-ups on the website. January 2016 Navigans 14

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk I would like to pick one cruise in particular to tell you about, which was taken by one of our newest members, Tim Wood. I’ve been provided with a short account of Tim’s epic 8000-mile journey across the Atlantic in a Sadler 34. Their voyage started in 2012 from Mersea. Thinking they had run aground, they actually hit a whale in Biscay and continued to the Canaries. Crossing the Atlantic they had a knockdown but arrived in Antigua just 12 hours before the flight home. They left Antigua in May 2015 for Bermuda, travelling back across the Atlantic with a total of 40 days at sea. Another knock down had damaged the engine so they had a non-stop voyage from Bermuda back to their Marconi mooring completely under sail. So I would like to award the seamanship trophy this year to Tim Wood for his amazing achievement. The catamarans, dinghies and cadets have also been hard at work representing the Club at local, national and international events as well as competing in our own regular racing schedule. More information to follow in the Sailing Secretary’s report. I would now like to award the Commodore’s plate, and this year it is going to someone a little different. As I’ve been forcibly on the sidelines for much of this season, I’ve watched with great admiration all of the cadets that are regularly out racing when the ‘oldies’ are sat upstairs complaining of cold, too much or too little wind, whilst nursing their hot cup of coffee. For me, Jason Clarke has stood out in particular. Jason is always there, eager to help and never gives up. If he isn’t out racing, which is rare, then he’s on a support boat or doing something else useful around the Club such as waiting at the gate for over 2 hours for an ambulance to arrive during cadet week. I remember one very windy Wednesday night race this year, one of the first races back in my laser and I was ready to call it a day. On my way back to the hard I saw Jason, still struggling along in his Topper after his umpteenth capsize and he just wasn’t giving up - that day I turned myself around and carried on racing because lets be honest, no cadet in a Topper is going to out-do the Commodore! I’m pretty sure he beat me by a country mile in that race. So Jason I think you are an inspiration to the many cadets coming through the ranks so please accept this years Commodore’s plate. Moving onto the East Coast Piers Race. As always, thanks are due to Clive Shenton and his huge team, which will include many of you sat in the audience today, for organising another superb event. 2015 saw an impressive increase in entries with 76 dinghies and catamarans on the start lines. Yet again we had some excellent results from Marconi teams in the race itself. I am sure you will be interested to know that the Friends of Cirdan Sailing Trust have had an exceptionally good year for raising sponsorship in the name of the ECPR, in that we have just presented the Trust with a cheque for a staggering £33,850. On top of this we have also donated £500 for the Essex Air Ambulance. Sail training and Oppi club have seen a steady growth this year and we had another busy and successful cadet week. Thanks are due to John Nickalls, Fia Barnes, the cadet week committee and their extensive teams for providing such great training for our young people. They are the future of our club. Another important development this year has been the purchase of MSC’s very own rowing gig. Elettra was specifically built for us by the Pioneer Trust and was funded by a £10k Sport England small grant. We hope this gig will enable more members to take to the water and that the opportunity to race in local competitions will encourage the growth of paddle sports at Marconi. As sports with no harmful conflict of interest to sailing, we feel that rowing, stand-up paddle boarding and canoeing for example are great additions to the Club’s offerings and may encourage new members who would relish the opportunity to row or paddle on tidal waters. Elettra will be taking to the water after the AGM with a short naming ceremony for those who wish to see her afloat. A more high profile, formal launching event is planned for the summer months where the aim is to ask Princess Elettra, Granddaughter of Marconi herself to formally name the gig. Shore side the bar has seen record takings, especially over ECPR weekend, so thank you to all for contributing. Another successful and varied social calendar, including the open day has meant there was rarely a dull weekend at MSC this year. It has been great to see all the fleets socialising together and I look forward to seeing many of you at our annual winter dinner and dance in January. I would like to end my report by sharing some of our plans for next season. I will describe our ambitions for capital development later in the meeting, where we aim to grow and improve our facilities for training, safe storage for club equipment and spectating. Most of you will notice that the galley has grown in size this season and there is a total refit planned over the winter to ensure this facility is fit for purpose. In terms of sailing, we intend to initiate the rowing section of the Club and are also considering the concept of a Club owned Robber. We plan to continue with our annual open day and also to hold fewer but bigger events, such as a 29er Open that is taking place in March 2016. This coming season will also see a change to Club racing, for example with retimed and fewer starts, which is all part of the process to reinvigorate dinghy racing. As always training takes a prime position in our objectives and we will continue to deliver and develop sail training as well as offering formal courses throughout the year for skills such as power boating and first aid. Overall Marconi Sailing Club has had a successful year and I look forward to the year ahead. Thank you for your kind support this year and for listening to this report. I am happy to take any questions. Michaela Dowley Commodore, Marconi Sailing Club January 2016 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk > Marconi Sailing Club Ltd Marconi Sailing Club Ltd FINANCIAL SUMMARY ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING 29th NOVEMBER 2015 As Finance Director of Marconi Sailing Club Ltd, I present a financial summary along with the accounts for the year ended 31st August, 2015, for approval by the members. The accounts as distributed to the members are set out in the prescribed format ready for submission to Companies House and to HMRC. Independent Review The accounts have been reviewed by John Bird, Chartered Management Accountant (former member and Treasurer). Income (top half of page 4) Overall income from subscriptions and fees stands at £137,654 (£142,879 less Member Loan Discounts of £5225) as against last year’s income of £141,801 (£147,651 less Loan Discounts of £5,850). Although the level of membership – 401 -is nearly same as last year, the income has reduced. This is partly due to the lower proportion of cruiser members and also to new members joining the club later in the year. Surpluses on the bar, social events, camping fees, open meetings, Cadet Week and other activities amount to £13,123 (last year £15,541). Camping revenue has increased but the surpluses from Open Meetings have decreased. A straightforward comparison for the bar income and expenditure is not possible, as the amounts paid in and expended can fall just outside the accounting period, as is the situation this year. Overall therefore the club’s revenue has decreased to £150,777 (last year £157,342). Expenditure (lower half of page 4) Spending has been a little higher for sailing activities (up £459), representing necessary maintenance on the club’s fleet of dinghies. Spending on club and precincts (up £343) includes major improvements to the First Aid Room and the construction of a mezzanine floor in the Barn. This was offset by significant savings on cleaning and waste collection costs. There was an increase in rates but expenditure on electricity, gas and water were minimal notwithstanding higher charges. Social and publicity showed a decrease of £2,457 as there were no setting up costs for a new website this year. Administration expenditure no longer includes the income and expenditure relating to training. Net Surplus (bottom of page 4) Therefore the club’s surplus before interest and tax was £62,495 (last year £69,218). This amount includes contingency amounts for major repairs to the approach road, potential insurance claim and refunds for boat fees payable in December each year. It also includes a Sport England grant of £10,000 towards the purchase of a rowing gig which was awarded in April 2015. As the end of the financial year falls on 31st August, and subscriptions and fees are not due until 1st January thereafter, it is essential to ensure that club retains about £30,000 in the bank account to meet unavoidable expenditure for those five months (September to mid January) where little or no income is received. The annual budget plan is set to create a small surplus annually which can be put towards minor capital projects for improving the club infrastructure and/or as seed money to be used to secure grants such as the Sport England awards. The club continues at present to benefit from the historically low interest rates in the repayment of its development loan, but it is important to bear in mind that even a small increase in interest rates of 0.5% would amount to at least £3,000 p.a. extra per annum. There have not been any significant changes to the balance sheet during the year and the overall Net Asset Value of the club improved to a sound £352,571 (last year £319,026). This is approximately £881 per member! It is worth drawing members’ attention to the following areas: Capital spending (note 2, page 2): This has been fairly low this past year and includes £3,600 deposit for the rowing gig, £1,000 for a new club dinghy and the purchase of new mowing equipment. However some significant areas of expenditure have already been assigned this autumn including essential improvements to the main travel hoist (£6,500), maintenance of the access road (£10,000) and a major refit of the galley (£7,000 to £10,000). National Westminster and Members' loans (notes 4 & 5, page 3): The balance outstanding on the long term bank loan has reduced from £392,404 (2014) to £372,427, a repayment of £19,977. Repayment of £12,000 has been made against the membership loan which now stands at £104,500. The club's long term financing therefore is £476,927. When considering this figure members should compare it to the fixed assets total of £819,038 shown at the top of page 1. Essentially it is saying that the club's equity in all of its property and assets is now 41.8%. This represents a significant achievement since the members bought out the club 2003, especially in light of the developments undertaken. Sue Shenton, Director (Finance). 5) Marconi Sailing Club Ltd Marconi SC Sailing Secretary’s report 2015 Good morning everyone and it is my pleasure to present the Sailing Secretary Report for 2015. I am pleased to report that 2015 has been another very busy year for sailing across the club. I will endeavour to do justice to the range of activity but I apologise in advance for anything I may have missed. With support from the Board and Management Committee and encouragement from the RYA, the Sailing Sub-Committee set out to enhance sailing participation during 2015. There were four strands to this: To continue improving the club’s sailing equipment and capability To support activities to recruit new members; To introduce some new activities to encourage wider participation And to make our sailing activities more accessible for existing and new members to join in Throughout the year we have been having discussions about how we can improve racing and to try and encourage more of our members to get out there and to use those fantastic craft that populate the fields outside. The changes are still being refined but ultimately there will still remain similar fleets, however the number of starts will be reduced & the sequence will changed to 5,4,1, GO, to be more in line with the ISAF recognised sequence. The aim of this is to create busier start lines and ultimately to improve racing. This was also our second season as an official RYA Training Centre we have been delivering RYA accredited power boat training – thanks to the efforts of Bob Collins as Principle and Pat Shaw as our qualified instructor. We have taken this opportunity to train club members to RYA Powerboat standards and Bob and Pat will continue to expand this offering going forward. The First aider training is also going well, and next year we will be going into the next stage of getting those with certificates issued, renewed qualifications to keep them up to date. The open day was once again a great success, as Michaela reported, and saw many people sampling sailing for the first time or returning to a sport they once loved. The Friday Free4All evening sailing sessions continued this year, with the aim of easing the new members and less confident sailors into sailing the fantastic water we have just off the club, although they might not seem quite so appetising today. Next year they shall be known as Sunset Sail and Supper and with the galley providing an evening meal after sailing – it was pretty much the best way to start a weekend! The Sunday pursuit races continued again this year, an easier form of racing with starts from the hard, this saw good turnouts with 22 in one race. The weekly emails have continued this year, with Jenny kindly doing them until June when she handed over that responsibility to me, I hope you have found them both informative and enjoyable and have had as much fun reading them as I have had writing them. The idea of the emails is to keep you informed of both what to look forward to and what you have missed. And we have had plenty of activities to talk about in the weekly emails! From the cruiser cruising fleet there were many trips starting off in a shake down to Brightlingsea, The watercress run to Heybridge, A jaunt to Tollesbury. The summer cruise was across the Thames estuary to Ramsgate and then on to Queenborough, Chatham and finally Brightlingsea. The bank holiday cruise was to Ipswich, onto Wrabness, Walton and finally Brightlingsea. And one final cruise to Brightlingsea, just to make sure it was still there. The racing cruiser fleet had just as much fun travelling around the country, starting with the BJRC series, Blue Moon was the highest finishing Marconi boat, coming in 2nd in IRC and 4th in BJRC handicaps. Woozle Hunter was the highest finishing Marconi boat in the EAORA, offshore series, 2nd in class 3 and 4th overall. In the Fastnet Race, Woozle Hunter finished as 1st Marconi boat and in 188th position from a fleet of 309. Closer to home, Caroline competed at the prestigious Ramsgate Week, were she finished 4th in class. New this season, the highly successful Marconi Autumn Series saw 6 boats competing, with a further 4 in the Bart’s Bash event, 4 x boats were still in with a chance of winning come the medal race. Unfortunately the wind died on us, which saw Woozle January 2016 Navigans 19

Additionally, John Burgoyne, Dave Russell, Dave & Jemma Clarke and Sally Wilson, have ensured that Race officers and Support Boats were rota’d, that results were calculated and trophies organised. Whilst this is just a whistle-stop tour of 2015, I hope it does justice to the full range of sailing we have all been involved in. Categories to enter images into include: 1. Serious sailing - racing, race box madness, open meetings, competitions, safety boat operations etc. 2. People at work - unsung heroes involved in running the club events or site and boat maintenance eg. launching cruisers, laying moorings, OOD, race officers, galley staff, cadet organisation, management etc. 3. Graham Cross Rear Commodore MARCONI SAILING CLUB AND THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE AWARDED YACHTS AND YACHTING GOLD STAR AWARD. The East Coast Piers Race has been awarded a Yachts and Yachting Gold Star Award in the February 2016 edition of the sailing magazine. The award is for the large amount of money we raised in 2015 from the East Coast Piers Race. The BIG cheque for over £33,000 was presented to The Cirdan Sailing Trust just before the clubs AGM in November 2015. We smashed the £22,000 figure from the previous year. Proceeds from the race weekend and sponsorship go to The Cirdan Sailing Trust which provides sailing experiences for disadvantaged children. The East Coast Piers Race (ECPR) is a long distance race weekend with FREE camping held at Marconi Sailing Club in June or July. Traditionally there is in shore medium length racing on Saturday then the longer races on the Sunday. The event is open to fast dinghies and catamarans, there are three different course options of different length with the longest being 48miles. Along the course are a number of mother boats who are able to provide support with no penalty so the course is easy to follow. It’s a challenge but a manageable one. The race will be held over the 9th and 10th July in 2016. Andrew Dowley Marconi take part in the Burnham Gig Race This weekend Marconi Sailing Club made it’s world debut into the rowing scene, by entering our Harker’s Yard Rowing Gig in the Burnham Gig Race! Not one, but 2 races in fact, due to a last minute practice session of commands and technique organised by Tom Clayton on Saturday, we were able to add a “Mixed Crew” to our Men’s entry. There were 12 boats entered, 2 GRP Thames Class 4 man boats (which run in their own class) and 10 Harkers Yard class Gigs. We had set ourselves the task of “looking neat from shore” and “actually finishing” as being fair targets. The men’s race started at 12.45 Crew:- No.1 – Lee Hooper (Bow) No.2 – Roy Hardwicke No.3 – Steve Cleaver No.4 – Kevin Stubbs (Stroke) Cox’n – Tom Clayton It soon dawned on us that a race start would be more difficult than a sailing one, as with 12 boats mean 48 Oars to also keep clear of. The tide was due to turn 4 minutes before the start and we chose to get out early (avoiding the crew change on the pontoon from the first “Ladies” race). Our cox’n chose the far bank to start and we set off at a steady pace (so we had some hope of being able to last the distance) February 2016 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk As we only had one or two practice sessions each, we had not really tried a race pace, concentrating on basic technique first, so to me keeping breathing in time with rowing movement was the first challenge as we headed out to No. 3 buoy, seaward of the start. Fortunately for us Tom’s metronome had a miraculous improvement and we were heavily encouraged by Tom to keep going, time seemed to slow down and it seemed some while before we had even got 1/3 of the way to the turn. We could see the worry on Tom’s face as we closed on the turn, realising he would not want to be in the middle of the bunch for the turn around the buoy. For the return towards Crouch Y.C. we were pushed along by Tom, and managed to stay fairly close to the main bunch, and followed the north shore, it was certainly getting to the point for me not to be able to pull much faster when encouraged by the cox’n, but we were soon finishing about 15 seconds or so after boat No.11, with some strong encouragement from the supporters ashore (thankyou). After a quick crew change, the Ladies race started at 13.30 Crew:- No.1 – Rhiannon Hitt (Bow) No.2 – Lucie Walker No.3 – Tristran Hutt No.4 – Tom Clayton (Stroke) Cox’n – Kevin Stubbs As tide was building, about 2 knots pushing us over the start line, the start became more complicated to manage for me as Cox’n, plus the poor mixed crew (2 ladies,2 men) had me to drag along plus more work pre-race stemming the tide I decided we would row a 360 and then along the line for the start, and follow the deep water, we made a fair start, our rowers kept good time and we stayed relatively close to the bunch all the way downstream to the turn, where we arrived last but made a fast turn (“bow side” “ hold water”, “stroke side” “pull hard” and made up a length or two. Tactics split here and I decided to head close to the south bank against the tide going back, as the north side seemed a lot farther away. I did not get us over quite as far as I should but managed to tuck in eventually (the support Rib said by tucking in we gained a knot in boat speed to 3.5 Knots over ground against the tide. Our younger crew had great stamina here, credit especially to Rhiannon and Lucie, and by still responding to my gentle encouragement and “10 Good Pulls” (several times!) they gained over a boat on the North bank and we were not going to be last, the crew agreed to go harder and we finally crossed the line on the opposite side to our supporters AHEAD OF THE LAST BOAT!. (I have attached some “before” and “after” photo’s from the Mixed race, unfortunately the cameraman was busy rowing on the Men’s one). Immediately after the finish, having stopped rowing, we realised the full strength of the tide, and the distance to row back, so called on the services of a support Rib to tow us back. By the time they had tied us alongside we were halfway out to sea again but were glad of the tow. We have also noted that the last boat to finish can easily be a long time awaiting a trailer on a narrow slipway, waiting turns with a large fleet. We received some post race tips from other crews, some who have been racing 2 seasons now – interestingly one was “Why are you using your practice oars?” – it turns out that our “One Class” Harker’s Yard boats can be used with hooked blade oars, which can give 10% more efficiency (they say…..), so our 12/12 and 11/12 was perhaps more respectable than we thought. – the bad news is we’ve now got to raise £2,500 ish for a set of Race oars! So, well done both teams – a respectable first outing, a few blisters to show between us and certainly a few aches already for me tonight. - a challenge is now set for at least a couple more ladies to come forward so we can field 3 crews at the next event (Maldon) 7th Feb – or Stone – 21’s Feb (Practice next weekend needs a careful eye on the weather plus how to fit around the Dinner Dance Saturday night too!) Thank you especially to Roy Hardwicke for fixing the roof of the Gig container mid week, and to Peter & Sandra for towing the boat both ways and providing invaluable support plus linking us in with the race schedule organisers. Elettra signing off now ._. Kevin Stubbs February 2016 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk April Issue copy deadline: Saturday 12th March Club Notices Frank Bennett Frank Bennett passed away on 22nd January 2016. His funeral, which was attended by club members, was held in Chelmsford on 2nd March. This tribute to Frank was put together by Ray Ball with contributions from Marconi Sailing Club members who knew Frank at work or at the club or both. ……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………….. No doubt Frank had a long career behind him before joining the Marconi Company but club members who knew him at work recall that he was a research engineer in the Radar Research Laboratory at the Marconi Research Centre at Great Baddow. He is remembered as cycling from his home in Old Moulsham to work in Baddow wearing shorts whatever the temperature. We are told that he continued wearing his shorts even in the office or laboratory. To those who remember Frank at the club that will not come as a surprise. He was well known for wearing shorts when others were shivering with cold. Frank joined Marconi Sailing Club from the Royal Burnham Yacht Club. He built his Solo sailing dinghy which he sailed at the club for many years He also bought a Halcyon 23 called Sundowner in which he ranged far and wide on the East Coast; often on his own. It was typical of Frank that instead of putting up with what he saw as shortcomings in the way Sundowner handled, he decided that the designer did not know his business and removed the keel and moved it back by 6 inches. Apparently this modification was successful. Frank was treasurer of MSC from 1989 to 2002. During that time Marconi Sailing Club was the sailing section of Marconi Athletic & Social Club and was not allowed its own bank account. Frank spent many hours at Beehive Lane ensuring that the interests of the sailing section were given due consideration. He was a supportive and loyal member of the committee. When, at the start of this century, there were some doubts about the future of the sailing club at Stansgate Frank gave his full support to the small group who got together to form what became known as the Lifeboat Committee. The Lifeboat Committee ultimately arranged a members buy out creating the independent Marconi Sailing Club that is enjoyed by members today. Frank stood down as treasurer in 2002. At the annual general meeting in November 2002 the commodore, Neil Pembleton, thanked Frank with the following words: (The first paragraph is a little ‘tongue in cheek’ as Frank would have been in his mid-50s in 1989.) [Quote from AGM, November 2002] Finally, before I close the meeting, I must return to Frank Bennett. It was just over fourteen years ago that I stood down from the post of Treasurer and was introduced to a young lad wearing shorts, quite obviously fresh out of school. In the last fourteen years this lad has blossomed into the fine figure that we know today. I cannot believe that there is an area of the club which has not received his magic touch, be it from chucking lighted paper into the hole we dug to replace the water main to check that we had not punctured the gas pipe, designing and building the gate and clubhouse locking system, maintaining the sewage system and many other jobs. At the same time there cannot be many members who have not benefited from Frank's knowledge and experience. I personally, and I am sure that all other previous Commodores, members of the Executive and main committees, have welcomed his calm, careful analysis and advice over the fourteen years. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk May Issue copy deadline: Saturday 16th April Club Notices Club Secretary EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD I issue this warning every year but it may be useful for new members and perhaps a timely reminder for older hands. The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius. On sunny spring days it is easy to be fooled but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim. Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the wind chill. There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm. TENDERS ARE OFTEN JUST THAT! Every year it seems we have at least one incident when someone is either going from tender to yacht or vice versa. It’s easy to get complacent (well we do it every weekend, right) but probably most of us have had a near miss at some time but got away with it. Some are less fortunate and end up in the drink. Please take care in your tender where you are probably most vulnerable and possibly alone. As the man said, lifejackets are only useless ornaments unless they are worn (or words to that effect). Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk June Issue copy deadline: Saturday 14th May Club Notices Club Secretary CLUBHOUSE SECURITY There have been occasions recently when members have come on site early in the morning to find the front and back doors of the clubhouse unlocked. The doors may have been unlocked overnight or even for several days. We all have an interest on maintaining the security of the clubhouse. When you are the last to leave the clubhouse please ensure that all the exterior doors are locked. It is worth checking the back door and the external doors to the changing rooms even if you haven’t used them yourself. It only takes a minute or two. Lock up even if there are still members on site. Anyone entitled to be in the clubhouse will have their own access card. MAMGU BAR SECURITY Users of the bar are asked to ensure that the external patio doors are properly closed and locked. The leaver needs to be pushed fully down (to at least 45o or more) before the key is turned. The last centimetre or so is quite stiff. Double check by trying to lift the lever after the key has been withdrawn. If the leaver is not fully down it is easy to open the door from the outside with obvious potential consequences. CAMPING AT THE STAR, STEEPLE I have spoken to The Star and they have confirmed that their campsite is for adults only. That is nobody under 18. They have taken this decision due to damage in the toilets and shower block. They have accommodation in rooms and that accommodation is available to families. It would pay to book in advance. The Star is under new management and the new managers are continuing with this policy. It is important to spread this news as widely as possible as some of our members and guests have used The Star campsite in the past. It has been used as overspill by those wanting to do Cadet Week but have been unable to get a pitch at Stansgate. I believe that some ECPR visitors have also used The Star. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Cadet Fleet RHS TEAM RACING APRIL 2016 On Saturday 23rd April Marconi sent a group of six cadets to a team racing regatta hosted by the Royal Hospital School on Alton Water. This was a competition in which our team of three Fireflies sailed against a series of other teams in races where it was often more important to slow down the opposition than to sail fast ourselves. The team consisted of Dan Nickalls, Will Harrison, Jack Collis, Charlie Collis, Hannah Bard and Sam Featherstone. A total of 12 teams from various clubs and schools competed in group stages, with the top four teams in each group then going through to knockout stages. Through the day we raced five races, winning two of them – a great outcome for such an inexperienced group of team racers. This meant we were fourth in our group and qualified for the silver sail-off, but unfortunately a scoring error meant we did know this until some of us had left for home. The team had a great experience in some fiercely competitive and very enjoyable racing, as well as learning a lot about the tactics involved in team racing. We will definitely be returning for another go next year! John Nickalls ale Sprint 15 SPRINT 15 TRAINING DAY – MARCONI SC Saturday 16th April 2016 Six local sailors and eight visiting sailors arrived at Marconi SC on a decidedly chilly Saturday morning for a Sprint 15 Training day at Marconi Sailing Club led by Howard Hawkes. A pre-session briefing took place over coffee and bacon rolls which is, as we all know, a mandatory part of any proper training. Participants had been asked to pre-register to give an idea of the range of experience and what people wanted to gain from the day. It was quite a diverse spectrum from learning how to tack/gybe effectively, some racing practice, how to return to shore in an onshore breeze plus a slightly more broad comment of “why am I always at the back of the fleet”. The training started in earnest with a shore-based session running through boat set up, the importance of having a very tight trampoline and talking through how to tack without stalling. All of which is a lot easier to do when everyone is stood around a boat on dry(ish) land. The fleet then took to the water for the morning session. The wind had eased from quite strong to fairly light and the water was flat – making for nicely manageable conditions for the first sail. A proliferation of Go Pros on the RIBS meant that (a) we would be able to review the sessions when we came off the water (the reason we gave to the participants), (b) everyone was on their best behaviour and (c) potential opportunities for future website / magazine / blackmail material were maximised (the real reason but don’t tell them). A triangular course was set to provide tacking, gybing and three points of sail practice with the RIBS following and filming. The fleet came ashore for lunch and took the opportunity to review some of the footage from the morning session – particularly around tacking and trim when sailing downwind. After lunch, the wind had freshened making for ideal sailing conditions on the flat water. A committee boat and race course were set up and a series of short one lap races were run to give a good opportunity for practice starts and sailing in fairly close quarters. During the first race, Rob Bailey from Thorpe Bay kindly provided excellent footage by turtling in the middle of the river, which Howard naturally filmed for future training (blackmail) purposes. With some cajoling from the team on the coach boat and the committee boat – participants were encouraged to keep a very tight pre-start sailing area and after a couple of races, the start line was nicely busy and competitive. The coach boat also took the opportunity to follow different participants to film and offer some tips. After a good afternoon’s sailing, the fleet headed ashore to debrief over coffee and cake. The majority of visitors left their boats at the club to take part in the Traveller Event the following weekend which was fantastic. Unfortunately, we forgot to film the sailor who got his Transit stuck in the mud in the cat park (until a tractor was arranged to come to his aid) – so I can’t officially use that for blackmail material. A big thank you to our guests – Paul Shields (Seasalter), Andrew Berisford, Gordon Deuce (Brightlingsea), Donald Sloane, (Felixtowe Ferry), Chris Tillyer, Steve Healy, Rob Bailey and Darren Fitchew from Thorpe Bay. Well done also to Andy Perks, Dave Clarke, Antony Bailey, Nick Pavitt, Dani Pavitt and Steve Thomas from Marconi who are all very welcome additions to our fleet! Thanks to Howard for heading up the training – to David Ball, Kevin Kirby, Liz Jackson, Pete Richardson and Fenella Miller for assisting and Dave Russell, Abbie Russell, Jason Clarke, Paul Metcalfe and Pat Shaw for providing support boat cover. May 2016 Navigans 5

SPRINT 15 TRAVELLER EVENT 2016 – MARCONI SAILING CLUB 21 competitors took part in the first 2016 Summer TT at Marconi SC on 23rd and 24th April. We were particularly pleased to welcome a number of new faces – who had participated in the Association Training Day run by Howard Hawkes the previous weekend. A decent northerly breeze and cold temperatures meant it did not feel very summery but did provide great racing conditions across both days. Race 1 was a round the cans and the breeze fell away to fairly light conditions to start with. Jenny Ball led round the windward mark, closely followed by David Ball, Paul Grattage and Liam Thom. Paul and Liam pulled ahead on the downwind leg and led for the next two lap followed by Jenny, David and Chris Tillyer. For lap 3 a strong breeze filled in with a shift making for multiple changes at the front of the fleet - although Paul's lead was unassailable - Chris came in second followed by David and Kevin Kirby. Race 2 was the now legendary long distance figure of eight race around Osea and Northey Islands. With a strong if inconsistent northerly breeze, this proved to be one of the fastest round the island races with a fetch for much of the race. Paul Grattage took an early lead, chased hard by Kevin Kirby, David Ball, Chris Tillyer and Liam Thom. Stuart Snell soon caught up the pack and was in the front runners at the turning point at Northey Island. The rest of the fleet were close behind with a lot of position changes on the leg back round the back of Osea Island. After a real blast of a race, the fleet finished pretty close together with Paul Grattage leading followed by Kevin Kirby, Stuart Snell, David Ball and Liam Thom. The fleet headed in to thaw out over a well-deserved evening meal. Sunday morning saw another day of strong northerly breezes and flat water. The start of race 3 saw a bunching at the pin end of the line and a couple of boats tacked off from the rest of the fleet to get into clear air. Paul Grattage who went left up the course rounded the mark first followed by Jenny Ball who had gone right with the rest of the fleet close behind chasing down the reach. Paul Grattage continued to lengthen his lead with very close racing between Jenny, Steve Healy, Stuart Snell, David Ball, Kevin Kirby and Liam Thom. Wind shifts made for some interesting tactics particularly on the windward legs and very competitive racing throughout the fleet. Paul Grattage took first, followed by Stuart Snell, Kevin Kirby and Jenny Ball. For Race 4, the wind had strengthened including the odd Force 6 gust. Line bias again meant that the fleet bunched at the pin end, and this time a larger number of boats tacked off up the right hand side of the course with Donald Sloan and Erling Holmberg making good gains and coming in with the front of the pack coming in from the left hand side. David Ball led off on the reach closely followed by the rest of the pack. By the second lap, David had pulled out a decent lead with Paul Grattage and Liam Thom chasing – whilst Chris Tillyer, Kevin Kirby, Stuart Snell, Jenny Ball and Daren Fitchew battled out behind. Paul managed to work his magic again and eventually got past David to take the win, with Liam in third followed by Chris, Stuart and Kevin. The fleet headed home after an exhilarating weekend of sailing! Big thanks go to the Race Officer, Race Committee and Support boat crews who had a very cold time of it whilst we all enjoyed ourselves. Congratulations to the newer members of the fleet who found themselves sailing in breezier conditions than they were used to – but got on really well anyway! And Thorpe Bay made an impressive start to the newly introduced Traveller Team Trophy with a turnout of six competitors. Results: 1st – Paul Grattage, Shanklin, 2nd – David Ball, Marconi, 3rd – Kevin Kirby, Marconi, 4th - Stuart Snell, Grafham, 5th – Liam Thom, Shanklin, 6th – Chris Tillyer, Thorpe Bay. Jenny Ball Catbert 1917 May 2016 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk July Issue copy deadline: Saturday 11th June Club Notices Commodore I write this the night after our open day, held on 21st May, which was another resounding success! Many thanks are due to the army of volunteers, headed up by Graham Cross who helped to show our Club at its absolute best. 65 families signed in at our registration desk with plenty of people taking advantage of trips out on the water on a variety of boats. Our artistic youngsters created a beautiful mosaic in the arts & crafts tent, whilst the bouncy castle provided entertainment for the little ones and a Pimms tent for the older. It was also a lovely day for our members as all fleets really pulled together during the day and enjoyed a social event with BBQ in the evening. As you know, membership is our only real source of income so it is vital to the future of the Club that we proactively look to grow our membership - please keep supporting events such as open days in the future. Unfortunately I have to report that we were unsuccessful in our recent attempt to win a Sport England Inspired Facilities grant for £75,000 to invest in capital improvements to the clubhouse. There was fierce competition in this, the final round of funding. Although the outcome is disappointing we have a sound idea of what our priorities should be for capital improvements and I thank Sue Shenton for putting in a huge amount of time and effort into making our bid as strong as possible. Also thank you to all the members who engaged in discussions at the AGM and through our online survey earlier this year. We will continue to seek out grant funding in the future so please let us know if you hear of any potential funds we can apply to. In response to a query at the 2015 AGM, over the past couple of months we have carried out a survey of cruiser owners providing options for the development of mooring laying/retrieval at MSC. The results of this survey, which have been communicated to the cruiser fleet, include increasing mechanisation of the process in the near future and the potential to move to a 3-yearly cycle of laying/retrieval. These proposals will be discussed with the moorings sub-committee and at the cruiser AGM. We have also been discussing plans to build a ‘bridge deck’ above the western end of the support boat containers. The purpose of the bridge deck is to provide options for race control for opens hosted at MSC, including the East Coast Piers Race and also for one-off races in our own sailing calendar in the future. The plan is to begin construction over the winter season so keep an eye out for developments. Our calendar is packed over the remainder of the season with events such as the ECPR, cadet week and camping fortnight to look forward to. Please refer to our excellent website for up to date information on upcoming events and reports. Happy sailing! Michaela Dowley, Commodore Club Secretary OUT OF DATE FLARES According to the MCA rep at a meeting I attended recently, HMCG Walton will still take out of date flares for disposal. Walton is no longer operational as Thames Coastguard but they still have the premises. It is necessary to phone before going to arrange a time and date. Telephone number . TOLLESBURY PIER Due to some shifting of the river bed the remains of the old Tollesbury Pier have become exposed and pose a possible hazard to navigation. I understand that the southern extremity of the hazard is to be marked by a South Cardinal. Take care if sailing close inshore off Tollesbury. If you’re not sure where Tollesbury Pier used to be look at the old chart on the wall in the Mamgu Bar. DINGHY & CAT PARKS All dinghies and catamarans have been allocated a numbered space in the boat parks. The plans are on the club notice board and also available on the club website. Please ensure that you put your boat in the right space and clearly marked. Identifying ‘anonymous’ boats is a real time consuming nuisance! If you acquire a new boat (or sell one) please ensure that you advise Mike Turner (Membership Secretary) so the boat can be recorded on the membership database and the appropriate fees paid. You should also contact Bryan Spencer (Dinghy Park) or Kevin Dowley (Cat Park) to be allocated a boat space. June 2016 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk There is a reluctance amongst some club members to let the club officials know of boat changes meaning that the dinghy and cat park allocations have to be the subject of regular surveys. This often results in extra correspondence with members to obtain full details including insurance and more work for everyone involved. If you have any doubts about boat parking, please ask. RATS & ADDERS A reminder to be careful of some of our local wildlife. We need to be aware of rats and adders. If adders are left alone everything should be fine but all members, especially children, need to be aware of them particularly in long grass where they may not be seen or when reaching under boats. Rats will occasionally be seen running round the site. Care should be taken particularly with standing water for example in boats or on boat covers. Rats urine can convey Well’s disease so standing water and puddles may be contaminated. Cuts and grazes should be covered to minimise the risk of infection. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Fleet News Cruiser Fleet WOOZLE WINNING WEEKEND The East Coast offshore racing season got off to a good start over the May bank holiday weekend with the traditional Burnham – Mersea back to back races. Woozle Hunter was Marconi’s only representative in a fleet of 7 boats, but they set off out of the Crouch racing against some very experienced crews, which included one other closely matched Sigma 33. The Pattinson Cup race saw the fleet taking the tide up the swin in an attempt to beat the tidal gate at the North East Gunfleet mark. As was the pattern of the day, the wind was sometimes none existent and at other times saw boats heading down the wallet to finish at Mersea, some with kites up, others hard on the wind. After 48 miles of racing, Ian & Laura Ivermee and the Woozle Hunter crew finished in 9 hours and 14 mins, which on corrected time gave them their first overall victory of the season. The following day the fleet did it all again in the Ralph Herring race back to Burnham, but with slightly better winds towards the end of the race, Woozle was able to finish a little quicker in 8 hours and 37 mins. Their competitors also recorded faster times on the return, but it wasn’t enough, Woozle had done it again! 1st overall and of course the class 3 title as well which puts them in a great position to challenge for the 2016 series. NORTH SEA RACE WINNERS – WOOZLE HUNTER The RORC North Sea Race, the most prestigious Offshore Race on the East Coast, has been won by Marconi boat, Woozle Hunter in 2016. Ian & Laura Ivermee, joined by their Fastnet race crew from last season, set off from Harwich last Friday morning in a fleet of 30 IRC racers which included the best from Holland. The race, 180 miles offshore is a real test of seamanship, stamina, concentration and persistence and this year was no different, in what turned out to be a light airs race with very little shelter from the sun. Woozle, the slowest boat on handicap rating to finish the course, pressed on as they chased the fleet out to the South Galloper before turning North around the windfarms to head to Smith Knoll off Great Yarmouth, before turning to cross towards Holland. It wasn’t until 5:30 in the morning on Saturday that they managed to pass this most Northerly mark of the course, and as they were now way out of signal range, they had no idea of their position. Those ashore watched the race play out on the online tracker, which you can see here, and looking at the weather forecast, it seemed that the bigger boats would have light airs all the way with the possibility of slightly increasing wind later in the evening for Woozle. As it turned out, Woozle was still racing into the dark of Saturday evening when for a moment the wind died bringing the possibility of ruining their chances whilst the rest of the fleet had made Scheveningen. But the hole in the wind didn’t last long and at 10:30 in the evening Woozle finished after 36 hours of racing, to win the race outright, over 1 hour ahead of their nearest competitor on corrected time. A truly remarkable and well deserved achievement for the Woozle team, in particular skipper Ian who has spent many hours preparing both the boat and assembling his crew over the past 2 years. This must rank as one of the best, if not the very best achievement of a Marconi racing member from any fleet. The crew are seen here collecting the Goeree Challenge Cup and the Jan Moreton Salver, after the race. Later this month, they will be awarded with the Royal Ocean Racing Club Medallion at a ceremony on the 19th May at the clubs HQ in St James’s. Well done guys. You can see the full result here - http://www.rorc.org/raceresults/2016/ircoverall04.html June 2016 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk BLUE MOON WINS IRC CLASS – CAROLINE 5TH IN LH CLASS – BJRC RACE 2 Race 2 of the BJRC series drifted past the hard on Sunday 1st May, whilst many of the Marconi would be racers, worked to lay moorings or finish the late prep on their boats. The fleet of 15 boats, which included 8 from Blackwater SC, contained just Blue Moon and Caroline representing Marconi, but were hoping to be better represented in 2 weeks’ time. The drift continued all the way down to Bradwell, with the boats that ventured over to the Mersea shore losing out as the onshore winds started to fill. Eventually there was no need to shorten the course and some 7 hours later the fleet had all returned to the Osea line at good speed. Caroline was first Marconi boat home and finished 5th in the local handicap fleet, while Blue Moon came out on top in the IRC class, winning by just 6 seconds on corrected time. The full race results and report can be found here: MARCONI NUMBERS INCREASE IN BJRC RACE 3 After a late launch at the start to the season, 4 Marconi Cruisers took to the line and grew the fleet to 18 boat in BJRC race 3 on the morning of Sunday 15th May. With a lack of wind, the boats tried to stem the tide at the Stone line, but most resorted to kedge at the start. Eventually the fickle winds helped the fleet around the course which used all the inshore marks on the card, out and back, without going further than the turning mark at Bench Head. Monkey Business Heads Blue MoonThe Marconi boats returned after 5 hours of racing and Monkey Business and Blue Moon who were in close company around the course came out as best Marconi boats on corrected time. In the IRC rating class, Blue Moon finished 2nd to Absolution from Maylandsea Bay SC with Monkey Business in 4th place. In the BJRC local handicap result, Monkey Business turned the table, finishing 4th overall with Blue Moon in 5th. Crazy Suzy on her shakedown race, finished 10th with club boat Ned Kelly sailed by our new members successfully completing their first race in 16th position. The full race report and results can be found here: http://us6.campaign-archive2.com/?u=033143a6b9ffc5b475328b703&id=e4b86b36b4&e=e70fd24474 CRUISER SPRING SERIES – WEEKEND 1 RESULTS Six Marconi Cruiser racers set off early on Sat 21st May on leg 1 of the Spring Cruiser Series. Caroline, Woozle Hunter and Crazy Suzy, all sailing short on crew opted to race without spinnakers, and on the gusty passage to the finish line off Batemans Tower this proved to be a good decision. Crazy Suzy was first across the line, putting her new main sail to good use, whilst the rest of the fleet crossed closely bunched together. Ned Kelly, having issues with her main sail retired and took the short route inside Bench in order to get to the line in time for Leg 2 which started at midday. Leg 2 was a joint race with the Colne YC fleet and the 16 boats tacked out of the Colne, over the shallows to try and beat th e flooding tide. After Bench Head, and then on the return from WMYC No:10 where kites could have been flown, almost all opted to keep them in their bags. On corrected time Caroline, was highest finishing Marconi boat, 3rd overall in the LH class, with Woozle Hunter in 7th and Blue Moon in 10th. Crazy Suzy, Ned Kelly and Monkey Business were in 13, 15 and 16th place respectively. After a great social evening with the Colne YC fleet on saturday, the Marconi boats started leg 3 of their series in very light winds and against a strong flood tide. Once around the East Mersea point, the boats skimmed the bottom along the Mersea shore before finally making it out and around Bench Head. Monkey Business was having a great light airs day but as the tide turned and the winds died off Bradwell, all boats eventually retired, some after a long wait at anchor. Not the Woozle team though. After initially anchoring in 13m in mid channel, and then taking a very slow passage along the St Lawrence shore that saw them kedge another 3 or 4 times, they eventually crossed the line jubilant having beaten the conditions after 6 and a half hours of racing. There’s just one time that needs to be confirmed in leg one, but the current standings in the series show Woozle Hunter leading both the Local Handicap and the IRC classes. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk As well as the eclectic spectacle of barbershop quartet “Reunion” performing amongst the boats on the hard, it was an opportunity for MSC to formally name their newly acquired rowing gig “Elettra” aided by a recently successful Sport England grant. Graham Cross Getting to a World Championships At the end of 2014 we made an epic trip over to Perth in Australia to take part in the Tornado World Championships. This involved two road trips (there and back) to Southern Germany to load and unload the boat into a container, then of course th e flight to Australia (with a 3 month old baby). At the time I never wrote anything down about our preparation of getting to a World Championships and the logistics around attending. I thought this might be a useful read, whether you’re thinking of travelling to your first open meeting down the road or you’re looking at attending a World Championships. We’re in no way pros but we love our sailing and we like to sail with the best, watching and learning from further back! This year in early June we’re off to the 2016 Tornado World Championships in Lindau, Southern Germany. No flights involved this time, just a long road trip with a trailer (again), a toddler and a 3 month old (again!). So here are some tips on how we go about preparing for an event. FIRST STEPS Where is the event? What’s involved in getting there? What are the dates? Where is the notice of race? Sailing instructions published yet? Who are you sailing with? Collect all of the necessary information you need and start planning early. LOGISTICS With logistics, it could be an easy trip or it could be long and painful. This year getting the boat to the World Championships is in our own hands using the trailer we have, no containers, far away loading destinations or customs. Although in our own hands there are two boats travelling; Steve Glynn & Tom Duckmanton and Michaela & Andrew Dowley. We’ve also got the pleasure of bringing a new boat back for John Nickalls – welcome to the fleet John! Or maybe the boat is for David and Daniel? You really need to think about your timing with logistics, how long will it take you to get to the event? Although Google maps is useful, you usually hit traffic so make sure you leave plenty of time. I would recommend arriving a day earlier if you can, although that’s with a Tornado which takes some time to put together. I find if you build the boat the day before you can at least relax knowing you don’t have to rush before the first race the next morning because the boat is ready to go. Looking ahead to Germany, our friends at Google tell us it’s an 11 hour drive down to Lake Constance and we know it involves the M25, a ferry and a very long drive in Europe, probably around Brussels which isn’t great for traffic. TRAILER AND CAR My first thoughts always fall to equipment and prep for a road trip – the car is booked in for a service, the trailer has been checked over and we roughly know how we’re going to carve up the journey over the days depending on progress. Steve is towing the trailer and will leave on Tuesday morning, we will follow on Wednesday morning with the kids onboard (wish us luck). The first measurement day is on Friday so this leaves at least 2 days to get there which is plenty of time and allows for an overnight stop. Another important thing to always remember is a spare wheel for the trailer. If you buy me a beer in the Mamgu bar one night I’ll tell you the story of chasing a trailer wheel down the M3 at 11 o’clock at night. Buy me two and I’ll name the driver of the car. I would always make sure you secure the boat properly, get straps or non stretch ropes and plenty of padding. Make sure you also check your knots and straps every time you stop, it’s surprisingly easy for them to come loose on a long drive. June 2016 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk ACCOMMODATION Where to stay? Our most useful tool in previous years has been Airbnb, we found our accommodation for Ibiza and Perth here. Simply punch in the address of the sailing club and look for nearby places to stay. This year we’ve ventured elsewhere to book because there are no apartments around the area listed on Airbnb. We’ve managed to find an apartment 450 yards from the sailing club this year which is ideal. There’s also a pub less than 100 yards from the door – very important with us being sailing athletes! We’ve always had a few people travelling to the events over the years so we’ve gone for apartments which work well although they are self catering. Sometimes a hotel can be nicer but it’s obviously your choice. B&B’s are fantastic in the UK and are worth searching for, especially for a short stay. Of course, most events also allow camping in a tent – the Commodore (Michaela) isn’t too keen on this option. The key with accommodation is to work it out and book early, especially if you’re going to a big event. I’ve came unstuck previously at a large catamaran event where we had to stay quite far away from the club. Another useful tip is to speak to the locals and check out the club website for recommendations. BOAT AND EQUIPMENT One thing I’ve learnt is to make sure your boat is in the best condition it can be. Failing to prepare is preparing to fail and all that….. We took a boat to Perth which wasn’t in great condition, the World champion commented on the bad condition when it went back into the container to come home. The first thing I did when we got it back to the UK was took it to Graham Eeles, it’s amazing how a polish and small tidy up can make it look like new again. SIMPLE CHECKS Some of you may have seen me spending some time on the boat over the early May bank holiday. Okay, yes it was most of the weekend but we did hit some issues…. Make sure you spend the time, check each rope from end to end, your rigging, your sails, your blocks, shackles etc etc – the list is endless but just take some time to look in detail – it could save you an embarrassment when you get to the event. By typing this I’ve just jinxed us and something is going to break! SPARE PARTS Although it would be ideal you simply can’t pack a spare of everything! You know your boat, you know the bits you replace frequently and you know what could happen. Invest some money and get some spares. If you are short on cash to carry spares then there will always be a Chandlery locally, it might just mean you miss some races – not ideal if you only have one discard for example. Another option is to borrow, there are plenty of people who have the odd spare block hanging around they won’t mind you borrowing for a weekend or so. Along with spare parts make sure you have some tools with you, a small tool box with basic tools can really save your event. With some boats it’s also wise to carry some Gelcoat, filler or epoxy resin – a small dent or crack could be repaired at the event. INSURANCE Check your insurance paperwork – are you covered to sail where you’re going? You might need to pay a little extra if you’re going far away. Is your boat also insured while in a container? It’s worth speaking to your insurance company. PACK YOUR SAILING KIT First of all check you’ve got the essentials but then my advice would be to pack as much as you can (depending on the length of the event). You can never have enough gear, the more warm layers the better because at championships you’re going to be out on the water for lengthy periods of time. Try and find somewhere on your boat where you can store an extra layer, just in case. GOALS Ahead of arrival set your goals for the event. If you sail by yourself then you will know what you want to do and achieve. If you sail with a crew/helm then make sure you talk about it. Maybe it’s not to come last, or maybe you don’t care where you end up as long as you learn something new to bring back to Marconi. AT THE EVENT STUDY THE SAILING INSTRUCTIONS This document you get given is your bible for the event! The organisers have spent a lot of time gathering the info and pulling it together for you – make sure you read it along with your crew/helm. MEASUREMENT If your boat and sails need to be measured then it’s likely the organising committee will want the boat in bits again. Work out what’s needed and where you have to go. You may also need the boats original measurement certificate so make sure you pack that before your trip. TEST THE SAILING AREA June 2016 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Go out ahead of the event (if you can) and go exploring, wind patterns are often similar in the same conditions. If you’re sailing on a lake or pond then work out if there is a big tree that’s going to give you a nasty shift or lack of wind. GET ON THE WATER EARLY If you can push past the other boats it’s worth getting out on the water early. Go out, test the conditions, set the boat up as it should be for those conditions and practice, practice, practice. Think about how you’re going to start, where and what your tactics might be for the race. BUT make sure you also keep an eye on the committee boat incase the warning signal goes. TALK TO OTHERS I attended the 2010 Tornado World Championships to do some work for the organisers of Travemunde Week and the Tornado Class Association. Although frustrating not being on the water it was nice to be in the background driving a rib around the race course – you see things from a different angle. One of the best things I did that week was introduced myself to people and talked to the sailors about their race, why they made decisions and why they have their boat set up in a certain way. I learnt so much! I also ended up filming a Tornado tuning gu ide with the Greek Olympic team which has been viewed on YouTube nearly 8,000 times. ENJOY YOURSELF The most important thing is to go and enjoy yourself, there is no point putting in the effort if you don’t enjoy yourself. If you did have any questions, I would be happy to have a chat about this in some more detail. Sharing is caring! Although I have headlined this piece “ECPR weekend” I think it is worth reminding members that we now run three separate races on Sunday these are: - East Coast Piers Race (cats only) 48 Nm Colne Point Race (cats & fast dinghies with PY with 944 or faster) 27 Nm Bradwell Race (For dinghies with PY 980 or faster) 13 Nm There is also an inshore series of racing on Saturday. Since they had a major input in raising the money the majority went to Cirdan but we still able to donate £500 to Essex Air Ambulance. Each year the Cirdan Sailing Trust send us a file of letters from the underprivileged children and adults who have benefited from the money we have raised. With your help by entering the Race, drinking a pint(s) of Adnams, buying a raffle ticket or a polo shirt we can keep up our donations to our chosen charities. With your help and support it promises to be another great weekend. All we need is for the weather to deliver some wind. Clive Shenton Race Chairman July 2016 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Rubicon (8 metre yacht) from Stansgate to Dunkirk – June 13 through 20, 2016 Skipper: John Walker (JW) Crew: Richard D Wood-Kneller (RDWK) DAY ONE SUNDAY 13 JUNE We loaded our belongings at the Marconi Sailing Club, Stansgate at 16.00 hours and set off for a one hour sail down the River Blackwater to Bradwell Marina. We stayed there overnight and checked all the rigging and chart courses for the following day. DAY TWO MONDAY 14 JUNE We left Bradwell at 05.30 hours and set sail due East for the Eagle at the entrance to the Spitway. We passed South West through this narrow gap in the sandbanks and then headed due east again for Barrow Number 2. We passed over the Sunk Sand sandbank and continued South West to Foulger’s Gap. This entailed sailing through one of the multitude of Wind Farms in the Thames Estuary. We met all our Waypoints without difficulty up to Long Sand Inner at the entrance to the gap, but instead of Long Sand Outer we found Long Sand Middle. Our chart was a few years old, but this was one of only a couple of changes we encountered. From there we had a long run to North Foreland. A couple of hours later found us in Ramsgate Harbour at 13.30 hours. We had planned the tidal assistance carefully and this paid dividends. Our arrival at Ramsgate produced the first “incident” of our cruise. RDWK went to step down from Rubicon to make her fast at our pontoon; in doing so he looked down and his spectacles fell into the harbour and slowly disappeared from view. As these had cost over £500 a short time ago he was upset! A fellow seaman came over to enquire about the fuss and immediately suggested that we contact Terry Vickers, the local diving instructor. He quoted £175 and RDWK agreed. After a short while below at 8 metres in total darkness Terry found the glasses and handed them over to a much relieved RDWK. Terry reported that he had all but given up when his hand touched something and thus the day was saved. DAY THREE TUESDAY 15 JUNE We left Ramsgate at 11.00 hours with overcast skies and a wind forecast of force 5 gusting 6. Almost immediately we had doubts about continuing, but having started on the main reason for our cruise we were reluctant to turn back. We followed our SatNav course on the screen as there are no buoys between Ramsgate and Gravelines to act as waypoints. For a few hours the seas were large and the wind force six as forecast, but Rubicon seemed comfortable even if were not. About midway across the wind increased and at times was probably force 6 gusting 7 and this made life really uncomfortable. RDWK attached his lifeline to the boat, but the skipper’s was below and it was now impossible to leave the cockpit. We rigged a rope to act as his line and we both felt safer. We had been warned about heavy traffic in the shipping lanes, but saw only half a dozen ships and none of them threatened our progress. Needless to say, we did not see any other yachts from start to finish. By now the waves were considerably bigger than forecast and seemed to come from several angles making the helm hard to manage and it was difficult to keep our course. At one point Rubicon broached to and this was by far the most exciting moment of the whole journey. If we were alert before we were doubly so thereafter. To say we were concerned would be true, but Rubicon shewed her true worth then and throughout. She quickly lifted her skirts and righted herself much to our relief and we continued at a good pace on our way. Some while later the wind eased a little and this gave us a much needed respite and easier sailing. It was still too rough to leave the cockpit and so we had nothing to drink or eat throughout the crossing. It also meant certain other functions were more difficult than normal and left us with some amusing images of our epic voyage! JW found it less amusing, but that is another story. We had hoped the better weather would last until we reached Gravelines, but it was not to be and the last part of the journey was again hard work demanding 100% concentration at all times and no small amount of physical application as well. Changing helm was a particularly difficult operation. After about eight hours sailing the Skipper noticed that our SatNav was indicating a course that led us several miles up the coast and into Belgium instead of Gravelines in France. We could not alter the settings because of the weather and so abandoned it. As we could see the land in the far distance we decided to sail due south until we were near enough to the coast to locate our position. RDWK called the French Coast Guard on channel 16 and asked for our position. They replied that we were due north of Dunkirk and should call the latter on channel 9. We attempted this, but found that the radio would not stay on any station except channel 16. The coast guard than told us to call Dunkirk on channel 16, but there was no reply. In order to alert them we made a PAN PAN PAN call and at last they responded. Before they offered any advice they pointed out that there were dangerous shoals between us and the port and that they would only continue if we accepted full responsibility should we go aground. As we only draw just over a metre the Skipper decided to proceed. Finally, we spotted the harbour entry lights, but they were reversed, i.e. red was where green should have been and vice versa. Later, we found that this is due to the fact that entry to Dunkirk is along a coastal channel and not directly from the North. After some nine hours at sea we entered the marina in Dunkirk and tied up at the fuel pontoon for the night. DAY FOUR WEDNESDAY 16 JUNE Samuel awoke us at 09.00 hours and politely asked us to move as others wish to refuel. We did so and spotted numerous small boats flying the red duster. It transpired that a $150 million film was being made about Operation Dynamo and the “Little Ships” that transported tens of thousands of allied troops off the beach at Dunkirk in 1940 to avoid capture by the Germans. We spent the day sightseeing in Dunkirk and generally recuperating from our bruising battle with the waves the day before. July 2016 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk DAY FIVE THURSDAY 17 JUNE We cleaned up the boat and studied the operation of the SatNav until we mastered its somewhat complicated menu system. After various discussions with Little Ship Captains and local yachtsmen we decided on our course back to Ramsgate and entered it into SatNav. We also listed the headings, waypoints and timings on paper in case of any further machine difficulties. Most importantly we checked and found a loose wire on the radio which was easily fixed and meant we had no further radio problems. We also charged and tested our back-up radio. In the afternoon we hired a car to explore Gravelines and Calais. We missed the turning on the way home and only just returned the car in time. The weather forecast for Friday was good and we decided to head back to Blighty on the morrow, as did most of the Little Ships. DAY SIX FRIDAY 18 JUNE We were up early to refuel and fill up with water. Having made sure we had food and water easily accessible and the chart in the cockpit, we set off for home at 10.00 hours. The tide was against us as we sailed towards Gravelines and we were concerned that this might affect our timing later in the day. About two miles short of Gravelines we swung away from land and headed back across the Channel which had given us such a rough ride coming over. On this day the weather was perfect and it all seemed so easy. The only real risk was sunburn and we applied lotion early to avoid any problems. The equipment worked faultlessly and we only had to take avoiding action twice to give the big ships crossing in front of us a wide berth. We hit all our waypoints exactly on schedule and the passage was so calm the crew was able to sleep below for a couple of hours well-earned rest. Great care was taken as we moored in the harbour to avoid losing any spectacles and we celebrated the completion of our crossing with a good meal in town. DAY SEVEN SATURDAY 19 JUNE The weather forecast was bad and we decided to explore Broadstairs before making our way home on Sunday. In the evening we set up the SatNav and plotted our course for home. The engine was checked, minor repairs effected, the oil topped up and food prepared for the last leg. DAY EIGHT SUNDAY 20 JUNE The weather forecast was good and we set off at 11.00 hours. Again we suffered a small adverse tide to begin with, but benefitted later from a strong assist for the last leg home. We found all the waypoints without trouble except for one that was concealed by a wind turbine in one of the many wind farms that litter the Estuary now. It had taken us nine hours to reach Ramsgate from Bradwell on day two and we did as well on our last day, reaching the Marconi Sailing Club at Stansgate after ten hours. After unloading we shook hands on a mission accomplished and headed for home.
