Keith White RACE ee » East Coast Piers Race sponsored by Zhik 67 boats made their way to Marconi Sailing Club for the annual East Coast Piers Race over the weekend of the 9th and 10th July. The East Coast Piers Race is a long distance race weekend for fast dinghies and catamarans raising money for The Cirdan Trust and Essex Air Ambulance. East Coast Piers Race 2016With free camping available from Friday through to Monday many competitors arrived on Friday to get their boats rigged. After morning registration and a good breakfast on Saturday there was a midday briefing for a 1pm start with windy conditions forecast for the afternoon of racing where the race officer was hoping to get two races in. A course was set which took the sailors up and down the River Blackwater to give them a healthy warm up for Sunday. It was a breezy start to the weekend with a few capsizes in the first race, mainly around the windward mark in the larger chop. Many of the competitors thought it would be best to sit out the second race and prepare for Sunday. August & September 2016 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk At 6pm on Saturday the official race briefing was held in the marquee, with Adnams as a race sponsor it was rude not to have a beer in your hand during the briefing. As soon as the briefing finished the BBQ was ready and the sailors and their guests tucked in! After the BBQ the bar was continuing to sell beer where the visitors and Marconi members were making their donation to charity by drinking. Later in the evening a band came on and entertained everyone until very late. As per usual, and not at the request of the usual person, the camp site was woken at 6am by the sound of Sweet Caroline and Neil Diamond through the PA system. A firm favourite with many of the competitors, or maybe not but it’s becoming tradition. With the first race start scheduled for 8am an early start was unfortunately needed to match the tides. The East Coast Piers Race which takes sailors 48 miles to Walton and back was the first to start at 8am. Due to the wind forecast and possible force 7 gusts it was decided on Saturday that the course would be shortened to Clacton, making the race around 38 miles. The Colne Point Race (27 miles) started at 8.15am and then the Bradwell Race (13 miles) for fast dinghies at 8.30am. In the full ECPR race it was the Dinghy Rope Tornado which had the best start flying off the line with the Marconi Commodore at the helm. As the fleet reached Thirslet Spit they were over taken by John Gimson and Pete Jary sailing the big pink Nacra 20 Carbon. Closely behind were the Hurricane and Windrush Tornado followed by a fleet of F18’s. Through the Bradwell gate and out towards Colne Point the wind was building and the waves were getting bigger making a 2 sail reach very tricky! It was at this point that the foiling Nacra F20 overtook the Tornado and started to catch up the non foiling Nacra 20 Carbon. The two Nacra 20’s then started to pull away through the Colne Point gate and up towards Clacton pier which was the turning point. All the way back from Clacton it was a long beat with only 12 tacks made along a distance of 19 miles. As the ECPR fleet were heading back from Clacton they came across the Colne Point race boats which were going around the Colne Point marker and heading for home. This meant the fleets were arriving back in mass at Marconi after a long beat back. First back in the Colne Point Race were Kevin Dowley and Tom Brooks from Marconi sailing a Tornado. First back in the ECPR in a time of just over two hours were John Gimson and Pete Jary who took the line honours trophy. Due to the quick race the prize giving was held at 1.15pm, much earlier than usual meaning the sailors could head off home early. First up was the raffle where our race sponsors had donated some fantastic prizes. William Harrison was the lucky guy who took home the top prize of £750 worth of Zhik sailing gear. Results Saturday Cat Series Winners – Kevin Dutch and David Oakley – Tornado Saturday Dinghy Series Winner – Kyle Stoneham – Moth ECPR Winners – John Gimson and Pete Jary – Nacra 20 Carbon Colne Point Cat Winners – Olly Harris and Ben Harris – Spitfire Colne Point Dinghy Winners – Richard Smith and Elenor Smith – RS800 Bradwell Race Winner – David Chamberlin – Laser Vortex Full results can be seen on the ECPR website – www.eastcoastpiersrace.com It’s important to note that although this is a long distance event there are yachts anchored at every mile ready to give assistance along with a fleet of ribs in between them in key areas of the course. Marconi also ensure that essential safety gear is carried on each boat. A massive thank you to our sponsors for the weekend Zhik, Adnams, Dinghy Rope, GP Sails, Funky Monkey Boat Names, Yachts and Yachting and The Moment Images. August & September 2016 Navigans 3

Clive Shenton Race Chairman Fleet News Cruiser Fleet Well it’s been a busy month, 22 club members set out to drink the Ionian dry on 9 boats. The two weeks were full of amusing incidents ranging from watching a 60ft Belgian boat trying to anchor in 25m of water only to see his chain disappear in to the depths as the bitter end was not tied on and then asking a club member to free dive to collect it, to the same member throwing bread at a large turtle. I don’t know what turtles eat but it’s not bread. A diary can be found later in this report and also with pictures on the club web site. We also had our cruise to Tollesbury with 5 boats going into the marina and 21 sitting down for a meal in the clubhouse. This was organised by Cheryl Cutmore. The weekend after, the ECPR race had a large number of cruisers acting as mother boats. Thank you all. At the time of writing, the Heybridge cruise and bbq is in a few days with 14 boats booked in. Looking ahead, we have the Ipswich cruise on 27/28/29 of August which has been organised by Bob Godbold and the list is now on the club notice board. As I said at the last cruiser AGM, both myself and my deputy intend to stand down at the end of this year so two volunteers with lots of new ideas are needed. If anyone wants to know what it involves, please feel free to talk to me. Roger Camp Cruiser Fleet Captain BROWN CUP MCGREGOR WINS BROWN CUP. BLUE MOON & MONKEY BUSINESS 2ND & 3RD IN THRILLING IRC RACE. 19 cruisers passed the club on Saturday lunchtime, in what turned out to be a thrilling and close Brown Cup race between the Marconi representatives. Crazy Suzy and Monkey Business were at the head of the fleet with Blue Moon and McGregor 3 in hot pursuit. Sailing the longest course on the card, Ned Kelly had a close boat race towards the back of the fleet, whilst Caroline swapped positions throughout. After the turn at Wallet No3, Crazy Suzy took the lead all the way home on the windward leg, whilst McGregor 3 got ahead of all the other IRC boats on the water. Blue moon remained close on her transom, always close enough to be ahead of her on corrected time and approaching Colne Bar the team on Blue Moon looked as if they might have overhauled series leader, Absolution. Monkey Business then started her charge back up the Blackwater in an attempt to claw back her time, and by the time she had rounded No12 off Bradwell she had passed, Behave and McGregor. Absolution had got back into the groove on the homeward leg and was now 2nd on the water behind Crazy Suzy, it was now all about, how much time Monkey Business might get ahead of McGregor and Blue Moon whilst Triton, not far behind, would also have a say in the final positions of this exciting IRC race. Absolution (Eric Reynold – Maylandsea) finished 1st on corrected time after more than 6.5 hours of racing. Blue Moon (Richard Roberts – MSC) had a super race in 2nd place, beating Monkey Business (Dave Onyons – MSC) by 1:47 mins who were 3rd. Triton (Peter Copsey – BSC) was just 62 secs back in 4th place whilst McGregor 3 (Steve Purdue) was a further 70 secs behind. All 7 IRC rated boats finished within 20 minutes of each other on the water, and on corrected time, the first 5 boats were separated by just 7:48 mins Using the BJRC local handicaps on which all 19 boats in the fleet are scored, Steve Purdue and Monica Wolff racing McGregor for just the 3rd time, came out on top and are this years winners of the MLSC Brown Cup. The full results and report can be found here on the BJRC website. August & September 2016 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk WOOZLE HUNTER WITHIN REACH OF EAORA CHAMPIONSHIP Woozle Hunter finished 2nd in the EAORA Harwich to Ramsgate race last weekend, in a light wind passage race that saw many competitors, resorting to motor and a d.n.f. In typical ‘never say die’ attitude, Ian & Laura Ivermee and their crew which included Lydia Coffey (Ned Kelly Skipper), completed the race in 12.5 hours, in company with much higher rated boats, and just missed out on first place by 3 minutes on corrected time from Eclipse sailing out of the Haven Ports YC. With just 2 races left in the EAORA series, Woozle Hunter sits on top of the leader board and looks firm favourite to take the series win from Ape-X, another HPYC boat, 3rd in the race to Ramsgate, who needs to win both remaining races. It’s been a super series so far for the Woozles, and with 5 wins in a 7 to count series, there’s every possibility of them notching up a perfect score. Go Woozles! NED KELLY – 1ST MARCONI BOAT AND 6TH OVERALL – BJRC RACE 6 Lydia Coffey and her crew of new members were rewarded for their efforts this season by finishing as 1st Marconi boat, in 6th place overall in BJRC race 6 last Saturday. Ned Kelly, regularly seen training on none race weekends, have gradually moved up towards the fleet as the crews skills and teamwork have developed throughout the season, and on Saturday they made their mark. The teams day of success began by beating both McGregor 3 (Steve Purdue) and Caroline (Andy Ellis) to the first mark off Tollesbury, (WMYC No3) after kedging right on the start line. Then as the breeze returned on the passage out into the estuary, Ned Kelly was well ahead of similarly handicapped boats. John Littlewoods crew on Crazy Suzy were once again leading the fleet on both passes of North Eagle, whilst Richard Roberts on Blue Moon chased down IRC rivals Evolution (Maylandsea), who were themselves trying to shake off Triton (Blackwater). On the long return to the Tollesbury mark the lighter asymmetric boats of the local handicap class were seen to be doing battle among the IRC class. ‘It’s a pity that these boats didn’t have an IRC rating as seeing them in the result sheet would have made for interesting reading’, one Marconi member commented. Once past Bradwell, Crazy Suzy at the head of the fleet was the first to suffer the failing breeze. Luckily the tide pushed the fleet back towards the line, but off Marconi many of the leading pack of boats became tightly bunched as they tried to make the line at Osea. Only 30 minutes covered the 20 boat fleet after 6.5 hours of racing and in the local handicap result the Maldon YC Salver was won by Rod Martin on Moondance a First 21.7 from Harlow BSC. In the IRC class Triton (Peter Copsey BSC) came first, with Blue Moon (Richard Roberts) in 2nd ahead of Absolution (Eric Reynolds MBSC) But the honours of being 1st Marconi boat in the local handicap result went to Ned Kelly. Congratulations guys, and very well done! The Marconi cruiser race fleet will next race the Harwich passage race weekend on 13-14th August. Anyone interested in getting involved in cruiser racing should contact Peter Ward. There are team places available on a number of our boats. Peter Ward IONIAN ODYSSEY 2016 Holiday booked through Sailing Holidays that provided us with a very useful and comprehensive marina guide including excellent photographs of the majority of the marinas in the whole region. An enormous thanks to Jackie and Roger Camp for organising the most exceptional Summer Cruise. What an amazing fortnight. The scenery, the sailing, the weather, the food, the drink, the company. And of course an extra large portion of laughter. I can’t think of any way of improving it. Here is my diary style record of our two week holiday in Greece, starting in the Northern Ionian sailing to the Southern Ionian and back stopping at many wonderful places along the way. The Fleet: August & September 2016 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk KALAMAS (Lead Boat) Skipper: Kit, Hostie: Ellen, Engineer: Richard CORDELIA: Roger & Jackie Camp ISIS: Steve & Margaret Golding, Robin & Diane Good KALLONI: Derek & Hilary Gardner KASTRAKI: Sue & Peter Arnold MAZIA: Peter & Sue Booth NATALIA: Richard & Margaret Lee NATASSA: Roy & Margaret Bellord PELEKAS: Pete & Jan Reay, Mike & Cheryl Cutmore VANESSA: Peter & Sandra Clayton Plataria Our first taste of the Ionian. A beautiful bay skirted by mountains with a lovely shingle beach with restaurants spilling out onto it. We enjoyed our first meal at Olga’s on the marina. One of the local cats decided to pee through the pergola roof onto Jan causing much mirth and an interesting aroma. It was great to all be together if the restaurant had a problem with dealing with the volume of dinners ordered. We stayed another day in Plataria due to strong winds and rain in the morning. We gathered for a quiz after lunch then went out for a sail round the bay in the afternoon. We had a lovely dinner on the beach. It was q uite difficult sitting on chairs on the shingle beach and there was a dominos effect moment when Mike Cutmore toppled over and he and Cheryl tipped off their chairs. Was the wine to blame?! A great place to watch the sun go down and see the stunning sunset. Gaios Fabulous sail over. Gaios has lots of restaurants which early in the evening started to release the ever tempting smell of bbqed meat and many different shops selling a wide variety of goods. Somewhere that might be worth staying for another day. We had dinner at Genesis overlooking the the bay. Enormously pretty. All sorts of different craft moored against the long winding harbour wall with a pretty little beach tucked round the corner that was ideal for a cooling swim. Spartatahori Early start and big swell to Lefkas Canal where we were able to stop for lunch moored against the quayside before going through the canal and on to Spartatahori, Meganisi, Steve and Gerry’s Quay. – totally beautiful spot. Dinners were usually dip style starters, grilled cheese or stuffed vegetables. Fresh fish, squid and mussles could be had as well as popular favourites such as mousaka, kebabs and spicy meat balls. Spartahori was surrounded by stunning pine covered hills. We swam off the boat after mooring up and all got together for a joint meal. Walk up to cliff top in the morning before leaving to see view of the whole Ionian. Really beautiful (but isn’t it all!) Kalamos Georges restaurant – dinner on the beach with stunning backdrop of the distant misty mountains. Great sail down alongside Richard and Margaret. Did not find the bay with the church that was recommended for lunch stop. Lunch for us was usually local produce such as Feta cheese, olives, enormous fresh ripe sweet tomatoes , stuffed vine leaves with crusty freshly baked bread dipped in olive oil. A naked girl on the beach rather startled Richard when he swam ashore. He believes she may have had an accident with the strimmer. We swam off the boat and snorkelled round rocks. Later we all met in the local cocktail bar for pre dinner drinks. Vathi On our way to Big Vathi on Ithaka we raced to One House Bay. Had our usual lunch, snorkelled and fed fish. Woke to still flat calm and immense heat! Wide populated bay. Rafted on quay. Delish yoghurt with honey and fruit for breakfast. Some took 20 minute walk into village. It was way too hot so we made off and welcomed the cooling sea breeze. KionI Made off early for Kioni. Lunch stop then early in to port to find good spot and avoid mooring away from the quay and using tenders. Had to moor out with stern lines which made an interesting muddle to negotiate in the tender to get on and off. Punch party on the quay. Really good dinner at Three Windmills right by the beach. Had enormous fun attempting to get back on board the boats after a wine or two. Lots of shrieks of laughter from Sue Arnold and Sue Booth finding keeping dry impossible. Lunch stop in a pretty little bay just before Frikis. Moored up and got in the water for a swim and snorkel. As we entered the bay a young woman was waving at us. To our surprise the police turned up and moved us on due to mooring too close to the beach and being a danger to swimmers. It would appear the waving young woman was telling us to go away and called the police!!! Totally mad!! We moved onto an adorable little bay that was perfect. Decided to stay another day in Kioni to chill. All the fleet got spaces along the quay. Sampled the yoghurt and fruit and walnut for breakfast. A new take on delicious! All swam off the quay from steps down the rocks. Enormous racing yacht came into the bay and anchored but neglected to secure the anchor and the whole lot fell to the sea bed! Peter Clayton, in swimming at the time was asked if he could dive down for it. Naturally de didn’t! All met up for pre dinner drinks at Derek and Hillary’s boat. All had dinner at Avra. Lots of feline friends came to share with us! The wind got up and blew strongly all night. And kept blowing the following day. August & September 2016 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Sivota was the next stop. Sailing holiday base. Lots of Tavernas and shops fringed by wooded mountains. Small beach for swimming. Could buzz over the harbour in tender. Lunch swim in bay by Frikes avoiding nutty sunbathers. Preveza Stopped at Goat Bay for a swim. Went through Lefkas Canal 4pm opening. Wind speed had gathered. Great sail up to Preveza on foresail only. Moored on the quay. Very hot. Good town with lots of tavernas and shops. Great meal. Enormous mullet – delicious cool spot outside the restaurant and inexpensive. Busy night. Sue Arnold’s anchor was not holding and had to be relaid. Next boat to us decided to run engine at 11pm! Hot night had to spend time in the cockpit cooling off. Parga Early start for Parga. Possible stop at Two rocks bay. The bay was stunning. We swam snorkelled and had lunch. We were moored grounded on the beach at Parga and had fun on the paddle board. We caught the ferryboat into town. Large bustling town with Venetian fort on the hilltop. The majority of us went up for dinner in a restaurant by the fort with spectacular views over the bay. Bit of a challenge getting off the boats and shopping in the morning. Stopped at Emerald Bay for lunch on the way to Mongonisi. The bay seemed deserted then we were joined by a pleasure boat overflowing with people. The bay was transformed from a tranquil paradise to the local lido! Had a great evening in Mongonisi Greek dancing which started with a demonstration given by the locals after which we were all pulled up to have a go ourself. Much to all the ladies delight the local lad performed stripped to the waste exposing a gorgeous muscular torso that it would gave been rude not to have gazed at. Sivoter Muertos We hugged the coast of Mongonisi then took a 45 degree course to SM which enabled a sail over. There being no opportunity to stop in a bay to lunch and swim we had our lunch whilst under sail. This seemed rather decedent and definitely rather clever! We all assembled for a briefing ashore and Jan got a tart with candles for Ellen our hostess who was 29 that day. The girls donned wacky glasses and we were given ‘viagera’ shots by the bar owner. A few jokes were exchanged. We had dinner at George’s which was superb. A few shops to wander round and daft hats to try on. Plataria Dropped off for a swim after a yoghurt honey and fruit breakfast. Nice little beach just before Plataria then into Plataria stern to by Olga’s. The last evening of the most amazing holiday we all got together for dinner on the beach. There was some concern as it had rained earlier but the skies had cleared and we decided to take a chance. Was the most perfect evening. Food was fabulous. The restaurant put out oil filled torches to light the table then we dined and watched the most wonderful display of the day turning to night and the sun slowly sinking into the sea creating the most wonderful orange glow. Although this works OK, after many years sailing a Solo with a combined centre ratchet block and swivel cleat I would prefer this hardware set up. Is this possible, can available parts be used with the 4 screw holes that exist in the Pico hull? Recognise that this would probably infringe class rules - not a worry. Would much appreciate comments/advice on this subject please to A couple of images that may help: Tim Sweet Chernobyl Children On The Water At MSC As in the previous two years, MSC once again played host on Tuesday 5th July to twelve special youngsters from Ukraine, giving them an unforgettable lifetime experience, which for most of them was their first time on the sea. The children: six boys and six girls aged between 8 and 13, are on a one-month recuperative holiday organised by the South Essex branch of the Chernobyl Children’s Lifeline charity. They have all grown up near the ill-fated Chernobyl nuclear power plant, where local communities continue to be affected by health problems thirty years after the nuclear disaster. The children visiting are being treated at home for a range of health issues, and their time in England enables them to enjoy uncontaminated food and fresh air, whilst experiencing wonderful activities thanks to the generosity of organisations such as Marconi Sailing Club. Our young cadets (and slightly older volunteers) did a fantastic job of entertaining their visitors with a warm welcome which was reflected in the gradually emerging sunshine. The day started with a trip up the river on Top Cat, Jack B and the RIBs past Mundon Point to hang out with curious seals popping up for a peek at these young visitors from afar, and everyone enjoyed an exciting ride back for lunch… all against the backdrop of the beautiful Essex coastal landscape so utterly different from their home hundreds of miles from the coast in Ukraine. Not all could be persuaded to taste the salty water! The afternoon was spent in exciting sailing conditions in the club’s smaller dinghies, all the children were soaked but the big grins remained and they even tried their hand at crabbing. The youngsters, still excited by their adventure on the high seas, then treated the Marconi volunteers to a lovely rendition of a Ukrainian folk song as a thank you. They will go home refreshed, healthier, and with memories to last a lifetime. Thanks to all those that volunteered their time, energy and boats, and for giving our visitors such a great day. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Club Notices Club Secretary SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITY ON THE COAST I recently received the following request from PS Ben Felton who is a sergeant at Maldon. Ben is also a yachtsman who has an interest in local sailing clubs and marinas. Dear all, Sorry I have not been in contact for a while. It has been very busy so far this summer. Luckily I haven't had any intelligence to share with you all which I guess is a good thing. I am emailing today to ask for your continued vigilance around suspicious vessel or persons. In this time of heightened threat it is vital you are the eyes and ears of the coast. You know your area better than anyone. You know what looks out of place. Please don't hesitate to report anything suspicious to me or the marine unit, no matter how small. Today we had information regarding a yacht entering Tollesbury at night and the crew acting suspiciously. Luckily after checks it turned out to be a false alarm and the crew were in order. But that is exactly the sort of information we need. I would rather every call turns out to be a legitimate yacht rather than miss that one vital piece of information so please keep it coming. You can visit the Project Kraken website for more information. Please use my email or contact the Essex Police Marine Unit via the 101 non-emergency phone number. If you believe it is an emergency please dial 999 and let the call taker assess the information and respond accordingly. Thank you for your support. I hope you are all having a busy and profitable season. Regards, PS 74973 Felton B1 Shift LPT Maldon Police Station BenjaminFelton@essex.pnn.police.uk 101 x412120 ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING – SUNDAY 4TH DECEMBER 2016 Elsewhere in this issue of Navigans you will find the formal notification of the AGM. Roger Camp Cruiser Fleet Captain y = lof etn” Sprint 15 TEAM MARCONI AT THE SPRINT 15 NATIONALS! The Sprint 15 Nationals were held over the August Bank Holiday weekend. Kevin Kirby, Pete Richardson, Jon Pearse, David Ball and myself - with support crew of Liz Jackson and Fenella Miler made the journey up to Pwllheli in North Wales - which is a beautiful sailing location with sandy beaches and the back drop of Snowdonia. And, defying all known precedent, we had dry and warm weather and plenty of sun across the three days! We found ourselves sharing the boat park (not as big as we are spoilt with at home!) with 120 RS Teras, their sailors, parents, RIBS etc So it was a bit cosy for the 40 Sprint 15s but we all fitted in somehow. Racing: Racing format was a practice lap followed by two races on Sunday, three races on Monday and two races on Tuesday - all sailing back to back out in the bay. Sunday was fairly breezy with a solid force 4 and some stronger gusts blowing through. Monday dawned with no wind so the racing was postponed until the afternoon when a light but sailable wind filled in. The thr ee races were mentally taxing as it required a lot of concentration to try and find the best air and get ahead of the other boats. Tuesday had a lovely force 3 - 4 breeze with some larger waves that Pwllheli is famous for from previous events! A cracking two races saw strong placings from all Marconi boats. With all 7 races sailed, there are two discards so the best 5 results counted. Results: The National Championships were won very convincingly by father and daughter team Sean and Sophie McKenna (aged 8) from Shanklin, IoW - the first time since 1987 that a two up boat has won the Nationals! The agenda and resolutions for the 2016 AGM and the minutes from the 2015 AGM will be sent to members in a separate mailing; as will the Year End Accounts. This mailing will be distributed in the same way as Navigans. Please bring these documents and your membership card with you to the AGM. SELLING BOATS AT STANSGATE If you sell your boat to a non-member you remain responsible for it until the boat leaves site or the purchaser becomes a member of the Club. A member’s responsibility does not just end when the deal is done (bylaws 3.1.4 and 3.1.4.1 refer). Members’ gate cards are personal and must not be loaned to others; for example to a non-member who may want to gain access to work on the boat that they have just bought. If a non-member has bought a boat on site and wishes it to remain at Stansgate for a relatively short time they may apply to the membership secretary for Short Term membership. They will be granted Short Term membership for a length of time and for a fee which will be agreed in advance. If a non-member buys a boat at Stansgate and wishes to keep it at the club permanently they may apply for membership by completing and submitting a membership form. Copies of the form are kept in the clubhouse and are also available on the MSC website. If they have purchased a cruiser they should speak to the moorings secretary. Buying a cruiser from a member does not automatically mean that a mooring will be immediately available. There is sometimes a waiting list especially for deep water moorings. If they have purchased a dinghy or catamaran they should agree a dinghy or catamaran park space with the membership secretary and the appropriate boat park co-ordinator. All dinghy and catamaran park spaces are allocated to particular boats and members. It is essential that all information is kept up to date when boats change hands. Contact details for all club officials will be found in the yearbook or on clubhouse notice boards. OPERATION OF CLUB BOATS AND EQUIPMENT For information for new members and a reminder to older hands, there are detailed codes of practice and instructions for most activities at Stansgate from procedures for a flood alert to the operation of machinery. It is essential for the efficient and safe operation of club boats and equipment that users are familiar with the guidance. If you have a support boat duty, do read the guidance notes. Even if you have driven or crewed on support boats before it is worth reading the latest version of the relevant notes; they do get updated from time to time. Winches, tractors, mast derrick and boat hoists also have their own codes of practice and user guides which are regularly updated. Please read them. Their relevance to the operators of the equipment is obvious but it is also useful for boat owners to be familiar with the codes of practice. You will have a better understanding of the operation of the equipment, which is satisfying in itself, but also appreciate the operators’ point of view and the codes of practice under which they work to ensure the safety of all concerned. A paper copy of the codes of practice and user guides is kept in the upstairs lounge in the clubhouse but you can also familiarise yourself with them at your leisure in the members section of the MSC website. Go to Members Area/Document Library. The password for the Members Area will be found on Page 2 of the 2016 yearbook A document index may be found in document MSCP01. Ray Ball Company Secretary secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk Helm of the Year This annual sailing event sees the “winningest” sailor from each of the cat/dinghy fleets based on the Spring and Summer points series do battle for the coveted title of Helm of the Year. In recent years, this has also included a representative from the cruiser fleet. The event is completed in a one design class which is not regularly sailed by any of the competitors – as such, the “class of choice” for several years has been the Pico. The event was scheduled for Saturday 17th September but competitors arrived to a very blustery morning. The forecast was for the wind to decrease, so the Race Officer, Dave Clarke, very sensibly posptoned to the afternoon. However, with boats and competitors rigged and ready for a 1pm start,, it became clear that the conditions had not subdued at all. Eventually, it was decided to postpone racing until the following morning, ahead of Barts Bash. Sunday morning dawned with much lighter breezes and the fleet hit the water at 10am to give enough time to run the series before Barts Bash in the afternoon – plus one of the competitors had a county level football match he needed to compete in the afternoon. The Race Officer laid on five races – starting from the pontoon – with each competitor swapping boats in between races to ensure the playing field was as level as possible. The younger competitors Jack Collis (Cruisers) and Jason Clarke (Cadets) made an early impression scoring 1, 2 in the first race followed by consistently good positions in the remaining four races. The monohull sailors Bryan Spencer (Solo Fleet) and Rob Bard (Handicap monohull fleet) also seemed pretty comfortable in the Pico – whilst arguably the cat sailors (Steve Thomas, Medium Cats, Jenny Ball, Sprint 15s and Steve Glynn, Fast Cats) had a bit of a disadvantage sailing very small monohulls in light winds. But we were all particularly impressed when Steve Glynn (Fast Cats) not only capsized in Race 2 but also managed to go turtle! The racing was very closely fought with short races, light winds and a relatively strong tide – and the downwind leg against the tide from the penultimate mark to the finish line proving to be very tactical. After an extremely close series, the top two competitors – Jack Collis (Cruisers) and Jenny Ball (Sprint 15) had identical race results meaning that it literally came down to the results for the last race. A coming together on the start line between Jack Collis and Steve Glynn, allowed Jenny, Jason and Rob to get ahead of the fleet and, as a result, the final race and, the overall series went to the Sprint 15s by the skin of their teeth. As always, a great event! Many thanks to members who lent their boats – (David Ball, Dave Russell, Dave Clarke, Graham Cross, Sam Flaherty), to all the Support Boat crew and to Dave Clarke and Rory Thomas as RO and Assistant RO for running the event so efficiently. What advice would you give to anyone else considering taking part in their first traveller event? All in all a brilliant weekend. I came away much more confident. I had loads of encouragement from everyone and plenty of tips as well. 7. Any other comments? I would just like to thank everyone from my club who helped me get to the event and the rest of the Sprint fleet I meet at Grafham for making me welcome. Also Gafham Sailing Club for a great event. See you all again on the water soon. Andy Perks. JASON CLARKE (AGE 14) 1. How long have you had you Sprint 15? I do not own a Sprint - I borrowed one from someone at Marconi. 2. How much Racing have you done in you Sprint 15? I have done very limited amount of racing in a Sprint 15 3. What encouraged you to take part at Grafham as you first event? I was encouraged by my dad owning a Sprint 15 and I had just started to look at what options there were for boats to sail after moving out of old boat. Also there is a reasonable sized fleet that is very helpful at our club. They found me a boat I could borrow to do some club racing and also take to Grafham. 4. What were the highlights of the event from your perspective? My highlight was that wherever in the fleet I was there was always some that I could race Photo credit – Sara Townshend against. Ray Ball Company Secretary secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk Marconi Sea Wall Challenge and Winter Walks Following the news of a Marconi members breast cancer diagnosis some of us ladies came up with the idea for a sponsored walk for breast cancer charities. Our first idea was for a group of us to do the Moon Walk in London next May but felt this was a challenge too far for some and administration for a group was difficult to organise. We would therefore like to organise a walk of approximately 14-15 miles from Maldon to the club along the sea wall on 27th May 2017 (the Saturday of the 2nd May Bank holiday). I am also looking for non-walking volunteers with cars to act as taxi’s to drop people off at the start point and pick up stragglers along the way if needed, but also to run a registration process on the day. In preparation for the big walk I am hoping to arrange some monthly Winter Walks on a Sunday and would like to know who would be interested in these as well. I think it will be a nice way of keeping fit over the winter and keeping in touch with our sailing club friends. Hopefully we will be able to do circular walks along the shores of the Blackwater with a Pub or refreshments at the end. I am aiming for the first walk to be Sunday 27th November, meeting at Bradwell Marina car park at 10am to leave by 10.30. Club Notices Commodores Notes 2016 COMMODORE’S REPORT TO THE AGM Michaela Dowley 4th December 2016 Good morning and welcome all to the 2016 Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting. This report will comment on the main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season. As usual I will award a few coveted prizes and hope to enlighten you on our plans for the year ahead. Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board of Directors, and for the previous year has comprised these six people: Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing Graham Cross - Rear Commodore for events Sue Shenton - Treasurer Myself, Michaela Dowley - as commodore I am managing director and chair Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of the administrative burden of the Club. I can report that the Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like to extend thanks to all those who take the time to serve on the main and various sub committees. Usually I would move straight onto the main business of the Board over the past year, however I would like to pause for a moment to acknowledge the people here at the front with me today. Many of you know that I have been lucky enough to have two children over the past couple of years and although they are a joy it has also been hard work. I want to thank the rest of the Board for their support in allowing me to continue as Commodore during this rather hectic time and ensuring the club has operated as usual. It must be said that shouldering responsibility for a Club of this size is no small task and we each have commitments outside the club, whether it’s a full time job or family. I would like to give you an idea of what these people do; Murray is our go to man for everything around the site and probably drives more miles on the club tractor than in his own car. Peter leads on administering all things mooring related, health and safety and still finds time to tutor our smallest cadets during cadet week. Pat looks after all things sailing, is our power boat instructor having qualified 32 new rib drivers since the inception of our training centre, he’s carried out at least 21 support boat duties this year alone and is also administrating our club membership database. Graham coordinates our hugely successful open day, oversees our marketing strategy and all things social as well as helping to tutor during cadet week. Sue can tell us where each and every penny of club funds is, she has pulled together every application for grant funding we have made, and always has a strategic view on any decision. Ray keeps us all on track and makes sure nothing falls through the gap, he shoulders the time consuming administration tasks, as well as serving as ECPR secretary. I may have rattled through them here, however these are not jobs that take 5 minutes here and there but require a huge amount of time and dedication on top of attending a number of monthly meetings each. So although it goes against tradition I really do want to thank each of you for all the time, effort and commitment you give to the Club. Moving on I will now give you that all important total membership number. Bear in mind that in 2014 we had 392 members and 401 in 2015. So I am delighted to report that as of today there are 430 members of Marconi Sailing Club. Some of these additional members are as a result of another a successful open day and from our new crusier racing series. However we have also been working on new initiatives and improvements, which I will describe in a moment. An increase in membership is brilliant news as it is our only real source of income. However we must not become complacent. We have taken part in some RYA surveys this year and the feedback has highlighted that a number of sailing clubs both within our region and nationwide are in trouble and seeing declining memberships. We need to encourage all of our members to stay part of the club whilst also trying to attract new members. Some future plans to address this include a survey of our new members to see what we can do to integrate them better into the club, and also the possibility of re-introducing the new members evening. In line with a healthy membership I can report that our finances are in a good position. I will leave Sue to take you through the statutory accounts a little later in the agenda. You will see that the Board and the management committee are proposing a small increase to subscription fees for next year. Although our membership is healthy we do face increasing running costs, and I will leave Sue to give you further details. We have also proposed some changes to mooring fees in E and F row. The purpose of reducing these fees is to encourage new members to take out these drying moorings which are under currently under used. January 2017 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk I would like to now report on the major focal points for the Board and committees in 2016, which have all been in line with working towards our ambitions as presented to you this time last year. Club racing cruiser. In response to a need generated by new members who joined as a result of last years 1st Autumn cruiser racing series the Club purchased and financed restoration work of Ned Kelly, a ¼ ton Robber. There are several members who pay a premium to use the boat, which over time will cover the purchase and running costs. She has also been available for use by other members during certain times of the year such as cadet week. Ned Kelly has been a real success and seen some good results in BJRC races. We hope to grow our capacity in this area as the need arises. Overall we have been working to increase participation in sailing, whether racing, training or cruising. Some successes have been the Sprint 15 and Skiff fleets where we have seen an increase from 1 skiff last year to 11 and we now have 22 Sprint 15s sailing from the club. Cruiser racing has also gone from strength to strength with a further successful autumn series. Dave Russell collates monthly data to submit to the RYA which shows that we have seen a real increase in participation for both training and racing versus 2015. We have continued to broaden our training provision. We are actively working towards offering RYA dinghy sailing courses and have 6 newly qualified dinghy instructors who have already contributed to sail training days. The Club have now trained 30+ rib drivers in house and continue to offer first aid training where needed. We have also purchased a Wayfarer and additional safety boat to support our training endeavours. Another major focus has been improving the process of mooring laying and retrieval. As detailed earlier the first action here was to increase mechanisation of the process and reduce manual handling required. Duty offset with other, more able members is being considered and the move to a 3-yearly cycle for mooring laying and retrieval is planned in the future. Encouraging growth of rowing and paddle sports. Our rowing gig Elettra has been active in the local gig series, and was available during camping fortnight and our open day to encourage use. We also purchased 2 club sea kayaks which have been well used for leisure and supporting training activities. A rowing representative will also be joining the main committee from December to make sure this group are represented at a management level. Improvements to the site and clubhouse. We completely refurbished the galley to provide a fit for purpose facility, carried out a major upgrade to the travel hoist and purchased a new marquee. Those who read Navigans will know that we were unsuccessful in our application for the Sport England Inspired facilities fund for £75k towards a capital refurbishment project. However we continue to strategically build a capital reserve and are always looking for more grant funding. I will give some further details on our plans for capital projects a little later in this report. Of course this is all above and beyond out usual day-to-day club operations. A couple of other achievements to note this year include: The Wednesday team who have been as busy as usual keeping our club fit and well. A couple of projects from this year include carrying out much of the renovation work to the galley, which significantly reduced the potential cost to the Club and fitting a new pressure washer system. Also, after spending a few years establishing the Tony B, the Gang have spent much of this year restoring her again after she suffered a very sad sinking incident in March. I am pleased to report that we have had another resoundingly successful year of training including cadet week and regular and hugely popular sail training days. What is very positive to note is that by increasing our volunteer base and support boat availability, we have been able to cater for 3-4 different groups during training days. These include oppi Club, beginners, advanced and adult groups, which is a huge step forward in delivering much needed training. Of course I say ‘we’ have been able to deliver more training but what I really mean is that John Nickalls and his ever expanding team of volunteers have made huge progress this year so thank you to each and every one of you. East Coast Piers Race 2016 was another success, and although entries were slightly reduced we were still able to donate £300 to the Essex Air Ambulance and we have just presented the Cirdan Trust with a cheque for £13,200. As always, thanks are due to Clive Shenton and his team, which will include many of you sat in the audience today, for organising another superb event. Perhaps 2017 will see a Marconi crew win the main race rather than coming just a close second and third! I would also like to mention and thank our 3 new social secretaries, Sara, Claire and Julie. I hope you will all agree that the social scene at Marconi has been excellent this year with a huge variety of events taking place. Plenty of fun has been had by a lot of people so thank you ladies and keep up the good work! As for sailing, I am not going to burst Tom’s bubble and will leave it to the Sailing Secretary’s report. All I will say is that we have had a brilliant year for Marconi sailors in club racing, travelling to opens, nationals and other events from both the dinghy and cruiser fleets. Prizes I will pause here to award our 4 prizes as they all relate to sailing. On the topic of representation of the Club at regattas, I would like to award the Barograph trophy to Ian Ivermee and the crew of Woozle Hunter for their outstanding racing performance as 2016 overall EAORA (East Anglian Offshore Racing Association) offshore champions and class 3 champions. As I am not au-fait with the cruiser racing scene I will read out some of their truly remarkable racing achievements this season: January 2017 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Not only did they win the prestigious 180 mile North Sea Race against a fleet of 31 Dutch & British boats, but their list of offshore race wins this year is impressive. Pattinson Cup, (Mersea to Burnham around the Gunfleet); Ralph Herring Trophy; (Burnham to Mersea around the Gunfleet); Houghton Cup (Harwich to Burnham); Walker Challenge Trophy (Ramsgate to Harwich). For their overall win in the North Sea race, after 36 hours of racing, they were presented with highly prized Royal Ocean Racing Club medallions. As the smallest boat in the EAORA fleet and the only one to finish all 13 races, and Marconi's only representative, Woozle Hunter singlehandedly finished MSC as 2nd place in the EAORA offshore team result. Ian Ivermee was joined throughout the whole campaign and all 13 races by Laura Ivermee. Other club members joining them on at least one offshore race were, Andy Fowler, Lana Clarke and Lydia Coffey. Congratulations to Ian and crew! Sticking with the Woozle crew I am pleased to award the mamgu trophy for best log to Laura Ivermee for her very entertaining account of the RORC North Sea Race. If you have not read this log on the club website it will be available in the next edition of Navigans which will be available in the new year. Now moving from racing to cruising I would like to award the Seamanship trophy to Roger Gibson in recognition of his double Atlantic crossing in less than 12 months. Not only is this a great feat of seamanship but also project management and logistics. For 2 weeks Roger and Derek Brown were the only 2 crew on board the 40ft Dufour Antigua Kiss, operating a 4 hour on, 4 hour off shift system. A truly incredible achievement. Our final award is the Commodores plate which the prerogative of the Commodore to award, despite what the other Directors feel. However I am very pleased to say there was unanimous support for this years winner. Although not usually awarded to a member serving on a committee we feel that Jenny Ball has gone above and beyond in doing the most for the Club throughout the year. Jenny has spearheaded the revival of the Sprint 15 fleet which has seen a huge increase in activity both in club racing and also on the travelling circuit. The fleet have attended Nationals and Opens on mass, the highlight of which was the recent Grafham open where there were 9 Marconi boats including 2 of our cadets. As well as Sprint 15 captain Jenny also took on the mammoth task of administrating both the cat and dinghy parks last year. This might not seem like much but trust us it is a huge and not very easy or pleasant task! Jenny has also been instrumental in the success of a number of our open events this year, either by race officering, arranging prizes, stocking the bar or organising them completely. One statement I had given to me after our very busy weekend of 4/5 June when the Lark and Laser fleets visited and we hosted the Marconi Cruiser Regatta was that; ‘Once again Jenny had to pull things together in the background, without making a fuss just got it done. This happens much more than people realise.’ In fact the list seems endless, as I wrote this report I remembered that Jenny also runs our cadet regatta, is the better half of the bar manager and there are probably other jobs as well that I’ve not mentioned. So Jenny thank you for all your hard work. We really do appreciate it! Next I would like to comment on our plans for 2017 and the coming few years. We plan to introduce RYA dinghy sailing courses in the near future. This is the culmination of a lot of groundwork chiefly shouldered by Pat Shaw as Rear Commodore for sailing and Bob Collins as RYA training centre Principal. As a result of gaining Championship Club status we were able to run a subsidised dinghy instructor course earlier in the year and now have 6 very able Dinghy Instructors within the Club and a Senior Dinghy Instructor to work with them. In the course of 2016 we have purchased a Mark 4 Wayfarer and are in the process of purchasing a second, specifically to be used for training. We also have an additional rib to support this development. We have just submitted an application for another Sport England grant for £10k in order to help fund this project. In general we are also aiming to maintain and grow our training offering with courses for race officers, first aid and safety boat for example. This will give current and new volunteers greater skills and confidence. We plan to continue to grow the rowing section within the club and the rowing captain now has a seat on the main management committee. We also have a number of capital projects planned for this winter and next. These include improvements and general maintenance to the site such as the approach road, pontoon and cruiser park road. We will continue with plans to further mechanise and improve mooring laying and retrieval. There will be some aesthetic works taking place here in the upstairs lounge including improvements to the acoustics and general atmosphere and reflective film fitted to the eastern and northern facing windows to help with temperature control and glare. We also plan to construct a bridge deck above the large boathouse , and build a fit for purpose club boat gear storage area alongside the boat store. This will enable better use of club boats as access to sails and spars is currently far form ideal and involves climbing over or under ribs. Finally, although we were unsuccessful with our bid for an Inspired Facilities grant in order to build a viewing platform, we do still plan to go ahead with a scaled back project utilising club capital reserves over the next few years. We will also being switching over to a new membership database in the New Year which should offer good integration with our website and be easier for club administration purposes. Although we are not there yet, a huge amount of thanks are due to Pa t Shaw who is handling all the transfer of data for us. All of this is in addition to our usual full sailing and social calendar for 2017 so we have a busy year ahead of us to look forward to. January 2017 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk I would like to end my report on a couple of very positive notes. Firstly we have been nominated as Yachts and Yachting club of the year, mainly in light of the ECPR and fundraising in aid of the Cirdan Trust. It would be fantastic if we won and voting takes only a few minutes on their website, so please vote for us if you have not done so already. The winner will be announced at the London Boat Show and by voting you are entered into a draw to win a Wildwind holiday for two! Finally, during the summer you were invited via email to participate in an RYA consumer research pilot survey and they have provided the feedback to us, which has been very useful. There was an opportunity to leave general feedback on the Club and we were given some really positive comments along with some constructive feedback on where we can make improvements. I thought I would end by sharing some of the comments that I think best describe the club. These are totally anonymous so please do not ask who left them! ‘All round club; excellent dinghy sailing and ad-hoc training combined with a cruiser section who not only race offshore but would shame most professional marinas for care and maintenance. There seem to be a huge number of volunteers who support racing, launching and a cadet week which attracts 75 plus children. it is an extremely friendly club with a very positive outlook. Membes enjoy helping each other and participating in activities that need volunteers eg Cadet Week it is at a fabulous sailing location and very inclusive of all aspects of sailing - Plus it is a friendly, family oriented club where it is perfectly usual for three or even four generations to be members. Best family club in Essex, water there, all the time. Friendly people. Great team spirit. Marconi is a true community of sailors willing to help each other out, the sailing is brilliant and facilities are fantastic. Marconi SC is a very friendly, family based club with strong leadership who value all members and encourage everyone to take part in activities within the club. There is a very strong community feel and members of all ages and abilities are supported and encouraged with their level of sailing. There are so many opportunities to sail at whatever level and for the type of sailing that you are interested in. Visiting sailors always comment on how friendly and helpful the club is with great facilities. Friendly, helpful members; great access to tidal estuary; very good facilities; no blazers. ‘ So, in conclusion Marconi Sailing Club has had another successful year and I look forward to the year ahead. Thank you for your kind support this year and for listening to this report. I am happy to take any questions. Michaela Dowley Commodore, Marconi Sailing Club Roger Camp Roger Camp passed away at home with his family on 25th November 2016. He had been ill for some time but had remained active for as long as he could. Roger joined MSC in 1986. As well as being a good chap to know and very helpful in so many ways, he also carried out the following duties for the club: - clubhouse manager (and management committee member) from 2008 - security coordinator from 2008 - cruiser fleet captain from 2013 Roger attended his last management committee meeting in October 2016. His dry humour and witty comments as well as his contribution to club business will be missed. Roger was very involved in East Coast Piers Race both ashore as well as being the radio hub at Colne Point. I was always grateful for Roger’s help during the annual fitting out of the ECPR bus. Nothing was too much trouble. Roger’s control of ECPR from Colne Point was legendary. He was always calm and efficient even when bombarded with requests over the radio for weather reports, attempts to find 'lost' competitors, and so on. He last carried out this duty in July 2016. Jackie and Roger organised the Greek flotilla cruise that took place in June 2016 where 22 club members sailed on 9 boats. By all accounts it was a memorable holiday and Cheryl Cutmore wrote an excellent log of the trip which was published in August/September Navigans. With the willing support of other club members Roger was able to keep sailing until the end of the 2016 season. Clive Shenton (Vice President and ECPR chairman) paid the following tribute: January 2017 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk We are deeply saddened to hear of the passing of one of Marconi SC’s favourite sons. Unlike the two others who warranted such an accolade Roger has been taken from us cruelly early. Roger used his many qualities to add to Club life in a very positive way. We found him to be skilled, experienced, hard-working, decisive, good humoured and above all dependable in everything he did. As Safety Coordinator afloat in ECPR all these qualities were put to a test that he passed year after year. Roger knew when to lead and when to listen. Many years of leading us as Fleet Captain set a standard that will never be beaten. We cheerfully followed him on many Club cruises as did many other members and who can forget the leap into uncharted waters as he led the fleet across the sandbanks of the Thames. As well as family and friends there was a strong contingent from MSC. Our thoughts are with Jackie and family. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Fleet News Cruiser Fleet Ed: This account of the RORC North Sea race won Laura the Mamgu Trophy presented at the 2016 AGM THE RORC NORTH SEA RACE BY LAURA IVERMEE After a great start to our season the previous weekend, winning the first two races in the East Anglian Offshore Racing Association series, our 2015 Fastnet crew was reunited and hopes were high for the 180 mile RORC North Sea race to Scheveningen in the Netherlands. The conditions were good for a Sigma 33, light airs and good weather, which suited the smaller boats, but we were competing against a lot of very fast people! Delayed in the lock leaving Shotley Marina, we headed for the start line as fast as we could, other latecomer boats speeding along with us. In the distance the start line was a mass of boats on the horizon, milling around. Once checked in with the committee boat, we headed for the port end of the line and got a great start, working our way amongst many larger boats up to 1st place on the leader board. Then we tacked losing places to the faster boats. Most boats went around the Cork Sands, but as one of the smallest boats, we were able to sail over them, gaining back a few positions. Fantastic sailing weather for us and our colourful kite. Approaching the Black Deep Buoy, to round it to Port, the tide was against us, and the wind died. We dropped our kite too early and nearly failed to reach the mark, along with a couple of other boats with the same problem. We inched slowly towards the buoy, considering dropping the anchor at one point, finally rounding it after a very unwelcome delay. Once round, however, the tide was in our favour and we made great pace. We stayed in sight of the pack for many hours, though gradually the faster competitors disappeared into the distance. Another boat had a medical emergency during the night, and a helicopter was sent to airlift the casualty off. Night watch and a totally clear sky. Millions of stars, shooting stars, and a phosphorescent boat trail, until 3am and skipper wanted the kite up!! Kite flying in the dark? Fun!! A stunning sun rise, and other yachts amazingly still in sight as we made our way towards our Nemesis, Smith’s Knoll, a buoy notorious for problems rounding it, and which has cost us this race in a previous year!! Approaching Smith's Knoll, (also known as 'The Bastard'), this time, we carried a good speed to it with our kite flying and round beautifully at 5.45am. Now to head for Holland. One of the best sails in a long time. The boat behaved like a little darling. Still boats within sight after 24 hours!! A rare sight for us in other years! This year the boat was performing superbly, and was a pleasure to race. Eventually Holland appeared out of the murk, and we fought for every second in the final leg. At one stage, the wind dropped within sight of land, leading to much blaspheming!! Out came the Haribo, then kite up, and so far forward it was a real challenge to keep flying. 11pm (local time) and one mark to go. Round the NAM 22, kite up again and a flying dash to the finish. One of the best night kite sessions ever. We flew in the dark, heading for the lights of Holland. Every second counted, as much faster boats than us had already finished. And, across the line. Just over 36 hours of racing and a hyped, but weary crew. Sails down and into the marina. Heading for beer and results!! Boat tidying could wait!! We were met on the way to the bar by the RORC officials with the results, and .... we did it. We won. Beating over 30 boats to an overall win, and sailing less miles than anyone else. What an amazing result for a bunch of misfits in a 30 year old Sigma 33. The Woozle Misfits are: January 2017 Navigans 8

We’ve seen a more that 50% increase in participation both through the training we are laying on and the racing that is happening at the club. Our thanks must go out to Dave Russell for both collecting and sending that data off to the RYA, and it clearly paid off as in April we were pulled out of the monthly prize draw by the RYA for returning our participation data! We spent our prize on some useful race training marks. Last season we set about making changes to the racing that would hopefully improve the experience for those already racing and to try to encourage more people to use their dinghies in a racing environment. The number of starts was reduced down to 3 and the start sequence was changed to a 5,4,1, go system. So far it seems to have been a great success. We also introduced a mini closed regatta for the final bank holiday weekend which kept the racing really close and the prize-giving afterwards made sure we hadn’t forgotten why we were picking up trophies. The training centre side of things is going well, we have now trained up lots of eager RIB drivers and First Aiders to help save us when things sometimes go a little wrong. We are looking to expand this going forwards and hopefully will be running RYA sailing courses soon to teach, and to qualify those that already know how to sail. This year’s Open Day seemed to be even more successful than ever, there were lots of new sailors that came along on that day, took part in cadet week and have joined us again and again for our Sail Training days. Which have also seen record numbers this season, with the adults joining them for the first time, hopefully these are good signs for the future. The Weekly emails have continued in their interesting, informative and hopefully amusing vein. I hope you have enjoyed reading about everything that’s been going on in the Club. The Cruiser sailing fraternity have had a busy year starting with an early cruise in the Ionian Sea, exploring the Greek islands. It’s like the Walton Backwaters, but slightly warmer! They have also been on their traditional voyages up and down the east coast, with trips to Ipswich, Brightlingsea & beyond. Some of our members have ventured further afield and as mentioned previously, Antigua Kiss 2 has completed two Atlantic crossings, Locomotion is currently en route to the Med, and Woozle Hunter has racked up many miles offshore as well. This brings us nicely onto the cruiser racing side of things, Woozle Hunter have had a stellar year winning the EAORA championship. More locally we have had the BJRC championship and Marconi boats did well under the IRC handicap with finishers in 3rd, 4th & 6th place. The Autumn series was once again a great success, with many new people introduced to sailing and a tight series of races was enjoyed by all who took part. Those that joined last year had the opportunity to crew & maintain our new club yacht, Ned Kelly. They have had a fantastic year and have hopefully learnt a lot about racing. January 2017 Navigans 19

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Colin’s dinghy cruises are still a popular feature of the sailing calendar. They’ve been on voyages from the club to any pub that is willing to serve them, it must be getting harder to find these pubs as this year they even went as far field as Plymouth in search of the perfect pint. The windsurfers continue to venture out when most have given up all hope of sailing, but they now have some excellent club kit for use in lighter weather so that anyone can learn and see what they’re missing out on! The cat and dinghy racing scene have had an excellent year of sailing, we’ve coped with the changes and hopefully not put anyone off. The Sprint 15 fleet continues to go from strength to strength, and under the steady helm of Jenny Ball the newly formed fleet has grown to a force that is positively buoyant and encouraging more people to join in. The handicap fleet has been boosted in the later part of this year by a skiff revolution. The number of skiffs at the club has gone from 2 to 3 at the beginning of the year to at least 10 now. With a group of enthusiastic youngsters willing to learn, and some more experienced guys leading them, we should have a good fleet going by next season. The club has once again opened its doors to visiting fleets and the open meetings this year have been a great success. In mid-March we invited the 29er fleet to the waters of the Blackwater and 28 29ers were treated to some chilly conditions. We also had 21 Sprint 15s join us for their open on a marginally warmer April weekend preceded by some class training the weekend before. In June we had 15 larks visit for the first time, they were treated to some very competitive sailing in some difficult conditions. Of course we also had the East Coast Piers Race, another epic year with monster conditions Saturday and cracking conditions Sunday. This year I even got to compete for the first time, so would like to extend my personal thanks to everyone who made it possible! On the road our dinghy and cat sailors ventured up to Pwllheli for the Sprint 15 Nationals, down to Stokes bay for the Tornado Nationals and out west to Paignton for the 18” Skiff nationals to name but a few. Once again this this year year Tristan Hutt and team were named national champions in the 18” skiff class - well done! Bart’s Bash once again was a huge inter-club success. Being on the RIB this time gave me a fantastic perspective and seeing all those boats go out and round Osea Island was quite a spectacle. Congratulations to Nick Miller who won the Blackwater Bart’s Bash! Cadet racing continues to grow and the fleet have had a brilliant year, once again competing in the NSSA regatta at Great Yarmouth. Various individuals have also competed at open meetings and regattas around the country. Some have now moved into boats like the RS800 and Sprint 15 so it looks like we’ll be having some more competition in these fleets next year! And lastly as I draw to a close my report on what has been such a fantastic year I must say a big thank you to all who have helped. There are so many of you in the background and the foreground who have made this year so successful, I’d name you all but this isn’t an Oscars acceptance speech! Although this report is meant to sum up a year of sailing activity at Marconi, of course it can only be a brief snapshot of the events that have taken place. Here’s to 2017 - let’s hope it’s a good one! Tom Clayton, Sailing Secretary January 2017 Navigans 20

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Last Autumn in 2015, at times we had more people (guests) wanting to sail at the club as racing crew, than we had spaces available and every boat that sailed was fully crewed almost all the time. Ray Ball Company Secretary secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk The Blackwater as a London Airport The following is an article by Kevin Bruce published in The Essex Society for Archaeology and History, Summer 2016 Newlsetter. It was spotted by club member Jenny Ball, also a member of the society, and is reproduced here by kind permission of the original author and publication. Ed. Following the 2nd World War, the Government sought to improve transatlantic and long distance air transport. FLying boats were considered suitable and Saunders-Roe were approached in 1945 to design a suitable plan. The following year they received a contract for three of what were to be the largest flying boats – the S.R. 45 “Princess”. Steps were taken to find a suitable site for a Flying Boat air port to serve London. The Chichester Area and the Blackwater were the two suggested locations and assessments were made in 1947 of their suitability. Initial conclusions stated: “At Chichester, the ideal terminal cannot be provided without the engineering difficulties of building on reclaimed land. At Blackwater, it cannot be provided without a larger terminal basin and mooring area than is proposed in the Blackwater Survey Report. IF neither of these courses should prove practical, then, in terms of taxying distances, Blackwater, with a terminal at Bradwell and Maintenance and M.O.S at Ramsey, would be preferable to Chichester..... Extendability of Alighting Area - Chichester, once built could not be extended, whereas the length of run at Blackwater is practically limitless. March 2017 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Availability - Chichester would not be available for use until the end of a lengthy development period. On the other hand, most of the alighting area at the Blackwater is available now and would be so during the development period.” The three terminal sites suggested were at Osea Island, Ramsey Wade between Stansgate and Ramsey Island, St Lawrence and Bradwell Creek. The Bradwell basin would have utilised an enlarged creek. At Ramsey, it would have occupied the Wade, previously sealed off from the Blackwater in 1815. Both basins would have been deepened by excavation and at Ramsey Wade, the sea wall demolished to gain access. The plans do not indicate where the Osea basin might have been but the terminal would have been on the island itself with a new causeway constructed to give road access towards the A12. It was envisaged that the then redundant Bradwell Bay aerdrome could act as a feeder airport for the south bank sites. They estimated that the road journey from these two sites would take 3 hours compared with today’s 1 1/2 hours. Consultations were held between several government ministries and local authorities. Maldon’s MP Tom Driberg also requested to be kept informed. One consultee put forward the Medway Estuary as a better alternative. A precursor to Boris Island? The scheme came to nothing as it became obvious that the land based airfields would cater more economically and safely. Only one of the Princess aircraft ever flew, in 1952. Small sea planes did operate on the Blackwater during the First World War in conjunction with HMS Osea fast motor boat base. Sea planes may still return to the Blackwater as there is currently a proposal to operate a service between Osea and small airports around London. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk May Issue copy deadline: 18th April Club Notices Club Secretary SECURITY OF YOUR CLUB I recently had a call from an ex –member who was out for an early morning walk and noticed that the clubhouse door was open. He was good enough to phone me and offer to make the clubhouse secure. I gratefully accepted his offer. Unfortunately finding the clubhouse door and/or the gate open when there is nobody about is more common than you might think. It is essential that your sailing club site and clubhouse are secure. Do not assume that someone else will lock the clubhouse or close the gate if you don’t. A convoy of vehicles will drive through the gate and the driver of the last vehicle will assume that the gate should be open because that is how it was when they followed the other vehicles out. If in doubt close it. Generally the gate will only be tied back for open meetings or if a trades vehicle is expected. EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD I issue this warning every year but it may be useful for new members and perhaps a timely reminder for older hands. The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius. On sunny spring days it is easy to be fooled but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim. Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the wind chill. There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm.
