Ed Antonio and Bob’s French Canal Trip Bob Whittaker writes of a voyage through the French canals… Start date 1st Sept 2017 Yacht Sabre, Antonio and Bob departed Marconi SC at 8 am on the 1st September bound for Barcelona via the French canal system. The run down to Ramsgate was uneventful, motor sailing assisted occasionally by light winds. Since Sabre also contained Antonio’s entire collection of worldly good and possessions, space was somewhat limited on board. We became aware that Sable had a marked list to starboard and was somewhat stern heavy, the bows being rather higher in the water than the boats designers ever envisaged. On arrival in Ramsgate the cargo was redistributed and the problem solved although space on board was still limited. Setting sail for Calais the following morning in sunny conditions, light winds with little cloud cover. July 2018 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Crossing the first separation zone presented little difficulty, as we approached the second zone a cloud appeared. Almost round a kilometre in diameter, flat top and bottom and entirely jet black in colour. Although we had light winds at sea level the cloud was moving so fast it easily overtook a Polish bulk coal carrier travelling towards the Atlantic. It looked like trouble and it certainly was. As it passed ahead of the Polish ship wisp of cloud spiralled down from the leading edge. We knew what was coming; a Tornado. The wind hit us immediately, accompanied a few minutes later by heavy salty rain. Sabre picked up speed dramatically, water running along the deck, the boom skimming the waves. Fortunately we only had the main sail up at the time, we had intended to go astern of the Polish coal carrier, however the increase in speed meant we were now rapidly closing with it. An urgent change of course followed by an interesting ten minutes or so, then it was all over back to blue sky’s as if nothing had ever happened fortunately no damage was sustained we set a new course for Calais and continued on our way Calais Marina is well equipped, secure and well organised, we received no attention what so ever from the authorities regarding customs, fuel or passports. Antonio registered with the marina office and collected our permit to enter the canals (CIVINE) 100 Euros for 31 days Mast removal is carried out by the staff at the Chandlery situated within the facility, the travel hoist appears to be the sa me model as the one at Burnham Marina. The chandlery are specific in their instructions before leaving the pontoon, detach the upper shrouds completely, slacken the lowers, free up the split pins, motor under the travel hoist. Locate the strop under the spreaders, pull the split pins, remove any bolts. Lay the mast on top of the boat, all over in under ten minutes, pay the 60 euros job done. A French carpenter repairing a boat in the marina provided some second hand wood to support the mast free of charge, he was clearly impressed with Antonio, it eventually turned out he was Irish from Dublin. The weather was good as we left Calais, entering the Canal system it soon changed we had eight days and nights of rain, day time temperatures rarely exceeding 8C, everything was either wet or very damp, as we headed south the weather began to slowly improve but not fast enough by any means. It soon became obvious that most canal dwellers had either already headed south, gone home, or were sheeting up their boats for winter. As far as leisure boats were concerned we were almost on our own. The locks on the major canals are operated by VNF staff in control towers above the locks. The larger locks have lifting gates 20 metres high, controlled by a cable and winch system, resulting in large quantities of muddy canal water descending on our heads as we entered and left. Thankfully these locks have floating bollards to which the centre cleat is attached, the water flow is very controlled, these are amongst the easiest to use. They are however very muddy attempting to climb the mud encrusted ladders 16 metres to the top, in the event of an emergency would not be a good idea you would probably never make it. On occasions we were in locks with a 100 metre long 1000 tonne barge. that’s two 50 metre barges bolted together end to end and bound together with hawsers winched tight as banjo strings, the locks are only just wide enough to take these barges in many cases the Bargees don’t even moor up using forward and reverse to maintain their position the main objective is not to clout the gates. On one occasion we were the only boat in the lock I estimate that it took around 12000 cubic metres of water to lift Sabre the 14 metres. Just as well it had been raining for days, it has been known for the canals to run low on water during the summer months, not a problem we encountered, quite the opposite. The Canal de Marne which includes the Canal de I’Aisne a la Marne, the Canal lateral a la Marne, and the Canal entre Champagne et Bourgogne de la Marne. Is not as commercially important as it once was the railway and motorway which run alongside the canal, in many places have taken the cargo’s off the barges. Since the Marne’s 200 kilometres long encompassing 98 locks, 12 lifting bridges, and 6 tunnels the longest being 5 km. It’s easy to see why with few exceptions leisure craft transiting north/ south or between river systems during the summer months constitute the majority of the traffic. Subsequently the VNF who run the canals are heavily into head count reduction, the locks have been automated, operated by a remote controller supplied free of charge at the first lock in the series. Most of the lock keepers cottages are now boarded up, built in the 1880’s they require a considerable amount of work to make them habitable. A few have been sold off and updated no doubt at considerable cost to the new owners. It’s now clear that we had little idea as to the challenges the Marne would present. Most of the leisure craft on these canals are large steel boats entirely self contained with all the comforts of home, a cabin roof that the crew stand on to access the bollards which can be five to six meters above water level and 20 metre’s apart. At 27 ft Sabre was the smallest boat we encountered, fibre glass yachts are unsuitable for life on these Canals, far to light and to easily damaged as we found out. July 2018 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Canal de Marne locks are very violent, the sluices operated hydraulically, are either fully open or closed, the initial surge of water throws the boat around placing a considerable strain on the cleats, lines and crew until the flow subsides as the pressures equalise. Large round fenders 300 to 400mm in diameter four at least are required, the sort of fenders we use in north sea marina’s are generally as good as useless. Mooring and centre cleats with good reinforcing are essential as are strong mooring lines, anything less will be destroyed, An athletic crew member capable of climbing and descending five to six meter high ladders, up to 19 times a day is a great advantage, many of the locks are only 500 metre apart. Hardly time to make a cup of tea. It’s just as well Antonio’s has plenty of energy, some days she must have climb well over 95 metres in total and carrying the mooring ropes, and then she had to climb down again, no job for an OAP, I lost 14 lb in 26 days as it was. Owing to the heavy rains the water overtops the lock gates filling the lock 2 cm from the top. The fender are doing nothing, the hull rubbing against the concrete is all that’s restraining the boat. The same applies in the down locks we had to push the boat away from the concrete quay heading often reinforced with rusting railway track in order to deploy the fenders. Marinas as we know them are very few, many Canal side villages claim to have a marina with washing and toilet facilities and shops, we even took virtual tours of some villages using Antonio’s smart phone. On arrival you find four bollards on the side of the canal. The shops, café, and bars in the villages which once existed are with few exceptions now closed and boarded up, some with for sale signs attached for good measure Web sites have never been updated and are out of date, at one stage we ran out of food, a retired bargee living in a lockkeepers cottage informed us that it was 30km to the nearest shops, he was good enough to supply a loaf of bread we even had a choice white or brown. Larger canal side towns which can be many days motoring apart are well supplied with shops. The supermarkets where they exist are enormous and sell just about anything you could possibly want. A combination of Home Base, Tesco’s, B&Q and Doe’s Of Ulting as well as normal domestic items, mowing machines and agricultural equipment can be supplied from stock, no wonder the village shops can’t compete. The strange thing is their never seem to be many customers, generally only one checkout open and no queue I can’t understand it! Fuel is generally not available canal side or from marinas but has to be obtained from filling stations often some distance away. They are open 24/7 and are fully automatic (credit cards only) Fuel cans and a trolley to transport the cans are essential, we averaged ten litres a day. The Balesmes Tunnel on the Champagne to Burgundy section was the longest of the six we encountered, at almost five kilometres long with control canals either side the total length is 10 km it’s a formidable undertaking. From the check point at Vitry-le-Francois it’s a chain of 71 up stream locks to the tunnel under the Plateau De Langres. The traffic through the tunnel is controlled from lock No1 Heulley-Cotton on the upstream side, it’s the last lock before the control canal. The controller ensures that the canal retains sufficient water to function, the system holds 160,000 cubic meters pumped from the valley below. Once through the tunnel the Les Batailles check point controls locks 1 to eight of the 43 locks on the down side. The lock keepers in the control locks Numbers 1 either side issue verbal instruction regarding clearance to proceed, it’s one way traffic through the control canals and the tunnel. They also supply fenders in the form of bulks of timber with rope loops to replace the existing fenders, should the boats beam be considered too wide for the canal. Getting jammed in the tunnel is not advised The tunnel’s 8 metres wide with a 1.5 metre walkway along it’s length originally used by horses to pull the barges through in the 1880s now restricted to emergency use only. Unfortunately the lighting in all these tunnels with one exception is not all it could be, the lights in the Balesmes Tunnel are intended to switch on and off as you progress it’s length, the first section came on and failed to switch off the rest failed to light up, probably because Sabre had too lower profile to trigger the sensor. There is another explanation the tunnels are shut down for maintenance during the winter months and this was the end of the season after all. We used a torch to light up the side of the tunnel, progress was slow we took 2 hours 45 minutes to cover the distance, the maximum time allowed in the tunnel is three hours the whole operation take’s 4 to 5 hours including the control canals, As it was we had the place to ourselves just as well. This was the last of the five tunnels we encountered Several of which were built by criminals from French prisons most serving life sentences, I don’t think they had much say in the matter, they did an excellent job, as I understand it the mortality rate was extremely high. July 2018 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk On reaching Maxilly-sur-Soane the end of Marne you return the remote control by posting it into a large metal container which reads the unit automatically communicating with the control centre, once all are satisfied the lock gates open to let you out into the Saone. The only marinas we encountered worthy of the name were Calais and St Jean de Losne which have excellent facilities. We arrived at one marina on the Saone just after 6 pm on a Saturday only to find the sites facilities were locked and would stay closed until Monday along with everything else, despite the marina being full of boats and crews. Oh and by the way that will be eight euros for the night. Antonio sorted them out on the spot, we left the following morning for St Jean de Losne, we never did pay the eight euros. On reaching ST Jean de Losne some 50 km south of Dijon I handed over to Simon, heading for home on the train, leaving at 10.45 am I arrived in Chelmsford at 6pm that evening not bad at all. FLOOD GATES The Environment Agency requires that the flood gates must be kept closed between the 1st September and the 1st May unless the hard is in use. The gap in the seawall is vital to our club but it is a privilege not a right. We must be seen to be doing the right thing by keeping the gates shut which as well as meeting EA requirements also protects our club and our neighbours. Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk >PIERS. a ECPR 2018 Report The 2018 East Coast Piers Race weekend was another success with 86 boats registering to take on the challenge of long distance racing. The East Coast Piers Race is a weekend of sailing held at Marconi Sailing Club in Essex in aid of the Cirdan Sailing Trust and Essex Air Ambulance, all money raised from the weekend goes to support these charities in what they do. This year we were proud to also be Allen Endurance event, part of the 3 event series. With free on site camping available from Friday through to Monday many competitors arrived on Friday to take advantage of the glorious sunshine and to get their boats set up early. Mighty Oak Brewery very kindly donated 7 firkins of beer (over 500 pints) of beer to the event with all beer being sold at £2 a pint with all the money going to charity. Obviously this proved to be very popular and visitors to the bar made a fair dent in the beer supplies on Friday night. When Saturday morning arrived there was a light breeze coming from the East but it was building all morning. The race briefin g took place at midday with the first race due to start at 1pm. The wind direction was perfect for sailing up and down the river so the race officer set a course which went to Thirslet Spit mark and then back past Marconi SC to an inflatable. The first race was more popular than the second, mainly due to a game of football which was showing in the bar. The second race was a little more testing with slightly less wind on the race course but the approach of running average laps helped out the slower dinghies who didn’t have to go as far as the big catamarans. Overall it was David Annan in his Musto Skiff who took the dinghy win and Grant Piggott and Will Smith who won the catamaran racing. The race briefing for Sunday is always held on Saturday evening due to the early start of Sundays racing. The briefing kicked off at 6pm with a full marquee of competitors keen to understand the 3 race courses available. To cater for dinghies from a PY of 1030 or faster and foiling catamarans the 3 race courses are 48 miles, 27 miles and 13 miles. The end of the briefing was rudely interrupted by a charcoal covered gentleman shouting THE BBQ IS READY! Following the BBQ we once again had a the popular Monkies Wedding band who did a great job of entertaining the crowds while they slowly worked their way through the Might Oak beers. The early call on Sunday morning came at 7am to get competitors up and ready for the planned 9.30am start. Due to the long distances of the races we ask competitors to take certain safety equipment with them and each boat is checked through the gate in the sea wall to ensure everything is present and correct. There was no breeze very early but it was teasing the race officer with the sponsors flags starting to move on shore. He decided on a postponement of 45 minutes before we could get the races underway, it was tough keeping the competitors from crossing over the line with the tide but with a bit of rib support they were dragged back and all started the ECPR as planned. At this point the race committee knew there was 10 knots of breeze at Walton and that it was building. October 2018 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Colne Point race started 15 minutes later and was the race with the most sailors, this race is open to fast dinghies and catamarans and the 27 miles proves more popular than the 48 mile course. Next to start was the Bradwell Race – this was introduced a few years ago to cater for more dinghies and the PY was adjusted to allow boats of 1030 or faster to attend. This year we were pleased to see a 29er and Contender taking part in the shorter course. Due to the wind conditions and the time the course was taking the ECPR and Bradwell courses were shortened. The ECPR turned at Clacton Pier and the Bradwell Race sailors didn’t do the additional dog leg back up river. In the East Coast Piers race it was John Tuckwell and his crew John who took the line honours award. Mark Mawditt and his crew Tiffany took line honours in the Colne Point Race. For Bradwell it was the 29er sailed by Sophie Johnson and Dylan who came through the line first. OVERALL WINNERS: ECPR – Simon Northrop and Caleb Cooper sailing an F18 Colne Point Race for Cats – Rob Forrester sailing a Shadow Colne Point Race for Dinghies – David Annan sailing a Musto Skiff Bradwell Race – Sophie Johnson and Dylan Collingbourne sailing a 29er With Sail Racer supporting us with GPS tracking and with the support of Allen we were able to award some additional prizes based on the data collected from the boats. Anthony, a local Marconi sailor won the award for Best Display of an Allen Sticker, keep an eye on the ECPR Facebook page to see the photo. Prizes were then awarded for the fastest speeds on the courses and the fastest on corrected time. A raffle is also held over the weekend with this years prize being a summer clothing package from Zhik worth over £500. This year local sailor Kevin Kirby took the prize home – a massive thank you to Zhik who not only provided this prize but also loads of prizes for prize giving. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Topper NS1 at Marconi SC a Remarkable Success The weekend of September 8th & 9th saw the first of the International Topper Class Association National Series Events for the 2018-19 season take place at Marconi SC. This was the first time a Topper National Series Event has been held at Marconi SC and what an event it was. The class was out in full force with 155 boats registered to take part in the event. For many this was the first real experience of big fleet sailing at a truly tidal location this provided an extra challenge for the fleet which most seemed to handle without any great drama. It must be said that all at MSC where mightily impressed by the Topper Class Associations event machine, very organised and very positive – this made for a very good event weekend. The weather also played ball with mostly sunshine a decent breeze, this helped to make the weekend very enjoyable for the sailors who seemed to be having a very good time indeed. The only thing more impressive than the ICTA event machine was the sailors themselves, brilliant on and off of the water. The race officer remarked that being thanked by large numbers of the sailors as they crossed the line to return home after the days racing made an extremely pleasant end to to two great days of sailing and was very much appreciated. The recently finished Bridge Deck development was remarked upon as being one of the best facilities they have ever seen for visibility of the sailing area and radio communications. The large clear hard was also seen as being one of the best the well travelled fleet has enjoyed, if possibly a bit lumpy. The large amount of space was also enjoyed particularly as it is mostly grassed providing a boat friendly rigging surface. The sight of so many Toppers at Marconi was inspiring – perhaps even inspiring enough to be the start of more things Topper at Marconi SC. For a full race by race event report see the Yachts & Yachting write up. For more information about Toppers visit the International Topper Class Association Website Pat Shaw Helm of the Year 2018 The annual Helm of the Year event took place on Saturday 22nd September. The winningest helms from each fleet (based on results in the Spring and Summer racing series) represent their fleet in a closely fought sailing regatta in Picos. The event takes place over seven races, with competitors swapping boats each time to ensure no undue advantage/disadvantage from the boats. The goal is to see off the competition and become Helm of the Year. Serious stuff. Seven competitors took part – Jason Clarke (Cadets), Julie Spencer (Slow H’Cap Fleet), John Burgoyne (H’Cap fleet), Jenny Ball (Sprint 15), Steve Thomas (Medium Cat), Will Harrison (Fast Cat), Ian Ivermee (Cruiser). Nigel James was Race Officer, assisted by Jon Pearse and set a course off the club with a committee boat start and finish. Jason took an early lead in Race 1, closely followed by Jenny and John. Jenny managed to get inside Jason at the end of lap one and just about held off Jason and Jon to take the first win. Will Harrison led the start of Race 2 with Jenny, Jason and John October 2018 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk hard on his heels but he held his nerve and took the win. In Race 3, Jenny forgot that Pico’s don’t get the start line as quick as a Sprint 15 so was late starting. Will, Jason and John battled at the front with Julie and Ian not far behind and Will went on to take a second win. A change of course and the fleet went back out for Race 4 with Will taking a third win. The fleet came in for lunch and in view of the weather, Ian and Julie decided to quit before they froze in the drizzle. After lunch, the wind looked promising as the fleet headed out for Race 5. Will led off the line with Jason and Jenny close behind. This time John had got his times muddled up and was late for the start line. As Will, Jason and Jenny rounded D mark, the wind stopped altogether making it difficult to cross the ebbing tide on the way back to G. John, in the meantime, was able to round D about the time that a light breeze came back giving him yards of advantage over the top three. John sailed the light conditions extremely well to eventually take the win, with Jenny taking second. The fleet came back out for Race 6 in light conditions, and although the tide was not at its Blackwater strongest, it took patience and concentration to get the Picos over the line against the tide. Jenny managed to edge a lead at the first mark with John and Will close behind and Jenny managed to just hold them off to take the win. With discards, a quick calculation worked out that the title was hanging in the balance on the last race between Will and Jenny. In ever lighter conditions, the fleet changed boats on the water at the committee boat. Jenny, Will and Jason managed to get across the line and away – whilst John and Steve decided that a tow home was more favourable than another hour folded up in the front of a Pico. Jenny led to the leeward mark, turned for the finish and stopped in the tide. Will and Jason did the same. Then a breath came in from first the west and then south west which Will picked up first and got to the line to take a well deserved win of the race and the title. Big shout out to Ian, Julie, Steve, John, Jason and Will for some fantastic racing in light conditions that were not forecast (apart from the drizzle), to Dave Clarke, Tom Clayton, Lee Harrison and Pat Shaw for being shore support. Thanks to Nigel Baker and Tony Goode providing RIB support in less than ideal conditions. And massive thanks to Jon Pearse and Race Officer Nigel James for running the event and finding creative course to get all 7 races in despite the failing breeze. And congrats to Will Harrison for becoming 2018 Helm of the Year! Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Navigans Editor: David Ball navigans@marconi-sc.org.uk February Issue copy deadline: 18th January Club Notices Important notice to members The following notice was issued to members by email on 18 th December 2018, Ed. Routine testing of our water system this week has detected some growth of Legionella bacteria within the disabled showers. There have been no cases of Legionnaires’ Disease reported. MSC wishes to be completely transparent with our members. For information: Legionnaires’ is a very rare but serious disease caused by inhalation of contaminated water Symptoms appear within 2-10 days of exposure, with symptoms similar to pneumonia (fever, cough, shortness of breath) Those most at risk are the elderly, people with compromised immune systems or chronic lung disease If you have used the disabled showers and are at all concerned please consult with your GP What are we doing to address the issue? The disabled showers & toilets have been closed A specialist company with expertise in removing the bacteria will decontaminate the affected systems this week We will take further samples after the decontamination to confirm clearance of the bacteria from the whole site We will revisit our risk assessment for the prevention of Legionella at MSC and put in place further preventative measures to mitigate against the risk of future contamination Thank you for your understanding. If you have any concerns please feel free to contact Bryan Spencer either by using commodore@marconi-sc.org.uk or by phone . Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk Fleet News Cruiser Fleet CRUISER MOORING CHANGES 2019 We are in the middle of the changes for this year – along the lines outlined at the cruiser AGM whereby we are trying to get the bigger boats into A row and group where possible into like displacement types. This is not completely possible but this is our best shot. Normally we would notify you all individually of changes to your positions but because of the volume of changes this would be a lot of phone calls. You will still receive the final version as part of your membership pack. Please take the time to read carefully the information below – it contains information you will need for this season. THREE YEAR CYCLE OF MOORING LIFTING AND RELAYING In the season prior to our current system of lifting and relaying all deep water moorings, thirteen boats went adrift. This was clearly unacceptable so the decision was taken to lift and then inspect moorings annually, before laying. We are now in the position that breakaways are rare, mainly from chafe above the buoy. The current system involves a lot of work and is weather dependant, which can result in late laying and retrieval. It is also very difficult to set up alternative dates to get back on track. For several years now the mooring subcommittee have been experimenting with leaving the moorings down for longer periods. The visitor’s mooring which had been down for fifteen years, with cathodic protection on the scope, was retrieved this year. On inspection the main ground chain had deteriorated very little. I have inspected the mooring down to the centre at the beginning of every season and have had to replace the scope twice. This was done easily from the barge. The brand new mooring for the Tony B, which has a rope riser, has been down two winters and three summers. When it was retrieved at the end of this season there was again very little wear. Chafe was evident on the rope riser but this can be guarded against. If you order a new rope riser from EYE make sure that they fit anti chafe protection before they splice in the hard eye. The main problem we now have is with moorings that drag. This is random and happens if the anchor doesn’t set at laying. Once the mooring has been laid for some time and the anchors set they tend to stay there. At the moment we are lifting secure moorings with the risk of relaying and then dragging the following season. The mooring subcommittee have therefore decided that we should adopt a three year cycle for lifting and laying our moorings which is a common system in commercial moorings. For us it will mean that for 2019 season moorings in C row and the end of D row that use the barge will be laid with the aim of leaving them in situ for three years. They will receive an inspection down to the centre from the barge at the beginning of each season. The mooring owner will be on the barge for this and any remedial work will be carried out. This will apply to B row moorings from 2020 season then A row from 2021 and at the end of that season C row and Deep water D will be retrieved. For this to work the standard of the mooring equipment will need to have minimum wear at the point of laying. All shackles will need to be welded and ideally cathodic protection provided. To assist mooring owners the mooring inspection will take place one week earlier than normal and we will provide a welding facility with welder in attendance. Dates for this will be in the Cruiser Handbook as usual. Check your mooring early now is not too soon!!! If you need new chain or shackles let Bob know as soon as possible. January 2019 Navigans 4

It was a busy period for Harwich and we couldn’t get pre-booked in anywhere without going on swinging moorings or anchoring. Subsequent drop-outs meant we eventually booked into Lavington easily. Strong tides going into harbour but all safely arrived.15 boats in Southwold. One night the Commodore opened the sailing club for us to enjoy their hospitality and a Bar-B-Q behind the clubhouse. As boats dispersed we went onto anchoring some nights in the River Deben then onto the River Orwell. August bank holiday 8 boats turned out to Ipswich Haven Marina. Bar-B-Q in the old Yacht Club grounds. Weatherwise not great. Final trip to Brightlingsea 11 signed up but due to bad forecast had to cancel Low attendance numbers at the start of the season but increased as season went on. Hoping for better support next spring 5. ECPR – Clive Shenton 31st year of ECPR. Started in zero wind with the RO turning many a blind eye to get Race underway. Last year I was able to report a record entry of 86 boats. This year I am equally pleased to report that the 2018 equalled that record. This at a time when similar events are seeing entries in single figures. A feature of the entry list is that more than twice as many boats enter to Colne Point Race than the full course ECPR. ECPR was won by Simon Northrop who had won the F18 Europeans in Barcelona that week and trailed directly to Marconi to enter. Three reasons to run the Race: - 1. To give Club cat and fast dinghy sailors the chance to compete against the very best. 2. Run a flagship Event which fixes our Club firmly where it belongs in the forefront of British sailing. 3. To make money for the two charities we support. January 2019 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk I am pleased to report that we made almost double the profit of last year mainly due to generous donations of product from Adnams and Mighty Oak breweries and a large increase in sponsorship from GJW the Club’s insurers.The profit of over £5,000 has been distributed to our two charities, The Cirdan Sailing Trust and Essex Air Ambulance. The undoubted success of this Event is due almost entirely to the many members of the Club who freely give up their time to plan and execute the organisation. All sections of the Club contribute, but none more so than the Cruiser section. The work of mother boats and matriarchs both in giving physical aid and spotting the position of competitors along the course is invaluable. Your work not only gives reassurance to the organisers that we are in full control but also gives competitors confidence they are being looked after. My heartfelt thanks go to everyone who has given their time, effort and expertise. Cruiser racing – Peter Ward BJRC race one day 7 boats in 2 classes. IRC class (international rating system) and Wilco handicap system which is adjusted to give everyone a chance of achieving a win. In the IRC we were pipped to a win by ‘Evolution’ out of Maylansea Bay Club. ‘Monkey Business’ finished in 2nd overall with 3 points behind ‘Evolution’. ‘Blue Moon’ was in 3rd place with 12 points, McGregor was 4th and ‘Ned Kelly’ had 26 points. These are series wins and the club has had some race wins this year. The Marconi Cup was won by ‘Monkey Business’ this year and will awarded at the dinner in February next year. They also won the MarineStore ‘Shipmate’ Trophy and the ‘Challenge Cup. ‘Blue Moon’ had one race win the last race of the series and ‘Mcgregor’ won the first race of the series. In the BJRC handicap ‘Evolution’ also won on the local adjusted handicap system and Mcgregor was in 4th position , ‘Blue Moon ’ 5th place, ‘Monkey Business’8th ‘Ned Kelly’ in their first series with a new skipper Alana Clark was in 14th position and possibly will win the ‘rabbit’ trophy for the highest sailing new skipper. The trophies in the BJRC event Andrew/Caroline?? in a very windy race 5 winning the ‘Stone’ rose bowl, ‘Blue Moon’ winning the ‘Blue Mark’ trophy and for the first time in many years Marconi won the team race. ‘Blue Moon’ ‘McGregor’ and ‘Crazy Suzy’ made up the team. 2 trophies we have for the best positioned Marconi boat in the BJRC series. The winner for the IRC series is ‘Monkey Business’ Autumn series 7 boats and joined new long keel boat ‘Diana’. Lost one day due to ‘Barts Bash’ where it was extremely windy but had 5 races which were tightly fought to the end. Trophies awarded at the end of the series. It was close between ‘Blue Moon’ and ‘Monkey business’. As Dave was away he invited some previous cadets to sail ‘ Monkey Busness’ and just trounced everyone. Last of the year is discard race at double points and ‘Blue Moon’ just pipped ‘Monkey Business’ by 1 point overall in the series. Dan Dangerfield was awarded the trophy and Mike Turner with the ‘Crewmans’ trophy. 7.Mast Derrick and Scrubbing Richard Roberts All went well this year. No double bookings. 8.Moorings and haul out – Peter Clayton General report same as last year but going forward some amendment to the way we do things. Since taking over the mooring matrix hasn’t been changed regarding the spacing between moorings and boats are getting bigger. Propose to increase the spacing on A row to put the bigger boats out and to bring the lighter boats together. Will be as fair as possible moving between A row and B row and up and down the rows. Also been looking at 3 year cycling the moorings. At the moment we lift and relay everything every year, on retrieval this year we have had problems with the hydraulic system and are about 10 moorings behind schedule. More sessions will have to be included and very weather dependant. To try and reduce our work in future from next spring is to relay C row and leave in for 3 years, at end of season leave C row and lift B then following year relay B row and leave for 3 years and then A row would follow the sa me. So every year taking out just one row of moorings rather than all rows. When the mooring has been down for 12 months we will lift onto the centre of the barge for the owner to come and inspect and together look if any new chain needed. We haven’t had any mooring gear failures for several years now, the gear is getting better. We will do the inspection for C row next spring a week early. This will formalised in some sort of report. Several areas logistically we need to address, changing boat, moving or n eeding to retrieve/relay due to deterioration. We will pick the riser up down to the ground chain, inspect the bit of ground chain we can see and full inspection on the risers/buoys. At this point owners may want to take strops off for the winter. Still set up 3 sessions but instead of trying to get 20 moorings up or more, we will only be scheduled to lift about 10 on the tide so the team is under less pressure. Any shackles would be replaced on the water, if the whole riser needed replacing we would prep it ashore and take it out and attach it on the water. The ground anchors are the responsibility of the owners and we wouldn’t be laying any that has any doubt on the condition. There are anchors that have been down 40 years but they do have a shelf life. Retrieval of moorin g buoys and putting a temporary rope on the riser causes problems as they are more vulnerable to being lost and having to be recovered by a grapple. You can’t guarantee you get in the middle and could hook into the wrong mooring. Most problems used to be with the shackles but changing the source that problem has gone away over the last few years. Recommendations of new chain or new rope if leaving in for 3 years. New chain definitely but rope does not deteriorate so much other than chafing. If you protect against this they will last. Problems last year were EYE did not put protection around the hard eye, leaving the outside of the rope exposed. When it went slack the bottom of the rope was chafing so make sure they put protection around it before splicing up. Blow up buoys are subject to deflation and if they have damage they will deflate. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk 2018 Commodore’s Report to the AGM Michaela Dowley 25th November 2018 Good morning and welcome all to the 2018 Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting. This report will comment on the main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season. Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board of Directors, and for the previous year has comprised these six people: Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing Liz Kirby - Rear Commodore for events Sue Shenton - Treasurer Myself, Michaela Dowley - as Commodore I have been managing director and chair Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of the administrative burden of the Club. I can report that the Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like again to extend thanks to all those who take the time to serve on the main and various sub committees. It has been another exceptionally busy year for us both in terms of activities, events and also in projects and developments around the Club. My final report as Commodore will focus on those successes and set out our plans for the coming year. I am very pleased to report that our current membership stands at 445. This compares to around 436 in 2017 and 430 in 2016. We are now a little unsure of the accuracy of the 2016-2017 figures so in fact we think this is an even bigger increase that it seems. At our most recent management meeting no-one round the table could remember a time where membership levels were this high. This is a true achievement at a time where sailing clubs all around the country are struggling to maintain their membership levels. I went to a club conference yesterday where some clubs were discussing their minimum membership number required to stay afloat. This increase in membership hasn’t happened by chance and is thanks to our continual drive to move forwards within Marconi. From encouraging younger members onto our committees to running exceptional open days and building our training centre to name a few examples. Without stealing all the material from the sailing secretary’s report, some of our on the water highlights include: regular sail training, the East Coast Piers Race in July, Cadet week in August, our first RYA dinghy training courses being delivered, Topper National Series Event in September, Marconi leg of the Harkers yard gig racing in October, the Marconi keelboat championship held at Queen Mary in October and the massive increase in use of our club kayaks and stand up paddle boards. Everywhere we look there have been more and more opportunities for members to get out on the water. I would like to say a couple of specific thank yous. First to Clive Shenton, who has been Race Chairman of the East Coast Piers Race for the past 14 years. Clive, along with the ECPR committee have worked tirelessly over the years to keep this event running. It continues to be an internationally recognised event with competitor numbers increasing where many similar events are being scaled down and even cancelled. This is a testament to Clive’s commitment to the race and our charities, the Cirdan Sailing Trust January 2019 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk and Essex Air Ambulance whom we continue to support. Clive has been a driving force behind the fairly recent inclusion of dinghies into the race, which has served to further enhance the event. In addition I would like to recognise the team who organised the Topper National series event in September. This group was headed up by Adam Ferneyhough and Lee Harrison. It was an amazing feat and really has put Marconi firmly on the map as a venue that can host big events as well as being a friendly, welcoming club to. I would also like to say thank you to Liz Kirby for organising the 2018 open day which was another huge success and to Kevin Stubbs for orchestrating the recent Harkers Yard gig event in October. Finally, I would also like to extend our thanks to Tom Clayton who is standing down at this AGM as Sailing Secretary. Tom has been a breath of fresh air in this role and has run the sailing sub and supported Pat as Rear Commodore of Sailing in his own unique way. He is a man who is truly invested in every fleet in the club, being a keen rower, cruiser and dinghy owner and has been instrumental in progressing some of our recent sailing developments. Tom has also been responsible for keeping us all up to date with the weekly emails and he will be a hard act to follow. So, we have had a lot going on at the Club this year. We are being recognised nationally for our progressive efforts - in March of this year we were a runner up in the RYA Club of the Year competition and winner of the Innovation category, for which we had great publicity and got to take home a lovely shiny trophy at the RYA Dinghy Show. This was on the back of our efforts in keelboat sailing. The RYA are so impressed by us that they came down to make a video about our endeavours with keelboat sailing in August, which you can find on you-tube. As well as making the video we also gave interviews about how and why we think our club is so great. They were fact finding to see how we run our website and marketing, and how we are managing to increase our membership year on year when other clubs are struggling. So we are obviously onto a good thing. Sailing You may have noticed during the course of 2018 that we have expanded our offerings in terms of our RYA training centre. We have successfully run RYA dinghy sailing courses this year, which is something that was only a pipe-dream 5 years ago. We’ve come a really long way. This is thanks to our training centre team lead by Bob Collins and our head Instructors Jen Miller, Rhiannon Hitt and Pat Shaw. We also ran a female only dinghy instructor course during the summer so we are growing our own instructors, which is just great. As well as new courses we continue to train people in first aid and powerboats. In fact, to date, Pat has successfully qualified 53 members for powerboat 2, which is a huge achievement. So well done to all those involved. The RYA training centre runs alongside our ‘in house’ sail-training programme, which under the direction of John Nickalls continues to go from strength to strength. Huge attendance numbers and plenty of help from qualified and non-qualified instructors have been common this year. I believe that this balance of formal and informal training is one of our greatest strengths in terms of making new sailors and generating members here at Marconi, and I am sure this will continue to be the case. Cadet week is obviously the training highlight of the year and this year a new team took the reins. Here I would like to award the Commodores trophy to Dan Bard and Jemma Clarke. Dan and Jemma had big shoes to fill and they did a sterling job in running cadet week alongside Dave Clarke for over 100 of our young and slightly more mature cadets. As well as cadet week they are also involved in race results and support boat rotas and always around supporting sail training. They are a great example of younger members taking on responsibility in the Club and I am very pleased to present them with this award. January 2019 Navigans 17

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk I would now like to present the seamanship award. This is award is usually presented to someone who has, in the opinion of the Board performed an act of outstanding seamanship. In the past this has been awarded to sailors competing at international events, multiple Atlantic crossings, significant race or regatta wins etc. This year we would like to present the award to one of our newer members, Karen Corely. Karen came to the club with little sailing experience and in a few years has managed to take part in sailing activities in every single one of our fleets. She is a regular attendant at sail training, participant in cadet week, crew on Marconi cruisers, helper at ECPR and even had the pleasure of my company in the race box as an assistant RO. Karen has been involved in every aspect of club life and is now getting ready to take part in 2 legs of the Clipper Round the World race - pretty impressive for someone who has only been sailing for a couple of years. The cruiser fleet have had great success in local racing as well as further afield and have had a number of planned cruises this year. Here we would like to present the Mamgu trophy for best log to Bob Whittaker for his report of his voyage through the French canals. Returning to the UK, our dinghy fleets have also been travelling, most notably the Sprint 15s who have been to Weymouth, Grafham, Draycote and most recently Stone to name a few. They travel on mass with their distinctive purple t-shirts and have been scoring some great results. Within the club, the Sprint fleet are incredibly active with high regular numbers for club racing. From the outset Jenny Ball has orchestrated the revival of this fleet, both within the club and in terms of our sailors attending TT events. Regular communication, support of new sailors in the fleet and helping novices in their first traveller events are just some of her initiatives that have worked wonders. In view of her continued success and dedication to this area of club sailing I would like to award Jenny the Barograph trophy in recognition of going above and beyond for the Club. We have also seen enormous growth in the use of our club paddle-boards, windsurfs and kayaks. We have expanded our fleet to 4 kayaks, 2 SUPs and 2 windsurfers that can be paddled. During the wonderful long hot summer these were heavily used and have provided a great alternative for days when we can’t sail due to lack of wind. They have also been a great way to get our non-sailing members out on the water. To complete my round up of on the water activities I would like to mention keelboat sailing, which was something we only really dipped our toes in the water with in 2017. After some success/participation in the British Keelboat league in 2017 we entered another team in 2018. Peter Ward organised a keelboat league hosted by Queen Mary sailing club early in the season. Unfortunately, this event was cancelled due to lack of wind, however 45 competitors and race officials from the Club made the journey to compete in the rearranged event on a wet and windy October Saturday. It was a fantastic day, all be it a bit wet and has affirmed our member’s appetite for this type of sports boat, team racing. In light of our recent initiatives around keelboat sailing we purchased our own racing keelboat, an SB20, which has been a great addition to the club. The boat has been heavily used and although she suffered some quite severe damage recently, we hope to have her repaired and back out on the water over the winter. As well as the SB20 we have added to our growing fleet of club boats over the course of 2018 and these are available to all of our members. Capital projects There have been a number of projects undertaken during the year under the careful management of Murray and his team. To note is the Bridge Deck, which has been used as a race management centre for ECPR, race box for BJRC, rowing events and some club racing. It provides an excellent view of the whole river and is fully equipped to manage racing events. As part of this project we have also created a further boat store underneath to help house some equipment for the club boats, the idea being to make sails and January 2019 Navigans 18

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk spars for these boats more accessible. Another project completed this year is the updating of the upstairs saloon where we are sitting today. We have invested in new tables, chairs, décor and kitchenette area. We think this was an essential upgrade to our facilities as the previous set of tables and chairs were in a pretty dire state. I hope you agree that it has made a positive difference to the look and feel of the club. It is impossible to cover all of our projects and activities in this one report. However, I would just like to take a moment to thank our outgoing team of ‘social divas’ who have worked really hard over the past few years to put on some fantastic social events. Also changing for 2019 is our galley manager as Tina steps aside after over a decade of involvement in running the galley. We said a big thank you to Tina at her last event a few weeks ago. I think we can all agree that no one felt unwelcome in our galley during her tenure. 2019 Although I am stepping down as Commodore at this AGM, I would like to take the opportunity to talk to you about our plans for 2019, as these have been in discussion for quite some time. After a few years of experiencing a very cramped social space in the Mamgu bar, we have taken the decision to knock through downstairs to expand the bar area by at least the same size again. The plan is to create a multi-purpose room for both training and social use, as usually these two activities do not take place at the same time. On the back of a members’ survey carried out a few years ago, we have also decided to add a veranda to the northern aspect of the clubhouse, overlooking the river. This is something that we know the membership have been asking for and we are excited about this addition to the club’s premises. This project is in the early stages but we plan to carry out works during 2019. We also hope to expand our fleet of keelboats and will be looking towards grant funding and sponsorship opportunities to help finance these purchases. We also know that we cannot be complacent with our membership numbers and will continue to drive forward with new initiatives that we believe will make our Club more attractive to new members. We will also work hard to make sure we retain members. We have created a new role on the management committee of ‘new members liaison’ as we are aware that there has been a gap in this area - it’s really important that we keep new members engaged and integrate them into club life. Finally, I would just like to reflect on my 9-year term on the Board, the past 5 serving as Commodore. Starting at the beginning. I was a fresh faced 23/24-year-old just back from a gap year traveling round the world having completed a degree in Biochemistry the year before, when I took a surprise call from Simon Elwell. All I can say is that flattery will get you everywhere. As Commodore at the time, Simon had already managed to recruit some of my ‘millennial’ friends onto the management committee as a webmaster and social secretary and to be honest, I felt a bit left out. Simon told me there was a vacancy for Rear Commodore on the Board and knowing I was looking for a job, he said with great authority that it would be an excellent addition to my CV and I was just the type of person he was looking for. I had a lot of respect for Simon and although the world of biochemistry and helping to run a sailing club are miles apart, I did as he suggested and joined the Board. 9 years later (thanks Simon) and the club is almost unrecognisable, yet is still the same. Providing stability have been people such as Murray and Peter on the Board and the likes of Simon, Clive, Pat and Mike on the main committee, making sure we never strayed from the real ethos of our much-loved club. As a team we have achieved a huge amount over the past 5-10 years. We are no longer a cruiser club and dinghy club operating separately, but I think we are truly getting towards being fully integrated. January 2019 Navigans 19

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk We have an RYA training centre, our own in-house sail training programme, new, modern club boats, a vibrant social scene, kayaks, paddleboards, a rowing gig, national recognition for our new initiatives in sailing and a growing membership. Key interests were around the website and our use of social media, how we generated interest in keelboats and how we have managed to make sure our committees reflect the diversity within the club itself. On reflection it was a proud day as I could honestly tell the some of our large, neighbouring clubs that we haven’t just happened across any of these successes, they have taken years of strategic planning and work by our dedicated group of volunteer committee members. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk 2018 Sailing Secretary’s Report to the Agm Hi all, Well another year has passed and another season is over as I find myself once again in front of you to deliver my report as Sailing Secretary although sadly this will be my last one, for a while at least, I promise nothing! It’s been a fantastic year of sailing once again and it is now my pleasure to share with you what has been going on outside of your own experiences. There have been fewer changes this year but some of those changes have of course not been without controversy. We like to make sure that everyone is still awake and as such reversed the order of starts on Sunday dinghy racing. Mostly so that we stood a chance of being on time for the start but also it meant that there was less crossover between the fleets. The dinghy and cat racing fleets are still well supported and the extended season has meant that we’ve all had some good racing. The Solo fleet is still quite strong and the Sprint 15 fleet continues to grow, the medium cat fleet has less Dart 18s out racing sadly. The Sprint 15’s haven’t let the lack of organised racing at MSC stop them sailing and have been seen sailing down river to join in the polar series at Stone Sailing club, it’s great to see inter club collaboration. This year’s Open Day was seamlessly carried out by Liz and seemed to be even more successful than ever. There were lots of new sailors that came along on that day. Many new members took part in Cadet Week and have joined us regularly for our Sail Training days. These have also seen record numbers attending this season, with the adults joining in as well; all these are good signs for the future. The adult learners, or Turtles as they are known, these are a rapidly expanding group of adults who are showing great enthusiasm for learning to sail. They are so enthusiastic that there’s talk of them honing their skills during the winter months. We have had many graduates of this programme throughout the years and it really looks like there is a bright future for them, and the club going forward. The Training centre side of things continues to progress. We have trained up yet more Powerboat drivers under Pat’s careful tutelage and the dinghy courses were also a great success with many of the new members taking up these courses as introductions to sailing. Many thanks should go to both Bob Collins, as Training centre principal and Jenny Miller, who has taken over from Rhiannon Hitt as Chief Instructor, for running this aspect of club life. The Cruiser sailing fleet have had a full season of trips, this year venturing across the North Sea before the borders come down! Thankfully they made it back in time to provide their invaluable help with the ECPR as Mother Boats keeping an eye on the Cats & Dinghies as they race to Walton pier and back. There have also been the traditional rallies around the East Coast to Brightlingsea, to Ipswich and beyond although I believe he’s looking for more to join him on Rob’s tours …. It should be noted that Rob has gladly accepted Pete Clayton’s offer of organising the mother boats for the piers race and will this year be bringing this back under his role as Cruiser fleet captain. The Cruiser Racing fleet have seen a buoyant year of racing in the BJRC championship, which has seen a good turn out from Marconi boats with Monkey Business 2nd in the IRC championship and Blue Moon 3rd. The Autumn series was also well supported and went to Blue Moon in a close fought battle with Monkey Business taking it by only one point in the last race. Ned Kelly the club’s own cruiser, this year skippered by Lana, came home solidly mid fleet in 14th place of 28 starters. The British Keelboat League or BKL for short, saw us again send a team to compete in the local qualifier in Burnham and put in a sterling effort for a scratch team with very little experience sailing together. As a result of the interest drawn by the BKL Peter Ward organised a Keelboat championship for the beginning of the season to blow the cobwebs off. 12 teams headed to Queen Mary Reservoir in balmy April conditions but sadly the memo of wind didn’t make it and instead we sat waiting for the sea breeze to kick in. It was a long wait! Thankfully it was rescheduled and instead took place in the polar opposite conditions, good wind but pouring rain! It was really close racing and very little separated the teams at the front, it came right down to the wire with the youthful team of Nickalls and Jacks taking it. It was great to see so many people from different parts of the club competing against each other. There have been a number of opens held at the club this year, with Sprint 15’s visiting in April, the Larks in May and the bi g one the Toppers visiting in September for the first of their National series events. 148 sailors descended on us of which a couple of MSC members also competed. It was a great event generating income and positive publicity for the club. Of course we also had the East Coast Piers Race, another good year with great conditions for Saturday but Sunday was a little light for the start which meant that a lot of competitors had to be towed to the start line. But thankfully it filled in towards the end to create a great race. Bart’s Bash sadly had to be cancelled this year, and it’s the last time I trust a long range forecast of 2 days. Pretty much as soon as the joint decision to cancel happened the forecast improved, the 60 Mph winds disappeared and were replaced with pouring rain. So although it wouldn’t have been a particularly pleasant race it would have been manageable, ho hum hindsight is a wonderful thing. Colin Wardell’s dinghy cruises are still a popular feature of the sailing calendar. They’ve been on voyages from the club to any pub that is willing to serve them, they had to go as far afield as the West Solent this year! The quest to find the perfect pint continues and they will again be out next weekend when the cruiser members are lifting their moorings. Hardy Souls! January 2019 Navigans 26

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The windsurfers continue to venture out when most have given up all hope of sailing, and they have been using the excellent club kit to train up others in the hope that they also get the bug! These training sessions have been oversubscribed throughout the year even if the wind wasn’t so enthusiastic. Thanks to Nick and Vince for making sure these sessions went ahead. Lots of our sailors have been travelling up and down the country for various open meetings and national championships. The Sprint 15s had their Nationals at Weymouth with 11 MSC members taking part and bringing home the Team trophy, with the best overall results being Jenny Ball in 2nd and David Ball in 6th, special mention should go to Jason Clarke who finished 24th out of 45. The Tornadoes visited Brightlingsea for their Nationals and Andrew & Tom came home in 3rd with Marconi locking out 4th and 5th behind them. Dan Nickalls and Jack Wardell also attended their first event in their RS800, tackling the RS Games which was massive festival of all things RS and all their classes descending on Weymouth, well done to them. I hope you’ve been enjoying the weekly emails as I try to keep you up to date with what’s been going on or is about to happen. It’s not always easy keeping up with what you guys are doing as so much is happening but there is always something different to report on every week. Sadly however you may have heard the last of them from me as I move on to other literary endeavours, but they shall continue and I’m sure keep as entertained. And lastly as I draw to a close my report on what has been such a fantastic 4 years I must say a big thank you to all who have helped. There are so many of you in the background and the foreground that have made this so successful and our jobs more manageable. I honestly wouldn’t have been able to do it without you! Although this report is meant to sum up a year of sailing activity at Marconi, of course it can only be a brief snapshot of the events that have taken place. Here’s to 2019 - let’s hope it’s a good one! I’m going to have a nap! But please don’t Forget the Raffle for the RNLI £5 a strip £2 a ticket! The draw will be shortly before/after the prizegiving. January 2019 Navigans 27

WILDLIFE AT STANSGATE – ADDERS We share our site at Stansgate with a variety of wildlife. Indeed, it is their home whereas we only pop in from time to time. As the weather warms up adders will be coming out of hibernation and will be on the move. They will mind their own business as long as they are left alone. Be aware for example when reaching under boats or when walking in long grass where they may be basking. The younger members of your party should be warned. WILDLIFE AT STANSGATE – RATS For your own protection against being bitten be very careful when moving anything that could be hiding a rat’s nest. Obvious things are upturned boats, boats themselves if hatch covers have been left off, boat covers, piles of wood, trailers and anywhere else that might form a cosy nesting place for rodents. Warn your family, particularly younger members, who may move a boat without thinking. As well as the risk of being bitten the other danger when rats have been near standing water (puddles on boat covers or on the ground for example) is Well’s Disease. Well’s Disease is caused by rats’ urine in water. (There is a lot of information about Well’s Disease online.) Where there is water that has a high risk of rat infestation take great care not to ingest the water or let any wounds come into contact with it. The most effective way to protect yourself from Weil's disease is to avoid contact with infected water. However, there are steps you can take to lower your risk of infection. if you have cuts do not allow them to be submerged in the water; never swallow water unsuitable for drinking; wash all equipment and clothing in clean water; clothing that can survive bleaching should be disinfected or bleached to kill the bacteria; if you have a wound always use clean fresh water to clean wounds as soon as possible RACE OFFICER GUIDE The Race Officer Guide (MSCP13) has been revised and reissued. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Saturday dawned with a decent breeze, albeit with very murky weather conditions – but very welcome after the very strong winds experienced this winter. With the tide running against us – we were in for a weekend of clear starts. Race 1 got underway at a good pace with half the fleet tacking into the bay to find the slacker tide – and the other half opting to go up the lay line in stronger tide, but with more constant wind. Paul Grattage headed inshore first and although he had to put in an extra two tacks, rounded the windward mark first. Jenny Ball and Liam Thom tacked when they ran out of water and fortunately, this turned out to be a good line to clear the mark. Others who stood on further in the bay found the breeze got a bit softer whilst those who had gone up the middle found they were putting in extra tacks to clear the mark against the tide – so there was all to play for on the upwind legs, whilst the downwind leg were more straightforward. Paul held his lead to win, with Jenny second, Liam third and David Ball in fourth in a pattern that would repeat itself. Jon Pearse, Jim Bowie and Gordon Deuce were close behind. Race 2 got away swiftly with a similar pattern on the upwind leg. By the second lap, the front runners were opting to stay closer to the lay line, avoiding the softer winds right inshore and taking advantage of a slight lift off the shore about ten boat lengths from the windward mark. At the end of Race 2 Paul took first place, with Jenny second, Liam third and David fourth – followed by Jim, Steve Healy and Jon. There was then a slight pause to re-lay the windward mark for Race 3, during which Geoff Tindale kept everyone entertained by capsizing and getting his mast stuck in the mud. Race 3 was the legendary long distance race – a figure of eight course around Osea and Northey Islands. Following a short windward leg, the fleet turned at the mark and started the fetch up towards Maldon. The tide had started to turn so some of the fleet headed closer to the island but experienced more fickle wind so those who had stayed clear of the lee of the island fared better. By the end of Osea Island, Paul had created a solid lead which proved unassailable for the rest of the race. Behind him were Liam, David, Simon Hare, Gordon in the middle with Jenny, Jason Clarke and Kevin Kirby closer to shore. The fleet then turned and ran down the back of Northey Island - Liam and Simon rounded the far end of the island and crossed the causeway behind Paul and followed by Jenny, David, Gordon and Steve Healy. A little further back, some fleet members got a bit brave about which side they were going to leave the Causeway markers. Andy Perks rudders bumped the causeway – and everyone around him laughed until theirs did the same. Keith Chidwick later complained Jenny’s briefing said they would definitely clear the causeway – until it was pointed out to him she meant if you aimed at the bit that actually had water over it. The breeze had filled in nicely and was now against the tide, so conditions were a bit more choppy. The fleet stood on from the end of Northey Island and then cut across the channel to the other side of Osea Island – everyone carefully monitoring how others were faring on their different lay lines. Jenny tacked earlier at the end of Osea island, cutting the corner and catching up with Liam but with David, Steve and Gordon were catching up further out in the stronger tide and wind. Jenny put in another tack back out into the channel and just did enough to get ahead of Liam who followed in close pursuit all the way to the finish line. June 2019 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The final result was – you guessed it – Paul first, Jenny second, Liam third, David fourth with Gordon, Steve and Jim behind. Despite the race lasting over an hour, the fleet saw some remarkably close finishes. The fleet waved goodbye to Abbie Clarke, Geoff Tindale and Rob Wilson who sailed back to their neighbouring home club at Stone and then headed in for a well deserved dinner with plenty of good racing to talk about and looking at the more promising wind forecast for Sunday morning which was finally showing a bit more than 2 knots. On Sunday, there was indeed a decent breeze, albeit another grey and murky day. The Race team started laying the course but the wind unexpectedly died to nothing and with the typical Blackwater tide, the Race Officer decided to delay the start of the race and move the race course further out of the main channel. This proved to be wise as the wind filled back in again but from a slightly different direction which allowed the course to be set accordingly although a final shift at a minute to go made for an interesting start. A group of the fleet had opted for a port hand start whilst others started on starboard and then tacked off. The rain had caused everyone’s tell tales to stick to the sail making it tricky to find good boat speed in a light breeze against the tide. Jenny tacked first for the mark but it became clear she was not going to make it with the tide so the rest of the fleet stood on further. In the meantime, Steve Healy had headed straight up the middle of the river, tacked round the mark into a clear lead. Behind him, only David cleared the mark to go into a solid second place whilst even those who had stood on had to tack back one or more times and/or hit the mark. Paul, Liam, Jenny, Aaron Kirby, Jim, Kevin and Jon rounded in a bunch, although there were a few penalty turns to be done on the way to mark 2. Paul, Liam and Jenny set off in pursuit of Steve and David. On the penultimate lap, Liam and Jenny got a better breeze by standing further out. David tacked out to join them whilst Paul stood on – which allowed Liam and Jenny to move into second and third place with David and Paul fighting out a photo finish. But a great win for Steve. Newcomer, Abbie Clarke also fared well in the lighter breeze putting in an impressive 15th place behind fellow Stone sailor Rob Wilson and Shanklin’s Yvonne Pike – both of whom are also relative newcomers to the Sprint 15. The Race Officer re-set the course to take account of the new wind direction for Race 5 and again the fleet opted for a mixture of port and starboard starts. Gordon, Jon and Jason got great starts at the pin end and with the windward mark now on the far side of the channel, off the Osea shore, the fleet split significantly up the beat. Those who took the left hand side of the course fared better over the tide but this was offset by coming into the mark on port and having to duck the incoming boats on starboard. However, some of those coming in on starboard had misjudged the tide and either had to double tack or risk bumping into the mark. Gordon took the early lead but the upwind legs became the defining elements of Race 5 with places changing each lap and at least three different leaders during the course of the race. On the final upwind leg, a lift enabled Jenny to get inside of Liam and Gordon and get to the mark on starboard as Paul came in on port. Jenny just about held on to take the race win with Paul second, Gordon third, Liam fourth and Steve fifth. The fleet headed home after a great weekend of sailing! Big thanks go to the Race Officers, Race Committee and Support boat crews for setting up and delivering five great races in conditions that were cold, and at times, wet! Congratulations to: Abbie Clarke – winner of the New Comer Award – her first TT having only moved from a Topper to a Sprint 15 late last season! The catering was first class, especially the chocolate cake; it was worth the trip just for that. The early arrivals on Saturday were able to examine the effects of several force 9 squalls on the River Blackwater and were grateful not to be racing until Sunday. The fleet launched on Sunday into the forecast 10-12kt wind and prepared to do battle with wind and tide running perpendicularly to each other. Glenn Enkel and Julie Bachelor shot off into the lead chased by the Denchfield pairing. The Enkel boat pulled away for a comfortable win, which was to be the pattern for most races. Worthy of note was the performance of a very old Baker built Lark in the hands of club sailors Andy Perks and Sara Townsend. Race 2 wasn't quite a repeat run. The wind decided to do its own thing and rose to 18-22kt, creating some interesting water conditions for the run, especially where it crossed the main channel. Simon Cox crewed by 9 year old son George got into his stride, and took second place behind the flying Enkel boat. Race 3 began in similar wind, and whilst Enkel sailed away to secure 1st, Dave Russell and Clare Clarke found the go button and for most of the race were ahead of the Denchfields. The final run proved to be Dave's undoing and some good use of the tide allowed the Denchfields by. Race 4 was sailed in fewer breezes, but that didn't matter to the Enkel/Bachelor pairing, they picked up their 4th win of the day. Ashore, after a splendid roast dinner, the Larkies took part in a club social featuring a 80s quiz. We were hampered though by the lack of questions about Lark sailors in the 1980s. The final two races took place on Monday. Race 5 saw Enkel/Batchelor take a 5th win, chased home by the Coxes. The final race saw great excitement at the start with 4 Larks all aiming at the same patch of water at the tide biased starboard end of the line much to the amusement of the Cox boat that was clear of the ensuing carnage. The Denchfields were the recipients of two Larks barging in from windward whilst the third baled out. We won't say whose fault it was, but the Enkel boat was the first of the two to begin penalty turns. This allowed the Cox boat to take an early lead which much to young George's delight they held to the finish. Many thanks to Marconi for hosting a fun weekend that provided very different sailing conditions to the usual. June 2019 Navigans 13

Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk Nick Tovey You may have heard by now that Nick Tovey sadly passed away on 16th March 2019 aged 82. His funeral was held at St Andrews Church, Sandon, Chelmsford on 9th April and it was so nice to see a so many past and present members of Marconi Sailing Club attend. Thank you all very much for coming long. He was born and brought up in Surrey, Nr Guildford but came to Essex when he became an apprentice at Marconi Communications in the late 50’s. He lived with his new wife Daphne in Bicknacre. Their first child Fenella was born the year after they got married, then Peter a couple of years later. They later moved to Howe Green, Sandon where they lived for over 50 years. As a child part of his family owned a holiday house on the beach at Tankerton, Whitstable (called “Kiora”) where they all spent many happy summer holidays and this is where he learnt to sail. On our last visit to the area he related a story of helping to shunt steam engines in the coal yard beside Whitstable Harbour. As part of the Marconi Athletic and Social club there was a newly formed sailing section which he joined in 1959, picking up his new boat, an Enterprise (sail number EK 2353) also called “Kiora” on the same day as his Wife and new daughter, who was 10 days old, had been discharged from hospital. So after a few hours interval Fenella was introduced to the sailing club alongside his new boat. Daphne and Nick enjoyed many years of racing their Enterprise both at the club and at open meetings. Nick was also very active in the running of the club being made Sailing Secretary in 1963 and 64. This was the time when the club moved from the Barge “Mangu” at Heybridge to the current site at Stansgate in Steeple. He alongside his fellow committee members were responsible for the original lay out of the new club site including setting up the Race box, the mete and the di nghy park (now the cruiser park) and for the original laying out of the moorings, the foot prints of which remain today. He went on to become the Rear Commodore in 1965 for 3 years, then again in 1972. He was Vice Commodore in 1966, then a Vice President from 1970 to 1992. Nick and Daphne forged many longstanding friendships though their activities at the club. June 2019 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk By this time Nick has moved from Dinghies to Cruisers. His first cruiser was a Vivacity 20 called “Persephone” which he bought as a kit and fitted out himself, He went on to own a Westerly Jouster ( 21 ft) “Janthena” which he and his family sailed to France, Belgium and Holland in for 3 weeks. Nick, Daphne, Fenella and Peter spent many happy summers sailing up and down the East coast on various different boats. There was one occasion coming back from Ramgate they had to cross the Thames estuary in fog. Nick was able to navigate with very limited electronic equipment by taking echo sounding and managed to predict precisely when the Boat in front of them (Vic Tate’s “ Snow Goose”) was going to go aground on Black Tail Spit, on the edge of the Maplin Sands – she did! His great seamanship ultimately influenced the whole family in their own sailing careers. In later years Nick sailed “Northey” a classic ‘South Coast One design’ yacht with his friend Ian, and I am sure there could be many tales to be told there also! Outside of sailing Nick enjoyed bell ringing, eventually becoming Tower Captain at Sandon Church, where he and Daphne were very active in the Church community. They also had a love of dogs and was introduced to the Saluki breed by a friend of Daphne’s. They went on to show and breed a number of dogs, attending Crufts and many Championship shows across the country. As with all things they soon became involved in the committee and organisation of The Saluki and Gazelle Hound Club. Throughout this time Nick was still working for Marconi’s – now Marconi Radar, working on joint projects with the Royal Navy – which he loved. He would often go on Sea trials for the systems he was working on (mostly defence mechanisms) which at the time was all top secret. He would regale stories of having to do helicopter crash training and being hauled across to another ship while at sea using a harness, ropes and pulleys, suspended over the ocean! He retired from the Marconi’s in 2002 – a rare thing these days to stay working for the same firm for his entire career and was commended accordingly. He continued to attend the Church, ring bells at various local churches regularly, show dogs, and took great interest in the sailing antics of his children: Fenella Miller and Peter Tovey; and 5 grandchildren: Jennifer, Nicholas and Michael Miller, and Rebecca ( Leech) and James Tovey. He was immensely proud of every one of them and of all their respective partners who he warmly embraced into the family, attending three of their weddings in the last few years. It gave him great joy to see the family growing. He was always keen to know how the Sailing Club was developing and growing, and took great pleasure in watching the Wednesday evening racing in recent years. He lived his life to the full, making a difference to many people, in a quiet, modest and generous way, with a dry sense of humour and with paying great attention to detail in everything he did. He will be very much missed by all who had the privilege to know him and his legacy lives on in his extending family.
