Roger Mander (May 2019) The RYA Dinghy Level 1 Course – Start Sailing The RYA Dinghy Level 1 sailing course is designed to be an introduction to the sport of sailing. The course covers all you need to know to get afloat under supervision. Marconi Sailing Club are an RYA (Royal Yachting Association) training centre and offer the RYA Level 1, Level 2, First Aid and Powerboat courses to our members. THE SAILING COURSE Assumed knowledge: None Minimum duration: 2 days Minimum age: None (although under 14s may prefer to learn through the Youth Sailing Scheme) Course content: How to sail in all directions, including an awareness of launching and recovering Ability after course: Able to sail in light winds under supervision The RYA Level One course is for beginners who have done little or no dinghy sailing before. It is the first part of the RYA training scheme and its aim is to provide basic boat handling techniques and essential background knowledge. By the end of the course you will be able to sail safely under supervision. It is recommended that all participants consolidate this course with the RYA Level 2 (Basic Skills) course which gives you further skill to get out sailing proficiently on your own. WHAT WILL YOU COVER? You will cover a variety of topics both on and off the water. This will typically include: On Water: Sailing in all directions Turning the boat Confidence in the boat Capsize recovery Off Water – Knowledge in: Weather Tides Rules of the road Basic navigation June 2019 Navigans 17

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk East Coast Piers Race (ECPR) is a weekend of sailing held at Marconi Sailing Club in Essex, with all funds raised from entry and weekend activities going to chosen charities the Cirdan Sailing Trust and Essex Air Ambulance. ECPR 2019 was part three of the Allen Endurance Series. We’re pleased that so many boats pre-entered this year, it makes organising such a complex event much easier. The weekend kicked off early, with many competitors arriving onsite Friday to claim the best camping pitches and take full advantage of the stunning Essex sunshine to get boats rigged, tweaked and tuned ready for the weekend of racing. With several major competing events either side of ECPR we were glad to see the F18’s and RS800 fleet make small but strong turnouts to the event. DRINK MIGHTY OAK BEER, RAISE £££ FOR CHARITY Some keen sailors also opted for equipment test sails Friday afternoon, before settling down in the newly refurbished “Mamgu” bar for a pint (or three..) of Mighty Oak Brewery beer, who for the second year were incredibly generous in their donation of 7 firkins of beer (over 500 pints). All the funds raised from Mighty Oak’s excellent beers (at £2.50 a pint) going to charity. Of course, any socially conscious sailor can’t help but do their bit for charity in said scenario! SATURDAY RACING AROUND THE CANS Saturday morning saw many competitors still flooding in through the gates early, and lots of activity in the boat park to get ready for the afternoons racing around the cans. The Nacra 20 fleet turned up en-mass and dominated the boat park with length, width and height, making even a Tornado look small! Race briefing kicked off at 12:00 for the all-in Saturday races, with 43 boats competing. The breeze showed up and competitors were treated to good conditions. Race 1 turned into an epic 1 hour 45 minute marathon multi-lapper, in front of club, much to spectators and travelling family-member’s enjoyment. Race 2 was a considerably shorter affair to get everyone back for the #cometothebriefing for the Sunday long distance races. Overall Saturday winners in the Catamaran fleet and taking home the ‘Cool Cats’ trophy were Grant Piggott and Simon Farren on their Nacra F20 Carbon. Winner of the Dinghy fleet was Andrew Stickland in a Musto Skiff. As per the usual ECPR format, the race briefing for Sunday was held on Saturday evening due to the early race start on Sunday. This year was a particularly bleary eyed start of 8am… The briefing kicked off at 6pm with a full marquee of competitors keen to understand the 3 race courses available. To cater for dinghies up to 1046 PY and foiling catamarans the 3 race courses are 48 miles, 27 miles and 13 miles. ALLEN’S GENEROSITY GOES DOWN VERY WELL This year the race chairman, Andy Dowley, had a nice surprise to finish up the briefing on – Free beer! Race sponsors Allen, kindly contributed a £250 donation to cover the cost of 100 pints of the Mighty Oak charity fundraising beer. Inevitably there was the quickest exit from any race briefing, with possibly the most politest and orderly taking of free beer ever witnessed. Great job Allen and Mighty Oak, competitors and non-competitors saluted your generosity. Next up was the BBQ, getting our hungry sailors re-fuelled and ready for a night of live rock from, possibly the loudest band we have ever had a Marconi, Essex based ‘Stiff InThe Morning’. To say they rocked would be an understatement, they went down a storm, a personal favourite being their cover of ‘By the way’ by the Red Hot Chilli Peppers. THE SUNDAY LONG DISTANCE RACES The traditional ECPR wakeup call of ‘Sweet Caroline’ by Neil Diamond roused bleary-eyed sailors, much to the race organisers delight many boats were ready and waiting for the 06:30am opening of the hard and scrutineering. Due to the long distances of the races competitors have to take certain safety equipment with them and each boat is checked through the gate in the sea wall to ensure everything was present. The full distance East Coast Piers Race of 48NM started at 8am, with the fleet storming off, but the breeze was not going to last, and as the 27NM Colne Point Race exited the river so did the breeze. From that point on it was a case of finding and staying in the pressure, with mammoth holes appearing in the course. All races played like an accordion, compressing and expanding as they reached the front and back of the gusts along the course. The volunteers on the spotter mother boats moored along the course were treated to a slow but tight race. August/September 2019 Navigans 5

Andrew Dowley ECPR Chairman 30 Years on the Boards An event like ECPR involves a large number of volunteers performing all manner of vital jobs. Many of the volunteers have given many years of service. Here’s an inside story from two of them… Ed. Mike and I first manned the leader boards for the East Coast Piers Race in 1989. The control area then was upstairs in the clubhouse within a screened off area. This continued until 2001, Barbara Davies joining us in 1996. Not a lot changed in those years, reports came back from the “gates” via volunteers from the Territorial Army with old fashioned radios for a few years then by cadets using mobile phones. The large boards we used were revamped as they had been used by the club for many years at the Regatta which Marconi ran every May Bank Holiday. In 2001 the double decker bus was used as the control. It was driven to the club on the Friday evening after the school run and parked behind the sea wall at the end of the clubhouse. This gave us much more space and freed the clubhouse for increasing numbers of visitors using the galley. In the early years food was provided by a catering van outside the clubhouse. The three of us continued to work in the bus until 2018. In 2018 we were able to use the new race control which proved very good, great views of the Blackwater. So to 2019 our Swan Song! I think we have all enjoyed our years on the boards. We have seen the race develop from one race to Walton Pier and back to adding shorter Colne races for catamarans and monohulls and a Bradwell race. GPS tracking has been used and will in the not too distant future take over from the leader boards. There are also many other members involved in the running of the ECPR on the day and behind the scenes; preparations are already underway for 2020. Next year we will be watching from the sea wall, with binoculars but no pens or panic! Maggie Boreham August/September 2019 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Fleet News Keelboat GOALS SET & ACHIEVED! – A REPORT FROM OUR BKL TEAM The youth (U25) team for this event from stern to bow: Jack Collis, Daniel Nickalls, Jack Wardell and David Nickalls (author). Leading up to the weekend of the BKL qualifier we were fully aware of how under-prepared we were compared to the top teams competing. Making use of the club SB20 for a training day, we set ourselves two goals: Firstly, enjoy the event and come away with a ‘positive’ feeling. Secondly, come away in the top half with at least one race win. This would improve on our low finish and best result of second place from two years ago. We knew this goal would be hard, especially finishing in the top half. The format of the weekend was 11 teams competing in a round-robin, each sailing 12 races with 6 teams racing at a time. The racing was held at Royal Southern Yacht Club in RS21s. The weekend started with a glorious day, sun shining and a gentle force 3 blowing from the south. Champagne sailing conditions led to burnt shoulders and arms on both Jack Wardell and Jack Collis (known by the other teams as ‘vest-guy’; he was the only one in the entire fleer who dared to show his shoulders). The first race showed that our training had paid off, rounding the windward mark in second place. This was promptly shut down by a more experienced team turning up into our kite – red flag for us, penalty turns. We finished in fifth, feeling positive, but knowing that we still needed to learn a lot about keelboat racing. The next race saw an improvement, finishing third. Our third race saw a brilliant start, winning the pin end and sailing on for our first race win of the event – part of goal two achieved! We swapped off to watch some of the other teams compete. In the afternoon our first race started well, sailing clear ahead of all but one boat. The two lead boats were boat-on-boat the whole way round the course with the Royal Southern team (eventual champions) leaving us the wrong side of a port/starboard shut door on the final downwind. This tore a second race win from our grasp. We settled for second place and discussed how they managed to goose-wing faster downwind!? Clearly we are improving, but aren’t quite there yet. With a knot or two less wind the rest of the day our results didn’t improve. We managed to get one more second, losing out to the local team again! In this instance an August/September 2019 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk unfortunate umpire absence at a port/starboard incident inside the 3-boat length at the windward mark led to an ‘all-clear’ call. We felt this was an uncharacteristic mistake from an otherwise excellent race and umpire team – tough break. Our worst result of the day (and weekend) was a sixth (last), where we tried the ‘pro strategy’ of goose-winging to try to recover a place or two… it didn’t work out. Again, lots to learn! The second day was forecast for higher wind, but it did not appear! With only three races remaining we would have to push hard if we wanted to finish in the top half. The first race of the day did not go to plan. Shifty wind led to a biased committee boat start, one which we didn’t win. A heavy team in light air meant we struggled to regain places, only recovering one – thanks to a slick drop at the leeward mark. We finished that race with a fourth. Our tactics clearly had to change, we switched our focus to watching the wind, and choosing course tactics over boat-on-boat interactions. The second to last race of the day was another committee boat bias. We won the start and by this point had worked out that we were likely to be the second fastest boat in that fleet, the faster boat was (yet again) the locals! We hit the windward layline on starboard on a right-shift, forcing a port/starboard incident inside the zone, turns for them this time! We then sailed on to win the race. We watched, very impressed to see the Royal Southern team recover after their turns to finish in second, they’re a very quick team! The last race again had a heavy starboard bias, now with less wind and a building tide pushing us back from the line. After a poor pre-start we decided to start behind the fleet and tack off into a patch of wind on the right hand side of the course. With the wind further dropping into shifty patterns we followed our own race, gaining on all legs – both upwind and downwind (our previous Achilles heel). We eventually crossed the line first, an amazing way to finish the weekend, sailing from sixth to first! This would not have been achievable at the beginning of the weekend, showing just how much we’d all improved. Final result: 5th place, 3 race wins. Definitely fulfilled both targets. Individual race results: 531263245411 I’d like to thank Marconi on behalf of the team for their support in this event, it was an honour to be selected to represent the club. I also want to thank Royal Southern Yacht Club and RS, who made the event run very smoothly and welcomed us warmly. Thank you also Peter Ward, without your involvement and support MSC would have remained unrepresented at this event! David Nickalls MARCONI SC GRANT APPLICATION SUCCESSFUL Good News! Marconi SC have been successful in gaining a £10000 grant from Sport England towards our SB20 Keelboat Project. The project aims to secure the long term future of this type of sailing at the club by developing a fleet of boats. This follows the clubs commitment to this last season when an SB20 was purchased on a trial basis to gauge response. The response was overwhelmingly positive from all who managed to get out and sail the SB20. The grant enables the purchase of three more SB20s and the club will now be in a position to offer regular small fleet racing and one off events using these four boats. The award of the grant was the result of extensive work by Sue Shenton and the logistics involved in sourcing suitable boats and conveying them to the club has been taken on by Peter Ward. There is great support for this project from the board and the committee, it is intended to add an area of sailing to the club portfolio which up to now has been absent. The single SB20 which entered this year’s ECPR did quite well and came in second endorsing the suitability of these boats for our location. It’s planned that the boats purchased with the aid of the grant will arrive at the club shortly before Cadet Week and its hoped that the boats can be rigged and tested in order for them to be made available for organised sailing during camping fortnight. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Pioneer On 31st August, 11 Marconi sailors took a day trip on the Pioneer – a 70ft Essex Fishing Smack, the last of her kind, restored in recent years by the Pioneer Sailing Trust in Brightlingsea. Originally built in 1864 at Rowhedge, Pioneer was designed as a dredging fishing vessel, working out of Brightlingsea and dredging deep sea oysters. She was lengthened by 11ft in 1889 and a deep well was created which enabled her to travel further for her catch which could then be kept alive on the journey home – travelling around the British Isles and across to North Holland. She did not get an engine until 1929 but was decommissioned in 1939 and was used as a houseboat for just three years before she sank in the Strood Channel at Mersea Island. Fast forward to 1998 when an operation began to dig her out of the mud from where she was transported to Great Totham for a full refurb and rebuild and remarkably by 2004 she was fully restored, re-rigged and sailing again. And a very fine ship she is too. Pioneer is now moored off East Mersea and managed from Harkers Yard in Brightlingsea. In addition to restoring Pioneer, traditional boat building skills were rejuvenated at Harkers Yard who restore other traditional wooden boats and successfully built and re-introduced rowing gigs – including our very own Elettra. The Pioneer now takes primarily young people out sailing to learn the joys of being on the water and build new skills, confidence and make new friends and the boat yard continues to promote boat building skills, including recruiting apprentices each year. All of which was the perfect context for a group of Marconi sailors to book a day trip – Pete and Fen, Sam and Pat, Dave and Jenny, Dave, Clare and Jason and Gordon and Jane all turned up eager and ready for a great days sailing. We met with Carol, Lance and Brian who were going to look after us for the day and swiftly headed down to the launch to be taken out to Pioneer’ s mooring. It was a beautiful morning as we motored the length of Brightlingsea creek and across to East Mersea – bright and sunny but not much wind, although the forecast promised more to come. We were deposited on board and given a tour with various instructions – the most important of which was how to use the heads without breaking them - which of itself involved quite a work out using the manual pump. The next duty was to rig the mizzen, jib and staysail which involved most of us. Jenny however, disappeared below to fire up the cooker and the kettles. Which is just as well, because the wind shifted, all the sails had to be lowered again and we motored off the mooring – but at least we had tea and coffee. We motored out punching a strong spring flood – several of us had binoculars and were scanning the horizon to work out where any wind was and what direction it might fill in from. Meanwhile, Dave R, Jason and Pat got to work cooking vast quantities of bacon rolls. Once out in clear water, the mizzen, jib and stay sail were set (again) and we put Fen on the helm. Bacon rolls appeared and we were all very happy – although the wind was more reticent. But we thought it had appeared as we cut through the middle of a race course of racing cruisers at the Inner Bench Head buoy which happened to be their turning mark. So engine off and Jenny was put on the helm. And the wind basically went light and round in circles for the next two hours – or at least, that was Jenny’s excuse. Every time the breeze looked like it had filled in, it would back 30 degrees and then fall away. The only comfort was looking at all the other boats out on the water who were going through the same thing. Carol, the Skipper, announced that the helm had put them in the middle of the Sargasso Sea and was officially useless as a result – which was a bit harsh. At one point, we even got overtaken by our own tender (about the size of the Workboat) – progress was very slow. August/September 2019 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk The Skipper and Crew decided to put out the dredge nets and Jenny was abandoned at the back of the boat as everyone else crowded round to see the catch. Which is just as well because Jenny cannot bear the sight of fish or sea animals generally so she was quite happy. Various star fish were cleared of mud, examined and then released back to their home territory. The wind was bending round from the west to the east and we thought a sea breeze would come in but then it shifted back to the west, the boat tacked without moving and it looked like the breeze had come in properly and heading straight out of the Blackwater. Cue lots of people suddenly interested in helming now that there was actual wind and less risk of abuse from Carol. Pete was up first and enjoyed a steady breeze for about 5 minutes – which then promptly headed so he handed it over to Gordon. It appeared that the East Cardinal mark which marks the Mollyette had turned into a magnet because as the wind bent and no matter whether we bore away or got headed onto the other tack, we still seemed to be aiming at her. Fortunately, we managed to keep clear enough not to bounce off her. By which time we needed to turn around and head for home against the strong ebb. Jane took over the helm and headed us back towards the Colne Bar. Jason then took the helm as we headed back past the Inner Bench Head and despite a decent breeze, found that the spring ebb tide was really very strong. Dave Clarke then took over for a bit, followed by Clare – before Carol resumed command as we got closer to East Mersea and needed to head towards to the mooring. As we approached, the mizzen was stowed and the plan was to sail onto the mooring with the jib and staysail. The jib was stowed as we approached the mooring but this proved to be a mistake as the spring ebb tide proved too strong for the staysail alone and the Pioneer started to drift backwards. So reluctantly, the engine was switched on in order to get us to the mooring. After an efficient pack down, it was back aboard the launch for the final journey back up Brightlingsea creek to Harkers Yard. We all had a wonderful day’s sailing and our hosts, Carol, Lance and Brian were fantastic company. MSC Oppi Club and Sail Training’s 8 sessions ran from March through to October this year. As always, participation was a little weather dependent but there was always a strong core of keen sailors turning out. We registered a fantastic 178 different participants attending at least once through the year. A very encouraging trend was that, whilst attendance by youngsters held up very well this year, we saw a strong increase in the number of young-at-heart sailors giving it a go… and often coming back for more! Oppi Club, for the very youngest recruits, was very active. The groups we ran this year were: Oppi Club, for the very youngest, run by Fia Southgate the younger learners and improvers group, in small boats, 1 or 2-up, run by Dan Bard and Jemma Clarke the group for learners and improvers, in larger boats, run by Bryan Spencer the race training group, for all ages wanting to develop independent sailing skills, shouted at by John Nickalls. A very encouraging shift was the number of adults joining the more ‘racy’ group, which grew through the year with fantastic progress made. This group’s not just for those who want to race, it offers a chance to get real confidence in boat handling at close quarters (and to smile a lot). Sail Training relies very heavily on the great help we get from so many members… this year we gave tags to 31 on-the-water helpers, and alongside them was another army of helpers looking after everything shore-side. There are far too many to mention individually, but clearly Sail Training can’t go ahead without all this effort, and we are very grateful for their strong and consistent support. As well as spreading the catchment beyond the youngsters, this year saw the involvement of the Dinghy Cruising community. This was a huge help to Sail Training (it has been reported that some members find a Pico a little cramped, and that sailing is more fun in a larger traditional dinghy…) and seems to be providing a source of recruits for the dinghy cruises. We’re looking forward to this co-operation continuing in 2020. December 2019 Navigans 4

Ray Ball Company Secretary Tel: Email: secretary@marconi-sc.org.uk Nacra 15 – Story so Far… Adam Ferneyhough’s October update on Will and Isabella (MSC Cadets) and their adventures in the Nacra 15 class following the UK nationals and looking ahead to the worlds… The new Nacra 15 class has been introduced competitively over the past few year as a youth class pathway boat prior to stepping up to the full foiling Olympic Nacra 17 professional adult class boat. Of all the British Youth Sailing Team pathway boats, the Nacra is quite an elite class. The class is still in development and currently there are only 6 active competing boats in the whole of the UK. With such a small fleet, the racing is very close and competitive with lots to learn every time they hit the water. Recent changes in Olympic double handed racing rules and national competition guidelines now insist that the crew and helm must be of mixed sexes. Will has been sailing the Nacra for the past year or so, but his previous team partner has left to move into further education. Will and Isabella had sailed and raced a few times together at the club on the 29er and Nacra, then following some discussion decided to team up and start competing nationally and internationally together. They attended their first official RYA residential coaching/training weekend together at Calshot Activity Centre down on Southampton water, this proved quite successful for them. Soon after they made a decision to pursue the full competitive race circuit. Moving to the next step, they have just completed their first major competition, the Nacra 15 UK National Championships held a few weeks ago at Weston Sailing Club down on the South coast. For their first event, the weather was not kind to them, the wind was blowing 20-30 knots all weekend. The Nacra being a high performance demanding boat with 3 sails, twin trapeze and curved semi-foiling boards. This meant that they were flat out working the boat for two full days with no time rest or lose concentration. It’s fair to say, their fitness levels was tested to the limits. It was a very enjoyable weekend also being part of a general catamaran open competition mixing the starts with Shearwaters, Dart 18’s and Nacra 20 carbons to name a few. All 6 UK boats competed and despite snapped trapeze line taking them out of 2 races, they still managed to finish in 5th place overall. The icing on the cake was due to their much younger comparable ages of 15 and 13. They won the special Junior champion trophy, giving them the official title of National Junior Champions for the coming year. December 2019 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Following the excitement of the Nationals, they put an application into RYA British Youth Sailing Team for a place in the official National Youth Squad. We knew it was a bit of a long shot, as they hadn’t competed much together. This made us even more surprised when they wrote back to us offering them a place. Now one of only 3 Nacra teams officially supported by the RYA racing organisation. Now no time to relax, this weekend they are squad training down at the National Sailing Centre in Weymouth before we travel over to the South of France the week after to enter the Nacra 15 World championships. The event is being held at the future 2024 Olympic sailing venue in Marseille. A week long competition with 2 days of measurement followed by 5 days of racing. Around 100 Nacra 15’s will be competing from 17 different countries from across the world, it’s all very exciting. Wish them luck…. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Commodore’s Report - AGM 2019 Bryan Spencer 23rd November 2019 I would like to welcome you all to the Marconi Sailing Club 2019 Annual General Meeting. My report will comment on the business of the Board and the Management Committee over the last year. The responsibility for the club rests with the Board of Directors for the last year has been with Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after the premises and the site. Peter Clayton – Vice Commodore looking after the moorings and equipment. Pat Shaw – Rear Commodore for sailing. Liz Kirby - Rear Commodore for events. Sue Shenton – Treasurer. Myself, Bryan Spencer – as Commodore I have been the Managing Director. Ray Ball – once again has served as the company secretary, providing invaluable support to the committees and taking on the bulk of the administrative work of the club. I can report that the Board and management committee along with the sailing subcommittee have met regularly since the last AGM. I would like to thank all members have served on all committees. Murray is standing down as vice commodore having carried out many roles over the years. The latest being: Vice commodore 2005 – 2019 Tractor coordinator 2003 – 2018 Cruiser park coordinator 2016 – 2019 As well as leading the Wednesday Team in projects such as the bridge deck To show the club’s appreciation of his many years’ service to the club Murray has been presented with a painting. The club is pleased that Murray has agreed to be a vice president. The last year has been very busy on and off the water. On the water we have sailed a full programme along with open meetings. Once again, the East Coast Piers Race was a great success. Cadet Week was again a great success. Sail training was very well attended, both with the cadets and adults of all ages. This year has seen more of the newer members buys their own boats this is one of the reasons why we have seen the dinghy park grow. The dinghy cruising group once again has been very active. In addition to their dinghy cruises they have helped at the Adults sail training which has given invaluable help this season. Allowing more training to take place, a number these have now gone on to buy their own boats and have been taking part in the dinghy cruises. The club also held an Open Day which again was very successful, Thank you to Liz and team for all the hard work. This year the membership has been maintained high at 448. This is as a result of all the hard work over recent years and continued this year driving the club forward. We have a new sailing secretary this year Nigel James who will be reporting in more detail later. But I would to congratulate David Ball on winning the Sprint 15 Nationals for 2019. Will Harrison and Isabella Femeyhough came 5th in the Nacra 15 Nationals overall They won the special Junior Champion trophy, giving them the official title of National Junior Champions for the coming year. A few weeks later they came 40th out of 81 boats in the Nacra 15 World Championships 2019 Marconi also entered a team a British Keel Boat League at the Royal Southern YC on the Hamble. They came 5th overall. December 2019 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk SB 20 keel boats I am sure that you would have noticed that we now have 5 boats. Last year the club were able to buy one SB20. This year we were very fortunate in being awarded a Sport England grant of £10,000. With part funding by the grant and the club, 3 more boats were purchased leading up to Cadet Week giving us a fleet of 4 boats. Hot on the heels of the introduction of our SB20 fleet to our members, news of our initiative has spread quickly within the sailing community. David Armitage, retired teacher, RYA Instructor and sailor of many classes throughout his 80 years, heard from his south coast home, of the work we were doing to develop youth sailing. Recently deciding that it was time to cut back on his own time on the water, David kindly offered to donate his SB20 to Marconi SC. David said, " I really wanted to give up my boat to someone who would make best use of it, and Marconi's initiative looks like it will certainly do that " The club gratefully accepted David's generous offer and we very quickly collected the boat and we had a fleet of 5 boats. I would like to thank Pete Ward and Sue Shenton and team for the work that went into securing the Grant. Pete Ward and team arranged an SB20 Members Regatta on 29th September but this was blown out and rearranged a few weeks later. Which had almost as much wind. We look forward to next year’s programme for the SB20’s at Marconi. Off the water it has very busy. Last December a team lead by Richard Collis set out to transform the bar seating area, training room and 1st aid room this was completed in time for the Sprint 15 open meeting meal in April and has been used as a training area and for evening entertainment. Even the board has used this for meetings in the summer months. A big thank you to Richard and his team. The bridge deck has continued to be developed over the year, a big thank you to all that helped with this project. The purchase of the land. In February I received a letter from the Benn Family, informing the club that they wish to sell the pockets of land in the area of the hard which also included the coastguard hut. In September I visited the solicitors and signed the documents to complete the “Land purchase to secure our freehold”. This will mean that the club is protected from other 3rd parties having an interest in the land. This would not have been possible without the support I received from many members. I would like to thank the members of the board and the management committee along with membership as a whole for the support I have received allowing this purchase to take place. Marconi Sailing Club the Film set. As you may be aware the club was offered the opportunity to be used as a Film set for a TV series to be shown next year. The coastguard hut was included within the filming. This enabled over £10,000 to be put back into the club funds. I would like to thank Graham Cross for his part as he not only negotiated with the film company to the benefit of the club and made the whole thing happen but he also gave up his own time to be on site throughout the filming. Murray Bates and Mick Richardson were on hand leading up to the filming and while the film crew were onsite. A big thank you for all the other members that helped out. Before I finish, I would like to present the following awards. John and Caroline the Commodore’s Plate for all the work they put into the Sail Training. Barograph: Richard Collis for project managing and working on the creation of the new function room. Seamanship Trophy: Howard Rogers and Doug Turnnidge for leaving their own race and going to the assistance of another club member during the Pilots Cup. Mamgu Trophy: David Nickalls for his report on the MSC youth team taking part in the BKL youth championships at the Royal Southern Yacht Club in June. Thank you all for attending the AGM Before closing I would like to wish you a Happy Christmas and a Happy new Year Bryan Spencer Commodore December 2019 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Company Secretary's Report – AGM 2019 AGM Saturday 23rd November 2019 COMMITTEE The Board of Directors (your Executive Committee) met monthly throughout the year with the exception of August. With the exception of August, the Management Committee also met monthly to conduct the business of the Club. MEMBERSHIP The membership currently stands at 448 (445 in 2018. 436 in 2017 and 430 in 2016). Membership numbers are healthy and reflects the facilities the club offers. However, we cannot be complacent as we usually have 40 or so members not renewing their membership each January. They drop away for good reasons such as moving house, pressure of work, going to university, etc. On occasions previous members return to the club which is always gratifying. To maintain numbers, we need to keep working to recruit new members. Open Days are popular and result in many new members. Some sign up at the time but many come through afterwards and say they visited the club on Open Day. Open days are also a chance for club members to pull together to lay on a good event; which is always pleasing to see. Whilst on the subject of membership, please make sure that all the information the club holds for you is correct. Renewal invoices are being produced and they are based on this. You can check the data the club holds for you via the club portal. INSURANCES AND LICENCES I have to report that the club equipment and buildings are all adequately insured, and necessary licences are current. THANKS There are many members who carry out background tasks which are essential to keep the club running. Many of these administration tasks go unnoticed but the club could not operate without them. MSC is a registered company and a small business and insurance is essential to cover all club assets, directors’ liability, club members and various activities. Insurance cover also has to be arranged for special events such as Open Day and when club boats are taken offsite to other events. Some of the extra insurance matters are a little unusual such as covering the recent filming on site. The club’s fleet of boats is growing, all of which needs to be insured. Insurance is one of those issues which attracts little notice unless things go wrong. Pat Black manages all the MSC insurances and works closely with our broker. We are grateful to Pat and I am pleased to say that he has agreed to continue looking after insurance matters in 2020. Thanks Pat. Keith White supported by Susan has organised and administered the OOD rota again throughout the 2019 season. Thanks to all of you who did OOD duties in 2019. Having a duty officer on busy days is a sign of a well-run club and gives a point of contact during the day. Members are asked to do an OOD duty for one day every 2 or 3 years and it really does make a difference having an OOD on duty. New members need not worry as they are not asked to do an OOD duty until they have had 2 clear seasons experience at the club. By that time members have a fair idea of how the club runs. Keith has agreed to continue the good work in 2020 for which I am grateful. Thanks Keith. Mike and Rosemary Turner spend a lot of time corresponding with new members or prospective new members. When people are considering joining the club Mike and Rosemary are often the first people they talk to and first impressions count. Mike and Rosemary have agreed to carry on the good work with membership applications in 2020. Thanks Mike and Rosemary. David Ball edits and arranges the circulation of Navigans. A few issues have not been produced this year due to a lack of contributions. Navigans is a vehicle for members to submit articles of general interest or even humour so please use it. David is also involved in the weather station and other IT related matters. Thanks David. December 2019 Navigans 14

Ray Ball Company Secretary Financial Summary – AGM 2019 Marconi Sailing Club Ltd FINANCIAL SUMMARY ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING 23rd November 2019 As Finance Director of Marconi Sailing Club Ltd, I present a financial summary along with the accounts for the year ended 31 st August, 2019, for approval by the members. Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk As the end of the financial year falls on 31st August (2019), and subscriptions and fees are not due until 1 st January thereafter, it is essential to ensure that club retains about £25,000 in the bank account to meet unavoidable expenditure for those five months (September to mid-January) where little or no income is received. The annual budget plan is set to create a small surplus annually which can be put towards minor capital projects for improving the club infrastructure. Last year saw the completion of major improvements and enlargement to the bar area, first aid room and training space. In May, the club was awarded a further small grant of £10,000 to help develop the club keelboat racing fleet. A contribution of £4000 is required from the club to support this grant. Our Accountants have been able to negotiate with HMRC to reduce our corporation tax to £17.00 for 2018/2019 and hopefully to maintain this position for succeeding years. The club continues at present to benefit from the historically low interest rates in the repayment of its development loan. There have not been any significant changes to the balance sheet during the year and the overall Net Asset Value of the club improved to a sound £555,545 (last year £477,782). This equates to £1240 per member! It is worth drawing members’ attention to the following areas: Capital spending (note 2, page 2): The club has financed and carried out some major improvements over the past year. These have included:. £2,717 Club Structures including Lounge and Bridge Deck £25,827 Major Improvements to the Downstairs Bar Area & First Aid Room. £1,600 New Work Vehicle £4,193 (plus £10K grant) New Club Boats for Training and Member Use National Westminster and Members' loans (notes 5 & 6, page 3): The balance outstanding on the long term bank loan has reduced from £311,726 (2018) to £291,251 a repayment of £20,475. Membership loans stand at £81,000. The club's long term financing therefore is £372,251. When considering this figure members should compare it to the fixed assets total of £890,196 shown at the top of page 1. Essentially it is saying that the club's equity in all of its property and assets is now 58.2%. 2019/2020 Subscription and Fees Unavoidable revenue expenditure on areas such as Services, Rates, Insurance, Safety, Cleaning, Machinery, Mooring Fees, Fuel and Maintenance of Site, Buildings, Equipment and Boats increases year by year. This expenditure amounts to about £75,000 as against £62,000 in the previous year, an increase of over 20%. In addition it is vital to continue developing the club facilities for the benefit of members, and to replace ageing infrastructure and equipment as it becomes necessary. Therefore a small increase in subscriptions is proposed this year to allow the club to keep moving forward. We propose to introduce 3 levels of fee for dinghies according to size. There will be a small increase in fees for catamarans, and in the per foot charge for cruisers. Budget for 2019/2020 The Board receives detailed monthly budget reports where the income and expenditure to date is compared against the annual budget, which enables the directors to closely monitor the club’s financial progress. The annual budget for 2019/20 was drafted in July, discussed and agreed with the main budget holders, and ratified by the Board in early October. As Treasurer I have a very detailed and comprehensive picture of the club’s finances which informs future planning. I am pleased to be able to report that the club’s financial position is sound. The cash reserves together with the proposed changes in subscriptions fees will enable us to finance the projects outlined above in this report, and enable to the club to meet reasonable levels of emergency expenditure. Finally I would like to extend grateful thanks to Mike & Rosemary Turner for their work related to new members throughout the year. I would like to thank Patrick Black for dealing with the club’s various insurance needs. Finally I would also wish to thank Ray Ball as Company Secretary for his invaluable support to my role. Sue Shenton, Director (Finance). 23rd November 2019 December 2019 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk Sailing Secretary Report – AGM 2019 Another year has passed and the Summer sailing season is over as I find myself in front of you for the first time to deliver my report as sailing secretary. Having recently re-joined the Sailing club after a 20 year break, and taking on the Sailing secretary role, I am yet to fully understand and know all the details and personalities of the sailing activities at Marconi Sailing Club , so my first report maybe a bit brief but hopefully become more comprehensive as time moves on. I apologise to any individuals who have selflessly carried out activities at the club over the last year, that I don’t mention through this report. I took on the role with trepidation of following in both Jenny’s and Toms footsteps, but have been greatly helped and encouraged by Pat Shaw and the sailing Sub Committee, Thank you It has been a good year of sailing at the club once again and hopefully my brief report will inform and reflect on some of th e activities that have taken place during 2019. With the permanent move to the Bridge deck race box, came changes in the starting format and procedure’s, these seem to have settled down with minor problems being sorted out during the season. The new position of the Race box greatly enhances the Race officers’ control of the racing by being very central, it also enhances the safety of the competitor’s by being at a high vantage point. I have personally found that it is so much easier to manage the racing by not being so remote for hours on end, and help is never far away when required. The 2 major events of the Clubs Sailing calendar were again very successful and very well managed by Liz Kirby for the Open day and Andrew Dowley for the East Coast Piers Race. The Open day again was blessed by great weather and the very large numbers of club members organising and supporting all the activities on and off the water. This day really does promote to the visiting public the friendliness of the club. The East Coast Piers weekend again was very successful with large numbers of visitors and competitors returning, many very complementary comments were received on a number of social media sites. All the races were completed, and again there were countless volunteers from the club supporting the weekend, for which this great weekend would not be able to happen. Cadet Week again proved to very well supported and successful event with large number of youngsters and novices taking to the water over the week. Monthly Sail training continues to grow year on year with 178 individual participants being recorded over the 8 sessions throughout the year, this was well manged with 31 on the water helpers with many more assisting in the background. The Dinghy cruising section continue with their adventures and this year they have greatly supported the Sail training days with larger and more friendly boats to sail and learn in. Power Boat training has continued throughout the year, which allows the club to maintain the pool of rescue boat drivers to support the racing programme, and number of Dinghy courses have also taken place, which allows the standard of sailing and seamanship at our club improve year on year. The Dinghy and cat fleets are still well supported with a full racing programme being carried out apart form 2 competitions being cancelled due to very high winds. Midweek racing has continued to be one of the most popular series of racing throughout the year, with a good number of new and not so experienced members taking the opportunity to use the club boats and facilities to improve their skills. Sam’s team in the Galley provided excellent meals following the racing, which gave the participants the opportunity to discuss the finer points of the racing rules. The dinghy Handicap fleet has had a bit of a resurgence with an increase of Lasers taking part, so they are starting to have a competition amongst themselves, some of the fleet are currently extending their racing season at Maylandsea The Medium Cat has also seen a small resurgence of Dart 18’s which could potentially grow over the next couple of seasons Sprint 15s continue to have successful racing at both home and way, and are currently racing against the growing number of 15s at Stone in their winter series The SB20 fleet has grown considerably over the season with the help of a grant. Much training and practice has taken place on the boats over the year which culminated in all 5 boats taking part in their own mini regatta towards the end of the season. Perhaps one day some of these boats might venture down to the south coast to take part in SB20 class racing at Cowes week A small group of cruisers have continued to successfully represent the club in the BJRC series with Blue Moon taking part in all 8 races and coming 2nd overall, McGregor III came third On the Road this year the club members have been very successful. December 2019 Navigans 17
